FIG. 1.-Tom Sawyer solves a problem in applied psychology. To 

Tom life seemed hollow and existence a burden. Thirty yards of board fence six feet high to whitewash and nothing but trash with which to pay the boys to help. An inspiration! He took whitewashing out of the realm of work and made it a privilege. The boys paid him for permission to demonstrate their skill. Working in shifts, the boys paid him: an apple, a kite, a dead rat on a string, 12 marbles, part of a jew's harp, a piece of blue bottle glass to look through, a spool cannon, a key that wouldn't unlock anything, a glass stopper, a tin soldier, a couple of tadpoles, 6 firecrackers, a kitten with one eye, a brass doorknob, a dog collar, the handle of a knife, four pieces of orange peel, and an old window sash. He had a nice, good, idle time all the while-plenty of company-and, in the end, the fence had three coats of whitewash on it. 

(Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. New York: Harper & Brothers, 1917.

Preface 

"O give the student the essential facts about psychology in such a way that he can reach an understanding of himself and others, and to teach him how to increase this knowledge when his formal study of psychology has ceased-these objectives have guided the writing of this book. They have imposed three criteria on the presentation of material: to build upon experimental evidence; to make an impartial selection of source materials; and to encourage the reader to think independently. 

There are, of course, many gaps in the experimental evidence upon which psychology is based, and in indicating these I have tried to make clear the distinction between speculations which bridge those gaps and the basic facts. References to the source material will enable the student to trace the evidence for himself, although the names of the original investigators have been omitted from the body of the text for the sake of smoother reading.

In considering source materials I have uniformly weighed all the available evidence and have stated my interpretation as simply as I could. Obviously it has been possible to include only a small fraction of the original source material, but I have attempted to represent all vital areas adequately. 

The scientific method is emphasized throughout these pages in terms of an intellectual honesty that demands controlled and rechecked observations and experiments, that examines facts without prejudice and values them above any man's interpretation. In short, the student is encouraged to make the scientific method basic to all of his thinking. 

I have not attempted to favor any particular school of psychology. Although each instructor will vary his emphasis, the

vi 

PREFACE 

fundamental material is basic to all the various methods of presenting psychology. The writer of a textbook in this subject must therefore keep a middle course, careful to present all the essential material, but in such a manner that the individual instructor can add to it his own vital contribution. 

Without a precise vocabulary, accuracy in thought is impossible. Technical terms, therefore, in addition to being defined at the time of their first use, are placed in a general glossary at the end of the book for easy reference. 

Crucial experiments are presented in such a way that the student can discern the exact manner in which the results were obtained, and also survey the experimental methods critically in order to devise ways of improving upon them. The student who performs some of the simpler experiments himself will find the methods of psychological research a revealing and absorbing experience.

As is true of all subjects, certain topics are more interesting than others, which may, in addition, be difficult for the beginning student. Wherever it has been possible to do so, difficult sections have been alternated with easier materials so that the student will have an opportunity to review the perplexing topics while studying the easier sections. 

Practical applications of psychological truths are indicated throughout the book, but it is in the last chapters that they are most numerous. There the student explores the principles for clear perception, adroit problem solving, and satisfactory personal and social adjustments. It is appropriate that these "practical" aspects of psychology should be postponed until the student has had some training in the fundamentals of the subject, for without such a foundation no one can expect to understand, or apply, these rules for successful living. 

Evanston, Illinois

Chapter I  THE 

"HE life of each human individual is a process of continuous adjustment from the time he is conceived until he dies. 

This fact makes the topic of individual adjustment an essential focus for all psychological study. Whether an individual proceeds through life in a haphazard manner or according to well-established and beneficial principles will depend upon the degree of psychological insight possessed by his parents, nurses, teachers, associates, and by himself. Since one must live, and since living is adjusting, most persons pick up some random knowledge about human nature. Such learning is likely to be fortuitous and to contain misinformation and erroneous generalizations. Mistakes are sure to follow, and disclose themselves only after it is too late for the individual to correct them. Psychology attempts to organize the principles of human adjustment into sound and systematic form.

It has been found, for example, that many of the characteristics which seem to be an integral part of adult individuals originated in early childhood. An attitude of suspicion which is characteristic of one person may be traced to the deceit practiced upon him by an unscrupulous nurse. A fixed impulse to help the unfortunate may have originated in a childhood experience in nursing a motherless pup. A malicious desire to inflict physical pain upon others may have had its beginning in jealousy because of favoritism on the part of the individual's parents. Certainly, an objective and scientific attitude is of vital importance if the student is to study personality characteristics without preconceived prejudices about them.

Problems of social adjustment are becoming more and more difficult with the growing complexity of modern civilization.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Social, political, and economic theories all have their foundation in some sort of speculation about human nature. It is becoming apparent that we must substitute sound psychological principles for outworn superstitions if we are going to live together in peace and comfort. Practically any crackpot can refer to some aspect of "human nature" to support his wild ideas. But, unless a person has some background of sound information about psychology, he is in a poor position to know what to accept and what to reject. 

He judges on the basis of his own emotions, which may lead him to select ideas which are just as erroneous as those of the advocate of racial hate, violence, or world revolution. Human behavior is extremely complex, and no act can be explained by reference to one simple causal factor.

Many persons who have not studied psychology are inclined to believe that there are some relatively simple rules which apply to all individuals. For example, everyone has heard such assertions as: You cannot change human nature. Everyone loves flattery. All persons are selfish. Don't trust a person who won't look you in the eye. The greatest element in success is hard work. 

Clothes make the man. An infant instinctively loves his mother. 

Fat people are good-natured. Such statements are misleading and, at best, are but partial truths. It is vain to attempt to explain human behavior by reference to any such simple rules. The first task that the student of psychology should undertake is to rid himself of this common and almost irresistible urge to hunt for some simple explanation of human conduct. Why try to oversimplify a subject which derives its interest and its challenge from that fact that it is intricate? 

On the other hand, the admission that human behavior is bewilderingly complex should not deter one from attempting to ascertain why people act as they do. The student of psychology has a right to expect that he will learn something about human motives, why one individual is different from another, why some persons make good friends while others are always fighting, why some persons learn from experience and others do not, why some are happy and others sad, why some persons are trustworthy and others consistently unreliable, how time changes persons, how various circumstances affect people, and something about the degree to which human conduct can be predicted.

As a result of his study, the student should be able to work more efficiently, learn more quickly, reason clearly, contrive to use his emotions instead of being victimized by them, be more self-reliant, and be a better companion to those who have to live with him. In short, psychology offers boundless possibilities in the direction of personal advancement and in the improvement of social relationships.

WHY PEOPLE ACT AS THEY DO 

Psychology is concerned with the study of how people act and why they act as they do. A casual glance over the topics which we shall study will show how each one contributes something toward providing an answer to these how and why questions. 

An individual's behavior is partly determined by the kind of person he is. Man is not a billiard ball whose activities can be explained as a simple resultant of the physical forces acting upon him from the outside world. Psychology is most significantly concerned with individual differences and changes in the same individual as factors in influencing behavior. We shall find that a great many circumstances contribute toward making a man the kind of person he is. Some of these are listed herewith: 

1. A man's physical structure is partly determined by biological inheritance.¹ Having had human parents, he has acquired a human body and, therefore, cannot perform as a dog, a cow, a monkey, or a fish. Biological factors determine that he shall breathe air, walk in an erect position, eat certain foods, reproduce his kind, and eventually die. The study of psychology involves some knowledge of heredity. 

2. Developmental changes influence behavior in a variety of ways. A child cannot walk when he is born because the necessary equipment has not matured. A certain degree of maturation is a necessary prerequisite for speech. Nevertheless, it would be inaccurate to attribute such an act as speech to maturation alone. A child does not talk merely because his speech apparatus is full-grown, even though he cannot talk until it is mature. He 

1 The student is urged to use freely the glossary at the end of the book. 

All technical words are defined there. If the meaning of every word or phrase is clearly learned when first encountered, the student will find his study more interesting and enjoyable-as well as easier.

PSYCHOLOGY 

needs practice and instruction. Psychology must concern itself with maturation and with the effects of exercise upon the maturing organism. 

3. Behavior is influenced by certain needs of the individual. 

These range all the way from needs for chemical substances and for foods to highly developed and acquired wants, such as the desire for prestige. Consequently, psychology must concern itself with the intricate problems of motivation. 

4. Behavior is influenced by emotional tensions. Emotional conduct cannot be explained wholly in terms of the environmental stimulations or wholly in terms of the make-up of the individual. 

Certain conditions are exciting in and of themselves; but it is also clear that different persons show different emotions to similar situations, and that emotions change with the course of life. To understand human conduct, something must be known about human emotions. 

5. Learning changes people. Learning takes a variety of forms and psychology must concern itself with all these forms: motor habits, memorizing, ways of thinking, social adjustments, perceptions, rules for living, and the like. In fact, learning permeates all phases of psychology, even though we shall consider the main problems of learning in three chapters: Motor Skills, Memorizing, and Conditioning. 

6. Conduct is partly determined by the structure of the nervous system. The nervous system is the main instrument for co-ordinating activity. The student of psychology should have a clear picture of the general nature of the nervous system and its functions, even though the details of neural activity must be left to the physiologist. 

7. The structure and functioning of the sense organs affect behavior significantly. How each sense organ acts and how it contributes to our knowledge of the outside world is an essential aspect of any adequate psychological understanding. 

8. A clear picture of the way in which all these components are integrated into a unified personality is necessary in any study of psychology. The harmonious solution of personal problems is considered in the chapters on perceiving, intelligence, problem solving, and personality.

An individual's behavior is partly determined by the influence of external events and the presence and activities of other persons.

No man lives in a vacuum. Each person is being constantly affected by external circumstances and, no matter how well we may understand his organization and his ways of acting, such influences are vital elements in his conduct. A deaf and blind person will not act in the same manner as one who can see and hear, even though the two might be equal in all other respects. 

A boy who sits on a tack will not behave in the same manner as one who sits on a soft cushion. 

Nor does the same environmental circumstance affect all individuals in the same manner. This fact complicates the study of psychology and, at the same time, makes it more interesting. 

As an illustration, one experimenter was testing children to determine how easily they could solve a problem which involved the use of a stick. As a stick, she used a common yardstick. Whereas most of the children entered the game eagerly, one little boy cried and refused to try to solve the problem. This seemed strange until it was learned that his mother used a yardstick to whip him. 

After we have studied all possible aspects of the human personality and have analyzed all the environmental influences surrounding him, can we give a specific answer as to why a man acts thus and so? Only in a crude, qualitative, and conditional manner. In spite of the fact that our subject is so complex and the present state of our knowledge so inadequate that we cannot hope to reduce the explanation of any single act to a mathematical formula including all significant factors, the search for the most significant elements in any bit of behavior is an extremely fascinating pursuit. The answer is always elusive, but the search is only made the more exciting because of our inability to arrive at a definite answer. If you add two to two, you get four; and that is the end of it. But if you confront a child with a problem that is extremely difficult for him, you do not get a simple definite response, nor will you get the same response on repeated trials. It is interesting to watch what he does, but it will only detract from the challenge of psychological problems if the student attempts to arrive at some fixed answer.

In the face of this complexity of subject matter, the student must have some means for enabling him to steer a straight course.

PSYCHOLOGY 

The methods evolved by scientists provide the best answer to this need. Consequently, we shall devote some time at the very beginning of our study to an examination of scientific thinking. The student not only should understand the essentials of scientific thinking, he should absorb them to such an extent that the scientific attitude becomes a part of himself and dominates his thinking throughout the course.

SCIENTIFIC THINKING IN PSYCHOLOGY 

The elusiveness of psychological problems makes it particularly important that the student give attention to his thinking so that he will not go too far astray. Largely because of the complexity of human life, there are many superstitions, prejudices, and misconceptions to mislead the student. He should begin his study by attempting to think clearly, to make his vocabulary more precise, and to maintain an objective attitude throughout. He should attempt to keep his thinking on a scientific plane even though the interest of the subject matter should tempt him to leave reality and to permit his imagination to run riot. 

Sources of evidence. In his search for the truth, man has appealed to five sources of evidence: (1) customs and traditions; (2) authority; (3) syllogistic reasoning from self-evident propositions; (4) personal experiences; and (5) scientific inquiry. 

These sources are not of equal value. 

1. Customs and tradition. Customs and tradition rule a great part of our ordinary living, our clothes, speech, food habits, and social behavior. We follow customs because we know no better guiding principles, because we have no desire for other methods, or because we have not time to search for better ones. 

Following traditions makes life easier, but the fact that a belief or condition has always been maintained provides a flimsy argu ment for its truth or falsity. Dependence upon tradition leads to intellectual inertia. 

2. The appeal to authority. The appeal to authority is the device of the weakling in time of stress. Not knowing what to do, he appeals to some individual or source of power to give him aid. If we would arrive at the truth we must know more than that a well-known individual made a certain statement. We should base our credence not on the fact that he made the statement forw sonin or aut the pa possib cally, man's ask wh periend of erro a situa tion, a

Correct the old sense o accurat senses. they are veloped inquiry of scm resulting fects of Sir easy to it is imp ing. A scientific much wh Th many SC been for

The The orces Gr

2 ment but upon a critical evaluation of the evidence which he brings forward to substantiate his statement. 

3. Syllogistic reasoning. The appeal to syllogistic rea soning 2 is an advance beyond dependence upon either tradition or authority. Its weakness lies primarily in the possible falsity of the premises which lie behind the logical arguments, and in the possible ambiguity of the terms used in the arguments. Historically, it has had great value in that it directed critical attention to man's reasoning processes. When man studied logic, he began to ask why we knew certain truths instead of accepting them blindly. 

4. Appeal to personal experiences. The appeal to experiences has some fundamental weaknesses. The greatest source of error is that each experience is a unique event. To assume that a situation will repeat itself is certainly unwarranted. In addition, any interpretation of a personal experience is likely to be incorrect. When we come to study perceptions we shall learn that the old adage that "seeing is believing" is certainly unsound. Our sense organs are constantly deceiving us and we seldom know accurately the significance of what we do take in through the senses. Anecdotes of personal events make interesting stories but they are poor scientific material. 

5. Scientific inquiry. Scientific methods have been developed in order to overcome the defects of other methods of inquiry. Science has been defined as the systematic investigation of some specific field, together with the organized knowledge resulting from such investigation. It alone is free from the defects of the preceding four methods of searching for the truth. 

Since psychology is a field in which the student will find it easy to lose his way and to be unable to discern truth from fiction, it is important for him to know what is involved in scientific thinking. An intimate acquaintance with the rules that should govern e scientific thinking is especially important in view of the fact that much which is called science is anything but that. 

The rules of science. On the basis of the experience of many scientists through centuries, certain important rules have been formulated. [2]³ 2 The structure and use of the syllogism are explained on page 517. 

3 The numbers in brackets throughout the book indicate the exact original sources or supplementary information listed at the end of each chapter.

PSYCHOLOGY 

It is essential that trust be placed only in those observations which are repeated under the same conditions or under conditions which are changed by known amounts. Repeated observations are absolutely essential, but these would be misleading were not extreme care taken to control the circumstances surrounding such observations. An illustration will make clear the importance of this rule. 

At one time it was thought that dampness caused malaria because it had been observed repeatedly that malaria was more frequent in damp areas than in dry places. How could this proposition be checked scientifically? Select two groups of persons who were equal in all possible respects, have them live under similar conditions with the one exception-one group would live in a dry place and the other in a damp place. If an equal number of persons in each group contracted malaria, it could be concluded that dampness played no part. It was in this manner that this erroneous belief was overthrown. But other hypotheses were then advanced and each tested in the same manner. Finally, it was suggested that the mosquito carried malaria. Two groups were treated in identical ways except for the one factor to be tested. 

One group was protected from the mosquito and another group was exposed to and bitten by mosquitoes. Those who were protected did not develop malaria; those who were bitten did develop it.

It is just as important to consider facts which go against a proposition as evidence which favors it. It is possible to obtain proof for almost any hypothesis if a diligent search is made for supporting evidence, and if all contrary material is carefully avoided. The testimonial method for proving the value of a certain medicine is an instance in point. Suppose we have a vested interest in castor oil and would like to prove that it will cure malaria. If we give castor oil to individuals who have malaria, we will doubtless find that some of them recover. We might accumulate many testimonials saying that the patient took castor oil and subsequently recovered from the disease. Such testimonials are not only useless but actually misleading because we have ignored the negative instances, that is, those individuals who took the castor oil and did not recover.

How about indicating the percentage of patients who

recovered? If we can show that 60 per cent of all those treated with castor oil recovered, is not that evidence in favor of the treatment? No. This is a device commonly used and is extremely misleading. It may be that 60 per cent would have recovered without any treatment at all. How shall we ascertain whether our treatment was a vital factor or a useless gesture?

By the use of a control group. If more individuals recover in the group treated with castor oil than in the untreated group, this may be taken as evidence in favor of the treatment. Even if 99 per cent should recover in the treated group, no faith could be placed in the efficacy of the treatment if 99 per cent should also recover in the untreated group. 

It is important to avoid preconceived ideas and prejudices. 

Skill in making accurate observations involves getting away from emotional bias. A calm attitude may be easily obtained when one is studying chemicals, physical stresses, rocks, or plants; but it is peculiarly difficult to remain impassive when studying ourselves or human beings like ourselves. A motion picture of an ape playing with a child is much more likely to entertain a class of students than it is to stimulate an unemotional study, such as a cool analysis of the fact that the ape can outdo the child in many respects. It is easier to overestimate the intelligence of a person if he is handsome and agreeable than if he is ugly and mean. 

Admonitions to be unemotional are not sufficient to overcome this universal tendency. The psychologist has, for this reason, been driven to evolve all sorts of techniques and devices to accomplish this end. The eternal question in psychology is: 

By what method were those facts obtained? The validity of any psychological item depends upon the prejudice-proof nature of the method used in securing it. 

An artificial word has been devised to designate the substitution of emotional thinking for logical thinking. The word is "thobbing." It is made up of the initial sounds of the words thinking, opinion, and belief. It is defined as thinking misdirected by emotion, prejudice, the will to believe, or other nonrational factors. The scientific thinker is constantly on guard against the dangers of thobbing.

Inaccuracy of observation, inaccurate instruments of measurement, dependence upon subjective judgment, estimates, and

PSYCHOLOGY 

guesses may prejudice results. It is important to count cases or measure results accurately. Psychology has a hard time living up to this requirement. It is not easy to measure a fear or to count the number of times a child must be thwarted before he develops stubbornness. Great progress has been made in developing devices to measure precisely some of the more easily controlled types of behavior in human beings and animals in the laboratory and, for this reason, psychology has some definite conclusions to offer in relation to reaction times, to methods of learning, and to sensory discriminations. Ingenious methods have been devised for measuring some of the more complicated forms of behavior but much still needs to be done. These needs will be easily apparent to the alert student as he proceeds with his study. 

The failure to distinguish between assumption and law should be avoided. The part that assumption plays in the different stages of scientific thinking should be clearly recognized. 

Most scientific thinking, in its earliest stages, contains considerable speculation. Theories are propounded and generalizations are made which are only vaguely suggested by the available facts. Such speculations are valuable if they are not taken too seriously and if they lead to further search for evidence both for and against their verity.

If the insecure basis of speculation is recognized, a speculation becomes a hypothesis. A hypothesis is a preliminary and tentative presupposition, or principle, adopted for the explanation of observed facts.

With increasing accumulation of factual evidence to support a hypothesis, a general formula or principle may be propounded to express it; which formula or principle may be dignified by the name of theory.

Finally, when extensive research has demonstrated a fundamental uniformity in nature, this may be stated in the form of a law. In other words, there is a gradation depending upon the increasing adequacy of evidence (as demonstrated by rigidly controlled procedures) from speculation, through hypothesis and theory, to law. [8]

Laws are not unchangeable. They merely represent the best statements of facts accumulated to date. In every branch of research laws are being modified continually; old statements must

give way to new formulations. The younger the science the more rapid are such changes. Psychology is a relatively immature science. The student will learn some principles which are on a fairly secure foundation, but he will encounter also some relatively new and less stable hypotheses. It is, consequently, important that he should learn to weigh evidence, to adopt an intellectually critical attitude toward newer theories, and to avoid the idly complacent belief that the last word has been said. 

THE METHODS USED BY PSYCHOLOGISTS 

Each branch of science has to develop its own tools. The general purpose of such tools is to increase the accuracy of observation and to reduce vague qualitative values to quantitative form. 

The astronomer uses the telescope to bring the stars nearer. The biologist uses the microscope to enable him to see micro-organisms. 

The physicist uses scales and meters to measure and to count so that his observations may be made with greater accuracy. The tools that the psychologist uses have been borrowed largely from other sciences. He has, however, shown ingenuity in developing devices to control the presentation of stimuli to his subjects and to make accurate recordings of the reactions to such presentations. [5] 

Regardless of the mechanical devices used, psychological information is gleaned by two general methods, which may be used separately or in combination: introspection and objective observation.

Introspection. The examination of one's own feelings, sensations, efforts, ideas, or imaginations is called introspection. 

In some instances it is the only way in which we can learn about psychological facts. For example, we can tell better than any other person whether we are happy or sad, whether a color appears brighter or duller than another, whether we are hungry or not, or whether we love or hate a certain individual. To be sure, it is possible for an individual to deceive himself or to report incorrectly what he does experience. Consequently, psychologists do not always take introspective reports at their face value. They have been ingenious in the development of devices to overcome the influences of self-deceit, purposeful distortion, or dishonesty on the part of observers in psychological experiments.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Objective observation. Much attention has been given to methods whereby the behavior of others may be interpreted. Certain fields of study lend themselves to such methods more readily than do others. For example, improvement in motor skill can be studied without any reference to introspective reports from the learner. To be sure, the learner may make a contribution by telling about any change in attitude or about some change in method which occurred during the learning process; but much can be determined by objective observation in the absence of any verbal report.

Although both introspection and objective observation have their individual advantages in different experiments, more attention has been given to the latter in actual psychological research in recent years. There is no essential antagonism between the two methods. Instead, they should supplement each other, and emphasis on one or the other depends upon the nature of the specific problem that is being studied. 

SOME PSYCHOLOGICAL GENERALITIES 

Some studies are built upon self-evident truths which the student accepts without question. Psychology has no such axioms upon which to erect a system. However, there are some facts which can be so generally observed that it might be well to accept them without much question. At least, taking them for granted will not lead us astray in our study, and giving them attention at this point may eliminate some needless confusion. [9] 

1. The human individual is a unitary creature. It leads only to confusion to attempt to divide him into mind and body, into conscious and subconscious personalities, into the ego and the social self, or the like. A man is made of parts, but the parts have to be unified into a whole to make the man. He may do without some of his parts, but he must retain enough to remain a person. 

2. No two individuals are alike. It is a mistake to attempt to interpret the acts of others by attributing to them the motives that we think we observe in ourselves. 

3. Every person is continually changing. He can never be the same during two successive moments. Each experience leaves

its imprint upon him and he is different from what he was before that experience. 

4. Actions which appear very much alike may result from a different combination of causes. 

5. The same combination of causes may produce diverse actions in different individuals or in the same individual at different times. 

6. A stimulus from the environment "sets off" a response.

The stimulus acts as a release of energy which is already present in the individual.

DIVISIONS OF PSYCHOLOGY 

The study of psychology may be divided into different specialized fields. While these fields overlap, a brief survey of them will give the beginning student some conception of the broad scope of the subject upon which he is entering. 

General psychology is that branch of psychology which studies what is true of individuals in general rather than the way in which individuals differ from each other. It may deal with children, normal persons, or animals but, in any case, the emphasis is upon general factors found in the group studied. It is the opposite of individual psychology.

Differential psychology, or the psychology of individual differences, is the branch of psychology which investigates the differences in certain fundamental characters as manifested in different races, in social groups, or in individuals in the same group. It deals with sex, age, racial, occupational, social, and trait differences and with differences in the same individuals at different times.

Genetic psychology studies the origin and historic unfolding of the activity of the individual or of a group of organisms. 

It usually is divided into two divisions: (1) ontogenetic psychology, the study of the origin and growth of mental life and behavior in the individual; (2) phylogenetic psychology, the study of the origin and growth of mental life and behavior through various animal species. 

Child psychology studies the mental life and behavior of children from birth, or earlier, to maturity. It is sometimes included as a part of genetic psychology.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Animal psychology is the study of animal behavior. Animal psychology may be studied because of an interest in animals themselves, or because of the light that such studies throw on human psychology.

Abnormal psychology studies those individuals who are widely divergent from the typical individual. This includes those individuals who may be subnormal, supernormal, or qualitatively deranged. It includes pathological psychology (that is, the study of those persons who are mentally sick) and such mental conditions as dreams, hypnosis, hallucinations, delusions, and the like. 

Physiological psychology investigates the functions of the nervous system, the sense organs, the motor organs, glands, and other physiological organisms in their relation to mental life and behavior.

Social psychology is that branch of psychology which studies (a) the behavior of an individual in so far as his behavior stimulates others or is affected by others, (b) the behavior of individuals in group situations, (c) the study of personality as it develops in relation to the social environment, and (d) the interaction between groups.

Applied psychology is that branch of psychology which is devoted to practical rather than theoretical ends. It includes legal psychology, educational psychology, psychology of advertising, psychology of selling, industrial psychology, and clinical psychology.

PRACTICAL VALUES OF PSYCHOLOGY 

A course in general psychology will, not enable a student to solve all his own personal problems, nor will it enable him to organize any system which will bring order into a troubled world. 

Nevertheless, it should do some or all of the following things: 

1. It should make him keenly aware of the significance of individual differences. He will know that some men are bright while others are unintelligent, some are efficient and others inefficient, some are emotionally unstable and others placid, some can be trusted and others cannot. He may have an ideal of a social system where all men are alike; but he will know that any peaceful community requires a police system for the protection

of law-abiding citizens from those who have not learned to respect the rights of others. 

2. His study of sensations and perceptions should make him understand that the way in which we interpret our world depends upon a great number of factors. He should learn why he does not see and hear his universe in the same way as others around him. 

3. He should gain some insight into the significance of the complexity of human motivation. He may learn that even an enemy may have laudable motives. 

4. He should develop greater personal efficiency in many directions. He should find himself better able to organize a program of motor training. He should be able to study and to memorize more effectively. He should be able to make decisions more wisely and be able to substitute cool analysis for impulsive conduct. 

5. He should be able to improve his reasoning processes and his problem-solving ability. 

6. Finally, he should be able to develop into a better integrated, more wholesome, happier, and more congenial individual.

To be sure, his study may do none of these things. He may merely memorize certain facts, 'pass the course, and proceed to forget it all; but his work will be richer if he continually examines ways of applying what he learns as he goes along.

A word of caution! There can be unwise application of what one is learning. A tiny boy may attempt to apply his knowledge of how to use a saw by amputating the leg of his mother's grand piano. Nevertheless, such a possibility does not argue against the value of conceiving practical applications as one learns. The application of any kind or degree of learning presupposes a moderate degree of what is ordinarily known as common sense.

Chapter II  

"Some men are born great. 

Some achieve greatness. 

Some have greatness thrust upon them."

IN N SPITE of the implications contained in these lines that there are but three components involved in achievement, we all know that any man is the product of a great many factors which interact with each other in an intricate manner. We may try to classify all these into such groups as heredity, learning, and divine intervention; but such a classification does not solve any problems for us. What we plan to do in this chapter is to isolate some of these factors for examination and to try to understand why they function as they do. As a prelude to this task, let us review a few of the problems which will confront us. PROBLEMS

We have all seen men who were able to overcome the most inimical environmental influences in a masterful manner. Our admiration for such a person is often expressed by some such statement as "Blood will tell.” It seems, in such cases, that there is inside such a person some rare inherited quality which is more than a match for events which would crush a person with an inferior heritage.

On the other hand, we have all seen individuals, whose parents were certainly of inferior quality, who achieved greatness in spite of such an apparently poor hereditary background. Do we infer that such a person is an opportunist, that he had good teachers, or that his success is merely an accident? 

There is a widespread belief that inherited qualities cannot 19

PSYCHOLOGY 

be changed. If this is true, much of our educational effort is wasted. Instead of trying to teach those of inferior ability, it would be more profitable to perfect methods for detecting and segregating them and to devote all our energies to the education of the superior stock. But is it true that inherited qualities cannot be modified? And how much can they be modified, if it is shown that they can be?

Can learned habits be transmitted to the next generation by the mechanism of inheritance? Is there any foundation for the hypothesis, or belief, that if intense training in some special field (such as music) is continued for a number of generations, the results of this training are manifested in an improved natural endowment in the descendants? If this belief is without foundation, by what means may the human stock be improved? 

Are extremely unusual persons more likely to acquire their peculiarity through inheritance or from some environmental condition? Are criminals, geniuses, insane individuals, and idiots born or made?

Even a superficial analysis of most of the debates on the relative importance of heredity and environment reveals the presence of personal prejudices in these arguments. The individual who believes he has "blue blood" in his veins is likely to take comfort from this belief and to emphasize the importance of heredity. 

The one who is not so sure of his ancestors and who realizes that he must make the most of his opportunities is likely to stress the importance of environment. The one who knows he has inferior ancestors and who is placed in an extremely hostile environment is likely to hope that there is some force above, beyond, and superior to either; he hopes that some such miraculous force may intervene and enable him to rise above his apparently insurmountable difficulties.

It is natural that these personal considerations should creep into our beliefs about heredity, and they are pointed out not to criticize the individual who entertains one or the other prejudice. 

The recognition of their presence is merely a signal that care needs to be taken to survey the whole situation objectively. It is necessary to clarify the problems and to point up vague meanings. 

Problems of heredity will never be solved by emotional thinking and debate. 1

Essential components of the general problem. A clear conception of our problems involves three areas of clarification: 

1. A rigid definition of inheritance should be adopted. 

Using inheritance in its broadest sense, we can inherit anything we get from our parents regardless of the means of transmission. 

Thus, we can inherit a name, a title, real estate, money, or prestige. Such inheritance has been called social inheritance. But to the biologist, the use of the term "inheritance" is restricted to the transmission of characteristics from parent to offspring by the process of reproduction. There is no objection to the social definition so long as it is not confused with the biological one. 

Nevertheless, it is better for the student to adhere to the narrow definition of the biologist. Certainly, we should not permit ourselves to shift from one to the other. 

2. The notion that heredity and environment are opposed to each other should be eliminated. Misunderstanding often arises from an erroneous tendency to oppose hereditary factors to acquired characteristics as though they were mutually exclusive entities standing in opposition. Once this artificial antagonism is set up, confusion about their interaction arises. Thus, people often divide themselves into two opposed camps, the environmenmentalists and the hereditarians, and seem to have the conviction that the same person cannot be both. The antagonism is an unreal one, and a person should be neither one nor the other, but both. The germ cell does not develop in isolation, nor does the environment exert any magical influence.

Nor do we gain anything by attempting to decide which is more important. The hereditarian will argue that improvement of the soil is of little value if the seed is inferior. The environmentalist will argue that a good seed will produce an inferior organism if the soil is defective. Both contentions are true; so why should there be any argument? 

3. The concept of interaction between the organism and its environment should be substituted for the concept of antagonism between them. 

The problem should be stated as a question of adjustment. 

Given the seed for a human organism, is there any limit to the degree to which it can be changed by environmental influences? 

Certainly there are limits. No amount of external influence can

PSYCHOLOGY 

change a human embryo into a dog, a wolf, or an ape. But, within limits, the changes that may be wrought by environmental influences are striking. Any human being is the result of his original cell (the fertilized ovum) being nourished and helped, or being interfered with and modified, by surrounding influencesa process that is continuous from conception to death. 

We shall be better prepared to understand this entire adjustment process when we examine the mechanisms by means of which biological inheritance takes place. 

THE MECHANISMS OF INHERITANCE 

By some process of reproduction each animal organism is generated and, in turn, may reproduce offspring of its own kind. 

Nonsexual reproduction. The simplest type of reproduction of living tissue is accomplished by the division of a cell into two parts. These parts then grow to full size and, in turn, subdivide to form two more cells, each of these growing and subdividing into two more, and so on indefinitely. This process of simple cell division is called mitosis. The number of cells that can be produced by this process in a short time is enormous. For example, if mitosis should continue through twenty generations with no fatalities, one cell would produce 1,048,576 offspring.

Mitosis takes place in such a way that both offspring from a division are identical; and when they grow to full size, both are exactly like the original cell-barring, of course, any modification brought about by external or environmental circumstances. It is

dies. The individual does not transmit directly his bone cells, his nerve cells, and the like, to his offspring. Instead, the function of reproduction is entrusted to the specialized germ cells. Hence, if the offspring of a complex organism are to inherit any similarity to their parents, the means for accomplishing this inheritance must be found in the germ cells.

An interesting problem is the manner in which each parent by sexual reproduction is enabled to contribute an equal share to the offspring. The human egg cell, called the ovum, is much larger than the male germ cell, called the spermatozoön; yet each contributes equally to the characteristics of the child resulting from their union. This equalization depends upon a preliminary process in the germ cells before mating takes place, which process has been called maturation or the reduction division. The reason for the name "reduction division" is that the number of chromosomes in each of the germ cells is reduced to one-half its characteristic number as a preparation for mating. The process is shown in Fig. 5. In the human germ cell there are 48 chromosomes, arranged in pairs. In the reduction division the number is reduced to 24, one of each pair being retained. Consequently, when a sperm with 24 chromosomes is united with an ovum with 24 chromosomes, the original number of 48 is restored by this union. The fertilized ovum, therefore, has 48 chromosomes; but 

24 are from the father and 24 from the mother. [16] The process of fertilization is shown in Fig. 6.

Random combinations of factors in sexual reproduction. 

A significant question in biological inheritance is: What chance has a parent of producing a child exactly like himself? A number of conditions prevent exact similarity and the degree of similarity is determined by the random interplay of many factors. 

In the first place, each individual has germ cells which vary in the combinations of genes which they possess. Of a great number of germ cells, all capable of reproducing, only a few ever do take part in the process of reproduction. Hence, what the offspring will be like depends, in part, upon which germ cell happens to enter into the process of fertilization. In the second place, there are two cells involved, one from each parent. The traits of the offspring depend upon a chance combination of mother and father genes.

This process of random selection of factors in man is so complicated that it cannot be easily understood. In order to make it clear, it may help to use a simple illustration from plant life. 

The understanding of such a simple pattern may enable us to imagine, at least, what happens in man, although we must avoid jumping to the conclusion that the process works with equal sim-

PSYCHOLOGY 

plicity in man. The illustration we shall give involves only one pair of determiners and it should be remembered that as the number of determiners is increased the chance elements increase in geometrical proportion.

A cross involving one pair of factors. [16] A good illustration of the process of random selection in its simplest form may be found in an experiment by Gregor Johann Mendel (18221884), an Augustinian monk who crossed a tall variety of peas . with a dwarf variety. He found that all the resulting hybrid offspring were tall. When these hybrid tall peas were subsequently crossed with each other at random, he found, in this second generation, three tall plants to one dwarf. 

On further breeding, he found that the dwarf plants of this second generation, when bred with each other, produced only dwarf peas.

That is, they bred true. The tall peas of the second generation turned out to be of two varieties. One-third of them bred true and produced only tall plants. The other twothirds produced offspring in the ratio of three tall plants to one dwarf plant.

The law derived by Mendel from his experiments is known as Mendel's law and can be stated as follows: When parents who are opposites in a particular genetic character are crossed, the progeny of the first generation will all be like one of the parents with respect to the character in question. The character which thus impresses itself upon the offspring in this manner is calleđ a dominant character. The character which is suppressed is called a recessive character. When, however, the hybrid offspring of this first generation are, in turn, crossed with each other, they will produce a mixed progeny, 25 per cent of which will be like the dominant grandparent, 25 per cent of which will be like the other grandparent, and 50 per cent like the hybrid parents. The important element in this law is the fact that, while the hybrids of the first generation all look like the dominant progenitor, they contain both the dominant and the recessive factor in their germ cells. The recessive character will appear in the physical constitution of an offspring only when the dominant factor is absent. 

The process involved is illustrated in Fig. 7. Furthermore, which mating does occur will depend upon random or chance conditions. The possible chances are illustrated in the diagram

in Fig. 8. Putting together the results as shown in this diagram, the offspring will occur in the proportions of one pure tall, two hybrid plants which will appear tall, and one pure dwarf which will appear dwarf. In appearance observable to the experimenter there will be three tall plants and one dwarf.

If the inheritance of human traits depended upon some simple combination of genes, it might be possible to segregate these by some control of human marriages, and to effect matings which would perpetuate the desirable traits and eliminate the undesirable ones. No such situation exists. Even in dealing with animals which are much more simple in structure than human beings, it has been found that a character which is apparently simple is dependent upon large numbers of genes. For example, over fifty genes co-operate to produce the red eye color of a fruit fly.

Hundreds of genes co-operate to produce the straight wing on such a fly. [6, p. 17]

If, when only ten factors are involved, there is less than one chance in a million of securing an offspring exactly like his pure grandparent, the complexity of the combination of genes involved in producing a human trait makes the task of rational control of human matings a superhuman task. One is certainly not warranted in explaining how Mendel's law functions with a simple trait in a plant and then proceeding to the generalization that human traits are inherited in the same simple manner. The principles are probably the same, but the complexity of the problem grows in geometrical proportion to the number of factors involved.

THE TRANSMISSION OF ACQUIRED CHARACTERS 

Geneticists customarily maintain that each individual grows from the germ plasm, that the individual carries the germ plasm in a condition which keeps it immune from bodily influence, and that the individual passes on the germ plasm intact and unchanged to the next generation. This theory runs counter to a common and popular belief to the effect that the germ plasm may be changed by the activities of the individual who is acting as a car-

PSYCHOLOGY 

rier. For example, the popular belief is that, if a man becomes a mathematical expert by incessant application, his germ plasm will show the influence of his endeavors, and any offspring he may have will be likely to show original skill in mathematics as a result of the biological transmission of the effects of this learning from father to son.

Popular belief unsound. This popular belief is probably based on wishful thinking. Many individuals have wished that acquired traits could be passed on. Breeders who are trying to improve the strain of the animals with which they are working would have an easier time if the effects of the careful nurture of their prize animals could register in the progeny of those so reared. 

Physicians have hoped that a patient who is protected from some disease by the process of immunization could pass on this immunity to his children. Those who bring about a moral improvement in a man may well wish that this moral improvement could be transmitted through the germ plasm to the next generation. 

To console those who have a consuming ambition to contribute to the improvement of the next generation, it might be pointed out that such contributions need not be limited to biological heredity. A human being receives much more through social heritage than he does through biological heritage. For example, even if such a man as Pasteur could have affected his germ cells by his research and have passed on such changes, the effects of such biological improvement would have been infinitesimal compared with the contribution to human welfare which he passed on through the channel of social inheritance. 

Evidence against transmission of acquired characteristics. Practically every controlled experiment which has attempted 'to test the transmission of skill in some performance through the germ plasm has given negative results. Occasionally an experimenter has reported positive results, but later checks have invariably shown that there was some error in technique or in interpretation.

Gross mutilations of the body certainly do not affect the germ cells and are not transmitted by inheritance from one generation to the next. A bobtailed cat gives birth to kittens with normal tails. Certain races have practiced mutilation through centuries with no effect upon their offspring. For example, Chi- 1

nese have bound the feet of their women; Jews have practiced circumcision; breeders have docked the tails or ears of dogs, dehorned cattle, and the like; but in none of these cases has the genetic structure been changed by such mutilations. 

If the individual body could affect the germ cells, it would seem that an individual who manifested a dominant trait might influence the germ cell in such a way that the recessive trait which was present there could be changed toward the dominant. An experiment with the fruit fly shows that this influence will not operate. It has been possible to carry a recessive factor along through 350 generations in animals which showed the dominant trait in their bodily structure without those dominant characteristics modifying in the least the recessive factor. [15] 

The conclusion seems to be that the germ plasm is immune to any sort of ordinary influence from the behavior of the individual who carries it. It has been possible, as we shall show in the following paragraphs, to produce genetic changes by subjecting the genes to violent treatment, but this is a different situation from that involved in the proposition of inheritance of acquired characters as ordinarily stated. 

Effects of violent treatment of the germ cells. It has been shown that the germ cells may be changed in their structure by violent methods. 

1. It has been found that the genetic system may be altered in many ways by subjecting the developing organism to powerful X rays. [12] The animals are injured; many are killed outright, many are reduced to sterility, and many which are still able to reproduce pass on abnormalities of various sorts to their offspring. The X rays have been shown to cause the chromosomes to break apart, to cause recombinations of the chromosomes, and to destroy some parts of the genetic structure. 

2. An increase in the temperature in which a developing organism is placed has been found to cause decided mutations. [13] When the temperature is close to the lethal point many die; others survive with various abnormalities; and those who are still fertile may transmit changes to their offspring. 

These experiments show that the germ cells may be modified by the environment in which they are placed. It is significant, however, that in order to produce observable changes, such violent

PSYCHOLOGY 

methods must be used. A man may lose a leg or an arm, or suffer mutilation; he may fail in his vocation, become a drug addict, or otherwise mess up his life; he may be racked with disease and lack physical stamina; and still, in spite of all this, he may be competent to be the father of a normal child. Whereas some individuals may wish that they could pass on their accomplishments to the next generation by biological means, most of us should congratulate ourselves that the mistakes of our ancestors stopped with their bodies and did not affect their germ cells, and that our mistakes will stop, in a biological sense, with us. When we make mistakes we hope that other people will forget. Occasionally they remember for a long time. Fortunately, the germ cells do not have to forget; they simply do not learn. 

IMPROVEMENT OF THE HUMAN STOCK 

In spite of the apparent difficulties confronting the advocate of human eugenics, it has been contended that, even if we do not know exactly how to arrange the best human matings, it would be well to make sure that only the best citizens be permitted to reproduce themselves. It seems logical to suppose that those who have proved that they are competent individuals would be more likely to have competent offspring than those who have demonstrated their defectiveness. The problem is not solved so easily, as we shall see when we examine the issue more critically. 

We shall examine some of the methods used by breeders to improve the genetic strain of their animals, compare these methods with the method of widespread crossbreeding, and then measure these against the value of attempting to improve the individual by environmental influences.

Inbreeding. Inbreeding has been used by those who are trying to secure a pure genetic pattern in the offspring. By inbreeding is meant the mating of closely related individuals. There are different grades of inbreeding from the self-fertilization that may be found in many plants and in some animals, through brother-sister matings, to the mating of distant cousins.

Inbreeding functions by removing some of the chance elements in matings. When matings are truly random, the offspring contain genes in purely random patterns. When there is inbreeding, the range of variation is decreased and any trait is more

likely to appear in pure form than when there is wider mixing of strains or genetic patterns. If the traits thus produced are desirable, inbreeding may improve the stock; if they are undesirable, the stock will deteriorate. The latter situation is more likely to occur when the undesirable trait is a recessive one. If there is a wide mixture, the recessive quality appears in the individual more rarely than in a pure strain.

The rapidity with which a genetically pure strain is reached through inbreeding will depend upon the degree of inbreeding and the number of pairs of genes concerned. Self-fertilization, where 100 

Per cent homozygosity 90 80 70 60 50

When inbreeding is as far removed as second cousins, the percentage of pure offspring does not increase materially as a result of such matings. [15] The various percentages with different degrees of inbreeding are shown graphically in Fig. 9. 

Inbreeding may give rise to genetic stocks of unusual worth or it may give rise to striking defects. The results cannot be determined in advance. It is probably this factor which has made human beings look with disfavor upon inbreeding. While the

PSYCHOLOGY 

1 method has some value in animal work, it is literally out of the question with human beings. It would require complete control of all matings. It would mean the highhanded arrangement of marriages between brothers and sisters or parents and children in the same cold-blooded manner that the geneticist uses with fruit flies, pigs, or chickens. Even the most wild-eyed reformer would never advocate the use of this method with human beings. 

Selection. Selection may be of two types: natural selection and artificial selection. In natural selection, the choice of the ones who will mate and carry on the race is left to the operation of natural laws. In artificial selection, the choice is made by man. 

1. Natural selection. Many years ago, Darwin [1] evolved the theory of natural selection as a means for explaining evolutionary processes. His theory involves several definite factors: (a) Overproduction. The process of natural selection begins with the production of more individuals than can possibly survive in a given environment. The limitations of food and space make it necessary that some of the surplus be removed. (b) Variation. A second factor is provided in the fact that the members of a given species manifest variations. Some of the variations make it easier for the individual to exist in the strained circumstances in which he finds himself, whereas other variations may make survival more difficult. (c) Competition. A third factor is free competition between the members of the species to take advantage of what opportunities there are for obtaining food, space, and the other essentials for life. (d) The survival of the fittest. Given an oversupply of individuals who vary in their equipment for meeting the stresses of living, and given a situation of free competition between them, those who are more fit to meet the difficulties of the situation will survive those who are not competent. Those who survive will be the ones who produce their kind because the others will be killed off. Hence, the race gradually loses its weaklings; whereas the strongest members survive and reproduce their kind. 

It should be noted that, when this natural selection operates, strength or weakness is measured in terms of ability or lack of ability to meet the immediate difficulties in the situation. It should be noted, likewise, that this theory of the survival of the fittest does not imply the transmission of acquired characters.

The offspring do not acquire strength from the struggles of the parents. They live merely because their parents were strong enough to outlive the weaker members of the species. 

While natural selection may operate in wild animal life, it certainly does not function in civilized society. On the contrary, we do many things to prolong the life of the unfit and to destroy the fit. For example, medical science has contrived means for keeping alive many individuals who would have died under the conditions existing a few generations ago; whereas we have developed rigid selective methods for sorting out the best physical specimens for military service. We kill the best in war, and use our scientific knowledge to preserve the unfit. On the other hand, perhaps we do not want a race of beings whose essential virtue is physical fitness. Perhaps we want to develop brain workers with defective bodies instead of good physical specimens. Who knows? Let those who are too much upset by this issue take comfort in the previously cited fact that what the individual does leaves his germ cells intact. Perhaps the germ cells of the physical weaklings are as good as the germ cells of the stalwart heroes who die on the battlefield. 

2. Artificial selection. Sometimes man has found it to his liking to favor those characteristics which are not necessarily connected with hardiness or virility. This has led to the search for artificial means for controlling and directing matings, as well as to a search for the kind of knowledge which would enable man to predict what will happen when he does exercise his directing influence. Such artificial selection methods may be classified into three types: (a) Selection on the basis of physical characteristics. One of the oldest methods that man has used is that of choosing the best individuals of a group for breeding purposes. Those individuals who manifested most strikingly the desired trait were mated, while those who showed the least degree of the trait were not permitted to mate. This method will give results only when the individual bodily type corresponds with his genetic pattern, and this is often not the case. If the desired trait comes from a recessive character, then the method will give results. On the other hand, an individual may have a combination of dominant characters which will give him the appearance of approaching the

PSYCHOLOGY 

ideal which the breeder has in mind but, at the same time, he may have a combination of recessive characters which will make his offspring deviate from the breeder's ideal. The animals which take the prizes at a stock show may not be those who have the best pattern of genes for producing offspring like themselves. (b) Selection by the pedigree method. Another method that has been widely used is the pedigree method. This method is better than the stock-show method and it works fairly well when it is combined with the latter. However, even when a long family tree is recorded, the individuals may have a genetic pattern that will produce inferior progeny. (c) Selection by traits shown in the progeny. This is the best method for artificial selection. The only real test of the genetic value of a plant or animal is the offspring that the individual can produce. This fact is utilized in the progeny method of artificial selection. The method works in this manner: The same male is mated to a number of females and the quality of the offspring from each mating measured. The female which produces the best progeny is selected for further breeding. Conversely, the same female is mated with a number of males and the progeny judged. The male who has the best offspring is selected for further breeding.

When this method has been used through a number of generations, some remarkable results have been obtained. One illustration is an experiment on increasing the production of eggs. Eight years of breeding of prize chickens (the stock-show method) had failed to increase egg production. At the end of this period, males and females were selected for breeding based on the egg production of their daughters. After two years of this method of selection (the progeny method), egg production was nearly doubled. [15] The progeny method is based on sound fact. The student who has followed the description of the mechanism of inheritance in the preceding pages will recognize this. The other methods of artificial selection are based on the fallacious notion that an individual is very likely to produce offspring closely like himself. This is not true. Instead, he is likely to produce offspring whose genetic structure is like his. Unless he knows his own

genetic structure as well as that of his mate, he must depend upon chance to reveal to him what kind of offspring he will get. 

It is clear that this, the one successful, method of artificial selection cannot be used by human beings. It would involve the postponement of permanent matings until an examination was made of the offspring of a number of preliminary matings by the individuals involved.

These facts should give pause to the enthusiast who advocates the application of the methods derived from the study of animal breedings to the betterment of the human race. We do not know which human characteristics are most desirable and, even if we did, we would not be able to institute any genetic program to transmit them to our offspring.

Widespread crossbreeding. Certain students of eugenics, recognizing that neither inbreeding nor the different methods of selective breeding are practical in human life, have advocated extensive crossbreeding as a means for improving the human stock. In extensive crossbreeding all traits tend toward an average and the extremes are lost because, by mere chance, the genes mix indiscriminately. The extreme variants are hidden because they are outnumbered by those which are not so extreme. This phenomenon was observed by Galton, who gave it the name of filial regression. [4] His law may be stated as follows: Average parents tend to produce average children; but the children of extreme parents tend to inherit the parental peculiarities in a less marked degree than that found in the parents themselves. 

If this method is used, as it is in many countries without any effort or supervision on the part of anybody, there will be a reduction of the chances for producing geniuses but, at the same time, a reduction of the chances for producing freaks. Perhaps we are better off without either. 

Improvement of the individual. Regardless of any theories we may have for the improvement of the race by genetic methods, such methods are not being applied today; unless we accept the method of crossbreeding with its reduction in the number of freaks and geniuses as a genetic improvement. Therefore, why not devote our time and energy toward the improvement of those individuals who are born, instead of bemoaning the fact that they did not have better parents?

PSYCHOLOGY 

Improvement of an individual by environmental influences is based upon the thesis that an individual may be modified by his surroundings: by medical care, by proper nutrition, by social contacts, by educational procedures, by his experiences in overcoming difficulties, and the like. Is this viewpoint a valid one?

One reason why so much has been made of the importance of human heredity has been the widespread belief that inherited traits cannot be changed. We have seen that the germ plasm of an individual cannot be modified easily by what the individual does. We have found that the genes can be changed only by such drastic influences as X rays and extreme heat. Having been impressed by the stability of genes, unthinking individuals have assumed that the characters growing from the genes cannot be changed, that the physical characteristics of an individual cannot depart from the structure and pattern laid down by the genetic combination which obtained at the time of his conception. This false assumption is what has given rise to most of the misunderstanding and controversy on this subject. 

What the environmentalists really object to is the contention of the hereditarian that what one inherits he has for "keeps." 

What the hereditarian objects to is the contention of the environmentalist that he can mold an individual into almost any form he wishes with no regard for the hereditary factors. The hereditarian is inclined to regard the inherited mechanism as the kernel of real value and to regard the environment as a dangerous threat to the integrity of this original seed. He considers that the task of the organism is to adjust in an environment. He reluctantly admits that the organism is influenced by his environment, but tends to think this is unfortunate and sees in the organism devices which enable it to resist too much influence. The environmentalist, on the other hand, is often inclined to think the stock is pretty bad; and his urge is to change it for the better. The true picture is better expressed by saying that an organism adjusts to his environment instead of in it. 

Regardless of personal bias, it must be admitted that the geneticists have shown that the physical organism is determined in part by factors in the germ cells from which he originated. 

It may also be admitted that such an inherited structure predisposes an individual to act in a certain way. The inheritance of

four legs predisposes an individual to walk on all fours; whereas the inheritance of two legs predisposes him to walk on two legs. 

Nevertheless, it does not follow that an inherited structure cannot be used in different ways. A man may learn to walk on all fours, and a dog may learn to walk on two legs. The contention that what one inherits cannot be changed is a queer belief which continues to have adherents in spite of its obvious falsity. 

Experiments with canaries. This issue, is brought to a focus in some experiments with roller canaries. [14] These birds were raised in isolation from the time they were hatched, so that they had no opportunities to hear other birds sing. It was demonstrated by this means that it was not necessary for the male canary to hear the typical song of his species in order to produce it. He sang it without having heard it or without having been taught it in any manner. The song was a product of his organism.

Having demonstrated that the typical canary could sing without the environmental stimulation of other songs, the question was asked: Must this ability remain fixed throughout the life of the canary, or can it be changed?

In order to answer this question, certain of the birds who had been isolated were subjected to tones and to sequences which were different from their native songs. Their singing moved from their natural type toward the stimulating tones. That is to say, a bird inherited an organism which predisposed it to sing in a certain manner; but it could be taught to sing in a radically different manner. [9]

In another experiment, birds which had been isolated were put together in a cage where they could hear all the songs of the other birds. Such group influence tended to make the birds more alike. The birds which had sung faster than the average of the group tended now to sing more slowly. Those which had sung more slowly than the average now speeded up. That is, the unusual singer tended to give up his individualism and to drift toward the average as a result of the mutual stimulation of group life. [9] 

The conclusions to be drawn from such a study as this may be expressed as follows: Each individual has factors or characteristics which are fairly stable and which resist change when

PSYCHOLOGY 

exposed to environmental influences. Some of these may appear without particular training or stimulation from the environment to bring them out. On the other hand, an individual may develop a pattern of behavior as a result of environmental influence; which pattern, in turn, may manifest different degrees of resistance to change. The degree to which a pattern manifests stability is, consequently, a poor index of its origin. If a pattern does show stability, there is no justification in jumping to the conclusion that it cannot be changed.

CONCLUSIONS 

It is not wise to generalize too freely in the field of heredity and environment. Nevertheless, the following conclusions can be accepted without too many reservations: 

1. A human individual is the product of a great many factors. Some of these exercise their influence but once, some operate at various times, and others function almost continuously from conception to death. These factors are practically innumerable, but some of the most obvious are: the genes which were present in the fertilized ovum from which he started his life, nutritional and other conditions which affected his development in his mother's uterus, the surroundings in which he matured as an infant, his education, his adjustment to the physical and social environment, and any chance or accidental circumstance which he may have encountered. Furthermore, the individual we now examine may have been a different individual in many respects at previous times, and he is almost sure to be different in another hour, in another day, year, or period of years. No conception of human life which makes a man a static creature can be correct. In the next chapter we shall examine the way in which some of these environmental factors influence the growing organism. 

2. The combination of genes with which a man starts his life results from the chance mating of one of a great many ova from his mother with one of a great many sperms from his father. 

This chance combination plays an important part in determining his physical characteristics, and these physical characteristics may, in turn, make it easier for him to act in one way than in another. 

A canary finds it easier to sing like a canary than to bark like a dog.

3. The germ cells which an individual carries, and which determine the characteristics he will transmit to his offspring, are relatively free from influences derived from the activities of the individual who carries them. Consequently, the kind of children a person may have is determined by his germ cells and not by what he does. That is, acquired characteristics cannot be transmitted by biological means to the next generation. In human cultures social inheritance becomes of more vital significance than biological inheritance. 

4. The species can be changed only by changes in the genetic structure. Many of the changes in genes are minor in character and affect the species but slowly. If changes are too radical, the cell may be damaged and unable to affect future generations. 

This immunity of the gene makes for racial stability. 

5. The individual is more easily influenced by the environment than are his germ cells. Racial improvement is best achieved by measures which enable each individual to make the most of himself, instead of attempting to improve the genetic stock. 

6. Practical considerations make it almost impossible to apply to the human race what has been learned about breeding. 

Improvement is furthered more by social heritage than by biological heritage. There is no ground for the popular belief that what an individual inherits cannot be changed.
