Chapter III  

THR 'HROUGHOUT our study of the hereditary background of the individual we were confronted with the fact that the inherited structures were influenced by the biochemical environment in which they matured. We concluded that an individual resulted from an interaction between the growing organism and its surroundings. Now we wish to examine more carefully the essential features of this interaction. Those who have worked intensively upon this aspect of the developmental process have kept a number of definite problems before them. A statement of these problems may be in order as we begin our survey. 

THE RELATION BETWEEN MATURATION AND EXERCISE 

The problem involved here might be stated in this way: To what extent is the maturation of an organ or of a complete individual influenced by exercise during the process of development? 

Several possible answers have been suggested, each of which seems to have something in its favor. 

1. It has been suggested that maturation is a process determined wholly by the genes. We have already stated rather arbitrarily that this hypothesis is not a reasonable one, but we shall presently examine specific evidence on this point. A commonsense argument in its favor is that one cannot use such an organ as an arm before one has an arm; therefore, maturation must precede exercise and be independent of it. An argument that has been used on the other side is the well-known fact that if an organ is not used it atrophies. In rebuttal, it may be contended that, although exercise may be required to keep an organ alive and 46

in good health, this fact does not prove that exercise was a necessary prerequisite for its original development. The statement of these different arguments should make clear the complexity of the problem. Let us withhold final judgment until we examine the facts that bear on the question. 

2. It has been suggested that maturation is wholly dependent upon environmental stimulation. Those who favor this hypothesis contend that the reason for the similarity shown by different individuals is that they grow in a restricted and similar environment. If a developing organism is placed in an environment different from its normal one, will its maturation show the effects of such changed surroundings? We shall examine some interesting experiments which have been performed in an attempt to answer this question. 

3. Is there a definite time sequence between maturation and exercise? Is it possible that, as the organism develops, there is first maturation and then development through exercise? Does improvement through exercise require the cessation of development through maturation? Or, do the two operate simultaneously, but in different degrees at different stages of development? We shall review some interesting suggestions made in this connection as a result of experimental work with twins.

The problem of individuation versus integration. The two extreme viewpoints on this issue may be stated as follows: 

1. The theory of individuation. The theory of individuation states that activity in an individual begins as undifferentiated mass activity (the individual acting as a whole) and that specific or local activities grow out of this mass behavior. 

2. The theory of integration. The theory of integration states that activity begins in relatively isolated segments, and that development proceeds by means of the unification of these small units into larger and more complex patterns of behavior. 

These issues are vital. When we know to what extent the developing organism is influenced by environmental factors, we will be able to surround it with favorable influences. If we remain in ignorance we are likely to time our efforts poorly and to apply them in incorrect amounts. If education during maturation is beneficial, it would be a grave mistake to postpone instruction until development is complete. Furthermore, our educational

PSYCHOLOGY 

procedures must certainly be different, depending upon whether the important problem is to enable the individual to integrate tiny bits of experience or to develop through the process of individuation.

In spite of their importance, these problems cannot be solved if we confine our study to human beings. Human maturation takes place in a situation that is relatively hidden from the prying eyes of the scientist. Since more liberty can be taken with animals, much of our information must be gleaned from a study of lower organisms.

TECHNIQUES USED FOR STUDYING PRENATAL LIFE 

The degree of intricacy of the techniques that must be used to study prenatal life depends upon the conditions surrounding the embryo while it is developing. We shall begin with the simpler forms of life and proceed to those methods which have been used with the higher animals and with man. 

Direct observation. In certain lower vertebrates, such as frogs and salamanders, it is relatively easy to study the first stages of development because the eggs have translucent coverings, and because the early stages of growth take place in water where the investigator may observe directly what is taking place. [9] 

Making a window in the eggs of birds. A special technique is necessary to enable an experimenter to study the development of bird embryos. The shell of the blunt end of the egg is cut off as far as the inner membrane. Melted vaseline is applied to the inner membrane. This transforms the membrane into a clear transparent window and, at the same time, has no detrimental effect upon the egg. The incubator temperature keeps the vaseline at the proper consistency to maintain the transparency. [21] 

Observation of fetal movements. In mammals, observation of the fetal movements may be made by placing the mother in a position favorable for direct observation. Mechanical devices have been used to record such movements in certain mammals. 

Human mothers have been asked to keep a record of the movements which they feel. However, such methods are usually crude, time consuming, and unsatisfactory.

Listening to fetal movements by means of a stethoscope. 

While only a little more satisfactory than the method of crude observation, listening to fetal movements, to heartbeats and the like, by means of a stethoscope can furnish some information about fetal development and behavior. This method can, obviously, give but sketchy information.

Premature removal of the fetus from the mother. This method requires the immediate death of the mother and the rapid death of the fetus following removal from the mother. [2]

The fetus may be kept alive and studied for a short period of time after the operation but, since mother and offspring soon succumb, the knowledge gained from this method is likewise unsatisfactory. [9] 

Operative techniques. Observations of the fetal behavior while the fetus is still alive and attached to the mother have been made possible by means of elaborate experimental procedures. [12] The mother is placed under a deep anesthetic and the spinal cord severed. A deep incision is made which will give access to the uterus by a slight subsequent operation. The mother is then permitted to recover from the anesthetic so that the fetus will not show any effects of ether when its behavior is studied. After this, the fetuses may be taken from the mother, kept alive in saline solution and studied at some length while still attached to the mother. These techniques have been used with guinea pigs, rats, and cats. Even with these elaborate methods, however, it has not been possible to study continuously the development of the same mammalian fetus over long periods of time.

Pathological conditions in human beings. Except for direct observations of movements, by listening with the stethoscope, and by reports from the mothers, our knowledge of the development and behavior of the human fetus must wait largely upon accidental circumstances. Such unusual conditions include abortions, death of the mother during the period of gestation, and surgical operations upon the mother. However, the accumulation of data from such infrequent situations, added to the knowledge gleaned from experimental studies of animals, has furnished us with some fairly accurate information as to the prenatal life of human beings.

BEGINNINGS OF ACTIVITY IN LOWER ANIMALS 

The visitor to a fish hatchery is usually much interested in watching the newly hatched fish as they swim vigorously against a current of water. It appears as though the fish were born with a ready-made drive to swim upstream. Anyone who has seen a colt immediately after it was born will remember that, although it was wabbly, it quickly attempted to stand on all four legs. 

Does the fish swim because it has a tail? Does the colt stand because it has four legs? Certainly, the colt does not make the mistake of attempting to swim, nor does the fish attempt to stand on four legs. Does it not seem that the kind of movements that an animal makes is partly determined by the structure of its body? However, we shall soon see that much more is involved in the origin of activity.

A more fundamental question is: Why does the animal move at all? It has been noted by various observers that the growing embryo can be made to move by decreasing its supply of oxygen or by changing the surrounding temperature. That is, movement can be induced by environmental changes. It is probable, however, that, even if all environmental factors were excluded, the embryo would move because of chemical activities taking place within the organism itself. The question to be answered is how activities induced by such vague stimulating conditions as internal chemical changes, or external changes in oxygen supply or in temperature, can develop into useful acts such as swimming and standing. A partial answer may be found by tracing the early stages in the development of co-ordinated movements. 

How the salamander learns to swim and to use its legs. 

The way in which internal chemical changes can result in significant activity has been brought to light by an analysis of how the salamander begins to swim. [11] This animal is well adapted to the study of elementary behavior because it can be observed in stages of development which are simple enough to be comparable with the embryonic development of higher animals, The various phases in the development of its swimming activities are illustrated in Fig. 10 and may be outlined somewhat as follows: The first movements are initiated from processes within the organism. This is evidenced from the fact that they

begin at a stage of development when the animal is unresponsive to external stimulation. These movements consist of a simple bending movement, first to one side and then to the other, so that the animal alternately takes the form of a C and a 5 Brain Eye Ear -Spinal cord

C, the double flexure or swimming stage. This comes largely through an increase in speed of the alternations of flexure movements. Each flexure begins with the head and proceeds toward the tail. When a second flexure begins at the head before the preceding one in the opposite direction has reached the tail, an S-movement occurs which serves the function of causing the animal to move ahead. 

(From J. E. Coghill, Anatomy and the Problems of Behavior. The Macmillan Com pany.) (a reversed C). In these bending movements the tail tends to lag behind the head. Consequently, as the movements increase in speed, the head completes its movement to one side and starts to reverse to the other side before the tail has ended its first swing. This variation in timing between the two ends of the animal produces an S reaction, the head swinging to one side

PSYCHOLOGY 

while the tail swings to the other. Reciprocating S movements are literally swimming movements and the salamander is thereby propelled through the water. That is to say, the salamander learns to swim as a sort of accidental result of movements which had their origin in internal chemical processes. 

How does the salamander learn to use its legs? At the time of the first swimming, the limbs of the salamander are not sufficiently developed to function independently. They merely hang as useless appendages to a body which swims by writhing movements. With further maturation of both the musculature and the nervous system, the forelimbs gain independence of movement, followed still later by movement of the hind limbs. Furthermore, each limb develops in a characteristic fashion. First the limb moves as a total mechanism, then elbow flexion gradually appears, then wrist movements, and finally independent movements of the digits.

The analysis of this succession of activities in the salamander lends support to several generalizations: 

1. First, they seem to support the principle of individuation. 

Partial or localized activity patterns arise within a larger or total activity pattern and, by a process of learning, acquire varying degrees of specificity and independence. 

2. The end of the organism which takes the lead in activity becomes the head end of the animal, whereas the part which is slower becomes the tail end. Whether the initial lead depends upon advanced maturation or whether an accidental lead in activity produces more rapid growth is a question still to be answered. 

3. Development of an independent member begins as mass activity, the development proceeding from those parts nearest the main body and proceeding toward the remote parts of that member. 

4. In a general sense, development must precede function. 

There must be the growth of a body before it can make any swimming movements. There must be a leg or an arm before it can function. Nevertheless, specific movements do not seem to spring forth fully developed. They begin with general mass activity and become specific with exercise. 

Structure and function develop together in the chick. 

Prolonged studies of chick embryos [21] have corroborated the

conclusions that grew from the studies of the salamander. In the chick, it seems that practically every mechanism for activity is ready to function before it actually does function but that, in many instances, an organ which is still rudimentary in form will function in a crude fashion. 

The studies of the chick embryos have brought out another significant point; namely, that development of behavior is gradual and continual. An organ does not develop to perfection and then begin at once to function in a highly integrated manner. The structural development of any organ is gradual and function usually goes along with structural maturation. Perfection in form and function come slowly, progressively, and in conjunction. 

It seems safe to conclude that the early embryonic movements of the chick are elements out of which every later response of the adult chicken is developed. For example, many of the adult postures and attitudes of the chicken show a striking relationship to observed postures and attitudes of the chick before it is hatched from the egg. If we but had a complete and accurate record of every stage of embryonic development, it might be that we could discover all the intervening steps in development and that activities which seem to spring forth suddenly would appear as the growth from simpler patterns. The illusion of sudden appearance of fully developed activities would then disappear. 

Is the embryo driven by a definite purpose? Much elementary behavior has beneficial results for the animal who manifests it. This has led thinkers to speculate upon the theory that the animal has some foreknowledge of the results of his activity and works to bring about favorable ends. There is much evidence against such a theory, a sample of which comes from a study of the newly born marsupials. The opossum and the kangaroo are good examples. A marsupium is an abdominal pouch formed by a fold of the skin and enclosing the mammary (milk producing) glands. The young of animals provided with a marsupium are born in a condition of considerable immaturity and are carried about and cared for in this pouch. 

It has been reported that the newborn opossum travels from the opening of the mother's genital organ to the marsupium without the aid of the mother. Considering the immaturity of the newborn animal, and the length of the journey in comparison

PSYCHOLOGY 

to its size, this is a remarkable undertaking and has been used to support the theory of purposeful activity. A critical examination of this journey, on the other hand, reveals that the movements made are probably not purposeful at all. They are similar to an overhead swimming stroke in which the head sways as far as possible to the side opposite the hand which is taking the propelling stroke. With each turn of the head the snout is touched to the mother's body and if the teat is touched in one of these movements the embryo stops and takes hold. Once having obtained a grasp upon the nipple with its mouth, it stays attached in this manner for a period of weeks without ever once relinquishing its hold. [18]

The activity of the newborn kankagoo is somewhat similar to that of the opossum. It requires about thirty minutes for the newborn kangaroo to move from the genital opening to the pouch and, during the entire passage, the infant kangaroo receives no help from the mother. It moves very slowly, turning the head from side to side, the hands reaching about, opening and closing continually like a cat's paw.

Several points of similarity may be noted between these activities of the marsupials (in their journey from the birth orifice to the pouch and attachment to the mammary organ) and the beginning activities of the salamander. The head sways from side to side in a movement quite similar to the S movement by means of which the salamander develops his swimming skill. 

In both the salamander and the marsupial it is the head end which is most highly developed and the front paws are by far more highly developed than the hind paws. The front paws assume the brunt of the labor in the marsupials and the hind ones drag along in rather a useless fashion. 

This, again, looks like the process of individuation, that is, the emergence of specific activity out of general mass activity. 

The marsupial is probably stimulated to a varying type of writhing movement because of the hunger resulting from ejection from the uterus. The form of these movements is determined by the stage of development already reached by the newborn animal. Once having become attached to the mammary gland, the movements cease; and when the animal finally releases its

That the newborn marsupial is not driven by some definite purpose has been demonstrated by a simple test. The role of sensory stimulation in fetal development. 

Studies of the fetuses of white rats and cats have supported the findings from the studies of lower forms of life and, at the same time, have made a further contribution in that they indicate the part played by sensory stimulation. The best observations upon fetal rats and cats have been made by removing the fetuses from the body of the mother without breaking the placental connection, and observing the behavior of the fetuses while both mother and offspring were kept alive in a blood-warm solution. 

The first movements observed in the fetal white rat were slight lateral bendings of the head. [9 and 31] Clamping the umbilical cord increased the products of metabolism (metabolites) in the fetal system and thereby initiated more violent activity and changes in behavior. The appendages of the very young fetus moved only with the trunk in much the same fashion as the legs of the salamander moved when the latter was developing swimming movements. In short, these early movements of the fetal rat remind one very much of the bending and S reactions that were found in the salamander and marsupials. 

However, the students of the white rat have shown that the principle of individuation is not a complete explanation of growing behavior. The mass reactions are not merely broken up into specific patterns. Instead, some condition ordinarily arises which interferes with the primary mass behavior. This arrest of the primary or basic movement gives rise to secondary movements and specific patterns grow from these. In this progress the primary, basic, mass pattern of reaction is never quite lost, but the smaller, more specific activities develop relatively much more independence. These interferences with mass behavior arise from stimulation of the sense organs of the fetus. A study of

PSYCHOLOGY 

the fetal cat reveals the same general form and direction of development that has been suggested by the study of the more elementary forms of vertebrates. [12, 31] [12, 31] Here, again, the first fetal movements are found to be slight head flexions, followed by generalized trunk undulations, forelimb flexion, and rotation of the head and trunk. These primary movements are strikingly altered by sensory stimulation. 

In other words, it would seem that the principle of individuation may account for the segregation of action patterns from internal and structural conditions alone, but that stimulation from the environment adds other elements by interfering with these patterns and thus producing still other forms of activity.

Experimental interference with the growing embryo. 

Evidence is multiplying that environmental influences will change in a striking manner the developing embryo. Although the salamander is normally an aquatic animal, it may be made into a land animal by being fed, in its very early developmental stages, with thyroid extract. So changed, it will live on land and go to the water only to lay its eggs. If a pregnant rat is fed with a diet deficient in Vitamin B₁, the offspring are defective in neural development. A young animal which would ordinarily become a female will develop into a male if a male sex gland is transplanted into it before sexual development has progressed far. 

Probably the most striking experiments in this connection are the transplantation experiments performed upon animals in the embryonic stage of development. An illustration of such an experiment is the transplantation of an eye-bud. If an eye-bud, at just the right stage of development, is transplanted so as to lie under the skin of the abdomen, the skin and adjoining tissues are influenced in such a manner that a fairly complete eye is formed. That is, the eye-bud becomes a center of influence which acts upon tissue, which would ordinarily become abdomen tissue, and makes it into eye tissue. [29] 

HUMAN FETAL DEVELOPMENT 

The prenatal life of the human being is usually divided into three periods: the germinal period, embracing the first week and sometimes the first two weeks of prenatal life; the embryonic

period, extending from the third to the fifth or sixth week; and the fetal period, including the remainder of the prenatal period from the sixth week to birth. The normal term of pregnancy is usually given as 280 days, with variations in estimate between 

270 and 284 days. An infant born at less than 180 days of age is not likely to survive. 

Description of human fetal activity. During the germinal period there is little but a globular cluster of cells which are multiplying at a rapid rate. This cluster is free moving until the end of this period, when it becomes embedded in the tissues of the uterus of the mother. From this time until birth, the developing child exists parasitically in the mother. During the embryonic period the individual increases greatly in mass and attains considerable differentiation of structure. No spontaneous activity has been observed in this period. 

The earliest movement of the human fetus is reported for a fetus slightly less than an inch in length and at the estimated age of six weeks. By two months the arms and legs move spontaneously. The early movements are likely to be slow, irregular, unco-ordinated, lacking in precision, and diffuse. 

With increasing age, at approximately three months, the fetus may show more specific responses to definite stimuli. For example, the stimulation of one foot may lead to the movement of the arm on the opposite side of the body. Or, brushing the sole of the foot may lead to flexion of all the toes except the great toe. Later, it may be possible to elicit a movement of the leg by striking the patellar tendon (the tendon just below the kneecap), or a movement of the foot by striking the tendon of Achilles (the tendon just above the heel). Continuing up to full term, the fetus seems to make greater progress in his ability to react more specifically to local stimuli. These reactions have been called reflexes.

Conclusions from the study of fetal life. A significant result of the studies made of the human fetus has been a reformulation of the concept of reflex behavior in human life. It was formerly thought that reflexes constituted the elementary form of behavior. According to this old conception, a reflex was defined as a constant, congenital, relatively invariable, restricted, mechanical response which followed some specific stimu-

PSYCHOLOGY 

lus. A reflex presumably had its basis in some inherent mechanism the explanation for which was not clear. 

The newer conception of human development embodies the conclusions from the studies of animal fetuses. It holds that human as well as animal behavior is at first crude, undifferentiated, and likely to involve the organism as a whole. As structural development progresses, behavior becomes more specific and localized. These individualized patterns then become more complex and elaborate, owing to the interference of environmental conditions, including both stimuli from the outside and interferences with movement imposed by outside obstructions. The reflex is, consequently, not the primitive form of activity, but an advanced form which develops with the growing independence of various parts of the organism. The appearance of reflex behavior in the full-term fetus is in striking contrast with the diffuse character of the behavior of the very young fetus. 

It would seem, consequently, that the reflex is a more advanced form of behavior than is mass behavior, the reflex is not inflexible in its manifestations, it is not unlearned, and it may be broken down in times of stress and external interference and give place to more primitive reactions. In other words, a reflex represents a more precise, more efficient, and more localized way of dealing with a stimulus than can be accomplished by a mass reaction.

From this discussion, it would appear that growth is not to be considered as the mere unfolding of preformed materials, nor is it to be thought of as the imbuing with life (vital energy) of some prefabricated organ. It is rather the continual interplay of dynamic forces which form one system, only to be continuously superseded by newer systems as the result of changing relationships between the dynamic elements involved. 

These dynamic processes that begin with the fertilized ovum continue through life. Development consists of alterations in both structure and function of the organism which is living in a continually changing environment. The aspects of this development are exceedingly complex; the forces that operate are numerous; and progress does not proceed in any one direction or toward any one end. Through the development one may perceive the continuation of primitive mass patterns, and he can also dis-

cern the emergence of new, localized, and specialized patterns which are partially independent of the mass reactions from which they grew.

ASSETS OF THE NEWBORN INFANT 

Even after birth, the human infant retains many of the characteristics found in the immature fetus. His movements are still slow, asymmetrical, arrhythmical, and un-co-ordinated. 

His body is thrown about, curved, flexed, extended, and arched. 

His arms and legs merge with those of the trunk and are slashed and kicked, flexed and extended incessantly. The movements are not regular and there are no fine and precise gradations and little specificity in the reflex sense. All his activity is ineffective. 

The significance of an infant's behavior cannot be determined by the degree of efficiency he manifests. Instead, his relative immaturity guarantees to him the possibility of developing in different directions, his reflex patterns are easily modified into different forms of behavior, and he requires only enough supervision from adults to safeguard him from errors which might bring death while permitted enough freedom to attain breadth of experience. As we review the assets of the child at birth, we should keep these aspects of the significance of infancy in mind. 

Relative immaturity. Birth in itself does not represent any violent acceleration of the maturation process; it is merely the transfer of the developing organism from a restricted environment to a more complex and extended environment. The relative degree of maturity of the animal at the time that this transfer is made has some significance. While the marsupial is more immature than the human infant at birth, the marsupial remains in the mother's pouch, attached for a prolonged period to the mammary gland of the mother, and hence not being subjected to a wide environment in the same sense as the human infant. 

When the marsupial eventually becomes separated from the mother, it is more mature than is the human infant at birth. 

Since the human infant is born in an immature state, he has few activity patterns already established. He must learn his forms of behavior while being subjected to stimulations and interferences from a complex environment and has, for this reason, the opportunity to develop more complex activity patterns

PSYCHOLOGY 

than would be possible if he completely matured in a restricted environment. It is an advantage for the human infant to be born in an immature condition. Much of his later intellectual progress may depend upon this characteristic of the human species. 

Behavior of the neonate.¹ The neonate has few specific behavior patterns at birth. [5] Those which are present are likely to show a lack of uniformity at first, to manifest quick change, and easy modification when they have little value and are, consequently, not much exercised. An examination of some of the neonate's behavior will make this clearer. 

1. The sucking response. The neonate has a vague tendency to orient the mouth toward the stimulation of areas near the mouth. The order from the highest to the lowest frequency of response is made to stimulation of: lips, above lips, below lips, and cheek. [26] With increasing age the cheek stimulation is the first to diminish in the frequency with which it will bring about the turning toward the source of stimulation. With the placing of the nipple in the neonate's mouth there is likely, at first, to be a disorganized attempt at sucking which quickly, however, becomes definitely organized. 

The sucking response may be stimulated, after it has once begun and then tends to lag (as it is likely to do after the infant has taken some food and begins to relax), by a flash of light, pinching the toe, pulling the hair, making a loud sound, or any sudden or forceful stimulus. Mothers use these methods to keep the nursing child from going to sleep before he has received enough food. Sucking may also be augmented by giving the infant sweet or sour solutions, and it may be affected by giving solutions which vary from the normal temperature. 

In other words, sucking is not the fixed machinelike reaction that it is sometimes described as being, nor is it as rigid in its operation as the sucking reflex in some lower animals. 

2. The grasping response. The grasping response is the flexing of the fingers in response to contact stimulation of the palmar surface of the hand. 

1 The newborn infant is often called the neonate. This term "neonate" is used arbitrarily to designate the child during the period from birth until he is about one month of age. Some limit the use of the term to the first two weeks. of life.

This reaction is very marked in such an animal as an ape. 

He will grasp an object and easily support his entire weight. [20] The grasping response is, on the other hand, variable in human neonates. It is stronger in periods of excitement or hunger, and disappears in sleep. It is weakened when the child relaxes after nursing. It disappears entirely after about six months. [17] 

3. The plantar response. The plantar response consists of a flexion of the toes produced by stroking the sole, of the foot. 

In neonates the response of the toes has been reported to be quite similar to the reaction of adults (known as the Babinski sign) who have a pathological condition of the spinal column; namely, the flexion of all the toes except the great toe which is extended or turned up.

This result has been asserted to be due to the immaturity of some of the fibers of the spinal cord. This reaction in neonates may be influenced by immaturity, but it is also dependent upon the strength of the stimulus used in eliciting it. [27] In other words, this foot response is quite variable and is partially dependent upon the nature and strength of the stimulus and not entirely upon the degree of maturity of the neonate. 

4. The pupillary responses. In the human adult the pupillary response to light is one of the most regular that can be evoked. It consists of a change in the size of the pupil in response to a change in the intensity of the light stimulating the eye; a brighter light causes the pupil to become smaller, a reduction in the brightness of the light is followed by an enlargement of the pupil. This response, however, is by no means uniform in the neonate. Most investigators report that it is not present at birth, but that it develops during the first few days of life. [23, pp. 40–41] 

5. Other forms of infant behavior. Other investigators have reported such responses as sneezing, hiccoughing, yawning, crying, smiling, the sudden spasmodic reaction in response to a quick change of position (called the Moro, or fear, reflex), and the raising of the head when placed in a prone position. [5] 

The sense organs at birth. Since the reactions of the child provide the only means for interpreting the sensory acuity of infants, and since the reaction patterns are crude in their func-

PSYCHOLOGY 

tioning, it is difficult to gain any clear conception of the degree of accuracy with which the neonate is able to use his sense organs. 

1. Visual sensitivity. The infant learns to respond quickly to brightness changes and to changes in hue and reacts to these stimuli in a variety of ways. The pupillary reflex is quickly learned by the neonate; the blinking reaction (palpebral reflex) appears about the end of the second month of life; the ability to direct vision upon an object appears at about the third month; eye, and head pursuit movements in following a moving object have been observed at about two weeks of age; and a bright, intense flash of light may produce a general spasmodic reaction with clasping (Moro reflex) during the first three or four days of life. [25] This quick learning indicates that the visual apparatus is well developed at birth; but it is also apparent that the infant does not know how to utilize his vision without learning. 

2. Auditory sensitivity. Great individual differences in auditory sensitivity are manifested during the first few days of life. Some observers insist that the infant is deaf at birth, others assert that the ear is stimulated effectively during prenatal life. 

In spite of this uncertainty, it is evident that the neonate soon becomes sensitive to sounds. He manifests his susceptibility to loud sounds by blinking (the palpebral reflex), respiratory changes, circulatory changes, spasmodic muscular contractions, and the clasping reaction (Moro reflex). This sensitivity is more marked to high-pitched tones, and to sounds of short duration and high intensity, than to low-pitched, prolonged, and mild tones. [23, p. 52] 

3. Smell (olfactory) sensitivity. The neonate responds when stimulated with ammonia or acetic acid by throwing back his head, wrinkling or grimacing of the face, squirming of the body, respiratory changes, movements of the legs and arms, and by crying or sneezing. [26] Odorous substances which do not cause pain or discomfort in the adult do not produce a response in the neonate. It seems probable, consequently, that the neonate is responding to pain or discomfort rather than to the olfactory qualities of the stimuli. 

4. Taste (gustatory) sensitivity. The most common taste stimuli that have been used to test infants are sugar, salt,

quinine, and citric acid solutions. The reactions used to indicate responsiveness to taste have been facial reactions, changes in the sucking reaction, circulatory and respiratory changes, or bodily movements. [25] It is quite likely that the neonate is sensitive to salt. There is disagreement among investigators as to the neonate's sensitiveness to the other three basic tastes; namely, sweet, sour, bitter. 

5. Thermal sensitivity. To a general lowering of the environmental temperature the infant of only a few hours of age will respond by shivering and muscular activity. When a cold or hot stimulus, considerably below or above the normal body temperature, is applied to local areas of the body, vigorous movements of the stimulated part are produced. In addition, such local temperature stimuli cause more widespread responses, such as respiratory changes, circulatory changes, widespread movements, and, in some instances, crying. [25] 

6. Pressure or contact sensitivity. Responsiveness to various kinds of pressure stimuli, touches, taps, and strokings have been observed in the fetal period and are probably fairly well developed at birth. For example, the sucking responses, blinking, plantar, and palmar reactions may all be produced by tactile stimulations. [26, p. 186] 

7. Pain sensitivity. Premature infants are responsive to pain stimuli, but it is also true that sensitivity to pain increases with the age of the infant. It is greatest in the head areas and is less in the legs. The time for response is longer in the neonate than for the involuntary reaction found in adults. In addition, it is often necessary in the neonate to give repeated pain stimuli before a response is elicited. [26] 

8. Visceral sensitivity. There is evidence that hunger contractions produce increased general activity in the neonate. 

When substances are introduced into the stomach there is a cessation of such contractions and general quiescence. This relaxation may be interfered with by gas pressure after eating, which in turn is customarily relieved by placing the infant in a position where he can easily belch, euphemistically called by mothers, "bubbling." 

9. Sensitivity to changes in position. It is well known that swinging and rocking are effective in allaying crying in the

PSYCHOLOGY 

neonate. In the first two or three days of life a crying child will become quiet, and perhaps fall asleep, if he is taken up, rocked, or mildly jolted. All infants enjoy cradles and baby buggies. Experimental studies have been made of the effects of rotating an infant. After the rotation stops there is an oscillatory rotation of the head for about fifteen seconds in the direction opposite that in which the infant was rotated. This is known as nystagmus and is presumably dependent upon static sensitivity, or sensitivity to changes in position.

Dependence of the neonate. While the sense organs of the neonate are ready to function, the infant does not have the ability to react to complex stimuli by appropriate acts. It needs no experimental confirmation to establish the fact that the child must be fed, protected, and guided by adults or he would perish. 

The neonate has not the mechanical equipment required to enable him to move about in his objective universe; he has not the strength to move the body structure that he does possess; he has no well-developed reflex behavior patterns to enable him to react spontaneously and efficiently to various stimuli; instead, he must depend upon others to help him. He attempts to do various motor tasks, makes mistakes, tries other methods, makes more mistakes, and all the time is being given help from those around him. A colt or a lamb is much more efficient and independent at birth than is a human being. 

Finally, when the child does achieve independence, he shows certain effects of this gradual learning under supervision. His movements are in the nature of intelligent adaptations to problem situations rather than automatic reflex actions to fixed stimuli. 

The advantage of this sort of early dependence, and its consequent effect of producing intelligent responses instead of blind automatic acts, can be seen by contrasting the behavior of a human being with an insect. On a summer's night the insect will fly toward a light even though it may be killed by the heat as a result of its action. It has a fixed pattern of behavior in response to a light and it cannot modify that behavior. The human being has a thousand and one reactions that he may make to a light. To be sure, the entire difference between an insect and a human being is not one of relative dependence in infancy;

but the differences would not be possible were not the latter immature and dependent. 

The significant factor is that the child learns as he achieves independence just as he learns while he matures. A mechanical response to any situation incapable of being modified is a nonintelligent reaction. It might perchance be an efficient reaction for some specific situation, but an intelligent response is one that can be modified in response to a minor change and adapt itself to the needs of the moment.

THE COMPARISON OF AN APE WITH A CHILD 

It is a significant fact that man's superiority over the lower animals is not dependent upon physical strength, motor skill, or sensory acuity, but upon his ability to put these qualities to efficient and intelligent use. A clever, unique, and enlightening experiment has made these distinctions clear. An ape and a child were given identical treatment for a prolonged period in order to observe differences between the two. [20] A female chimpanzee was taken from her mother at the age of 72 months and “adopted” into the family of a psychologist who already had a son 10 months of age. These two "children" lived together as companions, playmates, and members of the same household for nine months. They were treated as nearly alike as was humanly possible. Each was given the same consideration, caressed in the same manner, engaged in the same games, ate with the same utensils, and slept in similar beds. During this time a continuous series of tests, comparisons, observations, and experiments was made upon the two. 

In the ability to grasp small objects and to make fine finger co-ordinations, the child is more adept than the ape. This, however, is practically the only aspect of motor behavior in which the child excels. The ape makes up for ineptness with his fingers by greater skill with his lips. In co-ordinated arm movements, the ape was more proficient at the age of 9 months than the child at 18½ months. She learned to eat with a spoon more readily than did the child. In walking erect and in skipping, climbing, and running the ape was far superior to the child. In physical strength the child was far behind the ape (see Fig. 12). 

The ape had greater sensory acuity in practically all sense

PSYCHOLOGY 

fields than did the child. The ape showed her sensitivity to light by turning her face from the source of a bright light, putting her hand, arm, or even her foot before her eyes to shade them. The child showed no corresponding sensitivity to light. The ape was much more sensitive to small objects, would stare and point at insects, or play with dust particles in the sunlight, and would notice immediately, and manifest curiosity toward, any new object in her environment. She showed interest in pictures and was much quicker in noticing her reflection in a mirror than the child. The ape, too, was much more alert to faint or weak sounds. She could detect sounds that were inaudible to adult human ears. In localizing sounds the ape was much superior to the child. In other spheres of sensation this same superiority was apparent. The ape seemed to have a better sense of equilibrium, learning to enjoy the dizzy sensation which comes from spinning, was more alert to smells, and seemed to be more alert to temperature changes.

It would be interesting to have such an experiment continued through a period of years in order to ascertain in what direction, and at what points, the ape and the child would diverge. 

We know that the child would have a marked superiority in his ability to utilize language, but it is possible that in some other directions the cleavage between the ape and the child would not be so great as we now are inclined to think. 

At any rate, it would seem that the important factor behind human achievement is the manner in which man learns to use the equipment that maturation has given him, rather than in the strength, agility, and mechanical efficiency of his body, or the acuity or discriminating ability of his sense organs. 

STUDIES OF TWINS 

In the attempt to determine still further the degree to which inherited structure may lend itself to individual variation through educational and similar environmental agencies, the psychologist has resorted to a study of twins. 

Some earlier studies failed to make a fundamental distinction between identical twins and nonidentical, or fraternal, twins. 

Identical twins have identical heredity, that is, they develop from a single fertilized ovum. Fraternal twins develop from two sepa-

rate fertilized ova and have no more similarity in heredity than do any other pair of siblings.2

It is not so easy as it might appear to be to identify identical twins. At one time it was assumed that when twins were identical, they would be enclosed in a single fetal membrane. All that would be necessary, according to this assumption, would be to examine the membrane at birth to determine whether both members of the pair were in a single membrane or in separate membranes. More recently, this assumption has been discarded. 

Identical twins have been found with each member of the pair in an independent membrane. Also, two membranes may fuse and appear as one so that some twins who have seemingly but one membrane may actually have two. The simple method of examining the birth membranes has been discarded. [24] 

The determination of identical twins. A substitute method has been to judge them on the basis of similarity. The characteristics that should be similar in identical twins are as 

1. They must be of the same sex. While twins of different sex cannot be identical, twins of the same sex may be nonidentical, or fraternal. This criterion can, consequently, be used to exclude some twins who are surely not identical. On the contrary, after the twins of the same sex are sorted out, these will include both identical and nonidentical pairs. 

2. They must be essentially the same in certain characteristics, such as: (a) hair color, hair texture, and hair form; (b) eye color and pigment pattern on the iris; (c) skin color, provided there has not been change by exposure to sun; (d) distribution of down on the body, especially on the face, neck, and hands; (e) facial features, such as nose, lips, chin, and ears; (f) type of teeth with same dental irregularities; (g) type and proportions of hands and fingers; and (h) friction ridges on fingers and palms.

The method of co-twin control. The most significant studies of twins are those using the method of co-twin control. 

In general, the procedure in these experiments is to give one twin special training as soon as he is mature enough to profit by it, to withhold similar training from his co-twin until some time later, 2 Refer to glossary at back of book for definitions of unfamiliar words.

PSYCHOLOGY 

and then to train the co-twin along similar lines. In one such experiment, training was given to one member of a pair of twins in climbing and in the manipulation of cubes; in another training was given in digit memory, object memory, ringtoss, paper cutting, and walking boards of various widths; and in another the special training was in language. [19] 

The most striking experiment using the method of co-twin control was that on the twins known as Johnny and Jimmy. [22] 

Johnny was given all sorts of special stimulation and training, while Jimmy was permitted to grow as an ordinary boy in a normal environment. At the close of the period of training in each activity the twins were compared. The experimenters classified the activities in which Johnny was given special instruction into two categories: (a) phylogenetic activities (those which are common to the human species), such as reflex reactions, locomotion, rolling over, reaching and grasping, and reactions to skin irritations; and (b) ontogenetic activities (those which are largely individual), such as climbing up and down inclines, climbing on and off stools, roller skating, swimming, finding hidden objects, jumping from a relatively high perch, and meeting difficult problem situations. At 19 months, Johnny could roller-skate, swim, drop from a five-foot perch, and persist in a problem situation for as much as forty minutes at a time. Jimmy could do none of these acts. In the phylogenetic activities there was little difference between the twins, the special training of Johnny in these produced little or no effect. 

Eleven months after the end of Johnny's training, Jimmy was trained in the same acts. After the completion of Jimmy's training, the twins were approximately equal in securing objects with sticks; in manipulating ropes, pulleys, and strings to procure objects; in size discrimination; and in intelligence tests. One difference persisted, however, and that was that Johnny continued to be more persistent and deliberate than Jimmy in his approach to a problem.

The conclusion seems to follow that motor processes that are particularly dependent upon special training do not come to life by the mere process of maturation of hereditary factors. It also appears as though some of the more obscure traits of personality, such as persistence and deliberateness, may result from the type

of training a person has undergone. Since Johnny was stimulated to learn a task when in a much more immature stage of development than Jimmy, it probably was much more of a challenge to him. We may suppose that his rising to such challenging stimulation helped to develop persistence and deliberation. 

However, we know little specifically of the development of such traits, and it could be that just a little more stimulation might have had a quite different result, he might have become discouraged and have learned to shrink away from challenging situations, or to have become resistant and stubborn. In any case, it seems apparent that identical twins can be made permanently different in personality traits by subjecting them to rådically different types of training. 

Results of comparison of identical with fraternal twins.

An elaborate statistical study was made in which fifty pairs of identical twins were compared with fifty fraternal twins. [24] 

The same investigators studied nineteen pairs of identical twins who had been separated from infancy and had been reared in different environments. Some general conclusions from their studies are as follows. 

1. Fraternal twins are no more alike than siblings. 

2. Identical twins resemble each other more than do fraternal twins or siblings. 

3. The resemblance found in identical twins is much more striking in physical characteristics than in mental or personality traits. Identical twins are practically identical in such physical characteristics as finger ridges; they are similar in height, weight, and head length; and they are least alike in educational achievement, personality, and temperament. 

4. Twins who have lived apart for a considerable time in widely different environments are less alike than those who have lived in similar environments. Social and educational changes. in the environment are effective in producing variations in such traits as intelligence, school achievements, and temperament. 

Environmental differences do not greatly affect likenesses in physical characteristics. 

5. Identical twins become neither more nor less alike as they grow older; whereas fraternal twins become less alike with

PSYCHOLOGY 

age in mental traits and in personality traits, but remain similar in physical traits. 

6. The degree of similarity in twins varies with the trait involved as well as with the nature of the environment. No amount of education will bring about differences in the finger ridges in identical twins; nor is it probable that environment can be kept so similar for identical twins that they will have identical temperaments when they reach middle life.

CONCLUSIONS 

1. Studies of the developing embryos of animals and of human beings indicate that activity is first initiated by chemical processes within the embryo. 

2. The order of development seems to be: (a) From crude mass activity to more specific and localized behavior. (b) From weak, un-co-ordinated, and variable responses to those which are stronger, better, co-ordinated, and more regular. (c) Progress is from the head to the tail regions. (d) In each limb development progresses from the part nearest the body and proceeds toward the more distal parts. 

3. Changes from mass activity to specific activity emerge from the interaction of two factors. The one is the maturation of more complex structures in the individual, including the development of the nervous system, the increase in acuity of sense organs, the enlargement of the bony framework, and the strengthening of the muscles. This maturation makes possible more complex forms of behavior. The second factor is the stimulating influence arising from difficulties in adjusting to the environment. Each stress provides the occasion for specialized and individualized reactions in place of the earlier crude mass actions, the response to a specific need by a more direct and localized response. 

In short, each demand for adjustment stimulates the development of activities which are less random and more intelligent. 

4. The relation between maturation and exercise is not a fixed one.

Maturation begins from forces present in the genes; but exercise begins before an organ is completely developed. Such

exercise may effect radical changes in the developmental processes. 

Hence, if the entire development of an organism takes place in a restricted environment, the organism will tend to develop according to a more rigid pattern than would be the case were it exposed to varying situations during development. When an animal is born while in a relatively immature state, he will have opportunities to vary his adjustment behavior patterns. This gives meaning to the fact that the human infant is born in a relatively immature state. 

5. Reflex behavior seems to be a more mature form of activity than undifferentiated mass activity. The reflex patterns in a human infant are less rigidly established than are similar patterns in the lower animals. The behavior of the human being is therefore more flexible than that of the lower animals. 

6. The comparison of an ape with a child seems to show that human superiority cannot be measured in terms of strength and efficiency. The ape is stronger and more efficient than the child. Instead, the human being, because of his variability of behavior, has a wider range of uses to which he can put his various capacities. It is flexibility rather than efficiency that is the true measure of man's superiority. 

7. A study of twins gives indications that physical characteristics are more dependent upon hereditary factors than are personality traits. The elements in human life which count for most are those which man gains through his ability to modify hereditary patterns in accordance with his own individual experiences.

Chapter IV INTELLIGENCE INT 

NTELLIGENCE is correctly attributable to a person in so far as he manifests behavior which we ordinarily characterize by such terms as: judiciousness, penetration, perceptual alertness, good memory, acumen, discernment, judgment, rationality, prudence, adaptability, and sagacity. Intelligence is purely a descriptive term and its application to an individual carries with it no implication as to the factors which contribute to the behavior upon which the description is based; it says nothing about the sources from which it may have arisen; and it implies nothing about its stability. That a descriptive term does not involve any implication of cause, essential components, or stability can be made clear by the use of a simple adjective such as clean. When it is said that a person is clean, it does not mean that he has a trait of cleanliness, that he derived his cleanliness from any particular source, that he has always been clean, or that he always will be clean.

When we attribute intelligence to a man, we are not asserting that it is something he possesses or that it has a power to make him act in a certain way. We can, nevertheless, proceed to hunt for ways of determining to what extent any individual is intelligent, to what extent individuals are consistent in being intelligent, the practical value to the individual of intelligence, and some of the factors that may contribute to the retention of intelligence. [16] 

TESTS OF INTELLIGENCE 

Attempts to measure intelligence have been made difficult because of the inability on the part of psychologists to delimit 75

PSYCHOLOGY 

the term. It has been variously defined as: (1) persistence, that is, the tendency to take and to maintain a definite direction; (2) adaptability to new situations and to new requirements; (3) the ability to criticize one's own acts; (4) the ability to learn easily and quickly; (5) the ability to utilize facts and activities already acquired; and (6) curiosity, that is, interest in, and desire to know about things. [11, 16] 

General approaches to the measurement of intelligence. 

Two general approaches have been used: the analytical and the empirical. 

1. The analytical approach. Before attempting to measure such a vague concept as intelligence, it would appear reasonable to attempt to define it more accurately or to tease out the component factors by some logical or statistical device. Having ascertained the components, one could devise tests to measure each; and the combination of these component measures should give a measure of the original concept. This is the reasoning behind the analytical method, and the logic certainly appears sound. In spite of this apparent simplicity, attempts to carry out the procedures suggested by such a logical analysis have not proved to be very successful. 

2. The empirical method. The empirical approach to the problem grew from a practical need. Alfred Binet was appointed by the French Minister of Public Instruction to membership on a committee which was assigned the task of finding some means for determining which of those children who failed did so from stupidity and which ones failed because of laziness, lack of interest, or some other factor. [3] 

With this problem to be solved, Binet, in collaboration with Simon, a physician, began to work from the basic fact that children increase in mental ability as they grow older in years. 

He made no assumption as to whether this growth was due to heredity factors, to physiological maturation, to educational stimulation, or to the serial ripening of new elements. He merely set out to discover tests which would be indicative of this growth in mental ability which was so clearly apparent as children grew older.

He proceeded as follows: (a) He gathered a large number of tasks ranging in difficulty from very easy to very hard.

INTELLIGENCE 

77 (b) He gave these tests to a large number of children of all ages. (c) On the basis of the performance of the children on these tests he selected those items which differentiated between children of different age levels, and discarded those which had no differential significance. That is to say, if a test was answered as well by children of all ages from three years up to eighteen, it was discarded. If a test could be answered correctly by a large proportion of six-year-old children and only by a minority of fiveyear-old children, that test was regarded as having discriminative or diagnostic value. It was on this basis, and this alone, that 

Binet made his selection of tests. (d) He arranged his tests in groups corresponding to the chronological age of the youngest group of children who passed them. A test that could be passed by from 60 to 90 per cent of a given age group was regarded as a suitable test for that age, provided it was failed by a large percentage of younger children.

These same principles have been used in constructing many other mental tests. The tests most widely used in this country are the Stanford revision [14] of the Binet-Simon scale and the Kuhlmann revision [9] of the Binet-Simon scale. It is important to keep in mind the empirical process involved in the construction of these tests and the implications which arise from this method of construction. With such a method the results are purely relative. All that is known is that, when one individual passes such a test with a higher score than another person, he is better than the other. The extent of his superiority is not known, nor can any deduction be drawn as to why the difference exists. 

Furthermore, when an individual is given a score on such a test, the only information given is that his score is the equivalent of the average score of children of a certain age level. Binet gave his scores in terms of mental age, and the Stanford and Kuhlmann revisions have followed the same method. Consequently, if a person is given a test and secures a mental age of six years, for example, all that is meant is that this person has obtained a score which is the equivalent to the average score of the group of six-year-old children on whom the test was standardized.

Sample intelligence tests. In the Stanford-Binet scale there are six tests for each year-level, except for some of the

PSYCHOLOGY 

younger years where six tests are given for each six-month intervals. A few samples of the items from the various scales as used in this country, one from each age level, will give some idea of the nature of the material used: 

3-month level: will carry hand to mouth by a definite rather than by merely a random movement. 

6-month level: will pick up a small test cube from the table. 

9 month level: will give definite attention to scribbling demonstration. 

1-year level: will imitate such a simple action as shaking a rattle or ringing a bell. 

2-year level: will identify by pointing such toy objects as the following when asked to do so: a cat, a button, a thimble, a cup, an engine, or a spoon. 

3-year level: will copy a circle. 

4-year level: will answer such questions as: "Why do we have houses?" or "Why do we have books?" 

5-year level: will copy a square. 

6-year level: after watching the examiner string a chain of 7 beads on a shoestring using alternately square and round beads, he will make a string just like it, taking not more than two minutes to do so. 

7-year level: will be able to point out similarities in answer to at least two of the following questions: "In what way are wood and coal alike?" "In what way are an apple and a peach alike?" "In what way are a ship and an automobile alike?" "In what way are iron and silver alike?" 

8-year level will repeat verbatim a sentence of about fourteen words, as follows: "Fred asked his father to take him to see the clowns in the circus." 

9-year level: will point out the absurdities in three out of four statements read to him, one example of which is: "Bill Jones's feet are so big that he has to pull his trousers on over his head." 

10-year level: will name at least 28 separate disconnected words in one minute. 

11-year level will be able to tell the significance of such a problem as the following: "Donald went walking in the woods. He saw a pretty little animal that he tried to take home for a pet. It got away from him, but when he got home, his family immediately burned all his clothes. Why?" 

12-year level: will be able to say backwards numbers of five digits after having them read to him, such as: 8-1-3-7-2.

14-year level: will be able to answer questions which concern orientation, such as: "Suppose you are going west, then turn to your right, then turn left; which direction are you going now?" average adult level: will be able to indicate differences between such abstract words as: laziness and idleness. superior adult level: will repeat correctly the thought of a passage read to him, such as the following: "Many opinions have been given on the value of life. Some call it good, others call it bad. 

It would be nearer correct to say that it is mediocre, for on the one hand our happiness is never as great as we should like, and on the other hand our misfortunes are never as great as our enemies would wish for us. It is this mediocrity of life which prevents it from being radically unjust."

Computing the mental age. In giving an age scale, such as the Binet-Simon test, the examinee is given tests to a yearlevel low enough that he passes all the tests in that year, and to a year-level high enough that he fails all the tests in that year. 

All the tests in the range between these two year-levels are given and the mental age computed by scoring the tests in this range. 

The final score is an average mental age, and is abbreviated MA. 

The process will be clearer from the following illustration. Suppose a child passes all the tests at year III, fails all the tests at year VI, and makes the credit shown below on the intermediate levels: 

Year III, 

Year III, Year V, Year VI, Years Months all passed. Basal year level.... 3 and 6 months (written III-6), 5 tests passed, credit 1 month each 

Year IV, 

Year IV-6, 3 tests passed, credit 1 month each 

3 tests passed, credit 1 month each 

1 test passed, credit 2 months. all tests failed, no credit.... 

Mental age 

Total credit... 

4 years, 1 month, written 4-1. сл 320 13

PSYCHOLOGY 

The fact that the score obtained in this manner is expressed in terms of mental age should not be permitted to mislead us into assigning it some unusual significance. It is merely a score made on a test and is no different in nature than would be the case if expressed in terms of percentage, the letters A, B, C, or D, some arbitrary number, or the like. Let us repeat: What a mental age score tells us is that the individual being tested made a score equivalent to the average score of children of that age on whom the test was standardized. In the case of our illustration the child tested made a score equivalent to that of the average child of four years one month. A striking advantage of this method of scoring is that it makes clear at once the meaning of the score in a way that a score as 75 or B would not do. On the other hand, the use of a mental age method of scoring should not lead to any unwarranted assumptions that mental age has some peculiar, subtle, or symbolic significance. 

Mental age is a score on a test and it is nothing more than that. 

The intelligence quotient. The brightness or dullness of an individual cannot be determined from the MA alone. An individual may have a MA of nine years, for example, and still be a genius, bright, dull, or feeble-minded. A four-year child with a MA of nine years would be an extremely bright individual; whereas an eighteen-year-old person with a MA of nine years would be very inferior. In order to give due weight to the chronological age (abbreviated CA) of the individual tested, it has been found convenient to use the ratio of the MA score divided by the CA. This ratio is called intelligence quotient and is abbreviated IQ. Taking the illustrations above: The individual with the MA of nine years and the CA of four years would have an IQ of 225. (The actual ratio would be 2.25. In order to eliminate decimals, the ratio is multiplied by 100 and the IQ expressed as a whole number.) With the same MA an individual with a CA of nine would have an IQ of 100. With a 

CA of 15, a person with a MA of nine would have an IQ of 60.

The practice has grown of translating scores to MA regardless of the way in which the actual test is scored. This practice brings up an issue which should be clear to anyone using mental tests with adult individuals.
