children of different chronological ages. As children reach maturity and grow on into adult life, the differences in intelligence between chronological ages becomes less clear-cut and less measurable. Some persons have thought that this fact indicates that intelligence ceases to grow after about middle-teen age. A better interpretation would be that as individuals reach and pass maturity they cease to develop mental ability in a uniform and measurable manner but, instead, spread out in such diverse directions that it is practically impossible to find any test which will correlate with this spread of abilities. In other words, no one has been able to differentiate in any understandable fashion between the intelligence of a twenty-year-old group and a thirty-year-old group, or between a twenty-five-year-old group and a fifty-yearold group.

There is no consistent relationship between intelligence and chronological age after about fifteen years of age. 

This does not mean that intelligence ceases to grow, but it does mean that it ceases to grow in such a straight and consistent fashion that it can be measured by a simple battery of tests. 

However, adults are frequently given mental tests and their scores recorded in terms of mental age. When this is done, it should be kept in mind that the statement that a person has a certain mental age means merely that he did a performance equivalent to the performance of an average child of that chronological age. For example, if a man of thirty has a mental age of ten years, it means that he did the same grade of work on the mental test that is done by the average ten-year-old child. Certainly, his mentality is not equivalent to that of the ten-year-old child, for the child is likely to continue to develop, whereas the thirty-yearold man is not so likely to make further progress in mental development.

Adult IQ's. Neither can a mental age score for an adult be translated into an IQ in the same manner that the conversion is made for a child. Nevertheless, there are cases of adult individuals whose ability to pass intelligence tests is poorer than that of a child of fifteen and it is often desirable to make comparisons of individual differences in adult ability which will be significant in relation to the abilities of children. To accomplish this a compromise has been effected for computing IQ's for adults. If an individual is older than fifteen, his IQ is found by dividing his

INTELLIGENCE 

87 

MA by fifteen. If the individual is between thirteen and fifteen, an adjustment is made in computing his IQ to allow for the approach to maturity. It is only when his CA is thirteen or less that his IQ is found by the simple process of dividing the MA by the CA.

FACTORS INVOLVED IN INTELLIGENCE TESTS 

It was pointed out at the beginning of this chapter that when psychologists attempted to devise intelligence tests by a logical analysis of the factors involved in intelligence, they did not achieve any very striking success. They have been more fortunate in the use of empirical methods. On the other hand, after having standardized tests by the empirical method, they are still confronted with the problem of stating what is being measured with the tests. [2]

Kinds of material used in tests. If one makes an examination of the kinds of materials used in intelligence tests, it is clear that these are so varied that they cannot be reduced to any simple category. A casual inspection will show that the Stanford- 

Binet intelligence test requires the following kinds of reactions from the person tested: (a) language ability, (b) motor skill, (c) visual and auditory discrimination, (d) comprehension, (e) memory, (f) ability to make comparisons, (g) ability to abstract, (h) problem solving, (i) appreciation of absurdities, (k) ability to copy, (1) ability to define words, (m) orientation, (n) arithmetic ability, and (o) reasoning ability. 

Statistical analysis of intelligence tests. 

Much work has been done in an effort to analyze by the statistical method of factor analysis the components of batteries of intelligence tests. 

The results are not in agreement. One group of investigators has contended that they have evidence for a common factor, which they call a g factor, and which is supposed to play a part in a great number of intelligence tests. In addition to this common, or g, factor, they find other specific factors (s factors) which work with the g factor in diverse ways. [11] 

After analyzing a great number of tests by a different factor analysis method, another investigator concludes that the tests he studied contain at least nine group factors which he characterizes as follows: [17]

PSYCHOLOGY 

1. S-A spatial factor. The spatial factor is characterized by facility in processes involving a high degree of spatial and visual imagery. 

2. P—A perceptual factor. The perceptual factor is charac、 terized by facility in perceiving details which are embedded in irrelevant material. 

3. N-A number factor. The number factor is characterized by facility in numerical calculation. 

4. V-A verbal relations factor. The verbal relations factor is characterized by facility in the use of verbal ideas and verbal meanings. 

5. W-A word factor. The word factor is characterized by facility in dealing with words, that is, with fluency. 

6. M-A memory factor. The memory factor is characterized by facility in recognition and recall. 

7. I—An induction factor. The induction factor is characterized by facility in finding a rule or principle. 

8. R—A resistance factor. The resistance factor is characterized by the facility to complete successfully a task that involves some form of restriction or obstacle in the path of solution. 

9. D-A deduction factor. The deduction factor is characterized by facility in finding a rule and then applying it to the given examples involved in the test.

The teasing out of these nine factors by the factor analysis method is not meant to imply that no other factors are involved in an intelligent response. It merely indicates that these factors are present in the tests constituting the battery used in making the analysis. Since the tests used were those which have demonstrated merit as measures of intelligence, the factors outlined above certainly are important, even though others may be discovered by subsequent research. 

In the attempt to analyze intelligence tests into their basic components, it should be clearly recognized that it is the tests that are being analyzed and not any trait of intelligence in the individual. The tests were selected in the first place by the empirical method, that is, because they happened to work. The fact that they were found valuable does not mean that they comprise all the qualities involved in successful adjustment by an individual. 

It is quite possible that qualities or factors are involved in indi-

INTELLIGENCE 

89 vidual adjustment which the tests do not touch. Hence, a factor analysis of a battery of tests cannot be considered to represent an adequate analysis of any personal trait. We still have unanswered the question of just what components are involved in adjusting to intellectual problems and what proportion of each is needed in any specific problem or test situation. Our intelligence tests give some fairly good clues as to what to expect from individuals who are confronted with problems, however, even if they do not tell us why a person fails or succeeds. 

THE SIGNIFICANCE OF A CORRELATION 

Many physical measurements are made by the direct application of a measuring instrument to the object to be measured. 

For example, the length of a board may be measured by placing a linear scale upon it and observing how many times a given unit, such as an inch, must be used to cover the length of the board. In psychology such direct measurements are impossible and it has been found valuable to utilize indirect method of measurement. 

The value of any indirect method depends upon the degree of correspondence between the scale which is used and the object or event which is measured. The degree of such a relationship is expressed as a coefficient of correlation. While the beginning student may find it advisable to postpone his attempt to compute such coefficients, he should understand their significance. [4] 

Relationships expressed by coefficients of correlation. 

Although relationships may vary in complexity and in degree of intimacy, it may be well to confine our attention to so-called "linear" relationships. A linear correlation may be illustrated by the relationship between the diameter of a circle and its circumference. This relationship may be expressed by saying that the circumference always equals 3.14159 times its diameter. It may be indicated by saying that the correlation between the diameter of a circle and its circumference is perfect and positive, or that the coefficient of correlation between the two is 1.00. 

A perfect negative correlation may be illustrated by the relationship existing between the weight of a board and the number of holes bored through it (assuming that the board is of uniform thickness and weight and that the holes are of the same size). 

If the board originally weighed one pound and each hole takes

PSYCHOLOGY 

out one ounce of material, the relationship at various stages of the boring would be as follows: 0 holes-16 ounces; 1 hole-15 ounces; 2 holes-14 ounces; 3 holes-13 ounces; 4 holes-12 ounces; and so on, until all the available space for holes becomes exhausted. Such a relationship may be expressed by saying the coefficient of correlation is —1.00.

An absence of relationship may be illustrated by correlating the order of drawing of numbers enclosed in uniform capsules from a bowl in which they had been thoroughly mixed. This absence of any relationship may be expressed by saying the coefficient of correlation is .00. 

In other words, coefficients of correlation may range all the way from a perfect positive correlation (1.00), through no correlation (.00), to a perfect negative correlation (—1.00).

The interpretation of coefficients of correlation. A coefficient of correlation may be used to indicate the degree of relationship between a test and the characteristic to be measured. 

Our task is not complete, however, when we have expressed such a relationship in the form of an exact number. We must know how to use the information which the coefficient of correlation gives us.

We can illustrate the problem by referring again to the perfect relationship between the diameter of a circle and its circumference. If we say the coefficient of correlation between the circumference of a circle and its diameter is 1.00, we mean that we can tell exactly what the circumference will be by measuring its diameter. If a correlation is perfect, we can predict what one of the factors will be by measuring the other. 

What would be the meaning of such a statement as: The coefficient of correlation between the thickness of a bundle of papers and the number of sheets in the bundle is .98? Or, what is the significance of such a statement as: The correlation between an intelligence test and success in high school is .60? These two statements, taken together, would certainly mean that we can predict the number of sheets in a package by measuring the thickness of the package with greater accuracy than we can predict success in high school by intelligence test scores. Nevertheless, the actual difference in the accuracy of prediction is not directly indicated by the difference in the correlation coefficients. The

INTELLIGENCE 

91 relationship of the coefficient of correlation with prediction efficiency (called the coefficient of "forecasting efficiency" or the coefficient of dependability) is as follows: 

When a correlation is 1.00; prediction is 100 per cent perfect. .98; 80 .95; 69 .90; 56 50 40 29 .86; .80; .70; .60; .50; .40; 30; .20; .10; .00; 2 0.5 

THE PREDICTIVE VALUE OF INTELLIGENCE TESTS 

The purpose of giving an intelligence test is not so much to determine what a person will do on that test as it is to use the test performance as a means for predicting what the individual will do in other situations. Will he succeed in school, in a certain profession, in meeting an emergency, in solving a problem of management, or the like? This leads to the question as to the degree of accuracy with which we can predict intelligent behavior from scores on intelligence tests.

Time intervals. When a child is tested and retested after a very short interval of time, it is rather common for the two tests to vary by as much as 10 points in IQ; the majority of cases, however, do not deviate by more than 5 points. As the length of time between tests increases, the probability of variation between test and retest increases. There will be a tendency for those who tested high on the first test to decline on the second test after an appreciable interval of time, and a tendency for those who tested low to test higher on the final test than on the first. 

When the retest is at intervals from 1 to 24 months, the correlation between the two tests is about .88. This means that the efficiency of the first test as a means of predicting what the

PSYCHOLOGY 

individual will do on the second test is about 53 per cent better than chance. When the retest interval is from 60 to 145 months, the correlation between the two drops to .60; that is, the predictive efficiency is only about 20 per cent better than chance. 

The above facts hold when the surrounding conditions, which might influence test ratings, are uniform. In individual cases it has been found that IQ may change by as much as 50 points in test-retest situations. In order to reduce the degree of error, tests should be given only by those well trained in testing procedure. The tests have been standardized and the scoring methods based on the assumption that they will be given in a precise manner by one who knows how to evaluate replies. A slight change in the giving of instructions may seem trivial to a novice, but such a deviation may have an important effect upon the way the testee responds. The responses that may be made are quite varied and one must be skilled and have extensive experience to know exactly when to give credit for a reply and when to refuse credit. 

Influences which may affect IQ. The probable truth is that the IQ is relatively constant just so long as the relation between the individual and his total environment remains relatively the same, but that the IQ undergoes change with marked shifts in the total situation. There have been attempts to determine which factors are most influential in producing such changes. 

What these factors are cannot be stated with any clearness, but some suggestive findings will be presented.

Age at which test is given. The predictive value of an intelligence test varies with the age of the individual tested. It is relatively impossible to give tests which have any significant value as instruments of long-time prediction to an infant who is less than four months of age. It is really not until the individual is about four years old that predictions can be made over a span of as long as a year with any hope of accuracy. 

Effect of nutrition. While studies of general nutrition have not given striking results, it has been found that where a marked change in diet was instituted with undernourished children, some improvement was shown with improved nutrition. On the other hand, it is probable that specific elements in the diet are more important than general nutrition. It has been found, for example, that vitamin B₁ deficiency has a strikingly deleterious

INTELLIGENCE 

93 effect on maze learning in rats. It has been suggested, although not demonstrated, that the nutrition of the fetus and young infant may have an influence on the manifestation of intelligence in later years.

Endocrine hormones. Several studies indicate that IQ may be influenced by the hormones from such endocrine glands as the pituitary and thyroid. In some cases of thyroid deficiency, for example, where thyroid extract has been administered, there has been found a striking improvement in IQ, as well as in bodily structure. These changes with hormone therapy seem to be most effective with very young children and to decrease with the age of the patient. The activities of these glands will be discussed in greater detail in the next chapter. 

Degenerative changes. In certain diseased conditions there is actual destruction of brain tissue. With such degenerative changes there is certainly a lowering of IQ. A loss of intelligence may be found in cases of deterioration with old age. 

Changes in social environment. A number of studies have been published in recent years which show that when individuals spend a period of years in a sordid and nonstimulating environment, their IQ becomes lower, whereas the IQ improves when they are reared in a stimulating environment. For example, five-year-old children in certain nonstimulating communities had an average IQ of around 90, whereas fourteen- and fifteen-yearold children in the same communities had an average IQ of around 60.

On the other hand, children who were placed in stimulating foster homes and in stimulating school environments when very young manifested an improving IQ with the passage of time. 

Constancy of the IQ. There has been much animosity shown between those who advocate the constancy of the IQ and those who contend that it may be modified by certain conditions. 

Taking all the experimental, statistical, and clinical findings into account, the following conclusions seem to be warranted: 

1. The IQ may be lowered by degenerative changes in the nervous system, by injury to the nervous system by mechanical means, by deprivation of essential food elements or essential hormones, by injury from poisons, and by deterioration with old age. 

No one will deny such changes in the IQ.

PSYCHOLOGY 

2. The removal of injurious agents may lead to improvement of the IQ. If the removal of a deleterious agent occurs after maturity, the assumption would be that there would be a stopping of degeneration. This has been experimentally demonstrated in clinical treatment of patients. In such cases, the IQ does not improve but it ceases to deteriorate. 

If the removal of such a harmful agent occurs in infancy or early childhood, what would be the logical effect? The deteriorating process would stop and at the same time it would be reasonable to suppose that the individual would begin to profit more from environmental stimulation and educational opportunities. Hence, improvement of IQ by removal of obnoxious influences is more striking, the younger the child. This seems logical and seems to explain the improvement found in glandular therapy and nutritional studies. 

3. If large changes in IQ can be produced by major influences, lesser influences may produce minor changes. To use an analogy, the finding that Niagara Falls is being subjected to the slow influences of erosion does not mean that the whole Falls is going to cave in shortly. The discovery that the IQ is affected by certain educational and social situations does not mean that in six months of exposure to such situations an idiot can be made into a genius, or a genius into an idiot. Conversely, because these changes are not violent is no reason for arguing that they do not exist.

In short, it seems perfectly clear that the IQ can be changed, and that the degree of change varies strikingly with the nature of the factors which bear upon it. 

RESULTS OF TESTING INTELLIGENCE 

Intelligence tests have been widely used in various ways. 

They have been used to study differences between various groups of individuals, to study individual differences for the purposes of educational or vocational guidance, for the selection of employees, and for the study of feeble-minded and superior individuals.

Intelligence tests as educational guides. Probably the greatest value of intelligence tests is in the accomplishment of the purpose which Binet had in mind when he began his experimentation on an intelligence test scale; namely, the determination of the causes why children failed to progress in their schoolwork. [7]

PSYCHOLOGY 

The relationship between IQ and ability to succeed in school is rather close during the primary and secondary grades, especially when each child is permitted to progress at his own rate and in his own way. The relationship between intelligence test scores and success in college is not so striking. A number of studies designed to discover the best means for predicting college success have shown that the best single indicator of later college grades is the first-semester or first-quarter college grades. The next best index is high school grades, and the third best is a content examination of one sort or another. In other words, intelligence tests indicate whether a person is likely to succeed in his earlier educational career, but as he gets to the college level, the best indicators are samples of the sort of thing he must do in college rather than intelligence tests.

The customary use to which tests are put in the study of individual cases is to give the intelligence test and to check the test scores with the actual progress that the student is making. 

If he is doing as well as the test scores indicate that he can do, little or nothing is done. On the other hand, if the test scores indicate that he could do better work than he is doing, an attempt is made to find influences other than intelligence which contribute to poor schoolwork.

In addition, it may be possible to analyze the results of test performance and to discover the particular factor that is contributing to the failure of a particular student. For example, if the tests in which the student made his lowest scores are primarily concerned with the verbal factor, this information may be used as a guide for further educational guidance. The student may either be given extra training in the factor in which he is deficient, or he may be guided into fields where that factor does not play such an important part.

Vocational guidance. Although vocational guidance specialists have found that the interests of the individual are of primary importance in indicating the probable success of an individual in a specific vocation, it is also true that the intelligence of a person has some vocational significance. [8] When men in different vocations have been given intelligence tests, it has been found that the averages of various vocational groups differ from each other.

Other studies have shown that men with low intelligence, when employed on jobs which require a higher average intelligence than they possess, tend to leave those jobs. In other words; the job itself tends to eliminate the unfit just as school requirements tend to eliminate those incapable of doing scholastic work. 

To hire men indiscriminately, however, and to permit them to stay on jobs until they manifest their incompetence is an inefficient procedure-unsatisfactory for the employee and costly for the employer.

It has been found expedient to determine the minimum intelligence requirements for a given job, to give intelligence tests to all applicants, and then to employ only those who are able to demonstrate that they have more than the minimum. Such a procedure may help the employer to eliminate those who are unfit for the jobs he has to offer, and may save some men from the disappointment which would result from failure on the job; but it does not contribute much to the guidance of the individual who would like to know for what occupation he is best fitted. Taking

PSYCHOLOGY 

a broad view, it would seem that individual vocational guidance is not helped much by the use of intelligence tests. If an individual rates very high, he may be directed toward some professional work; if he makes a very low score, he may be directed toward unskilled occupations. The specific occupation, on the other hand, cannot be selected by general intelligence tests. Some progress has been made by the standardization and administration of special aptitude tests, but these are still in the experimental stage and are not sure criteria for vocational guidance. The conclusion seems to be that the employer can get more help in selecting employees by the use of tests than can the individual who seeks vocational guidance.

Feeble-mindedness. One of the most significant values that has resulted from intelligence tests has been a more skillful handling of the problem of feeble-mindedness. Long before psychologists had devised tests to measure intelligence, it was recognized that there were extreme variations of intelligence, ranging from the lowest degree of feeble-mindedness to the cleverest genius.

Before the development of tests the different grades of feeblemindedness were defined in terms of the degree to which they could adjust to the social and economic order. They were classified and defined as follows: 

1. Idiots were those persons who were mentally defective to such a degree that they were unable to guard themselves against common physical dangers. 

2. Imbeciles were those persons who were mentally defective to such a degree that they were incapable of managing themselves or their affairs with ordinary prudence. 

3. Feeble-minded persons (corresponding to the moron group as defined by later writers) were those persons who were mentally defective to such a degree that they needed care, supervision, and control for their own protection or for the protection of others. 

The main reason why individuals had to be classified on the basis of the degree of success in social and economic adjustments which they manifested was that there was no way of measuring their ability. They were necessarily exposed to life and their intelligence judged by the way in which they adjusted. Now, we utilize tests to derive an index of their ability, and then direct

INTELLIGENCE 

99 them so that they are able to adjust to society. In other words, if we can determine by means of a test that a person is an imbecile, he can be placed in a carefully supervised job and will adjust to it perfectly. He need not be thrown into a situation which proves too much for him in order to decide the level of his intelligence. 

Consequently, the modern psychologist defines the various degrees of intelligence purely in terms of ability as manifested on a standard test. In terms of IQ the different grades of intelligence have been delimited as shown in Table III.

Since there are all levels of occupations in life, the important consideration is to see to it that each individual is placed in some situation which is not too much out of line with his ability. When a feeble-minded person fails, we no longer blame him for not being able to measure up to the responsibilities placed upon him. 

The blame lies on those who were responsible for such misplacement. The remedy, of course, is to see to it that he is placed in a situation where he can adjust. 

Superior intelligence. A very high IQ is no more a guarantee of success than a low IQ is a certain index of failure or delinquency. The high relationship between intelligence test scores and chronological age stops at about fifteen years. That is, there is no standard growth in a straight line after adolescence. Nevertheless, it is apparent that some men make striking progress through many years and up to old age. The puzzling part of this to psychologists is that they have not been able to measure those qualities which make for success in mature life. It would seem

PSYCHOLOGY 

that abilities spread out over a wide area and there are many types of wisdom as well as many types of folly. Now, it is true that many bright men have had high IQ's in childhood. It is also true that many other successful men have not had such high IQ's. It might be safe to say that a man who has a high degree of superiority in all the nine factors which have been shown to operate in intelligence tests has a better chance of succeeding than one who has an inferior rating in all of them. It is probably true also that the specialized work of adult life may call for high proficiency in some one type of activity which may not play too big a part in an individual's general test rating, but which he finds extremely important in later life.

The interest of psychologists is now becoming centered in those features of adaptability which play a role in adjustment which are not primarily reflected in general intelligence test scores. 

Some of these have been called personality traits or personality factors. We shall investigate some of these in the last chapter.

Chapter V  WHY 

HY do people act as they do? Why is one man energetic while another is lazy? Why can one man be depended upon while another is completely untrustworthy? Why will a man spend years in an attempt to accumulate property? Why do some men kill their fellows? Why do some persons gamble? 

Why do some become addicted to the use of alcohol or morphine? 

Why are some aggressive and others submissive? The reasons for any act are always complex and are usually hidden from outside observers as well as from the one who is driven to act. 

We usually understand our own motives as vaguely as we understand the reasons for the behavior of others. Too often the reasons we assign for our own are incorrect or, at best, but partial explanations.

Elusive as human motives are, they provide the key to an understanding of conduct. Just as the solution of a mystery story depends upon a correct analysis of the motives of all persons concerned, so the interpretation of any simple act of human behavior depends upon the true evaluation of each factor influencing the individual in that act. 

Classification of motives. Motives have been classified in various ways: (a) According to whether they are inborn or acquired; (b) according to the degree of dependability they manifest, that is, the degree to which they can be counted upon to function consistently; (c) according to whether they are immediate or delayed in their effect; (d) according to whether they stimulate a person to increased activity or tend to thwart activity already in progress (rewards and punishments); or (e) whether they have their origin without the individual or are due to some internal set or attitude. 103

PSYCHOLOGY 

Some persons emphasize the condition or state of an individual which makes him ready to respond in a certain manner, whereas others think of a motive as a sort of trigger that sets him off. It should be clear that the individual needs to be set to respond, but he also needs the spark or immediate incitement to set him off. Before a gun is fired, it must be loaded; but the trigger must be pulled before the powder can do its work. It would be better to think of our problem in terms of a group of factors working together rather than to attempt to isolate one element as the essential factor.

Definitions. Perhaps adherence to the following usage of these terms would help us to avoid confusion: Let "motive" be a general term to indicate any dynamic element in the whole setting. Let "drive" refer to the readiness of the individual to perform. Let "incentive" refer to the stimulus which sets off the energy already stored in the individual. Let "goal" refer to the thing or external situation which, when reached or secured, is followed by a reduction or complete cessation of goal-seeking activity. For example, if a man were running a foot race, the physiological processes which enable him to run would be drives; incentives could be such factors as competitors and the supporters who watch the race; the tape at the end of the race, the cup to be awarded to the winner, or the good will of some friend could be the goal toward which the runner was aiming. 

Two other words need to be defined because of their almost universal use. The term "want" (or its synonyms: wish, desire, appetite, liking, craving, longing, etc.) indicates the tendency in a person to secure goals which may or may not be good for him. "Need" (or its synonyms: requirement, lack, shortcoming, insufficiency, etc.) indicates a judgment passed, whether by a person himself or by others, as to what would be good or beneficial for him. A person may or may not desire what he needs. He may or may not need what he desires. If a want or a need has a driving force that impels an individual to act in a certain manner, what the psychologist wants to know is why and how that force. acts. It is an insufficient explanation merely to say that he acted thus and so because he needed something or because he wanted something.

A DYNAMIC VIEW OF MOTIVATION 

Motives are active agents exerting an influence upon an organism which is already in active operation. The resultant must always be considered as due to the interaction of a number of dynamic components. An almost universal misconception needs to be corrected before we can even begin to understand the motivating factors in human life. Whether stated or not, most of us act as though we believed that man is naturally an inert mass who needs to be prodded, pushed, or stimulated in some manner to get him going. We lose sight of the fact that, before a man is stimulated, he is already living; and living is activity. 

The most powerful of all drives is the drive to live. It takes precedence over any motivating factor that can be applied from the outside. Living is not a simple process. It comprises a group of processes within the organism (such as the processes of metabolism, growth, reproduction, food storage, and excretion) which, by their co-ordinated operation, serve to maintain internal harmony in the individual. Break down the intricate balance between these processes and the individual dies. Hence, vital functions take precedence over everything else and nothing must be permitted to stop them or to change them too radically. This being so, the effect of a stimulus will depend upon what is going on within the individual at the moment, as well as upon the character of the stimulus. Food to a half-starved man is different from the same food given to a satiated one. 

Relation between simple drives and complex motives.

Simple action patterns are important driving forces which are often ignored as factors in human behavior. These may be patterns which were established before birth or at any stage during the life of the individual. However, these simple patterns never operate in isolation and it would be a mistake to attempt to explain a complicated act by reference to them alone. 

As we found in the Chapter III, careful observation of a newborn infant will reveal certain reactions which are fairly consistent, such as: the contraction of the pupil to light, the movement of the toes when the sole of the foot is stroked, withdrawal movements in response to a pinprick or other painful stimulus, muscular twitchings when a tendon is struck, a closing of the

PSYCHOLOGY 

hand when the palm is stimulated, a startle reaction when dropped or stimulated by a loud sound, sneezes, coughs, yawns, cries, struggles in response to restraint, restlessness in response to hunger or thirst.

In spite of the fact that such simple patterns are easily elicited in later life, and although some complex adult behavior may be traced to origins in these simpler forms, any attempt to explain mature behavior in terms of these simple patterns is misleading and of little value.

A simple illustration will make the issue stand out more sharply. Suppose we observe a man eating with his knife, and ask: "Why does he eat with his knife?" If we adhere to the method of explaining conduct by some primitive pattern or urge, we may attribute his conduct to the hunger impulse. Nevertheless, the cogent reason for this man's unconventional method of eating does not lie in the fact that he is gratifying his primitive hunger. He probably is eating because it is mealtime and not because he is particularly in need of nourishment; and he is eating with his knife because he learned to eat with his knife instead of with his fork. The essential explanatory factor in this situation is a simple process of learning and not a possible dynamic factor which led to that learning. He probably would never have eaten if he had not at some time been hungry; but he eats now and in a certain manner largely because of habit. 

The essential factor in motivation is the arousal of some sort of irritation or maladjustment. A condition of maladjustment leads to some sort of response by the individual. If he has some simple patterns of response readily available, he may make use of one or more of them. If such acts remove the irritation, he will probably relax again into relative quiescence. If his response does not deal adequately with the irritation, other acts will be tried. [21]

In other words, a motive is an irritation which the individual tries to remove. Most of the irritations of later life are complex and are not met by such simple things as putting food in the stomach, by contracting the pupil, by pulling back the arm, or the like. The flight of a bug into a street lamp on a summer's night may be explained by reference to a fixed and relatively simple action pattern; but the persistent study of a student through four

years of college cannot be explained in any such simple manner. 

Elementary drives are not absent in complex behavior; but they become less significant in the explanation of intricate acts. The student should know what these elementary patterns are, and how they function, but he should not let their simplicity tempt him to rely upon them as complete solutions to the problems of motivation.

The fact of the matter is that modern civilization has become so complicated that these elemental drives have been pushed into the background. In spite of the logical case that can be made for their importance, man is more extensively occupied with sensory comforts, social approvals, aesthetic satisfactions, strivings for security, and the like than with the satisfaction of primitive urges. 

We want food, of course, but we want it served in a particular manner; we want it to conform to certain tastes, and we want to eat in the company of approved friends. We want not only protection from the weather and from wild animals, but we want to have certain types of homes with arrangements for physical comfort. We are motivated more by the standards of decency which we have set up than we are by primitive appetites 

THE NEED FOR MAINTAINING BALANCE 

There are certain processes that are called vital processes which must carry on in proper fashion or an organism dies. We shall find, as we examine some of these, that they function without conscious control, and usually with remarkable precision. It is only when something gets out of adjustment that vital mechanisms come to the attention of an individual and cause him to modify his conduct.

As a tentative hypothesis we may say that ordinarily a person is not driven by an urge to live, to keep his vital processes in operation, or to maintain a balance between vital functions; instead, any marked deviation from a wholesome balance may become a driving force in behavior until a condition of relative safety is again reached. Neither does one ordinarily stay pivoted; rather, he sways backward and forward around an optimal center between limits of danger, beyond which he dare not pass. 

This balance in change has been given various names: unstable equilibrium, adaptive stabilization, comfortable constancy,

PSYCHOLOGY 

and homeostasis. [4] All these terms imply two essential elements; the ability to change or adapt, and the ability to avoid dangerous excesses. Whatever it is called, this "balance in change" is present in all forms of life. It is relatively simple in the lower forms and becomes more intricate as one progresses from plant life, through the lower animal state, up to human life. 

Age seems to affect the strength of the urge to maintain balance. The ideal of older persons seems to be to make life secure and immobile. Youth, on the other hand, is impatient with security. The sane life should be a compromise between mature caution and youthful rashness. Precipitate change is necessary in emergencies and is customary in youth; while prudence is customary in old age and gains the upper hand as life wanes. Rashness and indiscretion may carry with them the seeds of selfdestruction because of the excessive changes which they imply; but, on the other hand, excessive caution may end in stagnation. 

The end in either case is death. Death may come quickly to the foolhardy, slowly to the cautious; but it comes inevitably, in time, to both.

In spite of the certainty of eventual death, the living organism is constituted with safeguards to enable him to ward off threats of destruction. Some of our fundamental drives to activity are protective devices. On the other hand, much of our behavior is not so narrowly restricted in its value; we do many acts whose purpose is to make living pleasurable. Most of us not only want to live; in addition, we want to live pleasantly. 

A brief survey of some of the body's automatic adjustment devices may lend support to the hypothesis that maladjustment or imbalance is a stimulus to activity. We shall see that such maladjustments have the effect of making the individual do something. Whether he does the right thing is another matter. 

The need for a proper amount of water. It can be shown that conscious thirst is a poor index of the actual need of the body for water. In the case of an accident, where there is a severe loss of blood, thirst comes only as a secondary reaction. Before thirst has time to function, or before the person is aware of his need, the process of coagulation begins to stop up the wound, there is a constriction of the blood vessels near the wound which decreases the supply of blood for bleeding, and water is taken from

storage in various parts of the body and put into active service to replenish the loss. Thus, the vital functions of the body are supplied with water in spite of the loss occasioned by bleeding. If such adjustments depended upon conscious control, most of us would be dead before now.

Thirst functions in a more leisurely manner to motivate the individual to replenish his depleted stores. Nevertheless, one may need water without being thirsty and he may be thirsty without needing water. For example, thirst can be produced by causing the mouth to become dry even though there may be no diminution of the general amount of water in the body. Other experiments have shown that a diminution of water in the body does not cause thirst if the mouth can retain its moisture. Nevertheless, under ordinary circumstances, a dry mouth does provide a signal of water need.

With lower animals, thirst can become a powerful drive to make the animal engage in violent activity, to overcome barriers, and to take punishment in order to alleviate his thirst. The thirsty human being, on the contrary, is likely to be exacting in his choice of liquids. He wants them to be the right temperature, mixed to suit his taste, and served in the conventional manner. A man would have to be parched with thirst before he would drink filthy water from the gutter. In ordinary civilized life, the only type of thirst that motivates individuals is the highly sophisticated thirst for artificial drinks.

The need for a normal supply of salt. Human beings are seldom aware of the need for a balanced supply of salt in the body. This arises from the fact that foods ordinarily contain enough salt to supply all bodily needs and the body stores salt so that the proper amount can be doled out as it is needed. It is only when some unusual circumstance arises that salt imbalance becomes a driving force. It is seen as such a force in animals. If an animal takes too much salt, it develops salt fever. If it is deprived of salt to an extreme degree, it will develop salt hunger. 

Animals will travel long distances to reach salt licks in order to supply this need and gratify their hunger for salt. 

Maintaining a balanced supply of oxygen. Experimental work with animals has demonstrated clearly that the breathing of the newborn animal is caused by oxygen need. In one experi-

PSYCHOLOGY 

ment, sheep embryos were kept alive in saline solution while still attached to the mother by the umbilical cord. While the period of gestation of sheep is 147 days, the movements of the diaphragm that occur with breathing could be induced as early as the 39th day by pinching the umbilical cord and thus cutting off the supply of oxygen. After the animal had begun to breathe by this means, it stopped breathing when oxygen was supplied by an injection of blood from the mother. This experiment indicates that breathing is the direct consequence of oxygen lack. [1]

Throughout life the adequacy of supply of oxygen is achieved by adjusting the speed and depth of breathing to the needs of the body. However, a complication arises from the fact that the breathing of man is not flexible enough to meet the widely changing demands made upon him. The oxygen requirement of a man of average size, while at rest, is about a quarter to a third of a liter a minute. When he exerts himself violently, he may need 

15 liters a minute. The most he can take in is four liters a minute. In other words, although he takes in 12 to 16 times as much oxygen during exercise as during rest, he may still be getting only a fourth as much as he needs. There is no storage of oxygen in the body to meet such an emergency requirement; so the adjustment is made in another way. The work that the oxygen needs to do is permitted to accumulate, to be done at a later time. 

The body takes on an "oxygen debt." This debt is in the form of an accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles which the oxygen taken in later will be required to burn to carbon dioxide. If the debt becomes too large, that is, if too much lactic acid accumulates, fatigue sets in, the muscular contractions become slower and less efficient and finally stop altogether. [4] 

It is clear that the regulation of oxygen supply is almost entirely out of conscious control. It is too vital a need to be trusted to human guidance.

One hates to contemplate what would happen if all the vital adjustments of the body depended upon conscious control and direction. Man brags that he is master of his fate, but this survey of a few adjustment devices should convince the reader that he does not control those adjustments which are essential to survival. 

The only aspects of life that man is permitted to control are those

which are less essential and which will permit a wider range of error without serious consequences.

HORMONES AS DEVICES FOR MAINTAINING BALANCE 

A hormone is a specific organic substance formed by the cells of one organ and passed from that organ through the blood or lymph to other organs, upon which it produces characteristic effects. Most of the hormones are produced in glands which have no ducts, but which discharge them directly into the blood. These ductless glands are called endocrine glands and the secretions which they produce are sometimes called endocrine secretions. These secretions play a large part in physical and mental growth, in bodily form, in mental alertness, and in the production of personality characteristics. [8, 11]

With a proper balance of hormones functioning in an individual, he has a good chance of developing into a normal person; but if some of the hormones are absent, or lacking in balance with others, the most grotesque results may occur. Persons with endoerine imbalances formerly provided most of the freaks for the amusement of royalty and circusgoers; whereas now they are being studied and many of them are being made into normal individuals by means of hormonic therapy. Even where the hormonic lack is not so striking as to cause bodily malformations and extreme mental aberrations, it is becoming more and more evident that the endocrine glands provide much of the driving force that makes an individual into the kind of person that he is. The psychologist is most concerned with the pituitary, the thyroid, the adrenals, and the sex glands. 

The pituitary. The pituitary gland is located at the base of the brain. It secretes a number of hormones with different functions. One of these hormones affects bony growth, one influences sex development, one affects sex activity, one modifies the production of fat, and others play a part in controlling the general tension of the body. 

The thyroid. The thyroid gland consists of two lobes situated one on each side of the larynx and upper windpipe. It produces a secretion, containing iodine in chemical combination with other elements, called thyroxin.

Excessive thyroxin will lead to increased heart rate, a rise

PSYCHOLOGY 

in the metabolic rate, an increase of sugar in the blood, a loss of fat, increased oxygen consumption, an increase of water in the body, an increase in bodily heat, and the stimulation of sexual maturation. It is generally agreed that the thyroid is the most important regulator of the basal metabolic rate of an individual, and consequently of his level of general activity. [18] 

The adrenal glands. The adrenal glands are paired glands located adjacent to the upper part of the kidneys. Each gland consists of two distinct parts: (1) an internal medulla, which yields adrenalin and (2) an external layer, or cortex, which yields a hormone necessary for life, called cortin. 

Adrenalin circulates in the blood stream in a quantity just sufficient to maintain normal blood pressure and to reinforce the blood supply in times of need. It plays an important part in emotional activity and is essentially the emergency hormone. 

Cortin, the hormone from the outer layer of the adrenals, plays an important part in regulating body tensions. When the adrenal cortex of an animal is removed, a definite train of symptoms follows: These are easy fatigue, loss of appetite, loss of interest, irritability, twitching, convulsions, and death. When animals from which the adrenal cortex has been removed are treated with cortin, these symptoms (except death) disappear in reverse order. [9]

When rats were experimentally subjected to excessive physical exercise, an overdevelopment of the adrenal cortex resulted. 

Also, the administration of cortin enhances the work capacity of an animal. When the adrenal cortex was removed from hibernating ground hogs, they lived through the period of hibernation in apparent good health. In early spring, when they renewed their customary activity, death occurred with the typical symptoms of adrenal cortex insufficiency. [2]

Another worker found that exposure of animals to cold, subjecting them to excessive muscular exercise, or giving them doses of poisonous drugs led to an overdevelopment of the adrenal cortex, suggesting an overstimulation of this organ in the attempt by the animal to meet these damaging stimuli. Furthermore, he found that animals who had been thus trained to adapt to these harmful situations would continue to adapt fairly well after the adrenal cortex was removed by operation; whereas other animals

who had not been trained, and whose adrenal cortexes had not been overdeveloped, died as a result of equal exposure to cold, excessive exercise, or to poisoning. [9] 

These experiments suggest that the adrenal gland functions as an instrument, which enables the organism to meet extraordinary difficulties; that it performs this function by working harder itself; and that it thereby causes extra resistance by the organism to these damaging stimuli so that it can carry on after the adrenals have been removed and can no longer help. [20] The adrenals apparently are more active in emergency situations than in regu lating activity in normal conditions. When we come to study emotions (Chapter VII) we shall see that both the thyroid gland and the adrenals play important roles.

The sex glands. A number of hormones are involved in the complicated activities of sexual development and reproduction. 

The pituitary gland secretes hormones which are essential for the process of maturation. The hormones from the thyroid play an important part in stimulating sexual maturation and activity. The cortex of the adrenal glands produces hormones which are essential in the development of secondary sexual characteristics, such as the distribution of hair, voice changes, and the like. On the other hand, the gonads produce sex cells which carry on the process of reproduction. Hormones from all these glands interact to produce a balancing of these intricate functions. 

Maldevelopments of the gonads may lead to significant changes in physical development and in psychological behavior. 

If there is an overdevelopment of the primary sex glands, there may be precocious maturation and an exaggerated sex urge. If there is an excessive development of the adrenal cortex, there may be premature pubescence, and the presence of secondary male characteristics in girls. On the other side, lack of gonad development in the immature person leads to underdevelopment of the musculature, striking alterations of primary and secondary sex characteristics at adolescence, slender build, and overdevelopment of the long bones. If the failure of gonad function begins in later life (principally after thirty), it produces adipose tissue. 

Hence, the sex drive depends upon the proper development and functioning of the pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, and sex glands. 

In the animal world, where sex behavior is not complicated by

PSYCHOLOGY 

conventional patterns, these structures and their secretions play the dominant, and almost exclusive role in the sexual drive. On the contrary, in the human species, sexual activities are by no means so simply explained. The child's sexual behavior is determined not so much by the glands of internal secretion as by the teaching of his elders. He is made conscious of his sex from the first by the emphasis given to it. He must act differently, must dress differently, and his behavior toward the other sex is made so complex by these insistent teachings that, when he comes to the age of adolescence, most of his sexual behavior patterns are established and the physical aspects play a relatively unimportant part. 

MEASUREMENTS OF THE RELATIVE STRENGTH OF DRIVES 

Psychologists have devoted much time and have exercised great ingenuity in their attempts to measure the relative strength of animal drives.

Description of methods. We shall describe briefly five of the most common methods that they have used. 

1. The obstruction method. The obstruction method is based upon the logical assumption that the stronger drives will be able to overcome more resistance, or opposition, than the weaker drives. Stimulate a drive, oppose its operation by means of a measurable obstacle, and the strength of the drive can be expressed in terms of the size of the resistance that the animal will overcome in giving play to the drive. So the argument runs. 

The customary experimental setting evolved from this reasoning is as follows: The animal is placed in a compartment and stimulated to move to another compartment in order to get to some desired object, such as food, an animal of the other sex, water, offspring, or freedom. The usual barrier between the animal and the goal is a metal grid, which is connected with a source of electrical current and may be charged with a current of varying strength. As soon as the animal touches this grid, he will experience an electric shock which can be varied by changing the strength of the current. The strength of the urge to get to the desired goal may then be measured either by the amount of punishment he will take, or by counting the number of times he will attempt to cross the grid. The general plan for one such obstruction apparatus is shown in Fig. 17. [24]

2. The free choice method. If an animal is confronted with the possibility of selecting with equal ease any one of a number of alternate objects or goals, it may be inferred that he will select the one that is most satisfying to him. 

This method has been used by placing the animal in a starting box and permitting him to choose between various kinds of food, between food and a mate, between food and free exploration, between a mate and freedom, and the like. This same method has been adapted for use in studying various preferences of children and adult human beings as well as animals. Interests, attitudes, d2 FIG. 17.-Obstruction apparatus used in measuring the strength of drives. A, entrance compartment; B, wires which can be charged with electrical current and punish animal which steps upon them; d₁, manually operated door between entrance compartment and punishment grid; E, plate which automatically makes an electrical connection when animal steps on it and thus opens door de; C and D, incentive compartments. (From T. N. Jenkins, L. H. Warner, and C. J. Warden, "Standard Apparatus for the study of animal motivation," J. comp. Psychol., 1926, 6, 366.) food preferences, moral opinions, religious preferences, vocational interests, advertising displays, racial prejudices and numerous motivating factors can be evaluated by means of the free choice method.

A practical everyday application of this method is seen in the buying and selling activities of human beings. If a man wants an object more than he does the money it will take to buy the object (providing he has the money or the credit), he will buy. 

If he values his money more highly than the product, he will not buy. Much trading activity and advertising is based on an attempt to change the urges of the other person. A man's evaluation of any element in life can be determined by the price he will pay for

PSYCHOLOGY 

it, in terms of money, sacrifice, other commodities, prestige, or the like. 

3. Comparison of the effects of different incentives on behavior. In this method the tasks assigned to an individual are equated as nearly as possible and the effect of each different incentive upon the efficiency of performance is measured. 

A task may be assigned to an animal (such as getting out of a maze) and he may be stimulated at one time by the offer of food, at another time by the offer of a drink, at another time by a mate, or at another with freedom. If all other factors are kept

4. Shifting motivating factors during activity. Valuable information concerning the force of a drive may be gathered by changing the motivating influence during the course of a work period, or during a learning experiment. If the introduction of a different motive retards or accelerates activity or learning, such a change may denote a significant difference in the force of the different drives involved. 1

Results from measuring the relative strength of drives.

The most clear-cut results from comparing the relative strength of drives has been done by means of the obstruction method with white rats. [16, 24]

The strength of the maternal drive was measured by taking a mother rat from her litter and making it necessary for her to cross a punishment grid in order to reach her young. The number of times she would cross the grid and take the punishment was used as a measure of the strength of the drive. The drive to obtain food was measured by counting the number of times the rat would take the punishment to obtain food after a fast of from two to four days. The sex drive was determined by placing a mate beyond the punishment grid. In similar fashion the other drives were measured. The results are given in Table IV.

For example, when a rat is placed in new surroundings, he will forgo either food or sex until he has first thoroughly explored the place. When an animal is intensely interested in his mate, he has little interest in food; and when he is hungry, and in the presence of food, he is little concerned with his mate. Making due allowance for incidental factors, it is revealing to know that the drives come out in the order given in the table. 

Even when an animal is not stimulated from the outside by any particular situation, and is not impelled by the presence of any specific incentive, he manifests a tendency to engage in a certain amount of motor activity. A rat in an activity cage will spend a good share of his time running in the wheel rather than sitting quietly in the stationary compartment. As we have pointed out before, living is essentially activity, and so it is reasonable that the living animal should manifest an urge to be active. 

It also has been found that thwarting will intensify an elementary drive. In fact, thwarting is effective in practically all levels of animal and human adjustments. If an animal is placed in a puzzle box, such as the one shown in Fig. 20, he needs no incentive to activity except a realization of the fact that he is.

unable to get out freely. Should he be slipped into the box when he is asleep, or is unaware that he is locked in, he will manifest no struggle. Let him attempt to get out and fail to do so, and his efforts will be stimulated by the thwarting. Hold a cat's tail in such a manner that he interprets it as mere petting, and he will offer no resistance; but let him feel a little tug on it, and he will fight to get loose. A newborn child will fight if his free movements are hampered. The most prized possessions of an adult are the things for which he had to strive, which did not come too easily.

ANALYSIS OF SOME TYPICAL DRIVES 

It is instructive to examine some of the components in drives which seem to be relatively simple, and to analyze some complex types of activity in which they play a dominant role. 

The maternal drive. The maternal drive, as measured by the obstruction test, may be regarded as the urge to take care of the young. It should not be confused with a desire to have children. There is no evidence for the latter desire in lower animals. 

The widespread desire for children by human beings is regarded by most writers as the result of cultural factors and not of any inherent drive in women. [10] 

Various theories have been advanced to explain the desire to care for children. One is that the mother desires the young because of the discomfort she experiences when the mammary glands become congested. Such a theory probably explains the frequent instances in which an animal will take care of and suckle an infant of another species. Having once cared for an infant, the mother usually shows the same solicitude for the adopted child that she would for her own. [25] This theory would not hold for nonmammals, such as birds. 

Another theory explains maternal behavior on the basis of internal secretions. An interesting experiment gives support to this point of view. A hormone extracted from the pituitary gland, known as prolactin, when injected into an animal will bring about behavior in that animal which is ordinarily described as maternal behavior. For example, such an injection will cause a virgin rat to manifest interest in young, it will cause broodiness in hens, and will make a male rat take interest in making nests for

young rats, in caring for them, and in licking them in a motherly way. [14, 19]

In human society, any such elementary drives are certainly modified, reinforced, or counteracted by many other considerations. It is, for example, conceivable that the encouragement which a little girl receives to play with dolls may affect her maternal behavior in later life. The hunger drive. Experiments have shown that hunger pangs are associated with the periodic contractions of the stomach walls. [3] These experiments were performed as follows: The subject swallowed a balloon made of very thin rubber and attached to a small rubber tube. The other end of this tube was connected with a recording device and the whole system inflated so that the balloon in the stomach would respond accurately to any movement of the walls of the stomach. A graphic record was thus made of the stomach contractions (see Fig. 21).

Are these stomach contractions dependent upon the need for food? There is evidence for both a positive and a negative answer to this question. When a small quantity of blood was taken

PSYCHOLOGY 

from a starving dog and injected into the body of a dog which had just finished a meal, the latter jumped up and started eating again. This seems to indicate that some condition in the blood is what causes the contractions. On the other hand, the contractions may be stopped by chewing and temporarily by swallowing. 

They may be slowed or stopped by strong emotions, by tobacco, by alcoholic beverages, by vigorous muscular exercise, and by strong tightening of an abdominal belt. The effectiveness of these conditions cannot be explained by reference to a change in the need of the body for blood sugar. However, such negative evidence does not disprove the theory that blood sugar deficiency is a major cause of hunger contractions of the stomach. These circumstances may be merely interferences which prevent the stomach from responding to blood sugar need. [5]

Furthermore, it is clear that physiological hunger is not related in any simple manner to conscious hunger or appetite. The amount of punishment that an animal will take in order to obtain food is not directly correlated with the degree of need of the tissues for nutriment. Animals were deprived of food for increasingly long periods until death from starvation resulted.

From the beginning of the period up to about four or five days the animals would take more and more punishment from an electric grid interposed between them and the food. From that point on to the period of death, there was a decline in the amount of punishment they would take to get to the food. It is probable that with increasing need there was also increased physical weakness, more fear of the grid, and less ability to tolerate unpleasant shocks. Initial hunger may be stimulating, prolonged hunger is likely to be debilitating.

We may still have an appetite after our hunger has been satisfied. If this were not so the phenomenon of overeating would not be so common. Experimental work with animals has confirmed this statement. It has been found that the amount of grain which a hen will eat is increased by enlarging the size of the pile from which she eats. When a hen has been permitted to eat all the grain that she can apparently consume from a large pile of grain, and another hungry hen is then placed with her and begins to eat, the first, or apparently satisfied, hen will jump up and renew her eating. When, however, several hens have eaten

to satiety and a hungry hen is then placed with them, the fed hens will not renew their eating. It would seem that it is the majority influence which counts with these animals and not the mere suggestion given by one eating animal. [13, p. 152] 

Relation between hunger and appetite. Man is equipped with no devices which impel him to eat the foods he needs; nor does he have any natural appetite which will ensure that he selects a balanced diet. Nevertheless, he does have a crude sort of hunger which makes him restless and this agitation incites him to perform acts which may eventually satisfy his needs and develop in him a serviceable set of appetites. 律 ​In some cases, individuals have been known to develop a keen appetite for substances which do supply a need of the organism. Rats whose parathyroid glands had been removed, thus causing a calcium deficiency, showed a definite increase in their appetite for calcium. Rats whose diet was markedly deficient in vitamin B₁ selected, by both taste and smell, solutions in which there was a large amount of this vitamin and drank large quantities of it. [17] Diabetic patients, whose sugar metabolism is out of joint, will develop an intense craving for sweets, in spite of the fact that the eating of sugar is harmful for them. 

How can a person develop such appetites? We have no definite experimental evidence on this point, but we may imagine a hypothetical situation in which such appetites could conceivably develop. For example, let us suppose that an individual, who is too lacking in training to have developed a salt hunger, has a genuine need for salt. His need may make him uncomfortable even though he does not know why he is unable to remain calm. 

He may be stimulated, because of this discomfort, to get up, move around, to make noises, wave his arms, drink, eat, tease someone, or to do any of a number of acts. Suppose that, in the course of these activities, he eats something containing salt. As a result he will feel better, and his agitation will decrease. When he next feels a similar need he may go through a similar series of random activities before he again becomes satisfied; but in time he may learn that eating is usually followed by relief from his discomfort and, further, that eating foods with a certain taste (saltiness) will bring about this relief quicker than foods which do not taste salty. This method of learning is called random learning or trial-

PSYCHOLOGY 

and-error learning. We shall encounter it again in different connections.

Suppose, on the other hand, that as a result of the restlessness caused by salt hunger our subject was stimulated to eat some ipecac (an emetic drug) and became nauseated as a result. It would not take him long to learn to avoid ipecac. In other words, the agitation brought about by a common cause-salt hunger in this case-might teach an individual to seek salt or it might teach him to avoid ipecac. It is evident, however, that the hunger was not the sole cause, or even the most important factor, in learning either the appetite for salt or the aversion for ipecac. The essential factor in each case was the experiences that the individual went through during the process of learning. Without the hunger drive he probably would not have learned, but with the drive and no expérience he would not have learned either. 

An experiment in infant feeding demonstrates' clearly the workings of this type of learning. [6] Newly weaned children were presented with an array of foods and were permitted to eat any or all the foods with perfect freedom. It was found that they ate heartily and selected foods which nourished them properly. It was often evident that they did not know at first which foods to eat for they often temporarily had an unbalanced diet. 

At times they showed a tendency to eat excessively of one food or another, but they soon evened off to a temperate amount of that food. These periodic spells of taking an excess of one food the experimenters called food jags-egg jags, meat jags, cereal jags, etc.

Similar experiments have been conducted with pigs, cows, chickens, rats, and mice. [15] Give a child or an animal a wide selection of foods and he will tend to learn to eat those which nourish him properly. After such learning, appetites and aversions may become reliable guides in the selection of diets. Nevertheless, we must not lose sight of the fact that many appetites and aversions have no relation to bodily needs and, for this reason, blind faith in appetites and aversions is not warranted. [7] 

In the development of appetites, more is to be considered than the mere satisfaction of an organic need. The child soon encounters all sorts of social traditions, prejudices on the part of elders and other children, and fears of an unbalanced diet on the part

of doctors and mothers, with consequent pressures and restraints. 

Eating becomes mixed with all sorts of restrictions as to the time of eating, table manners, scoldings, teasings, reprimands because of accidents with dishes, and the like. A child may hate a certain food merely because his father scolded him for spilling some of it on his new suit. The persistent and violent food aversions for certain foods which may be found in most adults are probably based on childhood experiences which parents regarded as trivial at the time. Not only may a child's enjoyment of mushroom soup be spoiled by a scolding for breaking the window next door, but the grown-up child's enjoyment of a meal served years later may be marred because the meal is begun with mushroom soup. In short, social and aesthetic factors greatly modify the hunger impulse in human beings. It makes a difference who is present, how the food is served, and what conversation goes with the eating. 

The driving force of routine and habit. Each organism, after a certain amount of familiarization with any type of activity, tends to settle into a pace which it characteristically uses for that activity. A great many elements may be thought of as contributing originally to the establishment of this pace; but it tends to be maintained, regardless of its origin, in spite of circumstances that might be expected to change it. For example, a person will tend to walk at the same rate uphill and down although different amounts of energy are required in accordance with the terrain over which he is walking.

This principle can easily be tested by setting a person at a totally new activity. He will work at different speeds until he gets his bearings and then will settle into a pace which seems to please him, after which he will tend to maintain it. The longer he uses that pace on a specific task the greater will be his tendency to resist any influence designed to change it. The tendency to maintain such a customary pace may become a powerful motivating factor.

Specific habits are even more effective as determiners of behavior. An illustration may be seen in the morphine habit. Continued use of this drug causes an individual to develop a need for it that is extremely powerful. Once having developed the morphine habit, a deprivation gives rise to hunger pangs which cause the victim extréme agony and even death. The effects of mor-

PSYCHOLOGY 

phine hunger upon various aspects of the individual's life are farreaching and tremendously powerful; he will lie, steal, and even commit murder to get morphine.

To be sure, most habits have no such dominant influence upon a person but, to a lesser degree, they do provide an important directive influence which cannot be ignored. A child, who has acquired the habit of going to sleep with a doll or a Teddybear in his arms, will have difficulty in relaxing if these companions are missing when he goes to bed. The mere fact that we are doing something makes us resent any interference with that activity. Our zeal for repeating customary procedures may not make sense; but we will still fight to continue such routines. 

The striving for rewards and the avoiding of punishments are largely habitual. It has been the custom for certain persons to attempt to attribute the dynamic force of rewards to efforts on the part of an individual to supply the needs for food, shelter, warmth, and the like; and the restraining force of punishments to the attempt to avoid starvation, cold, disease, and the like. Such factors may operate in a primitive civilization, but certainly in modern life a man's wages are spent for things he has learned to crave rather than for basic needs. He spends his money to buy food prepared and served in the approved way, to wear the clothes that others wear rather than to keep his body warm, to buy a car, to live in a fine house. We do not work to keep the wolf from the door so much as to keep the door open to people whose criticism we must avoid.
