Chapter VI SOCIAL MOTIVES 

THER persons may influence our behavior in a number of ways. (a) We act differently when other persons are present. (b) There are emotional interactions between individuals which modify the actions of all concerned. (c) Working together affects members of a group enterprise through such factors as competition and co-operation. (d) Direct pressure may be brought by one individual upon others through personal domination, leadership, suggestion, and competition. (e) Finally, each person is influenced in a striking manner by the customs and culture of the society into which he is thrown. 

THE EFFECTS OF BEING OBSERVED 

When we are alone we do not act in the same manner as we do when we are being observed. We have curtains on our windows to shut out the curious eyes of others in order that we may feel free to do as we please. The effect of being observed increases when we believe that the observers are critical or hostile. 

Even though our behavior may be circumspect, such observation makes us uncomfortable and, if we have some difficult task to perform, we may lose all self-control and be forced to stop our activities altogether. Stage fright is an illustration of the effect of such discomfiture.

Experiments have shown that an individual, when he is being observed, will work more rapidly than he will when working alone, but his work is likely to be of an inferior quality. [1, p. 269] Other experiments indicate that group situations make individuals work toward the group average. Persons who are better than the average when alone, do poorer work in a group situation; whereas those who do poor work when alone, improve 129

PSYCHOLOGY 

in the group. [7, p. 336] However, even though individuals tend to conform to a group average when they work together, the group is nevertheless a stimulus; for the group average is higher than the average of the performances of the individuals who make up the group when these same persons work alone. [7, p. 339] 

None of these experiments were conducted under situations where competition or group pressure of any sort was present. 

It would seem that individuals try to make a good showing when others are around. What happens when they become convinced that they are not making a favorable impression on those who observe them? Razzing is used in a baseball game to impair the skill of a pitcher. Does it affect other types of performance? 

One experiment attempted to answer this question by having subjects "razzed" as they worked. It indicated that razzing causes an improvement in tasks involving speed, whereas the steadiness or skill of a performance may be injured by razzing. [8] The conclusion seems to be that others make us self-conscious. This self-consciousness does not slow us down in motor acts. Instead, we are inclined to speed up. For example, we talk faster when we are confused than when we are calm. On the other hand, self-consciousness tends to interfere with motor control and deliberate thought. We become unstable, jittery, and jump to a conclusion which calm thought would tell us was unsound.

MOTIVATING FORCE OF LOVES AND HATES 

The most powerful social motives known to man are probably the loves and hates of human beings. The strange part of this situation is that psychology has little to say about these forces; romantic literature has much more to contribute than does psychology. The probable reason for this situation lies in the fact that these emotions are not easily subject to scientific experimentation. In the realm of clinical psychology, it has been found that many pathological conditions are centered in these emotions. 

These studies are all anecdotal in nature and are more akin to literature than to scientific experiment. These case histories have aroused much speculation and many hypotheses have been advanced which may, sooner or later, be subjected to the rigorous

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

131 tests of science. Until that time arrives, all we can do is to give a brief account of the probable manner in which these emotions act as motives in human life. 

Love is a feeling of well-being which comes about as the result of pleasing interaction with another person. Hate is an unpleasant feeling which results from real or fancied mistreatment by another. Neither of these emotions is inborn. They depend upon learning. We can be sure of this even though we may not be able to demonstrate such learning in the psychological laboratory.

The first love of a child is usually for the person who feeds him. His hunger makes him uncomfortable and he becomes restless as a result of this discomfort. If a certain person is the customary attendant when this discomfort is removed, he comes to respond favorably to this person as a result of this learning. 

The principle is the same as the one which operates when one feeds a stray cat. When the cat gets hungry again, he will return for more food. The child cannot return, but he can make positive reactions toward the one who fed him. The onlooker calls the behavior, of either the child or the cat, love. 

This is not meant to imply that feeding is the only way to produce a love reaction in a tiny child. It is merely an illustration of the way in which any alleviation of discomfort may produce such behavior on the part of the child. One psychologist [13, p. 

72] has contended that the only stimulus which will bring out a love response in a child at birth is touching or stroking the skin of the infant. The important factor is not what stimulus will cause such positive responses, but that they are always the result of stimuli which produce satisfaction in the child. The multiplication of a variety of situations in which the child is made comfortable by the same person produces a fixed habit of loving that person.

Hates are developed in a similar manner; the essential difference is that the hated object is the repeated means for making the child uncomfortable and unhappy.

Although a love or a hate is a specific reaction developed in connection with certain individuals, it may easily transfer to others. We love on sight a person whom we class in the same category as one we already love. Sometimes the classification is based

PSYCHOLOGY 

on some trivial factor, such as the color of the hair, the tone of the voice, the nationality, some chance word spoken, or the like. 

Furthermore, the individual often does not know why he reacts as he does and is inclined to explain it upon some apparent reason that is not the significant one. For example, it was found that a little boy hated his teacher, explaining that he did so because she was unfair to another boy. Investigation showed that his hatred was based on the fact that she looked very much like a maid whom he hated because of her mistreatment of him.

As we proceed with our study of the ways in which social motives operate, we should keep in mind that the forces of love and hate form a background of many of our social interactions even though they are covered by habit, convention, and a conscious attempt to disguise them. We do not know enough about them to evaluate them in any specific situation, but we all have enough common knowledge of human life to be aware of their presence. 

COMPETITION 

A prominent aspect of our civilization is the competition for prestige which may be defined as the aggressive enhancement of one's own ego at the expense of that of another. From very early life a great deal of pressure toward achievement is put upon all individuals. The child who fails to respond to this pressure by the development of ambition is regarded unfavorably by his teachers, parents, and comrades.

If efforts toward attainment are thwarted only by objective difficulties, the energies of the child are directed toward overcoming them; but seldom is there any striking feeling of resentment or hate toward such barriers. What does often result is a profound regard for work as a means for acquiring fame or success. 

The teacher and parent seem intent on getting more and more work from the child, he learns to discipline himself and looks upon his tireless exertion as a step in the right direction. Should he discover that his efforts are too slow or ineffective, he may learn the trick of exploiting others, getting them to work for him in such manner that, while they get some reward, he gets the lion's share. Teachers often encourage such exploitation as a manifestation of executive ability.

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

133 Means for inciting personal competition. In order to induce a child to compete, it must be made clear that the gaining of the reward is dependent not on how well he performs, but on whether he performs better than another. He may do his best and even do better than he ever did before but, if another does better than he does, he loses. The winner thereby becomes the one who deprives him of his objective. Were it not for the better man, he would win. There is little doubt that efficiency of performance is enhanced by such means, but some unfortunate social consequences also arise. The winner comes to gloat over the failure of his competitor. He may be encouraged to be generous with the loser, but his generosity becomes a sort of specious condescension, which aggravates the discomfiture of the loser. The loser is told to be a good sport, but most often he comes to hate his rival. We talk idly about being good losers, but the objective is to win.

If too much is done to mitigate the sting of failure, the stimulating influence of competition is lost. For example, one young man was heard to remark that he ruined his golf game one summer because he had devoted all his efforts toward pretending to do his best while seeing to it that his boss won. 

Jealousy and hate. The social attitude which grows from a competitive situation is jealousy of, and hate for, one's successful rival. This is merely another way of saying that jealousy springs from a background of personal comparisons. In an open contest the comparison is overt and easily recognized. In other situations the comparisons are more subtle. When a mother praises one child, for example, she may not think she is making a comparison of the praised child with the other, but such a comparison is implied.

Jealousy by children manifests itself in various ways. The jealous child may make bodily attacks upon the hated rival. He may ignore the presence of the other, or even deny his existence. 

Or, he may show no outward manifestation of jealousy or antagonism but develop a change in personality. For example, he may become a pouter, become delinquent in his behavior, become irritable, fail in his studies, and so on. The jealous child is likely to show, in addition to jealousy, one or more of the following characteristics: pugnacity, selfishness, overactivity, destructiveness,

PSYCHOLOGY 

troubled sleep, persistent bed-wetting, independence, and a craving for attention. The common factor that is behind all other manifestations, however, is hate for the rival who is presumed to be detracting from his prestige. 

There are a number of factors that have been found to affect jealousy in young children. When siblings are from 18 to 42 months apart in age there is more likely to be jealousy than when the age difference is greater or less. As the number of children in a family increases, the proportion of jealous children decreases markedly with each increase in number. Jealousy decreases as the family income increases. Oversolicitous parents are more likely to have jealous children than are others who are more easygoing. Jealousy increases with marital discord. All these factors have the common factor of making personal comparisons easier and personal rivalry more acute. [11] 

So long as a person feels that there is a possibility of outdoing a rival he may be stimulated by personal comparisons to work harder, even though he may hate his rival in the meantime. 

When prestige is lowered to an unusual degree even the incentive to compete may be lost. For example, it has been found that public reprimands, sarcasm, and ridicule cause the performance of children to deteriorate. There is little doubt that jealousies instigated by personal comparisons serve to arouse an individual to a high pitch of emotional tension and spur him on to his maximum effort; but the individual, class, and national hatreds which probably grow out of, or at least are accentuated by, personal hatreds cost exceedingly more than the increased efficiency produced by personal competition. [3, p. 83] 

Co-operation. Although much has been said about co-operation, we know relatively little about it from observation, statistical studies, or experiment. Time samples of the behavior of children from 25 to 60 months of age during free play reveals that there are frequent quarrels lasting on the average for about 23 seconds. Within this age range there are fewer quarrels as the children become older but those that do occur last longer. The majority of these quarrels begin as a struggle for possession of some article.

As children grow older they make more contacts with children of their own age and fewer with older persons. There does

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

135 seem to be some increase in sympathetic reactions between children. as they grow older. These are accentuated if the child is permitted to have an animal for a pet. At an early age children tend to warm up to those children who are compliant in their behavior, who seem to attempt to act in ways that the others approve, and who have respect for property rights; they withdraw from those who fight, who refuse to fight if they are attacked, who dawdle, or who prefer to remain aloof and play alone. 

It has been found that when a prize is offered to a group for good work, this motivation will induce them to work together to improve their score. The same improvement may be seen when one group is pitted in competition against another group. Those who have reported these experiments have been more concerned with efficiency than with the attitudes of friendship or co-operation engendered by such mass competition. The child who refuses to join in such activity is regarded as an enemy of the group and he is forced to join or suffer loss of prestige. [3, p. 82] 

AGGRESSION 

The term "aggression" has been given different meanings, and investigations of aggressive behavior have taken different directions depending upon the definition adopted by the investigator.

Definitions of aggression. Aggression has been used to designate the characteristic behavior of a person who tends to take the initiative as contrasted with the individual who habitually lacks initiative. In this sense, aggressiveness is usually regarded as wholesome and teachers and parents are likely to encourage it. It is merely the expression of animal vigor and denotes health and vitality. On the other hand, aggression may be the expression of acts of retaliation by a weak individual for a real or fancied wrong. It is a kickback against thwarting. This latter type of aggression has the greatest social significance. [3] 

Analysis of aggression. The important factor to consider in studying aggression is the attitude or motivating element in the individual who manifests the aggressive activity. Up to a certain point the overt activities may be quite similar and the motive behind the acts are the only distinguishing elements. In extreme

PSYCHOLOGY 

form the two types (the wholesome expression of animal vigor and the compensation of the weakling against thwarting) part company and can be more easily differentiated. Because this distinction between the motives behind aggression is not given due credit by those who instruct young children a great deal of confusion surrounds their instruction in competition in sports and other activities.

Some contend that competition is bad and point out the fact that in some sheltered situations it does not exist. For example, a study of Hopi children showed that it was normal and universal for them to show self-depreciatory attitudes. The ambition to distinguish oneself or to get ahead was absent. The children refused to engage in competitive enterprises and tended to praise the work of others rather than to look for approval for their own. [7, p. 106] 

Others place so much emphasis upon winning that a child is made to feel intense humiliation if he does not win. To be sure, the advocates of intense competition do not stress the need for humiliating the loser. In fact, they call attention to the need for teaching a child to accept defeat and talk much about the nobility of the boy who is a "good loser." At the same time the urgings to win, the setting of high rewards for the winner, the turmoil made about who will win is so intense that the child must win or feel deep chagrin. If all frustrations which a person encounters were due to nonhuman interferences, aggression would never lead to conflicts between individuals. It happens, on the contrary, that most of the difficulties of living arise because others get in our way. It is more often a person than an inanimate object that stands between us and our goals. 

To add to the confusion there is an extreme amount of inconsistency in training children in their social relations. The unaggressive child is an easy mark and children are taught to have little regard for the one who cannot defend himself. On the other hand, the child who is too aggressive is frowned upon. A child is thwarted by adults, and yet he is punished when he attempts to thwart other children in the same manner in which his. parents thwarted him. A child must be humble and not show off, and yet he is encouraged to search for popularity and to be a

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

137 leader. He must submit to parental authority and be obedient, and yet must not let another impose upon him. 

It must be admitted that psychologists have not solved this problem. However, a realistic view of the facts leads to the following conclusion: We are in a competitive society and the child had better be taught that all individuals are not going to sit back and encourage him to take his turn. Even if such universal unselfishness might be enjoyable, common sense tells us that it does not exist in modern society. 

Clinical studies of children have made it clear that it is a wholesome exercise for a child to meet and overcome obstacles. 

He can be challenged by difficulties in a wholesome manner and be stimulated to do better work because of obstacles than he would manifest were tasks too easy. We know this is true even if we do not know just how to achieve a balance between easy and difficult tasks. Case studies indicate a possible solution of the problem of aggression. The child can be taught the pleasures that may be derived from meeting and overcoming obstacles with less emphasis upon the specific objective attained and still less upon a comparison of his success with that of others. The type of aggression that distorts the personality of the one who develops it, and becomes a disruptive social force, is the kind that is the expression of the self-conscious weakling who has his attention centered upon the humiliation or defeat of another in order that he may thereby rise to greater power and thus increase his own self-satisfaction.

Forms of aggression. Because aggression has become a pronounced social force, it affects the lives of great numbers of individuals. It is of vital significance for the student of psychology to be able to recognize it in all its forms. 

1. The aggression may be directed at the frustrating agent. 

For example, the jealous child who feels that his brother has come between him and his mother may manifest his irritation by direct violence to his brother. 

2. The aggression may be directed against a substitute for the frustrating agent. Instead of hitting his enemy, a thwarted person may institute a lawsuit against him or start a scandal by talking about him. Furthermore, if any action against the frustrating agent is prevented, the aggressor may take it out on any

PSYCHOLOGY 

innocent bystander or on some inanimate object. One may kick a chair instead of his enemy.

An experiment was performed which illustrates how aggression may fall upon an innocent bystander. Rats were trained to strike each other under certain circumstances. If one rat was placed with another rat, each tended to hit the other. If, on the other hand, one trained rat was placed in the test apparatus with a doll, he struck the doll instead of another rat. [3, p. 42] Innocent individuals, groups, and nations are continually being subjected to indignities because they happen to be the substitute recipients of aggressive activities logically intended for others. There is a tendency on the part of farmers to vote political incumbents out of office following years with poor rainfall. It is well known that the public tends to vote against the party in power after an economic depression. These are illustrations of displacements of aggression from the real frustrating agent to innocent bystanders. 

3. Aggressions may be directed against oneself. It is not uncommon to hear a person say he hates himself for something he has done. Self-condemnation may lead to emotional depressions and even to suicide. Such aggression against oneself appears only after overt aggressions have been checked. For example, a frustrated child may respond by biting, pinching, and kicking the adult who began the frustration. If such acts are checked, he may hit other children or his pet or even his doll. 

If these indirect expressions are likewise checked, he may bump his head against the wall, pull his own hair, or make faces at himself in the mirror. Martyrdom probably has an element of aggression against the self in it. 

INFLUENCING OTHER INDIVIDUALS 

Whenever individuals meet, there is a resulting mutual influence of some sort. Whether the influence acts in the way in which one plans, whether it depends upon the giver more than the recipient, and whether it can be controlled, are factors which make the question of individual influence a complex one. Courses of selling which teach the salesman a set method of approach and make him memorize a set speech take for granted that persons are similar in their responsiveness. Such an assumption is contrary to the

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

139 facts. On the other hand, those who contend that the only prerequisite for becoming influential is to develop a striking and dominant personality are certainly in the wrong. All social behavior is reciprocal and personal influence is no exception. 

Individual differences in responsiveness to others. If we could measure the degree of readiness with which individuals respond to others, we would doubtless find that they range all the way from those who are extremely resistive to any personal influence to those who are extremely responsive. It is also probable that most individuals would fall somewhere between these two extremes and that a curve drawn to represent a group of individuals on such a scale would be somewhat like the ordinary probability curve, such as we get when we plot the distribution of individuals in height, weight, intelligence (page 95) and the like. Those who tend toward the responsive end of such a distribution have been called suggestible. Those who tend toward the resistive end are called negativistic. Most persons are partly negativistic and partly suggestible. The one who wishes to be influential in his dealings with another must first know the degree of general responsiveness of the other person, the kinds of things that will increase his responsiveness, and certain techniques for making his influence effective.

The habit of suggestibility or negativism. The degree to which one tends to be responsive or resistive to the suggestions of others is a learned habit. If a child is brought up in surroundings where people are trustworthy and kindly disposed toward him, he will learn to depend upon them. As he widens his contacts, he will tend to act toward his new acquaintances in a similar manner. Should these, in turn, prove to be trustworthy, his habit of responsiveness will be strengthened. Thus, other things being equal, a person's degree of suggestibility is in direct proportion to the degree to which his social contacts have tended to encourage him to trust others. If one could imagine a person who had attained maturity and had never experienced a single situation in which others had proved untrustworthy, it would be easy to understand how such a person would trust others to the extent that he would be an easy prey to any malevolent impostor. 

On the contrary, one whose early and later contacts had been with untrustworthy individuals would most likely develop an

PSYCHOLOGY 

attitude of suspicion, and would tend to resist any attempt on the part of others to influence him. 

However, such a habit is in the form of a generalized attitude which takes specific form only in individual situations and, because each situation is different, will not be a habit that displays itself with the same degree of uniformity as would a motor habit. In 

FIG. 22.-Diagram of the sway test for suggestibility. A blindfolded subject is told that he is swaying forward. Without his knowledge, the swaying movements are recorded on the kymograph. 

(From C. L. Hull, Hypnosis and Suggestibility. New York: D. Appleton-Century Co., 1933.) other words, while a person might tend to be negativistic more often than suggestible, he would probably adjust his responsiveness to the particular situation in which it occurred. He might be negativistic to most persons but relatively responsive to some one individual. In short, if it is desired to influence a person, it is not enough to decide whether he is preponderantly suggestible or negativistic; one must go further and try to determine under what circumstances, or to what persons, he is more likely to be responsive.

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

141 Attempts to measure suggestibility. Attempts to measure suggestibility have not met with striking success. One of the most promising methods has been the sway test. This method is illustrated in Fig. 22. The subject is blindfolded and, without his knowledge, a light string is fastened to his body and connected to a device which will record any swaying movements on a kymograph. The experimenter then suggests to the subject that he is moving forward or moving backward. It has been found that suggestible individuals tend to move in the direction indicated by the examiner, although they are not aware that they are doing So. It has also been found that negativistic individuals become rigid when told to sway and refuse to respond. Some individuals, who have been called negatively suggestible will respond by doing the opposite of what is commanded. When told to sway forward, they will sway backward. [5] Kinds of suggestion. The factors which may play a part in eliciting a response from an individual are so diversified that they cannot be placed into logical and mutually exclusive categories. Until someone devises some measure of suggestibility and dissects the component factors by factor analysis, or by some other method, the following four factors may be distinguished: 

1. The factor of directness. Suggestions may be given in a straightforward manner, so that the recipient knows exactly what is intended. Or, they may be presented by indirect means, so that the intention of the person giving the suggestion can only be guessed by the recipient. Where two individuals enjoy an association of mutual trust there is no reason why suggestions should not be direct and undisguised. 

2. The factor of awareness. Some suggestions operate even though the recipient is not aware that he received them, whereas others may be consciously discerned. Many acts of everyday life are probably determined in part by stimuli of which we are not aware. 

3. The factor of prestige. Prestige suggestions are those which result directly from the influence of one person upon another; nonprestige suggestions are those whose effect is not dependent upon any personal factor. When we obey a person because we like him we are displaying prestige suggestibility. 

When we refuse to respond to a person because we hate him

PSYCHOLOGY 

we are manifesting prestige negativism. Illustrations of nonprestige responses are the response to monotonous situations by becoming drowsy, by the watering of one's mouth at the sight of appetizing food, or by the desire for a new car at the sight of a handsome new model. 

4. The verbal factor. Suggestions may be verbal or nonverbal. A nonverbal suggestion is illustrated by an individual's gazing intently at a certain object and thus influencing others to look at the same object. A verbal suggestion is illustrated by the statement: "Look at that spot on your tie."

Generalizations. From the above discussion we may make the following generalizations: 

1. The ease with which any person can be influenced by others depends upon his habit of trusting others. To be balanced, this confidence should be determined in large part by an understanding of the motives of the person who is attempting to exert his influence. Hence, the readiness to trust others should be determined separately in each specific instance. It is more important to know something about the personal integrity of a salesman than it is to hunt for indications that his wares are as represented. 

2. If one is to exert personal influence successfully, he should understand others. Understanding is more important than the knowledge of devices for influencing others. To be sure, devices applied mechanically will work at times, but when a critical situation arises, genuine understanding must supersede any routine method of influence.

LEADERSHIP 

Leadership relates fundamentally to a social situation in which one person stands in a dominant relationship to others. 

Background of leadership. What is it that makes people follow another's lead? Essentially it is a real or imagined need for help. In times of crisis, it is essential for each person to do what he can for the common good. At. such times, the person with intelligence, energy, self-confidence, who is quick to decide and energetic enough to carry out his decisions, easily takes the lead. Others, feeling keenly the value of such services, accept his leadership willingly and even eagerly. Since these traits are not too rare, the best leader in any situation is the one who, in

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

143 addition to these traits, has enough insight into the immediate emergency to contribute materially. In each need there should logically be a different leader. 

However, things seldom work that way. Observations of children have shown that, once a child takes the initiative, that very fact changes his relationship to the others. He develops a feeling of superiority which he enjoys. The followers look up to him and, in the next crisis, turn automatically to him to lead; and he readily takes the initiative again. There is, in other words, a sort of halo built up around one who takes the initiative. [11] 

In adults the same factors operate, only in a more powerful manner. In political, economic, or social crises, the mass of individuals become demoralized through fear and grope blindly for someone to guide them. The greater the emergency, the less discriminating the needy ones become and the greater the likelihood that an individual who is motivated more by his desire for domination, than one who desires to contribute, will be able to gain control. So long as the emergency lasts, his excess activity will be interpreted as efficiency and he will be able to maintain his position. Since emergencies do not last, it has been the agelong custom for autocratic leaders to fortify their position by other means than their own ability. Robes, parades, insignia of office, inaccessibility, speaking only from a lofty position under circumstances calculated to intensify the submissiveness of auditors, and many other devices are designed to intimidate anyone who doubts the supremacy of the officeholder. In some situations, the ruler is so revered that any attempt to dethrone him is regarded as treason, punishable by death.

Another curious feature of this situation is that the initiative in attempting to displace a person in office is usually taken by those who themselves have a mighty zeal to rule. In short, the most striking characteristic both of the one who clings to his office and of the one who tries most zealously to displace him is a desire to dominate.

Ascendance-submission patterns of behavior. These facts about leadership lead to the conclusion that whether one leads or whether one follows is determined largely by certain habit patterns which he develops. The leader is one who has

PSYCHOLOGY 

developed habits of ascendance and the follower is one who has developed habits of submission. To be sure, persons become placed in social situations where they are not adjusted to these habit patterns; but when this happens, there is usually an attempt to get into a more congenial situation. The person who has the ambition to be ascendant and who is in a subservient position takes the first opportunity to dominate others; whereas the submissive person who has authority thrust on him seeks the first opportunity to retire in favor of another. 

It therefore becomes an interesting problem to study how a child learns to be ascendant or submissive. A study of ascendant and nonascendant children showed characteristic differences between the two groups. The nonascendant children showed fear of facial demonstrations of displeasure by their companions; they made frequent appeals to adults for help and attention; they followed adults or held on to them; they interfered with the activities of others with no apparent reason; they hesitated after starting to do something and, at times, failed to do the act after it was begun; they showed reasonless laughter or enthusiasm; they reacted strongly to criticism, ridicule, or threats by blushing, apologizing, or retreating. [11, p. 398]

This description will be recognized as fitting a child who lacks self-confidence. Two kinds of home background may foster feelings of insecurity: The first is the home in which the child` gets too much attention. He never learns to do anything for himself, feels more and more dependent as he gets older, and when finally he is thrown in contact with outsiders, he mistrusts his ability to get along with them. Too often his lack of confidence is intensified by his actual failure in social affairs. 

The second situation which will produce anxiety and feelings of insecurity is that in which the child is given no attention and is thrust into hostile surroundings before he is capable of working out a plan for taking care of himself. Children who are so lacking have been changed by special training designed to build self-confidence. Most effective was training in some simple skilled act. As proficiency increased the child gained poise and was able to prosecute his work in the presence of others with a corresponding loss of the symptoms enumerated above. To generalize, the nonascendant child is one who is hyperconscious of himself; he

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

145 is afraid of the criticism of others of a nearly-equal status; and he is dependent upon those upon whom he has learned to lean for support. Interest and skill in pursuing an objective task is the best cure for such a condition. Instead of wondering how others regard him, the competent person knows he is doing a good job.

Suppose that instead of being supervised by some understanding person who taught him to be efficient and poised, such a nonascendant child fell into the hands of a dominating person whose main objective in life was to convince others that he was boss. The result would be either an increasing submissiveness and subservience or, if the pressure became too excessive, a violent revolt. Such a revolt, instead of leading to poise, would result in an excessive desire to dominate others and probably end in another social situation where a new person, or group of persons, would fall prey to his compulsion to rule. The groundwork is laid for tyranny.

Many of these problems are adjusted satisfactorily by children themselves if the children are not thwarted by supervisors. 

A tyrant is recognized and the group "gangs up" on him. Likewise, the abused child is protected by those who see his plight. 

MOTIVATING FORCE OF CUSTOMS AND CONVENTION 

Types of uniform social behavior. Various types of uniformity in human behavior have been distinguished. [6] 

Chance uniformities. Chance uniformities are characterized by activities which are uniform but which arise from some factor in the environment that is not closely related to the thinking or attitudes of the persons involved. An illustration is the fact that men turn up their collars in a blizzard. 

Folkways. Folkways are better known as conventions.

They represent the traditional pattern of a group-the "proper" way of doing things. Usually they are not rationally thought out, but often arise from trial-and-error methods of persons in their attempts to meet their needs. They are uniform, invariable, and imperative. Folkways are not improved by laws which make the individuals in the group conform; but the one who makes the conventional error is laughed at as ridiculous, he may be shunned, or he may even be excluded from the group. Illustra-

PSYCHOLOGY 

tions of such conventions are: wearing shoes, shaking hands, kissing, eating with a fork, or using a handkerchief. 

Mores. Mores are customs which the social group regards as the only right ones, as vital to the welfare of the group, and which must be maintained at any cost. The negative ban against transgression of the mores is spoken of as a taboo. They are usually explicitly expressed and are thought of as codes for the direction of individual conduct. For example, monogamy is considered essential to the welfare of our society and polygamy is not tolerated. 

Institutional uniformities. In institutional uniformities there is more regimentation, more rational justification for the uniformities, and less emotional horror at a violation. Still, the group regards as important the submission of the individual to certain institutional patterns, while realizing that such conformity is a matter of expediency rather than of vital moral significance. 

The concept of institution applies to such cases of uniform behavior as those arising from membership in political parties, business corporations, schools, or churches. A person has a relative amount of freedom in joining but, having joined, he is expected to adjust his behavior to the requirements of the institution. 

Fads and fashions. A fad implies a more unstable pattern of behavior than does a fashion. Nevertheless, both are changeable and appear and disappear with little reason and with no apparent contribution to human welfare. While at the crest of their influence, fads and fashions do exert a powerful influence, different members of the society vying with each other to keep up with the changing tide. Common activities strikingly affected by fad and fashion are: dress, slang phrases, popular music, hobbies, recreation, tastes in food, parlor games, radio programs, dance steps, and literally hundreds of others.

Conforming behavior. An outstanding feature of this outline of uniformities in behavior is the fact that most of them are self-imposed. We attempt to find out what is being done and to do it. We find the group having the strongest influence and then join that group. Not being able to attain membership with the in-group, we may accept a position in the out-group. However, having done so, we tend to exert our efforts toward increas-

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

147 ing the relative strength of the organization we have joined and to supplant the in-group. 

Even after an individual has joined a group, has adopted a fashion, or accepted a conventional mode of behavior, there is still some variation in the degree of adherence to the uniformity imposed by such allegiance. He may submit because of expediency but, often, his own individual wishes cause certain reservations. Various kinds of pressure are brought to bear to restrain individualistic impulses, and the resultant behavior is usually some sort of compromise between the need for conformity and the tendency to be individualistic. A person may manifest some freedom in selecting the institutions which he joins; he may transfer from one country or state to another when he does not subscribe to the political system of the first; he may change his religion when he finds himself affiliated with one which does not suit him; he may change clubs, economic associations, join the Foreign Legion, or become a monk. Some of these affiliations permit a continuation of more individualism than do others, but no sane man imagines that he can live in association with others and still be a complete individualist. Life is a combination of freedom and the voluntary or forced restraint of freedom. What seems to bother many persons is whether their restrictions are selfimposed or are imposed from without. Such individuals prefer to join institutions which keep up the appearance of allowing their members freedom. Any restraint must be rationalized as expressing the will of the majority of the group, or the will of representatives of the majority.

Other groups of individuals have been brought up through childhood in institutions where they have been taught to believe the individual has no rights. They take for granted that some greater power has ordained the state of affairs and their only obligations are to learn what necessary restrictions exist and to adhere rigidly to these. 

In most situations there is neither strict regimentation nor strict individualism. Instead, there are certain aspects of life which permit great freedom and certain others which permit little or none. In such cases, it is interesting to study those segments of behavior which are restricted and to compare them with the nonrestricted areas. It is also interesting to ascertain

PSYCHOLOGY 

how the self-imposed regulation compares with the restriction which is arbitrarily imposed from the outside. 

The measurement of conforming behavior. If conforming behavior is measured and is plotted in the form of a distribution curve, it has been found that the general shape of such a curve differs strikingly from the distribution curve constructed from measurements of such biological functions as height, weight, or intelligence (Fig. 16, page 95). The form of the curve obtained from measuring a function which depends upon the chance operation of a large number of factors is the bell-shaped

FIG. 24.-A typical J-curve. Distribution of responses of 2,114 

motorists at an intersection protected by traffic signs. The departure from the normal distribution form and the approach to the J-curve form indicates the degree of responsiveness to factors which demand conformity of behavior. (After Allport, Dickens, and Schanck.) [2]

In other situations, where the compulsion exerted upon the group is not so severe, the piling of the individuals toward one end of the distribution will not be so striking. If enough pressure could be brought to bear, presumably every individual could be made to respond in a uniform manner. If, for example, it was made clear that all those who did not stop at a stop sign would be put to death, not many would fail to stop. The shape of a curve, then, becomes a fairly good index of the degree to which

PSYCHOLOGY 

a group accepts the pressures exerted to make their conduct uniform.

It should be clearly recognized, on the other hand, that such outward compliance tells nothing about the degree of inner compliance which the individuals in the group may have. While all persons involved might presumably do an act rather than die, there probably are all degrees of willingness to comply. Some attempts to measure attitudes show that these internal factors also may show the effect of conformity. It is quite likely that when an attitude is closely related to the mores of the group the tendency would be toward conformity because of the moral pressure. The curve recording the belief in monogamy, for example, would likely be a J-curve.

In brief, when the need for conforming is at a minimum, social activities are determined by thousands of factors inherent in the personality characteristics of the persons involved. When social pressure of any kind is brought to bear, such freedom is restricted and freedom in certain directions is hampered. The curve of distribution of an act may be taken as an index of the effectiveness of the pressure exerted in any particular situation. 

MOTIVATING IDEOLOGIES 

A commonly accepted belief is that a man's conduct is merely the reflection of his system of attitudes, his character tendencies, his philosophy of life, his conscience, or his religion, all of which may be included under his ideology. If this is a sound belief, the complete knowledge of a man's ideology would enable us to predict what he would do in a given situation. For example, if a crime has been committed and we know the ideologies of the different individuals who might have participated in the crime, we should be able to pick out the culprit. It is this procedure that makes detective stories so fascinating. The clues give a possible motive for the crime, the individuals are studied to find one who might have been driven by such a motive, and— 

Q.E.D.-we have the criminal.

Ideologies as disguises of real motives. In practice, the problem is by no means so simple. Any detective knows that real attitudes and genuine determining drives in an individual are seldom revealed in his expressed attitudes. The degree of dis-

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

151 guise may range all the way from that of the professional man who takes up religion to increase his clientele to the international spy who wins the love of her victim in order to gain military information for her country.

An even greater obstacle than intentional deceit in the way of true discernment of real attitudes lies in the fact that practically all of us engage in self-deceit, are sure that we entertain one set of attitudes when we actually are nursing others, and are so genuine in our convictions that the disguise becomes impenetrable. 

This statement, which may appear quite dogmatic, has been amply verified by clinical studies. A generalization, which it is probably safe to accept tentatively although it cannot be proved by statistics or by controlled experiment, is that the smoother the ideological system which a person presents, and the more zeal he manifests in defending it, the more one should suspect that his expressed views are disguises for attitudes which, if exposed, would not appear so praiseworthy. The reformer, the fanatic, and the opinionated individual are not likely to be actuated by a logical interpretation of the relevant factors in a situation, but by very personal and probably narrow emotional attitudes. 

The man who appears to be extremely interested in saving your money, in saving your soul, in tipping you off to a good investment, in warning you against your enemies, or in giving you a better government, is probably more interested in himself than in you, although he himself may be unaware of the real motives behind his apparent altruism. This should not be taken as an excuse for going through life with morbid suspicions as to the sinister motives in all our friends. It merely is a simple statement to the effect that personal emotional bias lies behind much of the conduct of all of us, and we should take this for granted as an essential part of social life. The honest man admits that he has personal interests in his attitudes; the dishonest man contends that he has no interest except in others. He has personal interests just the same, but they must be discovered beneath his disguise of pretended disinterest in himself. 

The driving force of defense mechanisms. Defense mechanisms may be defined as forms of conduct which tend to guard some aspect of an individual's personality from scrutiny by others, or by himself, by calling into play disguised acts. They

PSYCHOLOGY 

are forms of deceit. To the psychologist, however, the important consideration should not be that they are lies, but that they are probably the most potent motivating forces in human life. In line with these driving values, these defense mechanisms have been renamed dynamisms-a term that is probably more pertinent. [14, p. 150] To know what dynamisms actuate an individual, it is necessary to know the sort of person he is. Hence, we shall postpone a more extended discussion of these personality qualities until the last chapter.

INTERACTION OF MOTIVES 

It should be perfectly apparent, from the foregoing survey of the various motivating forces in human life, that any act is the resultant of a vast number of factors. Behavior cannot be explained by selecting one factor and ignoring the others. Neither can it be explained by enumerating all the elements in a given situation. The theoretical explanation of any act would require the knowledge of each influence, the direction in which it was exerted, the force of each, and the time relations between all of them.

Psychological valences. An analogy used recently in this connection was borrowed from chemistry. It is the concept of valences. As used by psychologists, a valence may be defined as the attracting or the repelling value of an object. [10] The possible combinations of valences may be outlined as follows: 

A simple positive valence. This is a situation where a simple stimulus elicits an approaching reaction. For example, when a girl is offered a doll, she will make a positive or approaching response. 

A simple negative valence. An illustration of this is the negative value of touching a hot stove.

Poise between two positive valences. A child may be offered a dime to drop his play and go to bed. He may want to continue to play and may want the dime. Consequently, he may hesitate which one to choose. If the two were of exactly equal weight and persisted through a period of time, nothing would happen. Usually there is no more than a momentary balance; one or the other will win.

SOCIAL MOTIVES 

153 Poise between two negative valences. A child may be told that if he does not do some unpleasant task he will be punished. 

He may take the punishment rather than do the task; he may do the task to avoid the punishment; or he may try to evade both the task and the punishment. 

In an actual situation, a great number of forces combine and the behavior is the resultant of all these forces. One objection to this analogy of valences is the tendency it breeds to ignore the factors within the individual. Not only should the student make an analysis of objective forces, but he should also consider the personality make-up of the individual upon whom these play. 

For example, the opportunity to get a dime may be a strong force for one child and not for another. It may have a powerful force at one time when the child needs money, but be powerless at another when the child is surfeited with wealth. 

Individual interpretation. The conclusion that stands out is that each situation must be analyzed as an individual situation if we are to understand the motives behind any bit of conduct. 

Analogies or attempts to simplify only mislead us. An immediate act is dependent upon the genes from which the person originated, the biochemical processes in his body, prenatal influences, maturation, care during infancy, the food that was eaten, the hormones secreted by his ductless glands, the attitudes he has developed, and the influences of other individuals. 

Is there any method by means of which the dominant trends in an individual may be discerned? An excellent opportunity to observe individual differences in adjustment tendencies comes when a number of persons are exposed to the same objective crisis. The behavior of each will, in a measure, reflect his essential dominating trends. Most persons can dissemble well enough under ordinary circumstances; but a crisis will usually break through any ordinary disguises. For example, a train wreck will bring out the worst and the best in those involved. To understand a person, observe the way in which he reacts to unusual or difficult circumstances.

Chapter VII EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

MOTIONAL behavior describes those forms of response which are relatively intense, random, unusual, disorganized, and indiscriminate. A person is emotional when he is in a stirredup condition.

Subjective and objective aspects of emotion. Emotional behavior has two different aspects. 

1. Subjectively, the individual is disturbed. He is aware of feeling of excitement; he is aware of increased tension in his muscles; and he is aware that his customary acts are disrupted and disorganized. 

2. Objectively, the emotionally aroused individual may be observed to do acts which are different from his ordinary manner of behaving. He shows his disturbance by his facial expression, by his postures, by loss of motor co-ordination, as well as by other actions. He may shiver, laugh, cry, run, whisper, or yell. Even when he tries to hide the obvious manifestations of an emotional experience, inadvertent acts may disclose his agitation to the critical observer. 

Emergency aspect of emotional activities. Behind these two aspects of emotion, the subjective and the objective, there is a deeper significance which arises from the reasons for emotional activities. When we view emotional behavior in its most primitive aspects, we may say that a person is emotionally aroused when he is faced by an emergency. If an individual has an adequate response for his present situation, his behavior is likely to be precise, mechanical, and orderly, that is, not emotional. proportion to the extent to which elements are introduced for which he is unprepared, which are unfamiliar to him, for which he has no ready response, or which are a threat to his safety, he In 156

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

157 must digress from mechanical, habitual, and orderly reactions. 

He does something different but, at the same time, he manifests considerable uncertainty as to just what he should do, or how intensely he should act.

All the terms that we have used to define emotional behavior are relative. There is no point that separates clearly the mechanical act from the haphazard act, the habitual from the nonhabitual, the orderly from the disorderly, the precise from the inaccurate act. There is no sharp distinction between tension and relaxation, between order and disruption, or between mild and excessive feeling tone; hence, it is futile to attempt to determine whether any specific activity is emotional or nonemotional. It would be safer to assume that there is some emotional aspect to all conduct and devote our efforts to determinations of the degree of emotionality in any particular situation. For a person to be entirely free from the emotional aspects of conduct would imply that he is perfectly adjusted. Since no living being is perfectly adjusted (life is a process of continual adjustment), the act with no emotional aspect becomes an absurdity. 

Emotional patterns. Emotions may be classified (a) in terms of the situation which produced the activity; (b) in terms of the subjective experiences of the individual; or (c) in terms of the outcome of his behavior. Most of the terms we find commonly used imply a mixture of these three factors. For example, fear might be thought to indicate a certain subjective experience the individual feels afraid. Nevertheless, to state that a person is afraid implies that he has experienced contact with some threatening situation (either real or imagined), and furthermore that he has not successfully met that threat. Anger implies a subjective experience; but it implies also that there is a frustration which the individual is actively resisting in some manner.

As soon as we attempt to give an emotion a name or to classify it, we encounter insurmountable difficulties. The main reason for this situation is that emotional behavior is dynamic and classifications are static. The only escape from this dilemma is to forgo all attempts to evolve a rigid classification and to be contented with a description of the dynamic aspects of emotional behavior.

PSYCHOLOGY 

For example, the use of motion-picture analysis has made possible the description of a startle pattern which might well be substituted for such an abstract concept as fear. When infants are stimulated by the sound of a pistol shot, they have been observed to show a pattern of behavior which includes various combinations of the following: shutting of the eyes; distortion of the features; a forward movement of the head; a raising and drawing forward of the shoulders; abduction, forward elevation, and inner rotation of the upper arms; a bending of the elbows; a pronation of the forearms; clasping of the hands; contractior: of the abdomen; a forward movement of the trunk; bending of the legs at the hips and knees; and random foot movements. All this is merely another way of saying that when the infant is confronted with a sudden stimulus for which he has no ready or adequate response, he reacts with many of the movements of which he is capable. Apes and monkeys as well as experienced adults show a similar combination of bodily movements to the firing of a pistol shot. [24]

If we proceed on the basis of such descriptive studies, we are almost forced to the conclusion that there is but one basic emotional pattern, which rests on the interaction of two opposing mechanisms. There is excitement, which leads to some variation of the startle pattern when one is confronted with a sudden, violent, or novel stimulus; and a tendency to relax when events move in a routine, mild, and familiar manner. Differentiation is possible only in terms of changes in the significance of the stimulating situation, in terms of some habitual way of responding to such stimuli, and in certain attitudes toward the outcome of the whole situation.

Emotions may, then, be differentiated on the basis of degree of disruption involved. In ordinary activity, for example, there is a minimum departure from habitual rhythms, orderliness, precision, and relaxation. Such calm behavior might be classed as nonemergency, or normal, behavior. At the other extreme of this continuum we have the activity resulting from major shocks, such as the exploding of a shell in a trench next to a person. 

Such major shocks may lead to extreme motor activity, a marked loss of co-ordination, or even physical collapse. Between these two extremes are all degrees of disruption. There may be medium

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

159 shocks, which could be precipitated by the slamming of a door or by some other sudden stimulus which is recognized almost immediately as harmless. Or, approaching the major shock area, there may be the sudden appearance of a real danger, such as the skidding of one's car.

This distinction between mild emotions and shock behavior will gain more significance when we come to discuss the mechanisms by means of which emotional behavior is accomplished. 

There is a system of organs which brings about an arousal of activity and another opposed system which brings about relaxation. It is probably best to permit the concept of emotional behavior to include both these sets of behavior rather than to call the operation of one set emotional and the other nonemotional. 

We may conclude that there are two sets of emotional activities which are continually balancing each other; namely, the exciting and the relaxing activities. [43]

PHYSIOLOGICAL PROCESSES INVOLVED IN EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

Emotional reactions involve the activities of numerous and diverse physiological mechanisms. Without some conception of the way in which each of these operates and how the different ones interact, an understanding of emotions is almost impossible. 

Skeletal motor activity in emotional behavior. Any part of the muscular apparatus of the body may be involved in an excited reaction. A person may run, may fight, may tremble, and in diverse ways use his skeletal muscular apparatus to respond to an emotion-producing stimulation. This is obvious, but it is often overlooked in our interest in the more subtle and evasive internal tensions and subjective feelings that go with many emotional situations. Instead of overlooking these skeletal activities, we should keep in mind that the ultimate emotional response is an overt act designed to deal with the emotional stimulus. A great many processes may be set off by some threatening situation, but these may all be regarded as contributing to the main response, which is a skeletal reaction to the objective situation. Excited behavior is essentially one aspect of a complicated adjustment process, and the fact of greatest significance is to get a complete perspective of this process and not limit our view to the subjective experience. It may be important to know that a person is afraid,

PSYCHOLOGY 

but it is also important to know what the person is doing about the situation causing the fear. It is a mistake to ignore the overt behavior of a person in any study of his emotional experiences. 

Visceral emotional reactions. When there is an absence of emotional excitement, that is, when there are no emergencies to be confronted, the internal viscera maintain regular rhythmic movements in their essential function of carrying on the metabolic processes of the body. These organs are composed essentially of smooth muscles whose period of contraction is much slower than that of skeletal muscles. These smooth muscles are very much involved in emotional situations. However, the sensations arising from visceral activities are so vague that they cannot be localized with accuracy.

Glandular reactions in emotion. A number of duct glands are influenced by emotional situations. The salivary glands secrete lavishly during emotional calm and diminish in their activity (so that the mouth becomes dry) during excitement. The tear glands may be stimulated during certain emotions, and may be inhibited in others. 

The most significant glandular reactions during excitement are the reactions of the endocrine glands. These glands secrete hormones which are discharged directly into the blood stream and, in turn, produce striking physiological effects upon various organs in widely different parts of the body. For example, thyroxin has a marked effect upon the basal metabolic rate of the body. 

The autonomic nervous system. The way in which these different mechanisms combine in emotional behavior is most interesting and explains many of the apparently queer reactions that the emotionally aroused person performs. This co-ordination of activity is controlled by the autonomic nervous system [11] The entire nervous system is usually regarded as being composed of two general parts-the skeletal system and the autonomic system. The skeletal system (also called the cerebrospinal system) has its centers located in the skull and in the spinal column. 

It receives fibers from the sense organs and sends fibers out to those muscles which move the bony framework of the body. It will be studied in some detail in a later chapter. 

The autonomic nervous system has its centers, or ganglia,

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

161 outside the skull and spinal cavities. Nerve fibers come from the cerebrospinal system to these autonomic ganglia and carry messages in one direction only, that is, from the cerebrospinal centers to the autonomic ganglia. There are no fibers which pass from the sense organs of the body directly to the autonomic ganglia; all messages to the autonomic system must come by way Association nerve fiber- Sensory nerve cell

FIG. 25.-Schematic illustration to show the comparison of the ordi- . nary skeletal reflex (left) with the autonomic reflex (right). In the ordinary skeletal reflex the impulse comes through the sensory fiber to the center in the dorsal (rear) part of the cord, is transmitted by means of an association fiber to a motor cell, and is carried out along a motor nerve to some muscle. In the autonomic reflex, the sensory impulse comes in through the dorsal part of the cord to the lateral horn of the gray matter in the spinal cord. From here an association fiber carries the impulse to the sympathetic ganglion, outside the spinal cord, where it makes connection with the smooth muscles. of the cerebrospinal system. The fibers from the autonomic ganglia go direct to the internal organs of the body, such as the stomach, intestines, heart, various glands, and the muscles around the hairs in the skin; that is, to all smooth muscles. In brief, the skeletal system controls those muscles which operate the bony framework of the body, whereas the autonomic system controls those muscles which operate the internal organs. The skeletal

PSYCHOLOGY 

centers receive messages from the sense organs; the autonómic system receives messages only from the skeletal centers. 

The way in which these two systems function is illustrated in Fig. 25. In the left part of the diagram is shown an ordinary skeletal reflex mechanism. A sensory nerve conducts the nerve impulse from a sense organ into the neural center in the spinal cord. Here there is an association fiber which conducts this incoming sensory impulse to a motor nerve cell, and the motor fiber then conducts the impulse out to some striped muscle. Such a simple mechanism is called a reflex mechanism. (In actual life simple processes of this kind never occur in isolation, but it is convenient to abstract such a simple elementary process to clarify our thinking.) On the right side of the diagram is illustrated what happens when an autonomic ganglion is involved. The association fiber carries the nervous impulse to an autonomic ganglion outside the spinal cord and from this ganglion the nerve impulse proceeds to the smooth muscles and glands. 

The general arrangement of the autonomic system is illustrated in Fig. 26. It is conventionally divided into three segments: (1) the cranial segment, which embraces those ganglia in the head region; (2) the thoracic segment, also called the sympathetic segment (as well as the thoracicolumbar), which embraces those ganglia in the central region; and (3) the sacral segment, which includes those ganglia in or near the pelvic region. 

Some writers, probably the majority, combine the cranial and sacral into one group and consider the whole system as having two separate parts: (a) the sympathetic system, which corresponds to the thoracic or central region, and (b) the parasympathetic, or cranial and sacral regions. This latter grouping has in its favor the fact that evidence seems to point to balanced interaction between the sympathetic and parasympathetic. 

The functioning of the autonomic system in emotional activities. There is reason to believe that the sympathetic segment (that is, the thoracic, or central, segment) is concerned with emergency functions of the organism, and that the parasympathetic segment (comprising the cranial and sacral segments) is concerned with routine physiological activities. A review of the behavior of these two segments will pave the way for a clearer
