understanding of the way an individual behaves in various emotional activities.

In emotional excitement it is important that widely scattered parts of the body act in collaboration. The fact that fibers run directly from the sympathetic ganglia to widely scattered parts of the viscera makes for immediate and widespread control. This wide distribution makes possible the following effects on organs served directly by fibers from unified centers: constriction of the small blood vessels of the abdominal organs, skin, and other parts of the body; acceleration of the activity of the heart; increase in the secretion of the sweat glands; the inhibition of the activity of the smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract; the liberation of blood sugar from the liver; the acceleration of breathing; the dilation of the pupils; the retraction of the eyelid and a projection of the eye forward, causing the wide-open bulging eye so characteristic of strong emotion; the stimulation of the smooth muscles around the hairs (making the hair to stand up or forming goose pimples); an inhibition of salivary and gastric secretions; and the stimulation of the secretion of adrenalin by the medullary (central) portion of the adrenal glands. 

All these activities have the common characteristic of being emergency functions. The effects are to mobilize energy and to provide methods for its ready utilization. Stimulation of the sympathetic segment leads to an increase in the available supply of blood sugar in the blood. It slows up or stops unnecessary activity in the digestive system. Circulation is modified so as to supply extra food and oxygen to the parts needed to carry away the waste products of metabolism more effectively. This is accomplished by acceleration of the heart action, constriction of the blood vessels not needed in the emergency (the digestive system), more active breathing and sweating. The sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system acts as a unit, and thus mobilizes all these forces, in such emergency situations, as: pain, asphyxiation, emotional excitement, vigorous muscular exercise, exposure to cold, and states of lowered blood sugar (hypoglycemia). The fact that emotional excitement and damaging circumstances produce the same physiological results is strong evidence in favor of regarding those emotions which affect the

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

165 sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system as emergency activities. [10] 

This emergency function of the sympathetic segment differentiates it most strikingly from the parasympathetic system. The parasympathetic is able to exert its effects upon single organs without, at the same time, affecting other organs, whereas the sympathetic calls a great many organs into violent activity in a relatively unselective manner. The parasympathetic system is parsimonious, whereas the sympathetic is extravagant. 

It has been experimentally demonstrated that the sympathetic segment is necessary in emergency conditions but that an animal can get along very well without it if he is shielded from emotional stimulation. [12] The surgical removal of the entire sympathetic system causes no striking alterations of the body. A number of animals have lived in good health for over a year after such an operation and, so long as they are kept under quiet laboratory conditions, they show no deficiencies in behavior. On the other hand, when such animals are confronted with some stressful situation they are at a decided disadvantage. In cold weather, they lose heat rapidly, and have a low body temperature. When threatened with some danger, their blood sugar does not rise, their hair is not erected, there is no rise in blood pressure, no great acceleration of the heat rate, no increase of secretion of adrenalin to hasten blood coagulation and to abolish the effects of fatigue. 

Although they show typical signs of aggression when confronted with an enemy, that is, they make the customary skeletal responses, they cannot summon the visceral support, which is under sympathetic control. Similarly, a cat which has been deprived by surgical operation of the sympathetic segment will be unable to erect its hair when confronted by a dog. 

DESCRIPTION OF EMOTIONAL ACTIVITIES 

Now that we know something of the physiological processes involved in emotional behavior, we may be able to sketch typical emotional patterns.

Nonemergency behavior. The greater portion of any individual's time is spent in conditions of relative calm, without any need for emergency behavior. Subjectively a person experiences a passive type of happiness which may be in marked con-

PSYCHOLOGY 

trast with some preceding condition of violent emotional tension. 

Objectively such a person appears relaxed, his movements are usually co-ordinated, free from tension, and relatively slow. His voice is relatively low in pitch and his flow of words suggests poise. His autonomic nervous system and the viscera and glands which it innervates are functioning in an efficient manner. There is a steady output of nervous energy which keeps the body in a state of even tonus. There is a sustained contraction of the blood vessels, the pulse is regular, the pupil becomes smaller than during periods of excitement and the eyeball tends to recede in its socket, the digestive processes proceed efficiently with strong peristaltic action of the stomach and intestines and free flow of digestive secretions, the smooth muscles of the skin relax and the skin texture becomes soft. 

In short, the individual is in a condition of vegetative happiness. This state is a relief if the person has just been through some violent experience. Ordinarily, it is sooner or later interrupted by some environmental stress or some internal conflict. 

The average person, however, does not attempt to maintain such a vegetative calm for too prolonged a period. He has learned to enjoy emotional turmoil just as keenly as he enjoys intervening periods of emotional calm. 

Various aspects of emergency behavior. Emergency behavior is never simple. Even in its early appearance in an untrained child it is complicated. It becomes still more complicated with experience.

An emergency implies exposure to a situation that is unexpected, violent, or contains some factors to which the individual has no means of quick or easy adjustment. 

1. There is a change in the overt skeletal reaction. This is the sort of behavior we have already described as trial-and-error behavior. The individual departs from organized and habitual reactions and makes random movements, usually increasing the violence and speed of his reactions. 

2. There is a stimulation of the sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system. This stimulation leads to the combination of visceral and glandular effects which we have already outlined.

There have been some interesting speculations as to how

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

167 and why a violent stimulation affects the sympathetic segment so strikingly. One older theory maintains that stimulation of the sympathetic segment in intense emotional situations is due to an overflow of neural energy when such energy cannot find an adequate outlet in normal skeletal reactions. In response to a mild stimulus a few reactions are usually made by a combination of skeletal structures which unite in a co-ordinated act. With more stimulation, such a response cannot take care of all the energy and so it spreads to other larger muscles and those not usually involved. When even a widespread skeletal reaction is incompetent to take care of all the energy generated by the exciting situation there may be a further overflow which brings about involvement of the autonomic system. 

A more recent theory is that of chronaxie. According to this theory, the pathway that a neural stimulation takes is determined by the relative chronaxie of the possible pathways. [45]

Chronaxie is the index of excitability of a tissue. It is found in this manner: The minimal current needed to excite the nerve is determined. Then a current twice this strength is applied to the same nerve and the time needed for the nerve to respond to this current (which is twice the threshold strength) is found. 

The length of time that this current must be applied to get a reaction is called the chronaxie of that nerve.

It has been found that the nerves of the cerebrospinal system (those going to the muscles which move the bones) are much more sensitive than the nerves which lead to the sympathetic ganglia (those affecting the smooth muscles of the viscera). 

With stimuli of minor intensity the easiest pathway will be to the skeletal musculature, a relatively small portion going to the sympathetic segment of the autonomic system. With an increase in intensity the more resistant sympathetic pathways may be made to function. [45, p. 13] 

3. The activity of the sympathetic mechanisms reinforce skeletal activity. The various emergency functions of the sympathetic segment supply energy for violent activity by the whole body. Vegetative processes are slowed down or stopped and the bodily forces are mobilized for intense activity. These adjustments require much more time than do skeletal acts. Hence, while the first skeletal responses to an emergency are soon made, the

PSYCHOLOGY 

surging up of reserves takes considerable time. Smooth muscle reacts much more slowly than skeletal muscle, and it takes still longer for the ductless glands to become active and to affect the organism through the influence of the hormones secreted. It is this difference in time that gives emotions some of their most striking characteristics. After the initial stimulus has come and gone, perhaps, the individual stimulated becomes aware of the surging up of tension, and of changes in a great many physiological processes.

To summarize the situation briefly: An individual is confronted with some situation and responds with the mechanism شره 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 160 180 200 220 240 260 280 300 320 Seconds

FIG. 27. Curves showing time relationships between (A) skeletal, (B) visceral, and (C) glandular components of emotional reactions. 

All three are initiated by a stimulus acting at the extreme left. The skeletal movement is completed while the visceral movement is getting started and long before the glandular reaction becomes manifest. 

The height of the curve represents degree of excitement. that is capable of the quickest and easiest reaction. This is the cerebrospinal skeletal system. If such a reaction is completely adequate, the situation is no longer an exciting stimulus for the individual. If such a simple skeletal action is inadequate, those centers which offer a higher resistance to stimulation also respond; namely, the sympathetic centers. As shown in Fig. 27, the smooth muscle and glandular reactions require much more time to manifest their influence; hence, emotional behavior based upon their activity appears with relative slowness. In fact, these may be reaching their peak of activity long after the original emergency has passed. Hence, we have the anachronism of getting ready to deal with an emergency long after the crisis has passed. 

These considerations have been checked by the experimental observation of animals in the laboratory. Emotional tensions in animals have been observed to persist for as long as twenty minutes after they received the emotional stimulation.

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

169 These time relations have led to some erroneous interpretations. Because overt behavior comes quicker than visceral reactions, it has been thought that the skeletal activity caused the visceral response. The preceding discussion should make clear the fallacy involved in such reasoning. The emotional stimulus sets off the entire emotional pattern, including the skeletal reaction, the smooth muscle response, and the reactions of the endocrine glands. The internal responses are just as much a response to the original stimulus as are the skeletal reactions. The reason they come later is because they require more time to function. 

The older theories were based on the old fallacy which assumed that, if one event preceded a second event, it was a cause of the second event. 

4. There is a subjective aspect to emotional experiences. 

The subjective experience of emotion is probably dependent upon a number of elements of the total emotional pattern. An individual is certainly aware of the overt activity in which he engages. 

The first overt response he interprets as a reaction to some specific exciting situation. The change in visceral activity and the other aspects of autonomic function he can discern in the form of visceral tensions, changes in general tonus, and in changes in metabolic processes. While there has been a tendency in the past to identify these subjective experiences with emotion, and to exclude the skeletal adjustments, such a limited conception is not warranted. To hit an enemy is certainly as integral a part of an emotional adjustment as the feeling of tension in the pit of one's stomach.

VARIOUS ASPECTS OF EMOTIONAL LEARNING 

While an adult's emotional reactions should be different from those of an infant, some adults are relatively immature emotionally. Just as one may find adults who are incompetent to use language, to read, to operate a typewriter, to hit a target, or to perform a problem in algebra because of a lack of adequate training, so one may find adults who fly into a useless rage at the slightest thwarting, who scream with terror at the sight of a harmless insect, who tremble at a peal of thunder, who hide from people, or who literally collapse at the slightest discomfort because of a lack of emotional education. Furthermore, much adult

PSYCHOLOGY 

conduct called emotional is far removed from anything that might be described as emergency behavior. Starting with a common origin, various lines of development may be traced which eventuate in various kinds of behavior having little to relate them, except a common origin. 

Learning better methods for meeting emergencies.

Since the usual cause of primary emotional behavior is some threat, some thwarting, or some emergency, the most logical improvement in emotional behavior would be the development of better means for meeting emergencies. That is to say, the most rational type of emotional learning is learning to make more efficient overt reactions to the objective situation which made emotional behavior necessary. We do not improve our fears; instead, we learn better ways of dealing with those situations which make us afraid. We do not improve our angers; rather, we learn to deal intelligently with the situations that made us angry. The presence of an emotional pattern is evidence that the best overt adjustment has not been made. We should learn to substitute skilled, intelligent reactions for the disorganized behavior which characterizes emotional behavior. 

However, the substitution of a completely mechanical, unemotional, or habitual reaction for previous emotional activities should not be construed as evidence that the individual has made the best social, moral, or economic adjustment. It is easy to find a person who is completely complacent in the performance of an inefficient or immoral act. The elimination of emotion by overt adjustment means adjustment from the individual point of view. 

To increase the efficiency of a person who has got into a rut, it is often necessary to upset his complacency, to get him maladjusted, that is, to make him emotional, so that he may be incited to do something different from his routine performance, and possibly do a better performance. Motivation, as we have seen, is often a disruption of the complacency of an individual. 

Observation of rats in an experimental situation has verified the fact that there is an inverse relationship between emotionality and stereotyping of behavior. Emotional rats manifested greater variability than relatively nonemotional animals running in the same maze. If, through definite direction, the animal can be made to avoid emotional stimuli, he will develop stereotyped be-

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

171 havior; if an emotional stimulus cannot be avoided, the animal will manifest more variability of behavior. [23] Learning to disguise emotional behavior. Because of conventions, social pressures, and because frank emotional behavior places us at the mercy of our enemies, or because of selfdeceit, we soon learn that it pays to refrain from undisguised emotional expression. For example, the girl who guilelessly makes evident her love for a boy places herself at a social disadvantage. We must learn to mask our emotions if we do not wish to be ridiculed and victimized. 

The forms that such disguises take are exceedingly numerous. (a) A person may react to an indifferent situation in order to conceal the fact that he is really being influenced by another. (b) 

One may attempt to refrain from all emotional expression, giving himself away only by inadvertent movements which he cannot control. (c) Another may manifest one type of emotional behavior in order to cover a tendency to react in another manner. For ex- ample, hateful behavior may really be a cover for love. [42] 

The display of emotions to influence other persons. 

A child does not progress far in his life before he learns that other persons respond more readily to him when he manifests some emotion than when he remains unemotional in his behavior. 

Others respond to him when he cries, laughs, pouts, throws a temper tantrum, becomes angry, fights, becomes afraid, loves, hates, and the like. He soon learns to cultivate emotional behavior, not so much because he is biologically or physiologically maladjusted or faced with some emergency situation as because of the way others respond to his expression of emotions. It makes little difference whether the emotion is genuine or not; the important element is whether others act as though it were. 

The development of emotions of a child under such circumstances evolves from the close observation of others in order to discover how they respond to his emotional expressions. When the child is closely associated with a person who is sensitive to one type of emotion in others (love, fear, anger, or the like), he tends to develop the behavior which goes with that emotion, because he finds that such behavior influences the other person. The way in which children modify their crying in order to gain their way with other persons illustrates this principle. In the early stages of an

PSYCHOLOGY 

infant's life, crying is one element in the mass activity which follows a maladjustment of any sort. [7] Before the child is much more than three or four months of age, he modifies his crying to the sort of cry that will appeal to those around him. [5] 

This use of emotional expression is carried through all aspects of life. The impassioned orator can move his audience more than the collected speaker who deals in abstractions. Zeal is a part of good salesmanship. Tears will gain arguments better than logic. Smiles will often result more quickly in raises in salary than will efficiency. We gain help quicker by manifesting distress than by attempting to do the best we can in an emergency. 

Since most of us decry the unmitigated shamming of an emotion, most persons try to effect a compromise with themselves by attempting to support expression with a genuine emotion. As long as the emotion is real, it seems to be quite acceptable to utilize an emotion to gain our ends with others. 

Expression of emotions for the dramatic effect. The function of dramatic art is to convey a message to the observer. 

If this end is accomplished, it makes no difference whether the actor actually experiences the emotion he is enacting or not. To be sure, with the inexperienced actor, the presence of a genuine emotion is more likely to lead to effective dramatization than the absence of subjective feeling with entire emphasis upon technique. 

For example, when children act emotional scenes for motion pictures they are often given a real reason for crying or laughing which may have no relation to the plot. Experienced actors, on the other hand, may become so skilled in their art that they do not need to experience the genuine emotion each time they act a part. 

In fact, the actor accomplishes more by knowing the conventional way of expressing an emotion than he does by being genuinely emotional.

The cultivation of visceral tensions. In ingrown forms of emotional learning, visceral tensions become an end in themselves; the individual places himself in situations, and acts in such ways, that the visceral tensions become pronounced and lead to no relevant overt behavior. The cultivation of visceral tensions represents a secondary displacement of the original function of emotional behavior, namely, the adjustment to an emergency. 

Some of the reasons for such displacement are as follows:

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

173 1. Some ingrown emotions are cultivated because they are enjoyable. The beginnings of such learning can be observed in a child. He may inadvertently drop a tin plate. The noise frightens him but, after he discovers that no real damage has been done, a smile spreads over his face—he really enjoyed being frightened. 

Then he proceeds to drop the plate deliberately, showing signs of fright before it hits the floor, and laughing with glee at the sport of experiencing fright.

Adults achieve the same end by means of some of the devices found at amusement parks-being dropped in a parachute, being twirled around, having the floor suddenly drop, and the like. 

Daredevil, reckless stunts achieve the same end. Of course, these may be done for the benefit of the onlookers, but in many instances they are executed because the actor wants a thrill for himself. If he did not enjoy it more than the audience does, he would not be likely to continue for long.

The same process is found in more sophisticated form in such activities as reading novels, going to plays, visiting art exhibits, listening to fine music, and the like. These are all socially approved forms of ingrown emotional behavior. 

In most spheres the cultivation of internal tensions does no particular harm. In certain social situations, on the other hand, this emphasis often precludes a successful adjustment. For example, the adolescent may sit around studying his tensions, wondering "if this is love." When someone comes along who succeeds in making him feel good he believes he has found love. He fails to find the real social adjustment which comes from making overt adjustments to others. He loves himself, while believing that he loves another, because that other person makes him feel good. 

2. Some ingrown emotions are cultivated as an escape from the need for making an overt adjustment. Failure to deal adequately with an emergency situation accentuates the emotional tensions but, at the same time, the individual is aware that he is acting incompetently and is in a mood to welcome some means of avoiding further active attempts to adjust to the difficulty. Attention to the emotion itself provides a ready excuse for failure to make any further attempts. This is especially easy for one who has been taught that emotions are undesirable and should be con-

PSYCHOLOGY 

trolled. By devoting his attention to his own visceral tensions, such a person attempts to forget the actual emergency which confronts him. Furthermore, this substitution may be effective also as a means of diverting the attention of others from his real difficulty, when it is something he would rather not have known. 

He talks glibly about his fears, about his worries, about how he must try to control his temper, in order to hide the cause for his fears, worries, or his anger.

Such a device appears foolish when the nature of the emergency is extremely obvious. For example, if a person were confronted with a vicious animal, it would be ridiculous for him to devote his energies to overcoming his fears of the animal. What he needs to do is to deal adequately with the animal. 

As long as we maintain the tradition that certain emotions should not be permitted to function there will be a need for such disguises. In some cases they do no particular harm but in others they lead to chronic distortions of behavior and even to pathological mental conditions. The attempt to disguise or to distort overt expression leads to an accentuation of the internal tension even though adults may fail to recognize this relationship in complex situations. It is illustrated by the comment made by a little boy who was badly frightened by a dog and whose father, at the same time, was telling him that he should not be afraid. Finally, he said, "No, daddy, I am not afraid now, but my stomach still is." 

3. The fear of emotions often leads to the cultivation of ingrown emotions. Certain individuals become unpleasantly preoccupied with autonomic tensions. For various reasons they feel obliged to eliminate them. They may attempt to accomplish this end by avoiding emotion-provoking situations or by refraining from overt activity which might indicate the presence of the tensions. Attempts to evade in this manner are often unsuccessful. 

The attempt to avoid emotionally toned situations often ends in giving emotional significance to incidents which ordinarily would be commonplace. The attempt to refrain from overt expression while the aggravating situation remains unchanged often leads to an accentuation of the internal tensions. 

Whether the individual cultivates his autonomic tensions because of their pleasurable aspects or attempts to shun them because he regards them as unpleasant, he has distorted the function

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

175 of emotional behavior. He becomes preoccupied with his emotions instead of utilizing them as instruments to make better adjustments.

The effect of learning on the total emotional pattern. 

Whereas emotional behavior has its inception in the need on the part of an organism to adjust to some emergency or to some vital biological need, it may become so transformed as to make such needs appear insignificant. The individual may learn to deal successfully with the objective threats; he may become engrossed in disguising his behavior so that others will not know the struggles through which he is passing; he may learn to cultivate the expression of emotions for the purpose of influencing other persons for personal reasons; he may cultivate expression for dramatic purposes; or he may cultivate his own emotions for the enjoyment they give him, to escape from the dangers of overt adjustments to difficulties, or because of some learned moral inhibition against the emotions themselves. The changes effected by such learning processes may be so great that the resultant behavior bears little resemblance to the original emergency behavior of the infant. 

We all become adept at emotional distortion, and it becomes difficult to discern when a person is emotional and when he is not. 

These facts complicate tremendously our study of the emotional reactions of any one individual. When we find a person who has the habit of showing fear, for example, we cannot assume that he has been exposed to emergency situations which brought out fear reactions in him so repeatedly that fear became a habit. 

Instead, it could be that he has associated with a fearful individual and through this association learned to imitate the fear behavior. 

Or, it could be that he learned to enjoy the visceral tensions that go with fear and developed fear behavior for the enjoyment he derived from it.

Certainly, any attempts to change the emotional patterns of an individual should be varied according to which factor predominated in the original learning. For example, suppose a person is attempting to escape from persistent fears. If he developed the fears because he has been exposed to many emergencies, he could be taught other ways of dealing with emergencies. If he developed the fears because he enjoyed the visceral tensions which go with fear, he could be taught cther ways of enjoying himself. If

PSYCHOLOGY 

he learned to fear because his mother was responsive to his fear behavior, he could be taught other ways to influence his mother, or he could be made to associate with others who were not responsive to fear behavior.

It follows that it is not possible to judge the significance of an emotional act by a study of the act alone. For example, the fact that a person is crying tells one little about the significance of the crying. He may be crying because his eyes have been irritated by a bit of dust; he may be crying because he has suffered a bitter disappointment; he may be crying because he is extremely happy; he may be crying because he has been thwarted by some person; he may be crying because he is in love or because he has been disappointed in love; or he may be suffering physical pain. 

Every emotional action is a unique action and its significance cannot be determined arbitrarily 

THE EXPRESSION OF THE EMOTIONS 

Who has not been deceived in his attempts to interpret the significance of emotional behavior in others? We discover a person hates us after his behavior had led us to believe that he was kindly disposed toward us. An inner turmoil may be hidden beneath a smooth exterior. Joyful behavior may be a mask to cover sorrow. Has psychology any methods or devices which make it possible to look beneath these conventional masks and to interpret emotional behavior in others?

In judging an emotional activity it is almost impossible to separate the different aspects of the subject's behavior. (a) Some of it is essentially the subject's attempt to make an adaptive adjustment to the difficulty. (b) Some results from the autonomic activity and shows itself in such behavior as changes in breathing, pallor, flushing, and the like. (c) Some shows itself in what may be called by-products of the situation; namely, in-co-ordination, tremors, and apparently inane activities. [13]

Interpretation of overt emotional behavior of infants. 

The interpretation of the emotional reactions of infants and young children should be relatively simple owing to the fact that they have not learned how to disguise the real meaning of their acts. 

Experiments have shown that the problem is not so easy as it appears at first glance. The scientific advantage of the simplicity

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

177 of the behavior of infants has been destroyed, at times, by interpreting the child's behavior as one might that of an adult. For example, if a child acts in a manner similar to that of an adult who is angry, we have no warrant for assuming that the child is angry. If the child acts toward his mother in a manner similar to that of an adult who is in love, we may be entirely in the wrong if we assume that the child is loving his mother. 

1. The attempts to interpret emotions by tracing them to unlearned emotional patterns have not been fruitful. Some earlier psychologists thought that a neonate (a newborn child) could manifest emotions, such as the following, without any learning on his part: fear, anger, disgust, tender emotion, distress, lust, curiosity, feelings of subjection, feelings of elation, feelings of loneliness, appetite or craving, feelings of ownership or possession, feelings of creativeness, and amusement. [6] The best reason for rejecting the view that the child is born with such emotional patterns is that they cannot be found. Close observation of infants by one group of observers seemed to give evidence that three emotions were manifested: rage, fear, and love. Fear seemed to be elicited by loud noises or by loss of support; rage seemed to be evoked by restraint of movement; love seemed to result from stroking and fondling. The other eleven emotional patterns in the list just cited were strikingly absent. While these observations led to a radical departure from what had been more or less widely accepted, more careful experiments have thrown doubt on the presence of even these three original emotional patterns. 

2. Interpretation demands knowledge of stimulus as well as infant's reactions. The emotion of an infant cannot be identified correctly by the kind of behavior he manifests. One experimenter took motion pictures of infants after they had been stimulated by four different kinds of situations; (1) hunger resulting from deferred feeding; (2) sudden dropping through space calculated to arouse fear reactions; (3) the pricking with a pin to arouse pain; and (4) active restraint of movement of the head, designed to produce anger. These pictures (eliminating any part that would suggest the nature of the stimulating situation) were exhibited to college students. These observers were informed that the stimuli were limited to the four enumerated, and were

PSYCHOLOGY 

asked to judge whether the behavior shown in the pictures was the behavior pattern of hunger, pain, anger, or fear. Half the observers called hunger pain, a quarter of them called hunger rage. 

Less than a third of the observers named the behavior after restraint of the infant's head as anger, and almost as many called it pain. In short, the observers could have guessed at random and have replied almost as accurately as they did by inspection of the pictures. When they were permitted to see the situations which gave rise to the behavior they judged more correctly. That is, when the observers had knowledge of what caused the behavior, they named the emotion in accordance with what they thought it should be under the circumstances. [43] 

This inability to judge correctly the significance of emotional behavior in infants may be interpreted in two ways: It may be argued that the results depend largely upon defective judging ability on the part of the observers. The second possibility seems to be the more correct one; namely, that infants vary so much in their emotional reactions that consistent interpretation is impossible. Emotional behavior is judged more by the situation to which the individual is reacting than by the particular form of behavior that he adopts in meeting that situation. We call angry behavior anything that a person does when he is thwarted. We say he is afraid when he is confronted with a difficulty so overwhelming that he can make no adequate response. 

3. The emotional activities of infants have meaning if they are regarded as varied and changing attempts to adjust to emergency situations. An infant's responses to emotional situations are likely to be random and nonspecific, varying in intensity somewhat in proportion to the challenge inherent in the situation. His responses are likely to be either aggressive or docile. Docility may be the consequence of situations which seem to offer no challenge, such as mild tones, soft touches, rocking movements, and the like. 

Aggressiveness is likely to be the reaction to violent situations. 

A retreating response which may superficially resemble docility is likely to occur when the child has made an attempt to meet a challenge by aggression and has failed. Such a response may come initially when the infant is confronted with a situation so sudden or so violent that any aggression is overpowered at the first instant. Instead of naming these three forms of behavior

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

179 rage, fear, and love (which involves reading adult feelings into them), it would be well to consider them as crude classifications of reaction to situations with varying amounts of challenge. In a soothing situation, an infant tends to relax and go to sleep; in a challenging situation, the infant tends to increase his motor responses in an unpredictable manner; in a situation that is overwhelming, the infant manifests violent motor activity interspersed with a cessation of behavior but with an increase of tension which shows itself in indirect signs of inner tension and in later overt activity of a still more violent sort. 

To summarize: When the observer discerns the situation to which the infant is reacting, he designates an emotion which fits in with that situation. When he sees only the behavior of the infant without any knowledge as to the antecedent circumstances, his judgment of the emotion constitutes a guess as to what the situation was. His guesses are not accurate because the behavior of the infant is so indefinite and variable. 

The facial expression of emotions. It is common knowledge that emotions are shown in the face, but the degree to which the observer can correctly interpret facial expression has been vastly overrated. The facial expressions of athletes during strenuous competition and after partial collapse from such competition show extreme tensions in the facial muscles during strain and lowered muscle tonus during extreme fatigue and partial collapse. [36] Are there general laws of facial expression?

Variability of facial expressions. Extensive studies have shown that there is a great deal of variation in the kind of facial expression that may be made to similar emotional situations. 

There is really no facial expression typical of any situation. Furthermore, when the subjects who have been utilized in an experiment with real emotional situations are recalled and are asked to repeat the emotional expression that they had shown when stimulated before, their expressions are not the same. It would seem that the actual expression and the traditional expression are vastly different. It also has been found that most subjects have but two or three facial patterns which they tend to use in all situations whether these situations are designed essentially to call forth pain, surprise, anger, exasperation, crying, disgust, sex responses, or revulsion.

PSYCHOLOGY 

In spite of these variations, no matter how much the expression of an emotion may be inhibited, modified, or intentionally assumed in the social relationships of adult life, there is a language of expression which seems to remain behind these disguises.

Methods used for studying facial expression. This being the case, psychologists have concerned themselves with attempts to determine the way in which facial expressions of emotions are produced, the accuracy with which their meaning can be understood by others, and the way in which skill in such understanding is acquired. The general procedure that has been used has been to give subjects different kinds of emotional stimulations and then to attempt to obtain records of the combinations of expression which they manifest. This reduction of a dynamic process to a static record, or cross section, of that process involves a loss of one of the most significant elements of emotional behavior; namely, the perspective which comes from viewing the entire emotional sequence.

We usually judge an emotion by the features in motion, by the play of expression, and not by any static pose. A motion picture is likely to be more significant than a still picture; a motion picture with sound gives more emotional expression than one without sound; the observation of the whole person in activity is more revealing than a momentary cross section of isolated parts. 

Even though admitting this need for complete perspective, investigators have felt that it is necessary to break down the total performance and to study the parts separately. 

1. Drawings. Various methods have been used to obtain a static representation of emotional expression. The Rudolph sketches represent a pioneer attempt in this field. [41] This collection contains 68 drawings made by a painter who retouched and somewhat idealized them to fit his conceptions of anatomy and emotional expression. He believed that all facial expressions were based on a few primitive types which could be classified as reactions of approach or of withdrawal. Fourteen of these pictures have more recently been selected and incorporated into a test of ability to read the significance of facial expressions. [32] 2. Facial models.

The way in which the different com-

An early form of such a model shows the face in profile and divides it into four parts: the mouth, the eyes, the brows, and the nose. A profile supposed to represent anger was judged correctly by only 14 persons out of 716, that is, by about 2 per cent of the subjects. Some of the other profiles fared a little better: one designed to express horror was judged correctly by 57 per cent of the subjects; disgust was judged correctly by

[9] Another experimenter showed that the ability to judge the intended expression of these profiles was strikingly improved when the experimenter gave the subject definite suggestions. It would seem that when one is given the meaning of an emotional expression, he reads into the face what he thinks it should mean. [25] 

More recently, a facial model has been constructed using front-view parts. [22] The parts used in this model are shown in Fig. 29. By this means the number of variations may be increased and the expressive lines of the face can be made much more pronounced. Even with this improvement, it would seem that the use of such a model should be limited to demonstrating how facial expressions may vary with different combinations of component features, and that it should not be used to test the ability of individuals to discern the significance of emotional expression. [21] 

3. Photographs. A number of psychologists have prepared sets of photographs taken while subjects were being emotionally stimulated. By this means, attempts have been made to analyze the parts of the face used to express different emotions. [18] Others have taken photographs of persons who consciously posed in an attempt to express certain emotions.

The judge may not get the exact emotion that the photograph is designed to portray, but he is likely to guess correctly within a general area. For example, a photograph designed to express love was judged as love by only 10 per cent of the observers making judgments, but it was judged happiness by 68 per cent of the observers. A photograph designed to express mirth was judged happiness by 51 per cent and mirth by 49 per cent. In other words, observers differ in the fine shades of meaning given to photographs designed to express different emotions, but they agree fairly well in the general type of emotional pattern. [46, p. 251] 

We may conclude, therefore, that a posed emotion can be fairly well recognized from a still photograph of the actor's face. [27] 

There is evidence that the person expressing his emotions through his face learns to conform to conventional forms of expression, and that the individual who attempts to understand the significance of such facial expressions acquires interpretative skill through learning. All individuals tend to use certain muscles, muscle groups, or expressions in the majority of their expressive reactions, to the exclusion of other muscle groups. Most persons are poor actors because they have learned but a few forms of facial expression. There is a language of the face which the good actor must learn. Most of us could say more to our associates by means of facial expression if we studied patterns of facial expression and learned how to use them more appropriately. [29]

Children improve with age in their ability to judge the significance of posed photographs. [20] In one experiment, six posed photographs from a standardized collection were presented to children ranging in age from three to fourteen years of age. It was found that laughter is the easiest pose to recognize and contempt the hardest. Laughter was recognized at three years, pain at five years, anger at seven years, fear-horror at nine years, surprise at eleven years, and contempt at fourteen years. [39, pp. 258-259] · 

Adults improve with practice in their ability to interpret the significance of posed facial expression. Training on alternate days through a period of ten days increased accuracy by 51 per cent in one experiment. Those who were poorest at the beginning of the training made greater improvement than those who were

PSYCHOLOGY 

good at first, showing that practice tends to produce uniformity of judgments. It also was found that those who make snap judgments based upon the total impression judge much better than those who take an analytical attitude. [21] 

Summary of studies of facial expression of emotions. 

The findings in connection with facial expression of emotions may be summarized as follows: (a) While a posed emotion can be fairly well recognized from the still photograph of an actor's face, the face reveals the significance of emotions best when it is in action, by the play of expression rather than by a static pose. (b) Judgment is more accurate when the entire facial pattern is considered than when an attempt is made to analyze the significance of the various components. (c) While there are great individual differences in the way the face is used to express emotions, there are conventional patterns which the individual learns to use and which observers learn to interpret. There is a vocabulary of the face. It would seem that one could learn to make his face more expressive through training. (d) The conventional facial expressions are quite different from the original patterns upon which they are based. That is to say, facial expressions are used by adult civilized humans more for the purpose of transmitting messages to others than to express their own emotions. 

Vocal expression of the emotions. It is a commonly accepted fact that a person reveals his emotions definitely through his voice. Is the voice a primary factor in such expression or is it merely an adjunct to other forms of expression? If the voice is important in and of itself, what qualities of the voice contribute most to its effectiveness? 

1. The infant's cry is of ambiguous significance: One experiment with infants shows clearly that listeners cannot tell, from the sound that the infant makes, the significance of his cry. When the cry alone was heard, about one-fifth of the listeners ascribed the infant's crying to colic; whereas, when they saw what had happened to the child to make him cry, none of them mentioned colic, although the sounds were identical in both tests. It seems that the infant does not know how to make himself understood by his crying alone. [43] 2. Meanings of vocal expressions are learned. Another experimenter has shown that school children improve in their ability

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

185 to interpret the significance of vocal expression. These children were given the task of interpreting the emotional significance of letters pronounced by individuals attempting to express such emotions as happiness, unhappiness, anger, fear, and surprise. There was an increase in accuracy of judgment with age, school experience, and intelligence. [20] 

The analytical study of the voices of singers and orators supports the theory that vocal expression of the emotions is a learned and highly sophisticated art. The impassioned speeches of actors and orators show an unusual mobility and range of pitch in vocal expression; whereas an increase in the emotional fervor of an unsophisticated individual is more likely to result merely in raised pitch or an increase in intensity. [37] 

3. The vibrato is a learned technique of emotional expression. Trained musicians manifest a peculiar ringing quality, which is accepted as a form of emotional expression, and which has been called the vibrato. It is a periodic rise and fall in pitch, or a periodic waxing and waning of loudness, or both. The listener often cannot distinguish whether the effect is achieved by pitch or intensity pulsations. The rate of these pulsations is from 

5 to 10 per second (usually 6 to 8); and the pitch variations may be from 0.1 to 1.35 full tones (usually between .25 and .85 full tones). The vibrato, so widely accepted as a conventional form of emotional expression, is not a natural reaction resulting from emotion; instead, it must be carefully cultivated and can be perfected only by intensive training. [38]

In short, the use of the voice for emotional expression by adults, and especially by singers and orators, is a highly artificial and specialized performance. Nevertheless, these sophisticated sounds are better understood by the listener than the more primitive forms of vocal expression because civilized man has been trained to interpret them. 

THE UNMASKING OF EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

Overt emotional behavior is much more easily controlled or disguised than are some of the internal visceral and glandular reactions. While a person may be insulted by a friend and may have the impulse to hit the offender, he may learn to refrain from such overt assault, although he may still have the visceral tensions

PSYCHOLOGY 

and glandular reactions which naturally result from such an insult. 

It may appear to an observer that the insult is being taken with a good grace, whereas the underlying resentment may be acute. 

Psychologists have, therefore, been much concerned with devices for detecting the internal emotional responses of an individual when these do not harmonize with observed conduct. Some of the devices that have resulted from these endeavors have not had any practical value, being too cumbersome and intricate for anything but laboratory use. Other devices which seemed impractical at first have turned out to be easily adapted for common usage. 

We shall describe some of the most common of these devices. 

The psychogalvanic reflex. The psychogalvanic reflex (abbreviated P.G.R.) is the change in electrical skin resistance which follows sensory stimulation or accompanies thinking proc- 6v.

Other names which have been given to this phenomenon are: the galvanic skin response (abbreviated G.S.R.), the electrodermal response (abbreviated E.D.R.), the galvanic reaction, the orectic (appetitive) reflex, the general autonomic reflex, and the sympathetic reflex. This diversity of names is indicative of the widespread differences of opinion as to the nature and significance of changes in the electrical potentials of the skin occurring with certain types of nervous activity. 

Methods for obtaining the psychogalvanic reflex. By one method this reaction is obtained by attaching electrodes to any two parts of the skin and connecting these through a galvanometer, without any other source of electrical potential introduced into the circuit. With a sensitive galvanometer, it will be found that there is a change in potential, as designated by a movement of the galvanometer needle, with sensory stimulation or with shifts

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

187 in mental activity. A second method consists of measuring the resistance of the body by the Wheatstone bridge method. This method is illustrated in Fig. 32. 

There is no disagreement as to the fundamental fact that changes in electrical potential do occur under either method. The disagreements that are found have resulted primarily from the fact that investigators have made unwarranted statements about the significance of the reflex. 

Psychogalvanic reflex depends upon changes in sweat secretions. The majority of the evidence points to the fact that the electrical changes are the result of changes in amount of secretion by the sweat glands. [46, p. 281] When the sweat gland activity is inhibited by use of atropin, the galvanic skin reactions are abolished or strikingly reduced. Motion pictures taken by means of a microscope show that there is an emergence of droplets from the sweat pores during the psychogalvanic reflex responses. [16] 

Finally, there is a latent time between the presentation of the stimulus and the galvanic reaction, which would suggest that it is dependent upon some such slow reaction as the secretion of sweat. It is known that the sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system. It would seem, then, that the psychogalvanic reflex is dependent upon stimulation of the sympathetic segment. This has been verified by cutting the sympathetic chain of an animal in such a manner that all sympathetic fibers to a forelimb are severed. Such an operation abolishes the psychogalvanic reflex in the limb. 

Stimulation of the sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system has other effects than an increase in secretion of the sweat glands. For example, such innervation causes: acceleration of the heart, constriction of the blood vessels, rise of blood pressure, inhibition of digestion, contraction of the sphincters of the bladder and anus, dilation of the bronchi, the liberation of adrenin from the adrenal glands, the liberation of sugar from the liver, the liberation of red corpuscles from the spleen, the erection of hair or the formation of goose pimples, the dilation of the pupils. This combination of reactions occurs in emergency situations. If the psychogalvanic reflex is an indicator of sweat secretions, which is a part of the complex emergency pattern of behavior, it would appear that it might be an ideal index of the

PSYCHOLOGY 

innervation of the sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system and thus indicate the operation of emergency behavior, that is, of emotional behavior. 

An experimental check showed that there is not absolute uniformity in changes in the constriction of the blood vessels, changes in blood pressure, and the psychogalvanic reflex. [15] It would seem, therefore, that, while stimulation of the sympathetic segment causes a broad combination of responses, these do not occur in exactly the same time sequence or in the same degree. 

The use of the psychogalvanic reflex as an index of emotional behavior is, consequently, not infallible. In other words, sweat secretion is not the only factor affecting the galvanic skin responses, and emotions are not the only factors affecting the sweat secretions. With these qualifications it may be concluded that it is, nevertheless, a fairly good indicator of innervation of the sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system, and consequently of those emergency reactions which we call emotional. [46, p. 

284] It has not been found possible to use this reaction to indicate the kind of emotion that a person is experiencing or to give an accurate quantitative indication of the degree of emotional tension. 

It would seem safe to use the psychogalvanic response as an index that the individual may be experiencing a change in his degree of emotional tensions; but it would also seem to be chasing a phantom to attempt to reduce this response to such definite determinations as when the person had 10 units of fear, 20 units of love, 5 units of anger, or the like.

Respiration as an emotional index. While part of the respiratory apparatus is controlled by the cerebrospinal nervous system and is under conscious control, an essential part of it is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and, consequently, involved in emotional behavior. The smooth muscles control the bore of the bronchial tubes. These tubes open wide in emergency situations, thus reducing the resistance offered to the passage of air to the lungs and supplying the additional oxygen which the body needs when reacting to unusual situations. The diaphragm, intercostal muscles, and abdominal muscles, which are the main respiratory muscles, are controlled by the skeletal system. This arrangement accounts for a very frequent occurrence, namely the autonomic response of the breathing in emergencies with the con-

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

189 scious attempt on the part of the individual to control the breathing so that breathing changes will not be apparent to an observer. 

This dual control of respiration makes it appear probable that respiration would be a good indicator of any conflict between the natural emotional reaction of an individual and his efforts to suppress all evidence of such emotional behavior. 

Respiration affects emotional expression in another manner: through vocalization. We all are familiar with the emotional rising of the pitch of the voice in emotion, the choking, the catch in the voice, and the emotional stuttering and shakiness of the voice.

Psychologists have studied the changes of respiration during emotion with this in mind. The study of respiration, along with

Apparatus used to measure breathing. Various devices have been used to obtain a graphic record of breathing. 1. The girth-recording pneumograph. This pneumograph is essentially a hollow rubber tube that is kept distended by a coiled spring which it surrounds. It is shown in Fig. 33. One end is sealed and the other end connects with a smaller tube leading to a recording tambour. The pneumograph is strapped around the body, around either the chest or the abdomen; or one may be used at each position to record both chest and abdominal movements. 

When the body expands in breathing, the volume of air in the tube is increased; when it contracts, with expiration of air from the lungs, the volume is diminished. It is this change in air volume which moves the recording arm on the tambour up and down and

2. The breath-current recorder. The subject wears a breathing mask, inhaling fresh air through one tube and exhaling through another. A one-way valve in each tube makes it possible for the air to enter only through one tube and to be exhaled only through the other. A side tube activates a tambour so that the slightest flutter of the valve in the breathing tube is graphically recorded.

Variations in breathing. Breathing may vary in three ways: in rate, in depth, and in form. 

1. and 2. Changes in rate and depth. Physical exercise and emotional excitement affect breathing in the same manner, they make respiration faster and deeper. However, the first shock of an emotional stimulus may produce a sudden and temporary stopping of the breathing. There is a catching of the breath. 

Then there is a speeding up. If the excitement continues for a long period of time there is likely to be a gradual slowing of the rate and a gradual lessening of the depth, which tends to bring it back to the normal rate and depth. Excitement does not persist

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

191 at maximum for long periods and this return of the breathing to normal with persistent excitement is merely a bit of objective evi-, dence of that fact. 

3. Changes in form. Changes in the form of breathing may well be observed by a study of the inspiration-expiration ratio, or by the inspiration fraction (see Fig. 35). In either case the time consumed in inhaling and the time consumed in exhaling are measured separately. In the inspiration-expiration ratio the FIG. 35.-Breathing records as affected by tension. The upper curve is a normal breathing curve taken when the subject was relaxed. The lower curve is a record of the same subject when under tension. The downward movement shows quick inspiration; the rising curve, slower expiration. time taken for inspiration is divided by the time taken for expiration. In the inspiration fraction the time taken for inspiration is divided by the time of the complete cycle. [46, p. 262] 

The portion of the whole breathing cycle that is devoted to taking in of air (the inspiration fraction) is very small in singing, while in sudden fright it is very large. The inspiration fraction has been used in attempts to detect lying. It has been found that the inspiration fraction just before a response is the same whether a person tells a lie or tells the truth. If he tells a lie, the inspiration fraction increases. Since the general conditions which cause such an increase are excitement or fright, it has been concluded that the liar is likely to be excited by his lie and thus manifest the incriminating respiratory change. [8, 31] Circulatory changes as emotional indices. Whenever special demands are made upon the body, the blood becomes an important agent in supplying those needs. Such function may be accomplished both by changes in composition of the blood and by the quantity of blood flowing through the vascular system. Since chemical analyses of blood involve intricate techniques and consume considerable time, they have not been satisfactory as indicators of quick emotional changes.

Measures of changes in circulation have been more satisfactory. The flow of blood depends upon two factors: the force of the heartbeat and the resistance encountered in the blood vessels through which the blood moves. Therefore, both measures of the rate of heartbeat and measures of blood pressure have been used as indices of the circulatory changes and have proved to have some value in studies of emotional expression. 

The heart works automatically but its rate is regulated by two sets of nerves. The innervation from the sympathetic segment of the autonomic nervous system tends to accelerate the heartbeat, whereas innervation from the cranial segment, through the mediation of the vagus nerve, tends to retard or inhibit the heartbeat. Various hormones, likewise, influence the heart action. The most notable of these are adrenin and thyroxin. Through nervous connections in the brain, the heart is responsive also to external sensory stimuli and to certain stimuli from within the organism, such as high blood pressure. 

The fact that the heart action is influenced by such diverse factors and through so many media should serve as a warning against any temptation to give a simple interpretation to changes in heart action. In spite of the great amount of work that has been done in an attempt to use indices of heart action as emotional indicators, two of which we shall review, the multiple control of

BEHAVIOR 

heart action should provide a wholesome damper against overoptimism.

Effect of emotional stimulation upon heart action. Because the heart is so delicately responsive to many influences, it is not reasonable to expect any close relation between specific emotional situations and some particular heart pattern. Experiments have definitely shown, nevertheless, that the heart is sensitive to any increase in general excitement. Startle causes a prompt acceleration of the heart action. After this first response there is a quick recovery, which is followed by a secondary increase that is smaller in amount but more prolonged. 

This was demonstrated by an experiment in which the subject was actually frightened. A trick chair was used to tilt an unsuspecting, blindfolded subject suddenly backward, as though the chair back had given way entirely. The pulse shot up from an average of 84 to 104 beats, receded promptly to about 87 and then rose again to about 97, and then remained in this area. When the subject returned the next day and was placed in the same chair, he showed a high pulse rate in anticipation of the fall of the chair. 

The heart will beat faster and blood pressure will rise as a result of excitement or anticipated excitement. [3] 

Changes in blood pressure to detect deception. A number of experiments have shown that a witness who tells the truth is likely to have a small rise in blood pressure, whereas one who tells a lie will have a rather significant rise. Critical studies point to the fact that such changes in blood pressure are probably due to the excitement involved in deception and hence may be used in the same manner as the inspiration fraction in attempts to discover deception. [14, 33]

The most modern method for detecting liars is to take a combination of respiration, blood pressure, and heart-rate curves on a polygraph (which has been called a lie detector) and to attempt to determine from a study of the whole pattern whether a person is emotional or not when he replies to a significant question. If he shows emotional behavior, he may then be led to confess. Two individuals who have made extensive use of this device in police work claim that they have failed to discover the liar in less than 10 cases in 10,000 suspects. [28]

PSYCHOLOGY 

The detection of emotions though involuntary movements. When a person attempts to restrain an overt skeletal reaction that would naturally arise in an emotional situation, he usually discloses the presence of emotional tension by the inadvertent movement of some other portion of his body, even though he may be pretty clever in withholding a direct response. The checking of some vocal, retort may give rise to tremors of the lips, movements of the throat, and the like. A tendency to strike with the fist may be suppressed, but reveal itself by biting the lip or by twisting the foot. The poker player may repress any expression in his face, but reveal pleasure or disappointment with his cards 

FIG. 36.-The automato graph. The arm rests on the board which swings freely, supported from above. Any movement of the arm is recorded graphically by the writing point on the writing pad on the table. by involuntary movements which may be understood by one who has studied him closely. 

Various devices have been utilized to attempt to interpret these involuntary movements. One form has been variously called an automatograph, a planchette, or an autoscope. It is essentially a device by means of which small, involuntary movements of a part of the body, usually the hand, can be made visible or recorded in some manner (see Fig. 36). Superstitious individuals have thought that some variations of these autoscopes, especially the divining rod, dousing rod, and ouija board, were possessed of mysterious power to reveal secrets; but all they can do is to make evident what the person whose arm operates the mechanism is feeling or thinking. These automatic movements probably are merely symptoms that the person has failed in making a satis-

Such a device may indicate the presence of a conflict or some emotional tension but it tells nothing about the nature of factors producing the emotion. 

Free association methods for detecting emotions. Free association methods for the purpose of detecting emotions have received their widest use in clinical work. They have the advantage of being less artificial than methods requiring the use of apparatus fastened to the subject. They have the disadvantage of being more qualitative than the methods which use recording devices. This drawback may be more apparent than real, however. 

An instrument which makes a precise record may create an atmosphere of accuracy that is spurious. For example, it is possible to obtain accurate records of the action of the heart and an experimenter may thus feel that he has an instrument of precision for studying emotional behavior. He has an instrument of precision, to be sure, but the records must be interpreted qualitatively and the relation between his records and emotional patterns may be remote and unreliable. This is merely another way of saying that the clinician uses qualitative methods and must guess as to their significance, but that his guesses may enable him to get a better perspective than the laboratory man who attempts to read a precise graphic record which is influenced by a great many unknown factors.

Continuous method. The continuous method requires that the subject, beginning with a word selected at random or because it may appear to be related to soine emotional situation, continue to give response words in an endless sequence as rapidly as he can. Whereas this requirement may seem to be simple, it is almost impossible for any one long to continue such a series without hesitation. These points of hesitation, or complete cessation of response, are regarded as the significant points. They presumably indicate the presence of some emotional factor in the subject which impedes his free output. For example: A person may be told to begin with book and continue his associative responses. Suppose he replies: book, table, newspaper, movie actress, show, dark—and then hesitates or stops. The implication is that dark suggested another word or situation having some personal reference or emotional significance. To be sure, the examiner has no notion what this means in any specific sense; all he

EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR 

197 knows is that the individual probably has some emotional reaction. 

The real danger is that the clinician may think he knows more than he does.

Discrete stimulus method. In using the discrete stimulus method, the examiner gives stimulus words, one at a time, and the subject responds to each word with the first word occurring to him. The presence of an emotional background to any such response is indicated in a number of ways: by the response word itself, by the time taken to give the response, by some indirect sign of emotion while responding (such as blushing, squirming, stuttering), by repeating the stimulus word as though stalling for time, by giving a number of responses as though trying to correct the impression created by his first reaction, by giving a response so far removed from the stimulus as to appear to be an attempt to hide a natural response word, or by a failure to respond at all.

In using free association methods, the clinician does not arrive at any conclusions on the basis of a few responses. Instead, he relies on the accumulation of clues from a great number of responses. When he finds that some common element is present in numerous associations, he takes that as a clue and makes a guess as to the general area of emotional conflict. Using this guess as a hypothesis, he continues to test the subject, centering his attack around his hypothesis, in order to determine whether it is true or false. A clinician, in using these methods, usually makes guesses upon little evidence; but neither does he take any such guess seriously until he is able to corroborate it by a great number of different tests.

THE Chapter VIII ACQUISITION OF MOTOR SKILLS THE 

HE perfect execution of an intricate motor performance arouses the admiration and envy of any spectator. Highly skilled acts are applauded because they result from arduous practice by one who could never have reached his present perfection without years of relentless effort and intelligent direction. At the same time that we recognize that motor skill depends upon hard work we also know that persistent effort alone is not enough to ensure mastery. Many persons practice with unusual zeal only to end as second-rate performers. An analysis of the processes involved in motor learning may indicate whether failure depends more upon original lack of equipment, improper procedures, lack of intelligent direction, or lack of persistence. Even if the reader has no intention of becoming an expert in any form of motor performance, he can utilize the principles of motor learning in his everyday life. He can learn to walk with more grace, to play some game or musical instrument better, to carve a turkey more skillfully, to eat a salad more neatly, to speak more fluently, or to drive a car more easily and safely; in fact, any motor act can be improved by an intelligent application of the principles which psychological research has brought to light. 

BODY MECHANICS 

Those activities which are easily observable are due primarily to the function of the skeletal musculature. Before we can understand the ways in which practice and learning will change the effectiveness of motor behavior we must know something of the manner in which skeletal muscles operate. 202

The arrangement of striped muscles. The bony skeleton furnishes a framework which functions much like a crane or a derrick, from which a system of movable arms or levers extends. Radius

Biceps- Scapula -Triceps -Humerus
