MEMORY FOR RELATIONSHIPS 

In immediate memory, in memory for specific sequences, and in memory for forms the subject is presented with materials and then tested for his ability to recall, to recognize, or to repro-

PSYCHOLOGY 

duce that material in the exact form in which it was presented. 

What is measured, in such cases, is the specific retention of assigned items or exact sequences of items. 

In many situations such exact memory is essential. For example, it would be of little value for a person to remember that six came somewhere near eight in the numerical series, or that three times seven was somewhere around twenty, or that one's birthday was sometime in December, or that the person to whom he was speaking had a name something like Fullerton (when in reality it was Lightfoot). In other instances, the important factors to be retained are not the specific aspects of the material but its setting, its relationships, and its significance in relation to other items or situations. 

Memory in problem solving. Solving a problem involves memory for relationships. As an illustration, a man who is working on a heavy machine drops a bolt into a hole in a part of the machine. How to get it out is the problem. He first gets his associative memories to work. He had learned something about gravity and it occurs to him that if he turns the machine upside down the bolt will drop out; but the machine is too heavy. 

He thinks of tweezers, but they are too short; he thinks of pliers, but they are too big; he thinks of putting sticky substances on a rod (chewing gum, molasses, glue), but they are not strong enough; if the bolt were softer he could drive a spike into it. 

Isn't there anything else that will grip iron? A magnet. He has it! He gets a magnet only to find that the magnet will not go into the hole, it is too big; but then he remembers that a magnet will hold up one piece of metal and that another can be attached to this dangling piece. He gets a nail long enough to reach from the top of the hole to the top of the bolt, touches the magnet to the nail and pulls the bolt out. He has utilized memories but not in any rote manner; he has dug into his memories for items related to the present problem. 

In the attempt to facilitate the learning of relationships, recent educational procedures stress the practical applications of material to be learned. The danger in this procedure lies in the fact that the students may merely recognize the few applications that are presented, whereas the objective is to discover as many lines of relationship as possible. The essential feature is not

MEMORIZING 

295 application, but to teach the pupil to discern a multiplicity of relationships. The ideal would be to teach one fact, principle, or situation and then to follow this with problems which involve the utilization of this fact. Add another and follow with problems which might utilize either item already learned or a combination of them. Another valuable procedure would be to stimulate students to search for lines of relationship so that when some item is presented they would try to formulate situations in which this item might be utilized. 

Analysis of associative memory. The older psychologists attempted seriously to discover the fundamental principles that could be invoked to account for the way in which items of experience were related. They attempted to reduce them all to one law, which was called the law of contiguity. According to this law, if two experiences have occurred close together in time or space, the recurrence of one leads to the reinstatement of the other. In order to account for the fact that some elements occurring together seemed to become more closely knit than others, they evolved subsidiary laws which stated that the closeness of association could be influenced not only by (a) time and (b) space, but also by (c) similarity, (d) contrast, (e) primacy of occurrence together, (f) recency of occurrence together, (g) frequency of occurrence together, and by (h) vividness, which would include factors of pleasantness and unpleasantness. 

Which of these principles seems to operate depends more upon the setting of the individual experiment and the purposes involved than upon the nature of the principle itself. In rote learning, frequency is important; in a highly emotionalized experience, vividness; in lists of nonsense syllables, primacy and recency stand out; in conditioned reaction experiments, time and space are important; and in problem-solving experiments, similarity and contrast seem to be important. 

More recently, psychologists have stressed the degree to which associations are restricted rather than the factors which might be accountable for their being associated. Classified in this manner, associations are either (a) free, or unrestricted, associations or they are (b) controlled, or restricted, associations. 

Free association. In the typical free association experiment, or free association test, the subject is not limited by pre-

PSYCHOLOGY 

​vious instructions to some specific kind of relation or to some sequence of items that he has been required to learn, but may respond with any word that comes to him. The memory experiment is concerned with the learning process, whereas the association experiment attempts to discover what associations have been formed in the ordinary course of life. 

Two general methods are used: (1) In the continuous method the subject is merely given a start and is told to continue a sequence of words as long as he can do so; (2) in the discrete stimulus method, the subject is given a word and is told to respond with the first word that comes to him. The continuous method is used more in clinical situations than in psychological laboratories. It does not lend itself to quantitative analysis as much as does the discrete method although it does give the subject more freedom to wander where he pleases in his reactions. (See page 

196.) The discrete stimulus method is the most widely used in laboratory experiments and various refinements of technique have been evolved. In the most elaborate setting the stimulus word is exposed mechanically and the subject responds into a voice key. 

The presentation of the stimulus automatically starts a chronoscope and the voice key stops it. In this way the experimenter not only obtains the response word but is able to measure the reaction time.

If a thousand persons are given the same stimulus word, there will be striking individual differences in the response word. 

When the word "needle" was given to 1,000 adults of both sexes, 72 different responses were given: 160 persons responded with thread, 152 with sharp, 147 with pin, 134 with sew, 107 with sewing. No other response was given by more than 53 persons and 35 words were given by one person only. These variations illustrate the great diversity of associations that may occur. [36] 

Many attempts have been made to classify responses into various categories. The most general distinction is between (a) the objective, matter-of-fact, or impersonal responses and (b) the emotional or personal responses. Some words lend themselves to one type of response more than the other. For example, such words as table, chair, and salt tend to bring out objective responses. Some of the words likely to give rise to personal

MEMORIZING 

297 and emotional reactions are: love, marriage, friendship, quarrels, injustice, ridicule, contempt, pity, danger, expense, money, and death.

Certain individuals tend to give individualistic responses to more stimulus words than do others. If a particular individual tends to give personal reactions to a large number of stimulus words, this fact can be used as a means of making a clinical evaluation of his personality. In order to accomplish this purpose, frequency tables have been constructed which indicate the number of persons in a thousand actually tested who responded to each stimulus with other words. [36]` 

Controlled association. In the controlled association experiment the subject is given instructions which restrict his response to certain categories. In some situations the response is completely restricted and in others there is opportunity to select from equally correct alternatives. The subject may be instructed to give the word that bears the following relationship to the stimulus word: 

Relationship asked opposite synonym part-whole whole-part verb-object verb-subject genus-species Stimulus tall eat book house eat swim animal

Possible response short devour library room apple fish dog Where the restrictions permit of only one reply, the fixity of the association is usually measured by the reaction time. Such restricted associations appear when a person reads a passage; when he multiplies, adds, or divides numbers; when he gives the capitals of states; when he names forms or colors; and the like. 

RECALL 

Recall has been utilized as a means of determining the relative efficiency of different methods of learning and to measure the degree of retention. If we can recall practiced material, the assumption is that we have retained it; and if we can recall material better when it has been learned in a certain manner than when learned in another, we can conclude that the first method

PSYCHOLOGY 

was more efficient. On the other hand, if we fail to recall some material, it does not follow that it was not well learned or that we have failed to retain it. In other words, recall is not an automatic process that comes inevitably and mechanically. Everyone has been unable to recall some learned facts at one moment, only to have them come back with great clearness later on. It is, consequently, important to know something about the process of recall and to understand those influences which favor recall and those which interfere with it. 

Circumstantial recall. Whether we are learning intentionally or merely drifting from one activity to another, there is usually some memory of the temporal sequence of acts. An individual can relive a series of events in his memory even though he did not consciously try to learn that sequence as the acts were occurring. Circumstantial recall is the type of recall determined largely by the order in which the events occurred previously. 

In children, and in adults of inferior intelligence or little education, this type of recall is common. Living to these persons is a sort of straight-line, single-track process with few collaterals; they recall events as they lived them. 

Nevertheless, this type of recall may be of great value in finding some lost article. For example, a student happened to miss his fountain pen. All attempts to recall directly where he had placed it failed. So he started from the time he last remembered having it and traced, in memory, his every act from that point on. By this method he recalled where he had left it. The direct question, "Where is my pen?" did not evoke the proper memory, whereas a review of the sequence of events did. He had not tried to remember the sequence of acts he had executed at the time he performed them, but there was enough incidental memory to enable him to recall them in proper order. 

Effect of set or attitude on recall. Recall is definitely affected by the general set, attitude, or mood of the individual. 

The closer this set corresponds to the set which normally surrounds the material to be recalled the better the chance of recalling it. For example, suppose it is decided to recall the name "Steinberger." There is a gap, but the gap has a certain form into which the correct name must fit. There is a general feeling, perhaps, that the name begins with an S, that it is a long name,

MEMORIZING 

299 that it has a German atmosphere, that it has the feeling of a large building, etc. Stay in this atmosphere, keep in this set, and eventually the name "Steinberger" may come out. When the right name does not come directly and immediately; the right kind of name is likely to come, a name that is right in some particular-the first letter, the length, some outstanding syllable. 

In such situations there is often the feeling that one is just upon the name, that it is "on the tip of one's tongue," that a little extra push in the right direction will get it. Experimentally, it has been shown that a push in the right direction but too weak to be noticed by the individual will, nevertheless, enable him to recall it. This experiment was done with nonsense syllables. The subjects learned paired associates and then were given the first word with the task of recalling its proper associate. When they did not recall the proper nonsense syllable it was given through a telephone receiver or shown on a screen so briefly and so faintly that the subject could not discern it directly. This prompting, which was too weak to be discerned as a real perception, nevertheless enabled the individual to recall correctly. That is, a memory that is too vague to be recalled may become clear when reinforced by a stimulus that in itself is inadequate to be perceived. [65, p. 231] 

A certain set may, on the other hand, interfere with recall. 

When, in searching for a name, for example, the wrong name comes up, it is likely that this same name will continue to recur and will interfere with the recall of the correct one. At such times we may have the feeling that the recurring name is not correct, but we cannot get away from it. It is well to get clear away from the attempt to recall until the presence of the wrong name loses its effect. For this reason, recall is sometimes facilitated by a cessation of the attempt to recall. This temporary giving up enables us to escape the influence of the wrong association, the wrong clue, or the wrong set. 

Emotions may influence recall. The problem of the relation of emotion to recall has been investigated in several different ways. One method has been to assign subjects the task of learning material possessing differences in feeling tone from pleasant, through indifferent, to unpleasant. These experiments show that recall is most efficient for pleasant words, next for unpleasant

PSYCHOLOGY 

words, and least efficient for indifferent words. This tendency to recall pleasant more easily than unpleasant material has been found to exist both in children and in adults, [13] although one experimenter concluded that it is more evident in adults than in children. [25] 

Another method has been to test the emotional reactions of the subjects while memorizing, by measuring the electrical skin resistance. By this means it was found that words showing higher emotional values were more efficiently recalled than the emotionally indifferent ones. [5] Such an experiment does not distinguish between pleasant and unpleasant values. [35] 

Still another method has been to determine whether experiences which the individual regarded as pleasant were more easily recalled than those which were indifferent or unpleasant. For example, students were tested for their ability to remember good grades better than poor grades. After each quiz the student was told his grade and was asked to record his emotional reaction when hearing the grade. Later they were tested on a five-point scale for recall. Pleasing grades were recalled relatively more frequently than displeasing ones. Pleasant and unpleasant grades were remembered better than the more indifferent ones. [37] 

Personal experiences are recalled more easily than nonpersonal incidents, and emotionally toned events more readily than indifferent events. [12] There is some evidence that unpleasant events are forgotten more readily than pleasant events but this difference is not so striking as the advantage of emotionally toned events over indifferent events. 

Individual differences in the effect of emotional values are striking. One experimenter divides people into: optimists, who forget more unpleasant than pleasant experiences (about 56 per cent); pessimists, who forget more pleasant than unpleasant experiences (36 per cent); and indifferents, who forget the two equally (8 per cent). [48] The influence of emotional tone upon recall might be considered an extension of the general principle that recall depends upon the proper set or attitude of the individual. An indifferent attitude is probably least conducive to recall because it does not have the vitality to organize the directing influences which lead to a direct recall. In general, an unpleasant emotion would be less conducive to reinstatement of

MEMORIZING 

301 a previous experience than would a pleasant emotion. This would depend, nevertheless, upon the nature of the experience and upon the make-up of the individual. [58]

Imagination in recall. When recall takes the form of a particularly vivid or lifelike reproduction of the original sensory experience, the result is a memory image or an imaginary process. 

The use of an image as a basis for recall gives the individual a sketchy outline which serves as a starting point for detailed recall, but is ostensibly faulty as a guide for recalling specific incidents. 

In utilizing such a device the recaller is likely, therefore, to rearrange parts, to fill in gaps, and otherwise distort facts. [26] 

This leads to what has been called retrospective falsification. It is the process of making a good story from a few isolated remembered incidents. The narrator may be unable to distinguish the memory components from the fabricated part and may have a feeling of familiarity with the whole story as he tells it. A repeated story is especially subject to such distortion. 

Imagination leads to greater distortion in the recall of visual material than in the recall of verbal or motor experiences. The image is much more vivid than an abstract word symbol or the motor pattern. Hence, what we are all tempted to do is to take the word or gesture as a tool upon which to build recall and then to attempt to reinstate the memory in its original vividness. We read a story in which a villain plays a dominant role. From his behavior we catalogue him a villain and may, at first, recall some of the specific situations where he demonstrated his low character. 

As time goes on we forget what he did or why he is a villain, and merely substitute the visual image of some character with the facial characteristics of the traditional villain. It is risky business to judge the fidelity of recall by the vividness of the memory image revived.

RECOGNITION 

In recognition, the essential problem is to identify an object or to localize it in the setting in which it occurred in previous experience. There are varying degrees of clearness in recognition, ranging from a vague feeling of familiarity to the ability to recall the former time and place in which the object was experienced. Hence, recall and recognition may merge into each

PSYCHOLOGY 

other, the recall being involved in the more specific aspects of recognition, and recognition being the more simple process. The two are not necessarily involved in every instance of memory. 

There may be recognition without recall; as when you recognize a person, but cannot recall when or where you met him or his name. There may, likewise, be recall without recognition; as when you recall something you have heard or read, with no recognition. In fact, you may believe that the words you utter are your own when, as a matter of fact, you recently read them. 

Unconscious plagiarism is probably recall without recognition. 

Recognition easier than recall. The fact that recognition is easier than recall has been demonstrated by having subjects learn material under standardized conditions, and by following the learning with a recall test (by the method of retained members), or by a recognition test (in which the learned items are mixed with new items), or by both. With all kinds of materials the advantage is in favor of recognition. 

Recall score 

Recognition score

Syllables Words Proverbs 

12% 42% 39% 65% 22% 67%

When the cues used by a subject for recognition are obvious and distinctive, recognition is decidedly superior. Nevertheless, the superiority of recognition over recall may be materially reduced by making the new items that are interspersed with the old ones so similar that they can be distinguished only with difficulty. [46] 

In one experiment using colored designs where the new items were dissimilar to the old ones, the subject could recognize the original figure in 92 per cent of the cases. Where the new figures were similar to the old ones the correct recognitions were reduced to 29 per cent. [55]

Recognition often utilizes vague cues. Recognition may occur when some minor feature or some combination of features, which was a part of a previous experience, is perceived in the present situation. These may act as a sort of cue that one is "warm" or may be the starting point for a more specific recall. 

When material is learned verbatim, such factors as primacy,

MEMORIZING 

303 recency, length of list studied, and the like are more important than when they are learned for the general meaning. In the latter type of learning recognition is at a decided advantage as compared with rote learning. [1] In other words, if there is a need for recognition, the learner should stress the general feeling tone that goes with an experience without too much emphasis on specific detail or on verbatim repetition. 

Incidental memories. The alert individual takes in a great many details of his various experiences without making a definite attempt to discern or to memorize them. On the other hand, most persons ignore much that goes on and distort when called upon to report what they have observed. 

Inaccuracy of testimony. The ordinary person observes details inaccurately. For example, it has been shown that great errors are made in identifying persons. A workman came into the classroom during a class period and tinkered with the radiator. 

Sixteen days later this same workman and five others were brought before the class and the students were required to identify the one who had fixed the radiator at the previous session. This situation duplicated the customary police roundup. Of 117 students present at the second session, 69 per cent identified the workman correctly. This looks like a good proportion; but some glaring errors were made, enough to warrant skepticism about the validity of such identification. Seventeen students had not been present when the radiator incident occurred, yet five of these said they recalled the incident and tried to identify the man. [6] 

The reliability of testimony has been studied in a more formal fashion by exhibiting a test picture for about one minute and then obtaining a report upon what was seen. [59] 

Whether the events are staged as an incident, are presented in the form of a still picture, or are given in motion-picture form, the results confirm the fact that testimony is unreliable. 

The observer may be tested by obtaining from him a free report as to what he has seen or he may be asked specific questions about his experiences. The free report method lends itself to the making of a consistent story. The subject tends to simplify and generalize by combining similar items; he modifies details to make them more meaningful, he omits superfluous and incon-

PSYCHOLOGY 

gruous items; and he carries out the general meaning as he discerned it or as he happens to remember it. 

When specific questions are asked, the largely upon the nature of the question. [59] most confusing, the forms of questions are: errors depend

Children with a lower degree of intelligence are more likely to report incorrectly than children of higher intelligence. The effect of intelligence is greatest when the children are asked to report events they have witnessed and least when they are called upon to report material demonstrated on an object-card. [41] 

Temporary set affects incidental memory. When a person is set to memorize in a certain manner, or to observe certain aspects of a situation, he tends to ignore other aspects even though they may be essential. The performances of the magician or the sleight-of-hand performer are based upon this principle. 

A popular illustration of the influence of temporary set is this: "Listen carefully! A man was driving along a country road delivering and gathering milk cans. He had twenty-five cans in his wagon at the start. At the first farm he unloaded five and took on three. At the next farm he unloaded two and took on five. At the next he unloaded two and took on eight. 

At the next he unloaded four and took on three. At the next he unloaded three and took on five. At the next he unloaded four and took on four. At the next he unloaded four and took on one. 

How many times did the man stop?" If the questions are stated deliberately the listener will be concerned with counting the number of cans and, at the end, will be at a loss to know how many stops were made.

This has been tested in the laboratory by giving the student one type of memory test and then calling for recall of another

MEMORIZING 

305 type. For example, have the student learn paired associates and then ask him to repeat the entire list as though it were one series. 

Show him a card upon which are printed various objects and ask him to recall the objects he has seen, and then ask him to describe the border of the card or some irrelevant factor. All these experiments illustrate the fact that most of us tend to go through life with our intake limited by attitudes and specific sets, and to classify items into categories already established. This procedure may have some value but, at the same time, it limits the uses to which such experiences may be placed at a later time. 

Students are likely to specialize in specific memorizing or relationship memorizing. Instead, from the viewpoint of practical importance, they should learn to utilize both. Too often the student who makes an excellent record in memorizing materials makes a poor showing when he tries to utilize those materials in new combinations; while the one who enjoys utilizing new combinations disparages memorizing and so has little to recombine. 

The medical student who is best in memorizing anatomy may be a poor diagnostician, while sometimes the student who made a rather poor record in the first two years of medical school may turn out to be an excellent diagnostician. The best individual is the one who can memorize and then can utilize these memorized facts in solving a problem requiring a reconstruction of the elements.

Chapter XI  THE 

HE part of the body that makes possible the various psychological processes which we have been studying is the central nervous system. Up to this point we have made only incidental references to this system except in our study of the emotions. 

There we pointed out that there are two parts to the nervous system: the skeletal, or cerebrospinal, system and the autonomic system. Since it is difficult to understand the workings of emotional processes without reference to the autonomic nervous system, we gave a description of that part of the total nervous system in Chapter VII. The student is urged to review that section before proceeding with this chapter. What was given there will not be repeated here.

Thus far we have been studying the activities of an individual which can be observed by others-his behavior; now we plan to turn to a study of the ways in which an individual is able to receive messages from the external world-his sensations. In order to prepare for such a study of sensory processes, it is important that something be known about the central integrating agency-the central nervous system. 

STRUCTURE OF THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM 

In order to understand the workings of the central nervous system, some general picture of its structural arrangements is essential. [12] It can be divided for purposes of study into brain, spinal cord, and nerves. A general view of the nervous system is shown in Fig. 73.

Nerves. Nerve fibers may be grouped into sensory, motor, and association fibers. The sensory, or afferent, fibers carry impulses from the sense organs into the central portions of the 311

PSYCHOLOGY 

i.. 

FIG. 73.-General view of the nervous system, showing brain, spinal cord, and branching nerves. (From Martin.) nervous system. They are widely distributed and extremely fine at the sense organs themselves, but are organized into groups or bundles as they approach the central portions, and thus form the nerves.

The motor nerves, also called efferent nerves, carry impulses out from the central system to the muscles and glands of the body. They begin in large bundles and branch out as they approach their destinations.

Association fibers are found in the spinal cord and most profusely in the brain. They carry impulses between various other parts of the nervous system, thus making possible all sorts of intricate patterns of nervous activity. [17] 

The spinal cord. Most of the sensory nerves have their first switching center in the spinal cord; and most motor nerves pass out to the muscles from centers in the spinal cord. These centers in the cord are connected with other centers in the cord and with the brain centers by association fibers. 

The spinal cord thus has at least three functions: (1) It acts as a center for local action patterns. For example, in a reflex the impulse comes in through the sensory fiber to a spinal center and is sent out from that center to the responding muscle, as shown in Fig. 76 (page 318). Such a reflex can take place without any action on the part of higher centers, or on the part of the brain. (2) It connects centers at different levels of the body. For example, it connects the centers for the arms and legs by means of association fibers. (3) It acts as a nerve trunk line by means of which the fibers from the brain are connected with the local nerve centers. 

FIG. 74. The human brain. The shaded portion to the lower right is the cerebellum. All the rest, except the little part of the spinal cord, is the cerebrum. 

The brain. The brain is the mass of nervous tissue within the skull. Its general appearance can be seen from Fig. 74. Its main parts are: (a) The cerebrum, which comprises the portion most highly developed in man and by far the largest portion of the entire brain. It is the center for most of the processes studied in psychology, such as perception, reasoning, learning, remembering, and the like. (b) The cerebellum, which lies at the back

It is probably the main center for muscular co-ordination. [5] 

The neuron. The nervous system is composed of some 

14 billion highly specialized nerve cells. The mature nerve cell is called a neuron. It consists of a cell body and the nerve fibers which extend away from the central cell. The forms that these extensions take are very numerous. Some of these are shown in Fig. 75. 

The cell bodies are usually found in clusters with their branches intermingling with the branches of other cells. These groupings are most extensive in the outer layers of the brain and in the central portions of the spinal cord. They are the integrating centers to which sensory impulses are brought and from which motor impulses are sent. The processes which lead away from these centers are arranged in bundles of varying size. Even the slenderest nerve contains many nerve fibers; some contain as many as a hundred thousand. They vary in length from microscopic branchings to long fibers extending from the brain far down into the spinal cord, or from the spinal cord to the tips of the fingers or toes. Whether long or short, these nerve fibers end in fine branchings in the nerve centers in the spinal cord and brain, the branchings of many fibers all intermingling as the branches of the trees intermingle in a dense forest. This dense interlacing of the branched ends of the nerve fibers makes for a functional continuity between neurons, so that each neuron is so closely associated with other neurons that no part of the nervous system can be considered as functioning separately from the rest. The region of intermingling of the nerve branchings of one neuron with others is called the synapse. While the synapse provides a region of intimate functional relationship, then is no anatomical or protoplasmic continuity of neurons at the synapse. The different neurons come close together; they do not fuse. 1 

FUNCTION OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM 

Anything that can be said about the functioning of the nervous system must be highly speculative. No one has seen a nerve function and all that can be done is to make inferences from secondary data. Two essential problems are the nature of the

PSYCHOLOGY 

nerve impulse and what happens to this impulse at the nerve centers or synapses. [3] 

The nerve impulse. A nerve fiber may be excited by chemical, mechanical, thermal, or electrical stimuli when these are applied at any point along the nerve fiber. Normally, however, stimuli are received only at the terminal branchings of the neuron. 

Those branchings that receive the impulses are called dendrites; those branchings which transmit nerve impulses to other neurons, to muscle fibers, or to glandular cells, are called axons. Normally, the nerve impulse will go only in one direction across the synapse; namely, from the axon of one neuron to the dendrites of another. [4] 

The speed of transmission of nerve impulse varies with different nerves and in different animals, and may vary in the same nerve under different conditions. In human nerves it may be as rapid as 120 meters per second. The total time that would be required for passage through the fibers involved in an ordinary simple reaction is somewhere about 20 milliseconds, whereas the total reaction time is not less than 100 milliseconds and may run to nearly 200 milliseconds. Most of this excess time is taken up with delay in the nerve centers. In other words, something happens in the nerve centers which consumes considerably more time than would be required were the cord and brain merely switching centers. This makes it important to know what happens in the nerve, what happens in the synapse, and to understand thé significance of the difference between the two. 

The impulse which traverses the nerve on the way to the brain or from the brain is slower than an ordinary electric current and is faster than would be the case were the transmission purely chemical in nature. Every nerve impulse is, on the other hand, accompanied by an electric change which can be recorded by suitable instruments (see Fig. 80). These electric reactions have been called action currents. There is also a chemical change because the passage of a nerve impulse requires oxygen and generates carbon dioxide, although the amount is extremely small. 

The conclusion from these facts is that a nerve impulse is some sort of electrochemical change.

The nearest analogy to nerve conduction that is familiar enough to be commonly observed is the action of a fuse. Once

the fuse is ignited the passage of the action is determined by the internal constitution of the fuse and it travels onward in full force until it reaches the end of the line, or until some unusual circumstance stops it. Whereas a fuse is completely exhausted after it has fired, the nerve uses only part of its energy and recovers immediately. During this period of restoration it is unable to carry another current. This period of inexcitability immediately after the passage of a nerve impulse is called the refractory period. If a stimulus is applied during the refractory period, it is ineffective. It follows, then, that if a stimulus is continually applied to a nerve fiber it will produce an intermittent impulse. The nerve will conduct one impulse, take time for recovery, conduct another, take time for recovery, transmit another, and so on.

Since the transmission of a nerve impulse is dependent upon internal changes in the nerve fiber itself, it functions with full force once it is set off. This is called the all-or-none law. If the stimulus is too weak to arouse the nerve fiber, or if it is not applied long enough, no response is made. Once it is set off, the individual nerve fiber responds completely. Although the allor-none law holds for the individual nerve fibers, a measurement of the action currents generated in nerve trunks shows that these vary in magnitude. The amount of action-potential increases as a larger number of fibers are stimulated, as is the case when a strong stimulus is applied. Variations in the strength of a nerve current in a nerve trunk can be considered as a function of the number of fibers in operation.

Activity at the synapse. The stimulation of the dendrites of a neuron by an adequate stimulus sets going an impulse which does not stop until it reaches the branched axon end of the same neuron. What happens at the synapse is another story. 

The stimulus may be so weak, or may meet so much resistance at these junction points that it ends there. Or, it may co-operate with another nerve fiber which is already set to explode, and so start another current (or a number of other currents) which can be even stronger than it was. [16] 

To give a concrete illustration: A person may be almost unresponsive to the noise in a boiler factory and yet that same person may let out a blood-curdling yell if stimulated by a little

PSYCHOLOGY 

scratching sound when seated alone in a big dark house. To put it in still other words: The force of an explosion is determined by the amount of powder fired rather than by the size of the fuse. 

What happens at the synapse? That the synapse is a kind of switching center there can be little doubt. The microscopic structure of the neurons would make this seem plausible. The simplest type of connection that can be imagined is illustrated in Fig. 76. In actual living organisms, however, the central junction is filled with the branchings from hundreds of other sensory and motor neurons. No center can be affected only by a single sensory impulse from one neuron, and it is impossible for a nerve center Sensory neuron Y Skin Motor neuron Muscle

FIG. 76.-Diagram of con nection between sensory and motor neuron at the synapse. to affect only one motor 1.euron. A sensory impulse consists of a volley of impulses which reaches the center as a sort of pattern of stimulation, and the switching into other neuron stimulations must also be in a complex pattern.

By operative and experimental procedures, it has been possible to study the conduction through the synapse as compared with conduction along a nerve trunk. Compared with conduction along a nerve trunk, reflex conduction which involves passage through synapses: (a) is slower; (b) is more subject to fatigue; (c) shows a greater variability in the intensity of stimulus necessary to get a response (i.e., a greater variability in threshold); (d) is more subject to reinforcement by other influences; (e) is more subject to interference from other influences (that is, more subject to inhibition); (f) is more dependent upon blood supply and oxygen and more easily influenced by anesthetics; and (g) 1 1 1

permits current to pass only in one direction from the axon of one cell to the dendrites of another, whereas a nerve current will travel in either direction along a nerve fiber. 

This group of facts can be understood only on the assumption that the synapse is a switching center of a unique sort. 

Psychologists have sought here the explanation of many psychological processes: perception, learning, shifts of attention, memory, and the like. Their efforts have advanced little beyond the speculative stage, and the beginning student should be warned that when he reads about how certain mental processes are produced by some specific type of neural process he is reading speculation and not fact. 

VARIETIES OF NEURAL ACTIVITY 

In an intact human organism the interrelations of neurons are so intimate that the complications are tremendous. The varia- 

FIG. 77.-Diagram to illustrate simple reflex. The sensory impulse from the pinprick is carried to the spinal cord, affects the motor neuron, and the motor impulse returns to the biceps muscle, causing it to contract and pull the hand away from the pin. tions in such processes as reasoning, problem solving, performing highly skilled acts and the like provide evidence for this. In order to attempt to visualize what takes place in the nervous system, it is valuable to simplify conditions and attempt to construct what may happen in simple situations. 

The simple reflex. The simplest reaction which we can imagine is the simple reflex. If we could isolate a reflex pathway, it might be organized as illustrated in Fig. 77. The sensory

PSYCHOLOGY 

neuron carries the impulse caused by the pin pricking the sense organ in the hand to the nerve center. At the synapse a dendrite of the motor neuron is affected, the motor impulse passes out to the muscle and produces a reaction. 

Such a simple reflex action pattern is a purely imaginary abstraction-a device to clarify our thinking. The student should bear in mind that every action in the functioning organism is complicated by all sorts of interactions with other processes going on at the same time.

Simple co-ordinated movement. A single sensory impulse can affect a number of motor neurons at the same level and thus produce a co-ordinated response because of their combined response. The use of the hand for a co-ordinated act illustrates such a reaction. On the other hand, several sensory impulses might both converge on the same motor neuron and produce a common result.

Cerebral control. 

The more intricate the central connections the greater is the variety of complex behavior patterns which may be executed by the same organ. At the same time, these diverse connections restrict that organ so that it cannot be completely involved in some isolated type of behavior. To illustrate, the hand has various uses. Suppose that it became completely involved in writing and that such employment would make it totally impervious to any other need. An emergency might arise which would best be met by the individual's making a fending movement with his right hand. If the hand could not be diverted from writing, the fending movement would not occur and the person might suffer injury. However, there are neural connections to take care of such a situation. While the hand may be busy with one occupation, there are numerous higher brain centers which make it possible for nerve currents coming from the brain to stop such an activity as writing and to inaugurate some totally different kind of movement. While a motor organ may be relatively independent, it is also at the beck and call of other parts of the body.

This hampering of freedom by higher centers is illustrated in a simple manner by the results of severing the brain from the spinal cord. In an animal whose spinal cord has been severed, reflex behavior is not only possible, but the reflexes will be more

pronounced when the brain influence has been removed than when it is present. Being connected with the brain acts as a damping influence on the free activity of lower neural connections. 

Active inhibition or conflict. A good illustration of a conflict on the spinal level may be demonstrated by stimulating a spinal dog to scratch himself with both hind legs at the same time, as follows: If such a spinal dog is stimulated to scratch, he will shift his center of gravity and raise the paw on the stimulated side and scratch. If he is subsequently stimulated on the other side, he will raise the other paw and scratch on that side. 

If he is stimulated on both sides simultaneously, he cannot raise both hind paws. A conflict is thus brought about. What does he do? At first there is a delay, then he will scratch with one paw as though that were the only stimulus activating him. The winning of the one reflex totally submerges the other. After scratching, however, there is a refractory phase, during which the nerve that was just operative becomes inoperative. During this refractory phase the other reflex comes to the forefront and works at full tilt. If the stimuli are continued, therefore, the resultant behavior will be a sort of compromise so far as the observer from the outside is concerned. The dog will scratch alternately with each leg. [17] 

In short, the operation of one reflex is accompanied by total suppression of processes which antagonize that reflex act. Such ascendancy is short-lived. As soon as there is a completion of the ascendant process, it subsides and its antagonist takes the stage.

Learning. Learning of any sort implies that the individual is modified by experience and that these modifications are retained long enough to influence subsequent activities. By far the greatest part of such modification and retention takes place in the centers where the neurons meet. This much is known for certain. 

Just what takes place at the nervous centers to bring about these changes is not so clear. Some theories that have been advanced are given here: [11]

The new growth theory. This theory maintains that there is a growth of new processes at the synapses as a result of the passage of nerve currents. The main reason for rejecting this

PSYCHOLOGY 

theory is that learning is much more rapid than could be the case if it depended upon the actual growth of tissue. 

The movement theory. The movement theory holds that there is a physical movement of the dendrites or axons resulting from exercise by means of which they come into closer proximity. 

This theory has never received much favor because the branching ends of the neurons are so closely intermeshed that movement with exercise seems out of the question. For a time it was thought that there was actual continuity between neurons; but this idea has been definitely discarded. 

Electrical resistance theory. The electrical resistance theory holds that there is a change in electrical resistance with exercise. This view has taken various forms but, in general, the synapse is viewed as some sort of electrical condenser in which the two plates become charged, and the passage of current depends upon the capacity of the particular center. Exercise is supposed, in some manner, to change the capacity of the centers involved. This view might be credited if it were known that the nervous current is primarily electrical. We have already seen that it is not, but is a sort of electrochemical change. 

Chemical theory. According to chemical theories, exercise of a center is supposed to produce a chemical substance which has a semipermanent effect upon the ease of transmission. Chemical views are receiving more and more support by investigators. 

The advocates of chemical theories base their contentions on the fact that when a nerve impulse arrives at a neural connection, there is set free a chemical substance (called acetylcholine) which is effective in inducing nerve currents in other nerves which it contacts, or capable of causing muscular contraction when it contacts a muscle. They also contend that this substance is quickly destroyed by another substance (called cholinesterase). There is little doubt about the presence of these chemical substances. The argument centers around their significance. Those maintaining that neural processes are essentially electrical say that these chemical substances are merely by-products of the electrical activity; the advocates of the chemical theories, on the contrary, believe that they are the essential factors and that electrical changes are by-products. At any rate, the presence of both chemical and electrical processes is certain.

THEORIES OF BRAIN FUNCTIONING 

If one could imagine a novice, with no knowledge of radio and little knowledge of electricity, attempting to discover how a complex radio receiving set functions, and if one could multiply his confusion by millions, some idea might be obtained of the difficulties which scientists have had in trying to unfathom the workings of the human brain. 

The operation of any apparatus, no matter how complex, depends upon the interaction of its various parts, a process involving both spatial and temporal relationships. Parts must be placed properly in relationship to each other and their interactions must be timed properly. It has been difficult to study the anatomy of the nervous system because of its complexity, but great strides have been made in this direction. To understand the time relationships is exceedingly more difficult for a number of reasons. 

The greatest obstacle is the fact that the brain cannot be observed in operation. All that anyone can do is to observe the stimulus combination which activates the nervous system and then to observe the resulting activity. What happens between these two can only be conjectured. For these reasons, early theories of brain function were based largely on structural conceptions. The attempts were directed mainly toward localizing functions in various parts of the nervous system. 

Methods used in the attempt to localize functions. 

Various methods have been used to trace nerve fibers and to determine how they function. 

The embryological method. Nerve fibers in adults are covered with a white sheath called the myelin sheath. This sheath is not acquired until some time after the nerve fiber has developed, and different tracts obtain their sheaths at different periods. By examining a series of spinal cords and brains at different stages of embryonic life, individual tracts may be recognized. 

The method of degeneration. If a nerve fiber is severed, the fibers which are cut from their nerve cells degenerate; the part between the cut and the cell body remains alive, as shown in Fig. 78. By treating the nervous tissue with special stains after cuts have been made, the degenerated fibers can be traced through a series of microscopic sections.

PSYCHOLOGY 

The physiological method. In animals, or in human beings who have suffered head injury, different portions of the cortex may be stimulated and observations made of the resulting muscular responses.

Extirpation method. By this method certain portions of the brain or spinal cord may be removed and the resulting effect upon sensory discrimination or motor behavior observed. [2] 

FIG. 78.-Diagram to show the direction of degeneration on section of a nerve fiber. The cell body for the lower section. is in the ganglion to the right outside the spinal cord. The fiber disconnected from its cell dies, that is, the black area toward the cord. In the upper cut the parent cell is in the cord and the fiber dies to the right as shown by the black portion. 

Clinical method. The clinical method is especially applicable to the study of human brain functioning. When a patient is suffering from some known injury to the brain or from some disease which affects the brain in a known manner, the clinical symptoms which the patient manifests may be correlated with the disturbance caused by the disease. [9]

Specialized areas in the nervous system. These methods have demonstrated beyond any doubt that certain portions of the nervous system have definite functions. A general outline of some of these general functions is illustrated in Fig. 79. 

Anatomical and histological studies have shown that the fibers from the eye go to areas in the occipital (back) region of the brain. If these fibers are destroyed, the individual becomes blind. The auditory nerves from the ears go to the temporal regions of the brain. If they are destroyed, the individual becomes deaf. If the fibers from the motor area of the brain to the vocal organs are destroyed, the individual becomes aphonic (voiceless). If the motor fibers to the hands are destroyed, the person becomes so paralyzed that he cannot use his hands to write or to perform any other manual function. There is no question about these functions, because pathological conditions in

* 

human beings and experiments with animals have amply substantiated them.

The localization of functions within the brain is more complicated. Various areas have been suggested as association areas where the incoming impulses are co-ordinated and patterns of behavior organized. Destruction of vast areas supposedly necessary for such co-ordinating activity has been carried out with relatively little effect upon the behavior of the individual. There seems to be a higher relationship between the amount of cerebral

[10] It would seem that the central function of co-ordination does not depend upon specific fibers in certain locations but that this is a complex process of patterning which can be successfully performed by alternative areas. The general areas for the reception of visual, auditory, cutaneous, and olfactory stimulations are known. There is a region where motor impulses tend to originate. The greater bulk of the brain seems to have no specific function but to co-operate in many activities. [9] 

Since it has been demonstrated that a function cannot be

PSYCHOLOGY 

localized in a particular area of the brain, a theory has been proposed, called the theory of equipotentiality, which assumes that each part takes an equal part in each operation. This extreme view is no more required by the known facts than is the extreme localization view. Parts may co-operate in a function without all being equal in importance for that function. For example, legs are part of the mechanism needed to run a maze. One experimenter extirpated a part of the neural tissue of rats so that they became unable to use their legs. Instead of failing to go through the maze at all because part of the needed pattern was destroyed, the paralyzed animal dragged himself through the maze by pulling himself along with his front legs. You cannot localize the function of an automobile in the wheel, in the piston of the engine, in the spark plug, or in the battery. It takes the complete assembly for perfect operation, even though the car might limp along with part of its mechanism eliminated. [11] 

The function of timing in neural processes. Whereas a great portion of experimental work and speculation centered around brain anatomy for so many years, more recent emphasis is concerned with time relations in neural activity. This interest is the result of several groups of undisputed facts: (a) The discovery of brain waves has given impetus to a study of the importance of timing in neural processes. (b) It has been found that the impulse through a nerve fiber is customarily made up of a volley of impulses, which may be the composite of a number of other impulses of different frequencies.

BRAIN WAVES 

It is an undisputed fact that rhythmic electrical impulses arise almost continuously from the neural centers (the gray matter) within the brain and spinal cord. This continuous rhythmic activity occurs independently of incoming neural excitation and thus provides a background or pool of excitation which may act as a selective factor to incoming nerve currents. The facts about these waves, which we shall presently review, make impossible the old notion that the brain is merely a sort of relaying center which is inactive until stimulated by some incoming excitation. [3] 

Records of brain potentials may be obtained from electrodes

placed on the outside of the skull at widely separated places, as shown in Fig. 80. These records have been customarily designated electroencephalograms. They may also be obtained from electrodes placed directly in the brain tissue. These have been. Batteries Electrodes

Endot FIG. 80.-Diagram to show how electroencephalograms are secured. 

In the cathode ray oscillograph, C is the cathode, from which electrons are emitted. A beam of electrons passes through an opening in the anode, A, and falls on the screen, S. When changes in the electrical potential of plates + P and P occur, the beam of electrons is deflected, and when a succession of changes occurs, as in the case of brain rhythms, curves are traced on the screen. A camera, mounted to face this screen, will take permanent pictures of the waves. A sensitive galvanometer may be used in place of the cathode ray oscillograph, in which case records are made of the beam of light reflected from the galvanometer.

Hill Book Co.) called electrograms. In both cases the waves are greatly enlarged by means of vacuum tube amplifiers. [8, 14] 

Results of experimental studies of brain waves. Some general facts concerning brain waves may be expressed as follows: [6] 

1. They are present throughout the neural centers at all times. They are altered in character by different circumstances;

PSYCHOLOGY 

but from the highest degree of excitement, through sleep, to the deepest anesthesia, they are still present. 

2. Different kinds have been distinguished. They are: (a) The alpha rhythms. When an individual is in a condition of relaxation, waves with an average frequency of 10 per second are found, with a range of 8 to 13 per second. These are called alpha rhythms. (b) The beta rhythms. Beta waves are secondary rhythms superimposed on the slower alpha waves. They have an average frequency of 25 per second, with a range between 17 and 30. (c) The gamma rhythms. While not so universally found, there are sometimes waves with a frequency of 35 to 50 per second which have been called gamma rhythms. 

3. Children differ from adults in brain wave patterns. Brain waves are not found in infants less than a month of age. Infants below three or four months of age show slow, random waves with an occasional rhythm of three to four a second. The rhythmic waves do not appear before about six months of age and are then only about four or five per second. Not until about ten years of age does an individual show alpha waves of the typical ten-per-second frequency. [13] 

4. Adults manifest individual differences in brain wave patterns. These differences show themselves in the presence or absence of the basic alpha waves, changes in the frequency or regularity of the alpha rhythms, the way in which the alpha waves change in various situations, the frequency and change in beta waves, and the regional differences in these and other complex patterns. [18]

These individual differences are not due to any regular differences in structure. Instead, they seem to show some relationship to such personality differences as: differences in general tension, emotional stability, metabolic rate, aggressive-docile behavior, and the like. Such studies have not been carried far, but those that have been made suggest the interesting possibility that those characteristics that have been called basic personality traits may be related to differences in brain wave patterns. 

5. Circumstances affect brain waves. Numerous conditions have been found to affect brain wave patterns. Two of them are here discussed: (a) Relaxation is most conducive to a simple uncomplicated alpha rhythm. That alpha rhythms are indepen-

dent of external stimulation, and show themselves best when uncomplicated by other factors, is demonstrated by the fact that they increase in regularity and amplitude when the brain is completely severed from the rest of the nervous system. Sleep, sedative drugs, deep etherization, or any other condition which depresses cortical function tends to produce a slowing in the alpha waves. Conditions of worry, emotional excitement, acidosis, and sensory stimulation tend to increase the frequency of the rhythm or to cause it to disappear altogether in the welter of irregular rhythms produced by hyperexcitement and excessive cortical activity. [1, 15] (b) Intense mental effort will depress the alpha rhythm. Those stimuli have most effect which have attention or arousal value. That is to say, the brain waves seem to be related to psychological functions. When there is little activity, the waves slow down or disappear. When there is heightened activity, the waves no longer appear in regular rhythm but break up into all sorts of complex patterns. 

Theoretical considerations related to brain waves. The experimental facts concerning brain waves, which we have just outlined, have given rise to all sorts of speculations. These may be no more correct than those based on brain anatomy, but they are more exciting because newer and because they have injected a spark of life into what had become a sterile attempt to correlate mental functions with the details of neural anatomy. 

At least it seems logical to suppose that incoming sensory impulses, when they reach the brain, encounter neural processes already in operation, in the nature of waves varying in frequency and amplitude. It seems reasonable to suppose that the process involved in the reception of incoming impulses by the neural centers involves some sort of adjustment between the wave action already in process and the incoming wave action. The outgoing motor impulse can be interpreted in terms of the resultant of this fusion. 

In other words, the brain can be viewed as a kind of variable oscillator. The oscillations in operation at any one moment are the product of previous stimulations, other impulses acting at the time, general structure, metabolic processes, and the like. The incoming processes are due partly to the make-up of the specific

PSYCHOLOGY 

neurons involved but more strikingly to the stimulation of the sense organ.

According to this theory, cortical activity should be regarded as the product of a whole mass of oscillators whose activity can be expressed only as a spectrum of frequencies. Incoming nerve currents disturb the slow rhythms that exist in this spectrum in conditions of relaxation, and an adjustment must be made between the cortical spectrum and the volley of incoming waves. The motor discharge represents the resultant of this adjustment. This is all highly speculative and no details have been worked out, but it fits surprisingly well into many of the known facts of psychology. [7] 

In brief, the brain seems to be more like a radio receiving set than like a telephone exchange.

Chapter XII 

VISION

MAN 

AN receives impressions from the outside world, and from within his own body, by means of sense organs. 

Without such receiving devices he would have no way of adjusting to his environment. He would be about as isolated from life in general as a man without a radio receiving set would be from the radio programs which fill the ether. 

Several factors about man's sense organs are quite advantageous. (a) He has a variety of sense organs, so that he is not dependent upon one type of external disturbance to give him information about the world. He takes in waves of radiant energy through his eyes; he discerns sounds with his ears; he is aware of certain chemical stimuli through the sensations of smell and taste; he can discern heat and cold and touch by receptors in the skin; and he experiences pain when certain injurious situations are encountered. (b) His sense organs are selective. This selectivity enables him to respond to specific situations while remaining oblivious to others. It enables him to devote his energies to those stimuli which he does sense while ignoring others. Man has made up for many of the disadvantages which may arise from selectivity by devising apparatus to enlarge the range of his sensory capacity. He uses lenses to increase his visual range; he uses various electric contrivances to extend his hearing range. 

Such creations have more value than ready-made sense organs would have, because the latter cannot be shut off so readily. 

Man's most complicated and probably most important sense organs are his eyes. They are in the form of a receiving set designed to respond to light; that is, they respond to radiant energy within the wave-length range of 400 and 760 millimicrons, which travels through space at the rate of 300,000 kilometers, 333

PSYCHOLOGY 

Being or 186,000 miles per second. Being a good receiving set, the eyes are highly selective and are unresponsive to forms of energy other than light.

Parts of the eyeball. In principle, the eye operates in much the same manner as a camera. The rods of the retina of the human eye are 0.04 to 0.06 mm. long and about 0.002 mm. in diameter. It is estimated that there are 130 million rods in the human retina. 

The cones of the retina are shorter and thicker than the rods, as their name implies. In the human eye they are 0.022 to

The central part of the retina, immediately behind the lens, is different from the peripheral areas. This central part (about 

2 mm. in diameter) is called the yellow spot (macula lutea) because of its yellowish color. In the center of this spot is a small depression (a horizontal ellipse), called the fovea (fovea centralis), which is the area of sharpest vision and the center of fixation. The only light receptors in the fovea are cones which are closely packed. Passing from the fovea out toward the periphery of the retina the ratio of rods to cones increases until, in the outermost portions, there are very few cones. 

In each retina there is a small area that is not sensitive to light stimulation, which is known as the blind spot. It is the place where the optic nerve leaves the eye and is about 18° to the nasal side of the fovea. It contains neither rods nor cones.

The lens. The lens of the eye is suspended just behind the pupil. It differs from the glass lens in a camera in that it can adjust its degree of curvature and thus change in refracting power, whereas the curvature of the lens in a camera is fixed. 

The lens of the eye "accommodates" for distance by becoming thicker as objects move nearer to the eye (thus increasing the degree of refraction) and thinner as objects move farther away from the eye. Adjustments for distance in a camera are made by changing the distance between the lens and the sensitive film. 

The nearer the object to be photographed the greater must be the distance between the lens and the film. 

EXPERIENCES OF LIGHT AND COLOR 

The adequate stimuli for vision are the light waves which strike the retina of the eye. These waves vary in length and in intensity, and by variations in these qualities produce experiences of light and color in the individual whose eyes are affected by them. The light waves themselves do not possess qualities of light and color; they merely affect the eyes in such ways that the individual experiences these sensations. 

Surface, expanse, lustrous, and luminous colors. The kind of color or light which a person experiences is determined in part by the source of the stimulus. (a) There are surface colors, or object colors, which are determined in large part by the light reflected from objects in the field of vision. These surface colors are deceptive because we all tend to see a given object as though it had the color we are accustomed to attribute to it. 

For example, we will see the same rose as though it had the same degree of redness even though changes in lighting may produce radical changes in its coloring. (b) There is expanse color, free color, or film color, which is experienced when one looks at a clear sky, into a dense fog, when one's eyes are closed, or when one looks at a perfectly uniform surface through a tube. (c) There is the lustrous color that results when one looks at polished metal or at silk. The luster seems to be something added to the color reflected from the object. (d) There is the glow or luminous color that is experienced when one looks at an object

PSYCHOLOGY 

which produces as well as reflects light. A glow results when one looks at a bit of red-hot metal, into a flame, or at the luminous letters on the dial of a watch. 

Brilliance, hue, and saturation. Regardless of whether a light stimulus is reflected from a surface, whether it is a film. color, a lustrous color, or a luminous color, it may possess different degrees of three other qualities: brilliance, hue, and saturation. 

Brilliance is that quality of a color experience in respect to which it may be equated to some member of a series of grays ranging from white to black. Every color, no matter what other characteristics it may have, has some degree of brilliance. 

Absence of the ability to sense brilliance would mean blindness. 

Brilliance is determined most significantly by the energy of the light wave, although it is also affected by the wave length of the stimulus.

Hue is color tone. It is the sensory quality which varies. primarily with the wave length of the light stimulus. It is illustrated by those qualities of a color which we designate by such terms as red, yellow, green, blue, and the like. 

Saturation is the degree to which any color possessing a given hue differs from a gray of the same brilliance. Saturation is often referred to as the richness of the color. For example, two reds may be alike in brilliance and in hue and, at the same time, one may be a rich, saturated red, while the other is a washedout red barely distinguishable from a neutral gray. 

COLOR MIXING 

Colors may be mixed in various ways in the psychological laboratory. The one most commonly used is the color wheel (Fig. 84). It consists essentially of a motor that twirls cardboard disks which can be intertwined so as to provide various proportions of component colors. When this composite disk is rotated with sufficient rapidity the component colors fuse. 

Another method is to extract different rays from a spectrum and superimpose them on a dead-white surface or throw them directly on the same part of the retina. Or, various hues may be obtained by the use of filters. [4] The different results of color mixing may be formulated as follows:

ANALYSIS OF. VISUAL PROCESSES 

There is no doubt that the most important factor making for visual experiences is the radiant energy affecting the eye. The way in which a person senses light, however, depends upon a number of factors: individual differences in the presence and distribution of rods and cones, degree of general illumination, the part of the eye stimulated by the light, the way in which adjoining areas of the retina are being stimulated, what has preceded, the sequence of impressions, the similarity or difference of the stimuli affecting the two eyes, and the habits of sensing in certain ways. 

Since the influence of these various factors are interlaced they cannot be isolated for discussion, but they will come out in the discussion to follow. [10]

Distribution of rods and cones. Anatomically there are two types of receptor cells in the human retina, the rods and the cones. It is pretty well accepted that the rods are responsible for vision when the illumination level is low, or at twilight levels, and give rise to light-dark sensations but not to sensations of color. The cones, on the other hand, are considered the receptors for color or daylight vision and are inactive under twilight conditions. It is further thought by most investigators that the cones vary in their function, some being more responsive to certain color stimuli than to others. It is almost imperative to postulate some difference in the cones in order to account for the facts of color vision.

The fact that the ratio of rods to cones varies in different portions of the retina and that there are only cones in the fovea makes possible some crucial observations which support the theory that the rods and cones have these different functions. 

1. The totally color-blind person has poor foveal vision.

In color-blind persons, since the cones are the receptors for color vision, the fovea is either inefficient or inactive. Such individuals often manifest unsteadiness of fixation and must turn the eyes so that the object image falls upon the periphery of the retina to one side of the fovea. In order to see they must move their eyes to such a position that their rods can function. Night-blind 

2. Night-blind persons have defective rods. persons cannot adapt their vision to weak illumination and conse-

PSYCHOLOGY 

342 quently they cannot see at night. It has been found that such persons have a defect in the pigment layer of the retina which supplies the visual purple, that is, the chemical material utilized by the rods. This defect of the pigment layer may result from vitamin A deficiency. 

3. When the normal person is in a weak light he sees inefficiently with the fovea of his eyes. This has been definitely tested in the laboratory but a crude demonstration can be found in looking at a faint star. When the star is fixated directly, that is, when its image falls upon the fovea, it disappears: When the eye is shifted a little to one side, so that the image falls outside the fovea, it can be seen.

All these facts point to the conclusion that what an individual sees depends upon the kind of visual receptor that is stimulated. 

The rods are receptors which are limited in their function to brilliance discriminations, while the cones enable an individual to discriminate between colors as well as to give sensations of gray, white and black.

Light and dark adaptation of the eye. The eye adjusts itself to changes in illumination by compensating changes in the size of the pupil and by changes in the sensitivity of the retina. 

The area of the pupil changes from about 3 mm.² (or 1.9 mm. in diameter) in bright light to about 52 mm.² (or 8.1 mm. in diameter) in dim light. That is to say, in extremely dim illumination the pupil adjusts so as to admit seventeen times more light than it does in extremely bright light. While this seems to be a striking adjustment, it is relatively inefficient, for at different times of night and day the light affecting the eyes may change in the ratio of millions to one. 

The retina goes much further in meeting changing situations than do the pupils. As the light increases, the retina becomes less responsive. When there is a sudden change in illumination, vision is not so acute as it is after one has become used to (or adapts to) the new amount of light. This process of adaptation affects both the apparent illumination of the object seen as well as its hue or color.

A light-adapted eye is one that has been exposed to bright or intense general illumination. Such an eye becomes relatively insensitive to dimly illuminated objects and the same object seems 1

VISION 343 less brilliant than it did before the increase in general illumination took place. Walking into a motion-picture theater on a bright afternoon illustrates these effects. 

A dark-adapted eye is one that has been exposed to general illumination of weak intensity. Such an eye becomes more sensitive to faint stimulation and the same object seems more brilliant than it did before the eye became dark-adapted. The increase in ability to discern objects in the motion-picture theater after one has been there for some time illustrates these changes. As one emerges from the darkened theater into daylight, ordinary objects appear abnormally brilliant. 

The vision which occurs in faint light, or after dark adaptation, is called scotopic, or twilight, vision. The vision which occurs under illumination sufficiently strong to permit discrimination of colors is called photopic, or daylight, vision. 

That this adaptation takes place in the eye and not in the brain is evidenced by the fact that one eye can be light-adapted and the other eye simultaneously dark-adapted.

A dark-adapted eye and a light-adapted eye see the spectrum differently. When a beam of sunlight is passed through a prism and is projected upon a neutral gray surface, the different wave lengths of radiant energy become segregated and lie spread out in regular order. These wave lengths range from 400 to 760 millimicrons and give rise to color sensations ranging from red to violet. The wave-length values of the various colors are about as follows:
