In the light-adapted eye (that is, in photopic vision) the brightness value of the spectrum rises from each end and reaches its maximum at 560 millimicrons. With weak illumination (that is, in scotopic vision) a weak spectrum loses all its visible color and shows only a gradation of brilliance. In this situation the

PSYCHOLOGY 

spectrum shortens, because the red end becomes invisible beyond 640 millimicrons. At the same time that the red end disappears entirely the point of maximum brightness moves toward the violet end to about 500 millimicrons, or green. This changing aspect of spectral colors with changes in illumination is called the Purkinje phenomenon. It is illustrated by the fact that roses will disappear from view in a garden in twilight while the green leaves still remain visible. 

Another simple way to test the different aspects of colors with different illumination is to match a bit of red paper with a bit of green paper so that they appear to have the same brilliance in a bright light and then reduce the illumination. The green paper will appear brighter than the red with the decrease in general illumination as soon as the eyes become somewhat darkadapted.

It is an interesting fact that the brilliance values of spectral colors is the same for totally color-blind persons as it is for the normal person in dim illumination. Since the totally color-blind person has only rod vision, this would seem to provide further evidence that the retinal rods sense brilliance values only. The normal man in twilight vision and the totally color-blind man are both utilizing the same mechanism (the rods). Both discern only brilliance values and fail to see colors.

Dark adaptation not only changes the values in spectral colors but it also changes the sensitivity of the retina to light. As adaptation proceeds there is an increasing ability to see fainter and fainter stimuli. Both rods and cones take part in this changing sensitivity, but the rods play a much greater role than do the cones. Foveal adaptation (that is, cone adaptation) is very, very rapid and ends in about three minutes, after which time the eye can discern a stimulus that is about one-fiftieth as intense as the minimum stimulus before adaptation began. The adaptation occurring after this first three-minute period is wholly an adjustment of rod sensitivity. This rod adaptation proceeds rapidly at first and then more and more slowly, reaching near-completion in about 30 minutes. The change in sensitivity is enormous. The dark-adapted eye (after about 30 minutes of dim illumination) is able to discern a stimulus 1/50,000 of the value of the weakest

VISION 345 stimulus that could be seen at the beginning of the adaptation process.

The significance of sensory adaptation lies in the fact that it is an automatic adjustment to the environment. The sense organs are not merely gateways through which external, stimuli must pass; instead, they are adjusting organisms which respond, without any conscious control on the part of an individual, to changes in the external environment. 

Flicker and fusion. When successive visual stimuli come with sufficient rapidity they fuse, and the experience seems to be continuous. When they come more slowly they do not fuse completely, and there results a flicker. The frequency at which all flicker disappears is called the critical fusion frequency (or the critical flicker frequency) and depends upon several factors. 

1. An intense stimulus has a higher critical fusion frequency than a weak stimulus. With a visual stimulus of extremely low intensity, fusion may occur with a frequency as low as 5 cycles per second. With high intensities, the necessary frequency may run as high as 55 cycles per second. In motion-picture projection, freedom from flicker is secured when the pictures are shown at the rate of 15 to 20 frames per second unless the picture happens to be very bright. 

2. A stimulus that covers a large area has a higher critical fusion frequency than one covering a small area. That is, the parts of the retina seem to combine in a summation effect so that the stimulation of a large area has an effect similar to increasing the intensity of the stimulus over the same area. 

3. The fovea of the eye has a higher critical fusion frequency than the peripheral areas. For example, if a small beam of light is used as a stimulus, with an illumination strong enough to require a critical frequency of 36 cycles when it strikes the fovea, the critical frequency will be only about 22 cycles when the same light strikes the retina at a point 20 degrees above the fovea. 

4. The critical fusion frequency declines during dark adaptation and rises during light adaptation. 

5. The critical fusion frequency depends upon the relative duration of the light and dark periods. It is highest when the light and dark periods are approximately equal and declines when

PSYCHOLOGY 

either one becomes significantly longer than the other. For example, a motion picture would not have to show so many frames per second if the dark periods were much shorter than the light periods nor if the dark periods were much longer than the light periods. 

6. Once fusion is obtained, a further increase in the frequency of presentation neither improves nor impairs the excellence of the fusion effect. 

Whereas the effect of fusion in the production of motionpicture effects has been popularized, the use of fusion to make motion appear static has been largely confined to scientific laboratories. The instrument for effecting a static effect from a rapid series of visual stimuli is called the stroboscope. Everyone has seen a moving vehicle in a motion picture in which the wheels seemed to turn backward or in which the spokes stood still while the vehicle moved on. This is a stroboscopic effect. Its principle of operation can be made clear by a simple illustration. Suppose we have a disk which can be rotated on a color mixing motor and upon which is drawn a line extending from the center to the circumference. If, as this wheel is turned, it is illuminated by momentary flashes of light which occur only when the radial line is in the vertical plane above the center, and at other times the wheel is not visible, the illusion will be created that the line is stationary and is always vertical. It seems so because that is the only position in which we can see it. Now, if the wheel is turned at such a speed that the line comes to this position sixty times a second and the disk is illuminated by a light which flashes on at the same rate of sixty times a second, the line will appear to stand still. 

If the light flashes remain at the rate of sixty a second while the wheel is rotated fifty-nine times a second, it will appear to be turning counterclockwise at the rate of one revolution a minute. 

If the wheel is rotated at sixty-one times a second, it will appear to be moving clockwise at the rate of one revolution a minute. 

The stroboscope is used for such practical purposes as observing vibrations in high-speed machines, torque in crankshafts, the pitch of tones, and the like.

Visual aftersensations. Flicker and fusion demonstrate the fact that vision is not an instantaneous process. Instead, with each visual stimulation there is a time factor, during which the

LIVE

FIG. 86. Charpentier's bands. The reported effect produced by a brightly illuminated 12° slit rotating in a clockwise direction at the rate of two revolutions per second before a resting eye.

VISION 347 effect progresses from a minimum to its full value; and there is another time factor involved after the stimulus is removed, during which the effect of the stimulus recedes to zero. When the stimuli are not applied in rapid succession, this time lag produces other effects which are known as aftersensations or afterimages. 

When a single visual stimulus is instantaneously applied, the brilliance sensation rises rapidly at first and then more and more slowly until a maximum is reached. The total time for reaching this maximum is never more than one-fifth of a second. After this maximum is reached, the brilliance turns down rapidly and is followed by certain aftereffects. Most of these aftereffects are ignored in ordinary life and are apparent only when they are carefully sought. The train of effects can be described as a series of pulses of different speed and may be differentiated as follows: 

1. Charpentier's bands. If the stimulus is very weak there may be but one pulse. As the intensity increases there may be more pulsations which are briefer, more intense, and follow each other more rapidly. These can be demonstrated by rotating a brightly illuminated slit at the rate of two revolutions per second before a single resting eye. The reported effect is in the form of bands as shown in Fig. 86. They are known as Charpentier's bands. 

2. Purkinje afterimage or Bidwell's ghost. Next in order is the afterimage which has been named Bidwell's ghost or the Purkinje afterimage. It is best observed when the eyes are darkadapted, when the stimulation is brief, and when the eyes are fixated a little to one side of the object observed. It appears as a continuation of the object seen and is often of a complementary hue. It is probable that both rods and cones are involved. However, it is likely that the rods play the predominant role because: (a) It is seen most clearly when a peripheral area is stimulated (where the rods are most numerous). (b) It is very weakly present, if at all, in foveal vision. (c) It is best observed when the eyes are dark-adapted. 

3. The positive afterimage. The positive afterimage corresponds to the original impression in hue, saturation, and brightness. It can be ascribed to a continuation of retinal activity in the same direction after the stimulation has ceased. It is brief

PSYCHOLOGY 

1 in duration and is usually followed by a negative afterimage in which the qualities are reversed. 

4. The negative afterimage. Since the positive afterimage is so fleeting, it is hard to observe; but the negative afterimage may be clearly seen with a little practice. Look steadily at a square of red paper for sixty seconds, then at a neutral gray surface. There will appear a blue-green afterimage of a hue complementary to the original red. In other words, the negative afterimage is the complementary to the original stimulus. 

5. The flight of colors. Even more persistent is the aftereffect that follows the steady fixation of a bright white light. 

There is a flight of colors which may include any or all the colors of the color circle (red, orange, yellow, yellow-green, green, green-blue, blue, violet, purple, and gray) which follow each other in no orderly sequence and in a variety of patterns. During the first part of the period following the removal of the light, yellow may predominate over the other colors, then red, blue, or purple may gain the upper hand, and finally dark green. The changes occur most rapidly at first, then more and more slowly. There may be a core of one color surrounded by rings of others with a gradual interchange of places. Finally, the colors become darker and less saturated and end in a dull gray or black. 

Contrast. Visual contrast effects are usually classified into two categories: (1) Successive contrast refers to the changes in visual sensations which result from the influence of one stimulus on what follows. Those phenomena which we have discussed as adaptation and negative aftersensations are illustrations of successive contrast. (2) Simultaneous contrast refers to the mutual interaction between stimuli presented at the same time.

Contrast effects may also be classified into monocular and binocular contrast effects. Monocular contrast occurs when the two stimuli involved affect different parts of the retina of the same eye.

Binocular contrast occurs when one of the stimuli affects one eye and another stimulus the other eye at the same time. We shall consider binocular contrast later as a phenomenon of binocular vision.

Simultaneous brilliance contrast may be demonstrated by placing a small bit of paper on a background differing from it in brightness. If the background is darker, the paper will appear

VISION 349 lighter. If the background is lighter, it will appear darker. 

This can be clearly shown by placing a three-inch black square next to a three-inch white square. In the middle of each place a one-half-inch square of neutral gray paper and cover the whole with a sheet of tissue paper. The bits of gray paper which are really of the same brightness will show a marked difference; the one on the black ground will look lighter than the one on the white ground.

Simultaneous color contrast may be demonstrated by using backgrounds of different colors and placing the same bits of gray paper on the different backgrounds, covering the whole each time with tissue paper. It will be found that the following facts obtain: (a) The neutral gray square will tend to take on the hue that is the complementary of the background. If the background is red, the gray paper will appear to be blue-green. If the background is blue, the gray square will appear yellow. If the background is yellow, the gray square will appear blue. (b) Color contrast is greatest when the background and the small test square are of equal brightness, that is, color contrast is lessened by the presence of brilliance contrast. (c) The contrast effect is lessened if the two fields are separated by dark boundary lines and is heightened when the two fields are of the same texture. (d) Sat- urated colors produce a greater contrast effect than do unsaturated colors.

These principles should be given due consideration in the practical applications of the laws of color and brilliance contrast. 

In short, to enhance a color, place it in the company of its complementary. A red looks redder on a blue-green background; a white looks whiter on a black background; a blue looks bluer on a yellow background. The greater the difference between the color and the background the greater the contrast effect. 

BINOCULAR VISION 

When a robin looks for a worm, it attempts to see the worm clearly by turning its head so that one eye is directed toward the ground while the other one is turned upward. A bird's clear vision apparently involves the use of one eye to the exclusion of the other. When a person wants to see an object with the greatest clearness, he directs both eyes toward the object.

PSYCHOLOGY 

The way in which the two eyes co-operate in human vision has been the subject of intensive study. [2] Such co-operation is important in the perception of depth. We shall, however, postpone consideration of this subject until we take up other aspects of perception in Chapter XV. 

If the eyes are in the primary position (the position they assume when the head and body are erect and the eyes fixated upon an infinitely distant point in the median and horizontal planes), any stimulus will affect a certain area in each retina. 

Such paired areas are called identical retinal areas. If the stimulus is a single point it will stimulate identical points in the two retinas. Since the eyes are usually not in the primary position, the same stimulus ordinarily strikes points on the two retinas which are not identical. Nevertheless, the point will not be seen as a double point, even though nonidentical points on the two retinas are stimulated. That is to say, it is not necessary that identical points be stimulated to create a fusion of the two retinal stimulations. A pair of points in the two retinas which, when stimulated simultaneously, give rise to binocular fusion, or single vision, are called congruent points. 

When a visual stimulus falls on noncongruent points on the two retinas, it is seen as double; when it falls upon congruent points, it is seen as a single object. The reason that an intoxicated man sees double is that he has lost control of his eye muscles and cannot make them turn so that a single object will fall upon congruent points in the two eyes. Single vision, when congruent points are stimulated, is an illustration of teamwork between the two eyes; whereas seeing double demonstrates that such teamwork is limited and breaks down under certain circumstances. It is an interesting problem to determine to what degree the eyes act as independent units and to what degree they are unified in their action.

Binocular fusion. Under what conditions does binocular fusion occur? In ordinary conditions congruent points are stimulated by the same object and fusion is merely combining nearly identical images in the two retinas. 

When different stimuli fall on congruent points, what happens? When a stimulus of one brightness falls on one eye, and a stimulus of another brightness falls upon the congruent area of

VISION 351 the other eye, the resulting experience has a brilliance value lying between the two stimuli. It is a compromise between the two and not an addition of the two. This experiment shows that the stimulation of one retina is not added to the stimulation of the congruent point of the other retina. Binocular fusion is a compromise reaction and not one of summation.

Mixing colors produces a similar result. If red light falls upon one retina and yellow light falls upon the congruent area of the other eye, the result is an orange sensation. 

If one eye is

Binocular rivalry. When radically different colors or figures are presented simultaneously to congruent areas of the two eyes, they may refuse to combine in any manner; instead, they alternate so that the individual sees first one stimulus and then the other in fairly rapid shifts. This phenomenon is called retinal rivalry and can be readily demonstrated by means of the stereoscope (Fig. 87). The ordinary stereoscope is a device which places a prism before each eye in such a manner that one stimulus

PSYCHOLOGY 

can be seen by one eye and another by the other. Rivalry is best observed when the stimuli are not too intense.

With the stereoscope, two colors which are near together on the spectrum may combine and give the sensation of an intermediate color. When the two components are farther apart on the spectrum, they tend to alternate; the subject sees first one and then the other. -+- FIG. 88. Binocular rivalry. If the stereoscopic slide, as shown in the upper part of the figure, is presented, the subject will see alternately the combination shown at the left, in the lower part of the figure, and the combination shown at the right. That is, there will be an alternation in dominant position between the horizontal and vertical bars.

One interesting type of rivalry results when one eye is stimulated by a white surface and the other by a black. Instead of getting a plain neutral gray the result will be a lustrous effect. 

Rivalry is seen even more clearly when two incongruous contours are presented, one to each eye. If a heavy black horizontal line is shown to one eye and a heavy black vertical line is shown to the other they will not form a cross. The subject will see the ends of both lines but the point of intersection will change

VISION 353 so that alternately the vertical one will appear solid and then the horizontal one (see Fig. 88).

Binocular flicker. What happens when one eye is presented with a flickering stimulus and the other eye with one having the same rate of flicker but arranged so that it is bright while the other is dark? Do the two combine and thus eliminate the flicker or reduce the critical fusion frequency? Experiments have given a negative answer. There is some reduction, but it is so small that it can be said that the two eyes do not add together the alternating stimuli to form a continuous whole. 

FIG. 89.-Binocular perspective. 

If the upper slide is viewed through a stereoscope, it will appear as a truncated cone. If the lower slide is viewed through a stereoscope, the subject will seem to be looking into the large end of a funnel.

Perspective by retinal combination. The rule for binocular fusion and rivalry evolved thus far is: When the stimuli to the two eyes can combine in some manner, they tend to supplement each other; when they are too incongruous to combine, they alternate with each other. 

Under certain circumstances disparate retinal images combine and give the observer the impression of distance or depth of an object. Such experiences probably are based on the fact that, when a near object is seen, it is not seen the same with both eyes. 

Stereoscopic pictures illustrate such differences. Take two pictures of the same scene by means of two cameras placed apart by a distance equivalent to the distance between the two eyes and minute examination will show that the pictures are different. 

When these pictures are seen through a stereoscope, one picture falling on each eye, the observer will get the impression of depth. 

Look at the small end of a truncated cone with each eye, and

PSYCHOLOGY 

the difference in retinal images will be readily observed (Fig. 89). 

To the left eye the small section will be closer to the right rim of the more distant and larger section. To the right eye the small section will be closer to the left rim of the larger and more distant section. Seen together these two retinal images combine and the small section is seen to be nearer. Look into the large end of a funnel and the situation is reversed. With the right eye the small and more distant section moves to the right rim of the nearer and larger section. With the left eye the small and more distant section moves to the left rim of the nearer and larger section. 

When seen together the two images combine and the small section looks more remote.

Various effects may be obtained by reversing the pictures on a stereoscopic slide. For example, suppose the scene is a man sitting with his feet on an ottoman directly between him and the stereoscopic camera. The right camera would show the feet relatively nearer the right and the left camera would show the feet relatively nearer to the left in the picture. Seen through a stereoscope the observer would get a true perception of depth and would see the feet in front of the body. Suppose the pictures are reversed. The disparity of the images would tend to make the feet appear behind the man's body. But one does not ordinarily see the soles of a man's feet behind the body. The observer may see first the feet, then the body of the man; he may seem to see a transparent body with the feet behind; or, if there is enough incongruity resulting from the reversal of the two pictures, the observer will see merely a flat picture with no depth at all. 

These various phenomena of binocular vision suggest the conclusion that the combination of the sensations from the two eyes into a unified whole is the result of experiences of the individual which can be accompanied with success only when such a combination fits in with what the individual has learned about objects about him. The eyes supplement each other rather than add their experiences. 

We shall refer to the part that binocular vision plays in the perception of depth again in Chapter XV. Depth perception is a complicated process and binocular vision is but one contributing factor.

VISION 

355 

EYE MOVEMENTS 

Clear and distinct vision is possible only when and if the optical image of an object is motionless upon the retina of the eye. 

Vision is a chemical sense and time is required for a chemical reaction. Since the body is in continual motion and since external objects move, the eyes must be equipped with devices that will make continual adjustments possible if distinct vision is to be achieved.

Vision during eye movements. At one time it was thought that the eyes could not see during movement and that vision consisted of short periods of seeing interrupted by periods of blindness. Experiments have definitely shown that this is not the case. [12, pp. 576-594] When the retina of the eye is stimulated by a quick succession of stimuli (either because the eye moves, or because the objects move, or both), vision is blurred. 

If the eye moves at exactly the same pace as an external object in such a manner that the object stimulates the retina as though both were still, vision will be just as clear as though there were no motion.

A simple demonstration in the laboratory will provide convincing evidence of this fact. If a disk containing a series of converging lines, is whirled fast enough (in a clockwise direction) so that the lines blend, the observer will see only a uniform surface. If he fixates his vision on a point to the left of the disk and above the center of rotation and then quickly shifts to another fixation point to the right of the wheel and also above the center of rotation, he may see one or more of the converging lines of the disk as though it had stopped momentarily. He will see these lines clearly only if he happens to move his eyes with a speed equivalent to the speed of the disk and thus enable that part of the wheel to stimulate one portion of the retina during the movement of the eyes over the disk. Several attempts may be necessary before the two synchronize. The spokes of a wheel on a moving vehicle may sometimes be seen in a similar manner. 

Because movements of external stimuli and movements of the eye do not often synchronize, most vision during eye movements is blurred and hence ignored by the observer. Unless he

PSYCHOLOGY 

tries some definite experiment, such as the one just described, he believes he cannot see during eye movements.

Mechanical registration. One of the first methods was the attachment of a light rod to the eyeball by means of a polished bit of plaster of Paris. This rod then moved upon the surface of a smoked kymograph drum and provided a graphic record of

VISION 357 the eye movements. This method has been discarded for more efficient devices.

Photographic registration of light reflected from the cornea of the eye. A beam of light is projected upon the cornea of the eyeball and the reflection thrown on a moving film (Fig. 90). 

The operation of this device depends upon the fact that the eyeball is not a perfect sphere. If it were, there would be no change in the direction of the reflected light with a turning of the eyeball. 

Since the cornea projects forward, any movement of the eyeball changes the angle of its surface to the incident beam of light and thus changes the point at which the reflected light strikes the sensitive film. The film, of course, is moved in a vertical direction. 

Motion pictures. It is easy enough to take motion pictures of eye movements, but some difficulties are involved in measuring them. In order to obtain a point of reference it has been found valuable to put a small flake of China white on the cornea over the iris. When the pictures taken with this reference point are projected, frame by frame, onto a sheet of drawing paper it is relatively easy to obtain an accurate graphic record of the eye movements. Since some part of the movement may be lost between frames, it has been valuable, in some instances, to utilize two motion-picture cameras, each camera taking a picture during the movement, or dark period, of the other. 

Types of eye movements. The function of most eye. movements is to achieve the objective of obtaining clear images upon the retina and to maintain these for a long enough period to give clear vision. There are a few movements which do not directly contribute to this end, such as the slight upward movement of the eyeball during winking and the upward turning of the eyeball during sleep. Our main concern, however, is with the adjustments of the eye when it is being utilized as an organ of vision.

Movements during attempted fixation of the eyes on a stationary object. The eyes do not remain motionless when a stationary object is fixated for as long as a second on one fixation point. Instead, they move continually. Related to this is the fact that when the eyes turn repeatedly to the same object they are inaccurate in their ability to bring the object to the exact center of vision. This can be easily demonstrated. If an observer looks

PSYCHOLOGY 

at the setting sun, looks away, at it again, and away for a number of times, he will get aftersensations of the sun which do not coincide. The relative positions of these aftersensations give a graphic portrayal of the inaccuracies of his successive adjustments. Since the fovea is an area and not a mathematical point, this inaccuracy of fixation and unsteadiness of fixation does not interfere in any noticeable degree with clear vision.

FIG. 91. Convergence. When an object is moved toward the eyes, the eyes rotate so that the object remains fixated on each fovea, the optic axes converge, and the angle made by them becomes greater. 

Movements of convergence and divergence. Movements of convergence and divergence can best be understood by considering the movements of the optic axes. The optic axis is the straight line passing through the center of the lens and the center of the fovea. When a person looks at an infinite distance the two axes would theoretically be parallel. As the point of regard moves toward the observer, the eyes turn so that the optic axis for each eye is still on the object and the angle made by the two

VISION 359 becomes greater the nearer the object of regard approaches. This movement is a convergent movement. As the object moves away, the optic axes diverge, the angle between the two becomes smaller, and the two axes become more nearly parallel. These movements are illustrated in Fig. 91. 

There are some significant facts about adjustments of convergence and divergence. (a) Convergent-divergent movements take considerable time and are often interrupted by pauses. (b) 

The two eyes do not always keep step; one may pause while the other is moving; one may reach its destination and remain there while the other is still feeling around. (c) Convergence is a sort of tentative reaction and the object may appear double until corrections are made. Such readjustment may involve changes in the position of one or both the eyes. 

These facts have an important bearing on ease and efficiency in reading. If the book or printed matter is so held that one part of the printed line is farther from the eyes than the other, convergent-divergent movements would have to be made as the eye moves along the line. It would be more efficient and more restful to the eyes to make sure that the printed matter is so held that such movements are at a minimum, that is, have all printed matter equidistant from the eyes, especially from left to right. 

Saccadic movements. The sudden movement of the eyes from one fixation point to another is called a saccadic movement. 

It involves co-ordination of the two eyes and is the most frequent 

FIG. 92.-Record of eye movements made when the eye "sweeps around a circle." The lines are saccadic movements and the dots are fixation points. sort of eye movement. It is the type of movement that takes place in reading or in looking at various parts of a stationary object or scene. In reading a line of print the eye jumps from one fixation point on the line to the next and does not move evenly along the line. In "sweeping the eyes" around a circle the eyes make jumpy movements, stopping at various points, so that a graphic picture of such movements would be somewhat as shown in Fig. 92.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Improvement in reading depends in part (a) upon the improvement of saccadic movements in reading, (b) upon making fewer fixation points per line, (c) upon increasing the accuracy of such movements, and (d) upon increasing the speed of such movements. Certain facts about eye movements will show why improvement is not so easily accomplished as it might seem to be. 

1. They are only crudely recognized by the subject and are not directly subject to voluntary control. Nevertheless, a person may consciously determine the approximate location of his next fixation point and may attempt to space these points uniformly along the line of print. These saccadic movements are closely analogous to the ballistic movements described in the chapter on motor skills and are improved by corrections in aim and not by trying to make them into slow controlled movements. 

2. They start and stop quickly. Photograph records show that slow readers often take an undue amount of time at each fixation point and that this time is taken up with the sort of jumpy movements which take place when one tries to keep his vision fixed on a single point. Good reading, consequently, involves quick apprehension of what one sees as soon as the eyes come to a stop and the quick beginning of the next saccadic movement. The poor reader may continue to jump around at one spot before moving on. 

3. The speed with which the eyes move during the saccadic jump depends upon various factors. It is more rapid for longer jumps although the total time taken for the longer movement is greater than for the shorter movement. For example, a movement of 5° (which is the extent made to cover one inch on a page held a foot from the eyes) requires about 29 msec., whereas a movement of 20° (an extent of four inches) takes about 55 msec. The speed of saccadic movements is also affected by the reader's organic condition. These movements are slower when the reader is drowsy or under the influence of alcohol. 

Pursuit movements. In following a moving object, the eyes can continue to fixate upon that object and to keep pace with it by means of pursuit movements, provided the movement of the object is neither very slow nor very fast. Such pursuit movements are seldom perfectly synchronized with the movements of the objective stimuli; there is some tendency for the eyes to lag

VISION 361 behind and then catch up again by a saccadic jump. The combination of pursuit movements with saccadic movements can be seen when a person looks from the window of a moving vehicle. 

The eyes stay fixed on one object for a time by means of pursuit movements, and then jump to another object. 

A little experiment will demonstrate that, regardless of whether the eyes remain fixed or follow in a pursuit movement, clarity of vision will remain the same so long as the object remains fixated. Superimpose a sheet of transparent paper, upon which there is some printed matter, upon another sheet of paper containing printed matter. Move one sheet over the other. When a word on either sheet is fixated, the words on the other sheet are blurred. It makes little difference whether the fixated word is on the stationary or the moving sheet so far as clearness of vision is concerned. For clear vision the object must be stationary on the retina of the eye; it need not be stationary in space. 

Compensatory eye movements. If the head moves to the right, the eyes must turn to the left in their sockets to keep an object fixated. If the head moves up, the eyes must move down. 

If the head moves to the left, the eyes must move to the right.

These compensatory movements appear, on the surface, to be merely the reverse of pursuit movements. In pursuit movements, the object moves while the head remains still; in compensatory movements, the object remains still and the head moves. In either case, the eyes remain fixed on the object by means of the turning of the eyeballs in their sockets. In the pursuit movement, however, the adjustment is imperfect; it has a long latent time-requiring about one-fifth of a second to get going; and it must be corrected continually by the help of saccadic movements. In contrast to the awkwardness of pursuit movements, the compensatory movement starts simultaneously with the head movement, continues with the head movement, and maintains almost a perfect fixation on the object. The whole process works as though it were a single integrated unit. The head and eyes work together almost perfectly. This can be checked by reading while turning the head. 

There is practically no blurring. By way of contrast, watch a person attempt to follow the swinging of a pendulum by pursuit movements. A number of saccadic corrections will be seen; and

PSYCHOLOGY 

the observer will report difficulty in keeping the pendulum fixated clearly until he gets accustomed to it. 

Movements of nystagmus. Rotation of an individual causes a complex set of compensatory eye movements. When the head is rotated to the right, the eyes turn reflexly to the left and then, as the rotation continues, jump back by a saccadic movement. This alternation between a compensatory eye movement in the direction opposite to the rotation and the saccadic jumps in the direction of rotation has been given the name of rotation nystagmus. If the rotation continues long enough, the subject becomes dizzy and the eyes cease their movements and stare straight ahead. When the rotation stops, the movements reappear, but in reverse. The smooth movement is in the direction of the preceding rotation and the saccadic movement in the opposite direction, This is called post-rotation nystagmus. Movements of nystagmus are dependent upon the semicircular canals organs in the inner ear which are concerned with sensations of bodily movement and balance. They will be studied in more detail in Chapter XIV.

Chapter XIII HEARING THE 

'HE development of sound motion pictures and the radio has stimulated intense interest in the subject of hearing and, at the same time, has provided apparatus and techniques for the study of the physical and psychological aspects of sound. The progress from the crude squawkings produced by the first talkies and radios to the present smooth and pleasant performances has necessitated not only a perfecting of sound-producing apparatus, but an understanding of the hearing process by means of which sounds are heard.

Hearing depends upon the creation of a mechanical disturbance, the transmission of the effects of such disturbance to the ear by means of the air or some other conducting medium, and the reaction of the ear to this mechanical disturbance. Accordingly our order of study will be: (a) an analysis of fundamental characteristics of the mechanical disturbances which give rise to sound waves; (b) a description of how the ear operates; and then (c) a consideration of the significance of certain characteristics of sound such as pitch, intensity, and quality. 

THE FUNDAMENTALS OF SOUND 

All sounds, no matter how complex, may be conceived as the projection of uniform circular motion, called simple harmonic motion. [6]

Simple harmonic motion. The most elementary kind of vibration is simple harmonic motion. It is the kind of vibration produced by a tuning fork or by a pendulum, the only essential difference between the two being that of frequency. The undulating movement of a pendulum can be readily seen but is too 365

PSYCHOLOGY 

slow to make a sound that can be heard. The tuning fork, on the other hand, vibrates too rapidly for its oscillations to be seen clearly by the naked eye, but with sufficient frequency to be heard. 

If pendular motion is examined it will be found to have certain characteristic features: (a) Its swings are in a straight line; (b) it is vibratory, moving to and fro; (c) its movements are repeated regularly; (d) there is an instant of rest at each extreme of movement; and (e) starting from the rest at one extreme, the movement accelerates until it reaches the central point of its swing, after which it slows down until it comes to rest momentarily again at the other extreme. If a marking device is attached to a tuning fork so as to trace its swings upon a paper moving at a uniform speed, as is illustrated in Fig. 93, these characteristics of pendular motion can be readily seen. 

FIG. 93.-Graphic record of the oscillations of a tuning fork. 

An analysis of such a record of pendular motion will reveal that it is a true sine curve. Since a sine curve is the graphic record of circular motion, this fact enables us to make an accurate analysis of pendular motion and thus to determine the essential components of sound waves.

Simple harmonic motion is produced exactly when circular motion is transformed into rectilinear motion. This can be accomplished by tracing the path of a shadow (the light, of course, being at an infinite distance) produced by a rotating knob, as shown in Fig 94. A sample of the curve traced on the paper, moving at uniform speed, by such a shadow is shown at the lower part of the figure. When the knob is at the top position, the shadow will fall directly on the straight axis at A. If the wheel rotates in a counterclockwise direction for one-fourth of a revolution, or 90°, the shadow will be at B. When the knob has rotated one-half a revolution, or 180°, the shadow will be at C. When it has rotated three-quarters of a revolution, or 270°, the shadow will be at D. And when it has moved one complete revolution, or 360°, the shadow will be at E. Each complete revolution of

367 the knob is called a cycle. The sine wave representing such a cycle comprises one complete S-shaped curve.

These characteristics of harmonic motion, namely, frequency, amplitude, and phase, are the essential factors which account for differences in sound waves.

The production of a sound wave by harmonic motion. [7] A sound wave is produced when harmònic motion affects some material substance capable of being moved by pulsations or pistonlike movements. Any material which can be affected by these pulsations can also transmit these effects; and a sound wave is formed. The effects of pulsations from the human voice upon the air particles in front of the mouth are illustrated in Fig. 95. 

The most common medium for sound conduction is the air. 

The vibratory motion of the sound source may be conceived as giving a "push" to those particles in front of it, jamming them together until the stroke comes to its maximum point. On the return stroke of the piston, the particles tend to spring back and fill the space left by the recoil of the piston. If the stroke is repeated periodically, as occurs when we have a tone, there is an alternating period of condensation and rarefaction of particles and it is this series which constitutes a sound wave. 

The speed with which sound travels depends upon the medium through which it is passing. In air it is about 332 meters

C. A pure tone

FIG. 97.-Graphic representation of tone character. complex mixture of a number of harmonic waves differing in frequency, in amplitude, and in phase. In Fig. 96 the solid line represents a wave that results from a combination of the two simple harmonic waves represented by dotted lines. It is possible to analyze a complex sound wave into its simple harmonic com-

PSYCHOLOGY 

ponents by means of a harmonic analyzer. When a mechanical harmonic analyzer is used, the curve is traced with a stylus, the machine giving information which can be used to determine various components of the original curve. [6] Modern sound analysis makes use of electric wave analyzers. [7] 

The character of a tone is determined by the number of component harmonic waves, by the relative intensity of each, and by the pattern that they form. In the case of a noise, the components are so numerous, the patterns so variable, the components nonperiodic in form, and the duration of each so brief that the resultant is a hopeless jumble and the listener usually gets a feeling of unpleasantness from hearing it. On the other hand, a pure simple harmonic wave gives the auditor the impression of emptiness. A rich musical tone usually has a fundamental frequency combined with other higher frequencies which blend with it. The graphic representation of a street noise, a vowel sound, and a pure tone (in Fig. 97) will make clear these distinctions.

Overtones. Most bodies not only vibrate as wholes but various parts vibrate simultaneously with different frequencies. 

The basic vibration, usually the lowest audible one, is called the fundamental tone, whereas the tones produced by parts of the resonant body are called overtones. A stretched string, for example, will vibrate not only over its whole length, as shown in the top illustration in Fig. 98, but various segments will simultaneously vibrate at different rates, as shown in the other three diagrams. When the string vibrates as a whole, it gives its fundamental vibration, or its first harmonic tone. If the vibrating string is touched at its mid-point as shown at a, in Fig. 98, it will vibrate in halves as well as over its entire length. This will produce a tone of twice the frequency of the fundamental, and is called the first overtone or second harmonic. When touched at point b, it will vibrate at three times its fundamental rate, and this is called the second overtone or third harmonic. When touched at c, it will vibrate at four times its fundamental rate, and this is called the third overtone or fourth harmonic.¹ This illustration oversimplifies the facts. When a violin string is

Suppose the two tones of 256 cycles each are sounded together. They will be heard as one tone. If the frequency of one is changed gradually, beats will be produced whose frequency

HEARING 

373 1 corresponds with the difference in vibration rate between the two tones. If one is 256 and the other 259 cycles, there will be three beats a second. Such a slow beat will be heard as a change in intensity. It will be heard as a single tone which alternately swells out and subsides. This single tone has a pitch intermediate between the two components; it is called the intertone. 

As the difference between the two tones is increased, the beats increase in frequency up to about 16 per second, when they take on an unpleasant character and are experienced as a thrusting against the ear. The thrusting phase passes into a rattle when the difference is increased to about 30 per second. When the difference in frequency is increased beyond 30 per second, the f h FIG. 101. Representation of beats. The light solid line completes eight cycles while the dotted line completes nine cycles. At the areas marked abcd and efgh they are nearly in phase and reinforce each other. The resultant solid line is louder than either of the component tones. At m they are out of phase and tend to neutralize each other. The solid line is, therefore, almost motionless. The effect is heard as a change in intensity of a single tone. subject no longer hears the single intertone; instead, the two components are heard, but with a characteristic roughness. 

A good way to tune an instrument is to make use of this phenomenon of beats. Sound the standard pitch alone, and then sound the instrument to be tuned along with it. If beats are heard, they will indicate that the two are close together, but still mistuned. If a change in tuning increases the frequency of the beats, it indicates that the adjustment was made in the wrong direction.

Combination tones. Whereas small differences in frequency between the harmonic components of a tone will produce beats, larger differences will produce secondary tones called combination tones. The two most important combination tones are difference tones and summation tones. An illustration will make clear how they are produced. Suppose two tones, one of 400

PSYCHOLOGY 

cycles and one of 256 cycles, are sounded together. In addition to the two component tones there will be heard a difference tone of 144 cycles (produced by a high-frequency beat between the two components-400 minus 256 gives 144), a summation tone of 656 cycles (400 plus 256 gives 656), a difference tone produced by the difference between 656 and 144 (656 minus 144 gives 512) of 512 cycles, a summation tone produced by the sum of 656 and 144 (656 plus 144 gives 800) of 800 cycles, and a great many more such combinations of frequencies. That is to say, when a tone of 400 cycles and a tone of 256 cycles are produced together, tones of the following frequencies will be heard: 144 cycles, 256 cycles, 400 cycles, 512 cycles, 656 cycles, 800 cycles, and many others besides. Furthermore, there will be differences in intensity of all these tones. Some will be dominant and others so faint as to be almost indiscernible. These combination tones plus the component harmonic tones provide what is known as tone quality. 

Musical instruments producing the same fundamental tone will, because of their structure, produce different combinations of overtones, difference tones, combination tones, and incidental sounds. One would never fail to distinguish between a bell, a violin, and a cornet although we all three were sounding the same fundamental tone. 

Resonance. Resonance is the vibratory response of a body to harmonic motion imposed upon it. Resonance may be of two kinds: (1) tuned resonance, or sympathetic vibration, and (2) forced resonance.

Tuned resonance, or sympathetic vibration, results when the resonating body has a characteristic frequency that is the same as the inducing sound wave. Most solid objects have peculiar frequencies of their own; they are particularly responsive to their favorite frequencies and relatively unresponsive to others. The tuned resonance of such bodies can be well illustrated by the activity of a pendulum. The time required for the swing of a pendulum is a function of its length. Shorten it and the frequency of its swing increases. Suppose a pendulum whose rate is one swing a second is pushed by a force which acts once a second. The first impulse will give it a slight motion, but each succeeding push will be cumulative and increase the ampli-

HEARING 

375 tude of the swing (up to a certain optimal limit) because it comes at the right time. On the other hand, a succession of pushes will be relatively ineffective unless their rhythm corresponds in frequency with the natural rate of the pendulum or unless it is some multiple thereof. A tuned resonator is effective in the reception and interpretation of sounds, but it is a poor device to transmit sounds because it will distort while transmitting them. It will accentuate those components which correspond with its characteristic frequencies and dampen those which do not. 

Forced resonance takes place when the receiving body has a different frequency from that of the inducing sound wave. 

The best sound transmitters are those which have no characteristic frequencies of their own and will respond only by forced vibration. Air is such a transmitter. It is very responsive to sound waves without contributing much to the form of the waves which it transmits because it has no inherent favoritism for any harmonic frequencies. The eardrum membrane vibrates with forced vibration; within certain limitations, it does not tend to accentuate any sounds nor does it tend to dampen any. 

A resonator whose period is 100 cycles a second will be set in motion by a frequency in the surrounding air of 100 cycles and will respond only indifferently to other frequencies. If, then, we had a sound composed of a great many harmonic components and wished to discover what these were, we could make such an analysis by testing the effect of the sound upon resonators of all frequencies. Whenever we used a resonator whose frequency corresponded with one of the harmonics in the sound to be analyzed, it would be set in motion. A radio receiving set is based upon this principle. A highly selective set is tuned so that it will select waves of a certain frequency and will fail to respond to others. The ear is supposed, according to the resonance theory of hearing, to have a large number of resonators, each one tuned to a particular frequency. In a complicated manner, these analyze the incoming sound waves and transmit impulses to the brain in such a manner that the individual is able to discriminate tones and noises of various pitches, intensities, and qualities.

However, some students contend that the process of hearing is not that of the analysis of incoming sounds into components

PSYCHOLOGY 

by a set of resonators. Instead, they conceive of the ear as discerning differences in total sound patterns.

The human ear is a masterpiece of mechanical engineering. 

The sound waves that reach the ear are a complicated mixture of harmonic components. Their reception requires a specialized kind of mechanical system, which will be sensitive enough to FIG. 102.-Cross section of the ear. PITCH 

The most important factor in determining the psychological experience of pitch is the frequency of the sound wave. The relationship between frequency and pitch is so striking that it is often regarded as the only determining factor in pitch sensations..

HEARING 

381 Nevertheless, there is not a perfect relationship between pitch and frequency; other factors are involved. 

Factors which affect pitch. influence pitch are as follows:

Some of the factors which The relationship between pitch and intensity. When the frequency of a tone is around 2,000 cycles per second, there is little change in the pitch of the tone with changes in intensity. 

As the intensity of a low-pitched tone (that is, a tone appreciably lower in frequency than 2,000 cycles) is increased, the pitch decreases. Conversely, as a high-pitched tone (above 2,000 cycles) is increased in intensity, the pitch becomes higher. In other words, as the intensity of a tone is increased, its pitch tends to shift away from the central hearing range. 

The effect of duration on pitch. The duration of a tone affects its apparent pitch. In general, the apparent pitch of a tone falls when the duration of that tone decreases below 10 msec., the fall being especially rapid below 3 msec.

Stated another way, a tone must last a certain length of time in order for it to be identified with any accuracy. If a tone of 1,000 cycles is sounded for less than 2 msec., it will be heard not as a tone but as a toneless click. If it lasts a little more than 

2 msec. it takes on some tonal character but the pitch is rather indefinite. As its duration is increased the ability to discriminate its pitch improves. Furthermore, if two successive tones of equal frequency are separated by less than about 10 msec., they will be heard as one continuous tone. Lower tones may be separated for even longer intervals and still be heard as one uninterrupted tone. For example, two 100 cycles tones will be heard as a continuous tone if separated by as much as 30 msec. 

The effect of complexity on pitch. With an increase in the complexity of a sound it becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish its fundamental pitch. Sounds may vary all the way from the most simple tone, which is a single harmonic wave, to the most complex sound, commonly called thermal noise. We have already described a simple harmonic wave. Thermal noise can be obtained by amplifying and impressing on a loud-speaker all the random motions of electrons in an electrical resistance. 

If the amplifier and speaker have uniform characteristics, the resulting noise contains all audible frequencies at equal intensity.

PSYCHOLOGY 

It sounds much like a hiss or a shhh. It should be clear that the ear cannot distinguish any one pitch in a thermal noise, whereas it should be relatively easy to distinguish the pitch of a pure harmonic wave. In short, the more simple the tone the more easily can the ear distinguish its fundamental pitch. 

Moreover, the fundamental pitch that is heard need not be dependent upon that sound being produced directly by some instrument. For example, when a complex tone is composed of frequencies differing by a constant amount of 100 cycles or more, the apparent pitch of the complex mass of frequencies is that of a tone whose frequency is equal to the constant difference. Thus, if frequencies of 700, 800, 900, and 1,000 cycles are sounded together, the listener will hear them as a 100-cycle tone. If 400, 600, 800, and 1,000 cycles are sounded together they will be heard as a 200-cycle tone. If to 400, 600, 800, and 1,000 cycles is added a group containing 500, 700, and 900 cycles, the apparent pitch will drop from 200 to 100 cycles. Many radio receivers drop out the low fundamental tones without changing radically the apparent pitch of the tones that are heard. The same process can be observed in the laboratory by playing a phonograph selection from which the low tones have been filtered. 

Differential discrimination of pitch. Pitch discrimination is best in the range of keenest sensibility: between 2,000 and 

3,000 cycles. In general pitch discrimination improves with an increase in intensity of the tones to be compared. The ability to discriminate between tones is poorest at low frequencies and at low intensities. In the entire auditory area, as shown in 

Fig. 109, if tones covering the whole area are presented, varying them by minimum amounts in intensity and in pitch, the human ear can distinguish about 340,000 separate tones. 

There are great individual differences in the ability to recognize a certain pitch. Some individuals are so far superior to others in this respect that they have been given credit for the ability to name precisely the pitch of a musical note without the aid of any standard of reference. Even those individuals who claim absolute pitch have been found to be subject to the following types of errors: (1) confusion between octaves; (2) constant errors of a half tone in one direction; (3) errors of a half tone

HEARING 

383 downward in the highest part of the musical scale and a half tone upward in the lowest part.

LOUDNESS 

Loudness refers to the intensity characteristics of sound as experienced by an individual. Sounds of high sensory intensity are variously described as strong, loud, or intense; those of low intensity are roughly described as weak, faint, or mild. Loudness is chiefly a function of the intensity of the physical disturbance, but it also depends upon other factors, such as the pitch of the sound, the masking effect of other sounds, the overtone content, and the sensory acuity of the listener. [4] The measurement of loudness. The creation of a scale for loudness had to take into consideration the fact that the ear can detect an enormously wide range of energies. The ear can support a sound whose energy is a million-million times the least sound it can detect. Since the ordinary arithmetic scale could not easily cover such a wide range, a logarithmic, or ratio, scale has been developed. According to such a scale one sound is not described as containing so many more units than another but as having a certain ratio to another sound, such as twice as loud, ten times as loud, etc. Such a scale requires a definite reference level and that level has arbitrarily been placed at the threshold of hearing for a 1,000-cycle tone. That is, the faintest 1,000-cycle tone that can be heard by the average human ear.2 

The logarithm of the ratio between two sound intensities has been given the name bel and has come to be used as the unit of measure of sound energy. Since the bel is a ratio, it has no meaning unless the reference value is stated. Hence, it is important in using the bel in connection with hearing to remember that there must be a given reference point. The decibel is onetenth of a bel.

When the threshold of hearing is used as the reference intensity, and with decibels indicating the power to which a threshold sound must be raised to equal the other sounds, the following scale of values holds. 

2 In terms of physical energy such a sound can be stated as a sound whose energy is equivalent to the root-mean-square pressure of 0.0002 dyne per square centimeter.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Decibels 120 100 80 60 40 20 thunder airplane engine boiler shop elevated train pneumatic drill busy street conversation quiet automobile average office average dwelling whisper threshold of hearing 

Factors affecting loudness. Loudness is primarily a function of the amplitude of vibrations, but it is also influenced by the frequency, by masking, and by the overtone content. 

The factor of amplitude. The wider the swings of a vibrating body the louder will be the sound produced by its oscillations. It takes very little to demonstrate this fact. If a violin string, for example, is plucked gently, it will swing through a small space and the tone will be weak. Pluck it vigorously and it can be seen to swing violently and the sound will be more intense.

The factor of frequency. While the loudness of a tone is primarily a function of the amplitude of the physical sound wave, it is, nevertheless, partly dependent upon the frequency of the sound wave. The same difference in the physical intensity of two tones will be heard as a greater difference in loudness when the tones are of low pitch than when they are of a high pitch. 

Because of this fact the same musical selection will change in character with a change in the loudness with which it is reproduced by such a device as a radio transmitter or a phonograph. 

With an increase in the intensity of reproduction, the low tones will increase in loudness more than the high tones, whereas with a decrease in intensity, the low tones will decrease in loudness disproportionately. 

Effect of masking on intensity. 

Masking is the partial or complete obscuring of a given tone by the simultaneous presentation of a tone of different frequency. We have already seen

HEARING 

385 that when two tones have nearly the same frequency and nearly the same intensity they interact with each other and produce beats, rattles, or roughness (depending upon the actual difference between them). Such beating effects might be considered as an alternate reinforcement and masking. Masking is, then, a sort of interference between two tones. What factors favor such interference? 

1. Masking is greatest when the two tones lie close together in frequency but not close enough to give beats. 

2. A tone is masked more effectively by a loud tone than by a weak one. 

3. A tone of low frequency masks tones of a higher frequency, whereas a tone of high frequency does not act as a mask for a tone of lower frequency. Even when the high tone is very loud its masking effect on lower tones is slight. 

4. Masking has been explained by some students as the result of interference in the physical sound waves; [7] by others masking is attributed to interference within the individual. [2] 

Those who argue for internal interference cite the fact that a tone heard in one ear may be masked by a tone heard in the other ear (a phenomenon called binaural masking). Those who contend for interference in the physical sound wave explain binaural masking by bone conduction.

A good analogy to enable the student to visualize effects of masking is the action of waves on the water. Large swells (corresponding to low tones) can easily overcome the effect of ripples (corresponding to high tones). Ripples can hide broad swells only if the swells are not very deep (not very loud) and the ripples are quite vigorous (very loud). 

The overtone content changes the loudness of a tone. It is easy to increase the loudness of a musical tone by increasing its overtone content. Laboratory tests have shown, for example, that when a pure tone of 100 cycles is enriched by adding ten harmonic components, all equally intense, the loudness is increased to sixty times the loudness of the pure tone. 

Factors which influence the ability to discriminate loudness. The least amount of change of a given sound which is necessary to produce a noticeable change in sensation is influenced by several factors. [7]

PSYCHOLOGY 

1. The region of greatest differential sensitivity of the ear for loudness corresponds to the frequency range of greatest sensitivity; namely, the region of about 2,000 to 3,000 cycles. For the average ear it is possible to distinguish about 325 just-noticeable steps in loudness within this frequency range. This number diminishes as the pitch is increased or decreased. 

2. As the intensity of the tones to be compared is increased, the ability to discriminate differences in intensity improves. 

3. The ability to discriminate between the loudness of the two tones is better when both ears are used than when only one ear is used. 

4. Loudness discrimination is improved when the duration of the two tones to be compared is increased. 

5. Discrimination is best when the transition between the tones to be compared is instantaneous and silent. 

6. The readiness of the observer for making the discrimination is important. Keenness is increased when the individual himself operates the key that makes the change between the two tones, and when he is permitted to listen to the tones as often as he wishes before making his decision.

AUDITORY LOCALIZATION 

There are several facts which indicate that auditory localization is essentially a function of the two ears. In the first place, a normal person can localize sounds much better when they are to the right or to the left of the median plane. Many errors are made when the sound source is exactly in the median plane, and when each ear is, consequently, stimulated in exactly the same way. In the second place, a person deprived of the use of one ear shows poor sound localization immediately after his loss, although he is able to make some improvement after a lapse of time. These facts would indicate that the main factors in sound localization are those in which the two ears hear differently when there is a single sound source.

Factors which influence the localization of sound. 

Under different circumstances, the following factors play varying roles: 

Intensity as a factor in sound localization. When two tones, differing only in intensity, are led separately to each ear,

HEARING 

387 the listener tends to image the source as located toward the side of greater intensity. It can be shown that, when a sound comes from a source not in the median plane, the intensity of that tone is different at the two ears. Such differences are greater with tones of higher frequency than with tones of low frequency. 

The difference in intensity between the two ears is about 1 decibel for a 300-cycle tone, while it is about 10 decibels (or a power ratio of ten to one) for a tone of 15,000 cycles. 

Phase differs at the two ears. When a sound comes from the median plane, it stimulates both ears in the same phase. When it comes from a source outside the median plane, the ears hear it in different phase relations. In an experimental test, when two tones, differing only in phase, are led one to each ear, the listener tends to image the sound source as located toward the side, of the leading phase. Since phase differences become less with an increase in frequency of the sound, this factor should operate less as the frequency increases. Since phase effects disappear at frequencies above 800 cycles, the factor of phase can be operative only with sounds of low frequency. 

Time differences at the two ears. For complex tones and for noises, difference in the time of reception by the two ears becomes an important factor in sound localization. As the time difference in reception by the two ears increases, the source of the sound seems to move from the median plane toward the ear that is stimulated first. 

Complexity of sound. It is much easier to localize complex sounds than it is to localize a pure tone. When both low and high frequencies are present in a sound, the low frequencies probably provide cues in the form of intensity differences. In addition, the qualitative sound pattern comes to be connected with certain known sources, and this helps. 

Stereophonic effects. While localization is often tested in the laboratory with limited sound effects, in actual life the presence of multiple sources of sound gives an auditory perspective to most of our hearing. When listening to an orchestra one hears not only the summation of effects from the different instruments but effects based on their spatial relation. Pick up the music from an orchestra with one microphone and its broadcast will be flat and without perspective. Two or more microphones

PSYCHOLOGY 

set at different positions will add greatly to the quality of the broadcast. It is probably the difference in auditory depth, or perspective, that is most disturbed when a person is deprived of the hearing of one ear.

AUDITORY FATIGUE 

The ear suffers little from fatigue, in spite of the fact that we have no means of closing our ears against the constant bombardment of unwanted noises which may persist through both day and night. Violently extreme sound pressures may injure the auditory mechanism, but there is little temporary loss of sensitivity because of previous stimulation. 

There is some evidence that there is more fatigue from highpitched tones than from tones of low frequency. After an ear has been exposed for 2 minutes to a 94-decibel tone of 100 cycles, it will recover in 20 seconds; a tone of the same intensity but of 

4,000 cycles may take as long as 6 minutes for complete recovery. 

On the other hand, there seems to be an augmenting effect that works counter to any fatigue effects. After exposure to a loud tone the individual may not only return to normal but show increased acuity for tones of the same level of intensity and frequency.

Chapter XIV 

SMELL, TASTE, AND

SOMESTHESIS 

IN ADDITION to the senses of vision and hearing, there are a number of other sense modalities which enable humans to receive and interpret impressions from the external world. These include: olfactory (smell) sensations, gustatory (taste) sensations, cutaneous sensations, pressure and pain, visceral sensations, and sensations of movement and position. Somesthesis is a general term which includes all the body senses of the skin and underlying tissues and sensations from the internal organs. SMELL

The sense organs for smell are located in a little alcove in the upper part of the nose. They consist of nerve cells embedded in the mucous membranes of the nose with slender fibers branching out to the surface of this alcove. This alcove is off the main air passage to the lungs and it receives only eddy currents; hence, sniffing has value when one wishes to test the odor of any sub

In ordinary life odors are usually mixed with other sensations and an untrained person is unable to distinguish between smells and the taste, pain, and other sensations combined with the odors. Moreover, extensive experimentation has not enabled psychologists to reach any agreement as to the number and delineation of basic odors. It has been estimated that there are about 

60,000 different odorous substances, but it is quite likely that many of these owe their effect to such other sensations as taste, touch, pain, warmth, cold, and the like. If all extraneous influences could be removed, it has been estimated that the substances 391

PSYCHOLOGY 

which have no other sensory value than smell might be reduced to fifty.

The specific stimulus which affects the sensory end organs for smell are molecular particles which are liberated from their

These particles spread out in gaseous diffusion and are effective in extremely small amounts. For example, camphor can be perceived when in a dilution of 1 part to 400,000; or musk, 1 part to 8,000,000.

FIG. 111.-The odor prism. 

Foul Burnt Fragrant Fruity Resinous Spicy

Various lists have been presented as representing the primary odors. One which has been widely accepted is based on six qualities which may be arranged in the form of an odor prism as shown in Fig. 111. These six primary odors are.

Fragrant: as in lily of the valley, roses, or violets. 

Spicy: as in cloves, anise, or cinnamon. 

Fruity: as in lemon, orange oil, or ether. 

Resinous: as in turpentine, pine needles, or juniper.

Foul: as in decayed animal matter or hydrogen sulphide. 

Burnt: as in tar.

When odors are combined with other sensory qualities the following may be obtained: 

Odor plus sweet taste: as in chloroform, bromoform, iodoform, ethyl chloride. 

Odor plus sour taste: as in acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, and valerianic acid.

Odor plus cold sensation: as in camphor, menthol, phenol, eucalyptol, sassafras.

Odor plus warm sensation: as in ethyl alcohol, propyl alcohol, amyl alcohol. 

Odor plus pain: as in ammonia, chlorine, bromine, iodine, nicotine.

WWU ME FIG. 112.-The olfactometer. The bent tubes at the left are inserted into the nostrils of the subject. Tubes lined with some odorous substance are drawn over the straight parts of the tubes at the right. 

The amount of exposed surface is indicated on the scale.

The olfactometer, as shown in Fig. 112, is the standard instrument for conducting experimental work on the sense of smell. Tubes lined with aromatic substances are slipped over glass tubes leading into the nostrils. The strength of the stimulus is regulated by the amount of exposed surface over which the air must pass on its way to the nostrils. 

There are wide individual differences in sensitivity to odors. 

Some individuals are anosmic, that is, they are permanently

PSYCHOLOGY 

insensitive to odors of all sorts. Some have different values for ordinary odors. It also happens that the same odor may have a totally different quality for the same person depending upon whether it is received in small or in large quantities. For example, indol, when strong, has a fecal odor; but when properly diluted, it has a pleasant flowery odor. 

When different odors are experienced together they may blend, they may coexist side by side, they may neutralize each other so that the individual smells nothing, or one may entirely mask the other. Furthermore, adaptation to odors is rapid. 

Upon entering a room, one may be struck by the unpleasant odors but, after a short time, he becomes oblivious to them. 

For the most part, odors are in bad social and aesthetic standing. While we are all influenced by odors in a subtle manner, it would be bad form to comment too bluntly on most food or house odors. A girl may use perfume, but never to such an extent that it is obvious to others. It must seem that one is affected by her "personality" but never by her odor; even though it is the perfume that turns the trick.

In recent years odor engineers are beginning to realize that odors have a powerful influence upon human behavior provided they are presented in the right manner. Sales of a great variety of products have been increased by the simple expedient of substituting a pleasing odor for an unpleasant one. For example, smelly raincoats are made odorless, shower curtains are perfumed to give a pleasantly fragrant odor when water strikes them, stenographers are provided with spicy-smelling pencils and scented typewriter ribbons, shaving creams are made to smell fresh and less soapy, and hospitals are made to smell inviting instead of greeting the visitor with the ordinary smell of unpleasant drugs. 

These odor engineers have found that the introduction of perfumes must not be overdone, and that the individual is often unaware that the odor of an article has anything to do with his purchase of it. When women were asked if they liked perfumed hosiery, they all were against it. When, on the other hand, they were permitted to choose between stockings, identical except for the fact that one box was perfumed and the other retained the usual smell of finishing oils, they preferred the perfumed article. [5]

TASTE 

Most of the experiences which appear to be taste are, in reality, a combination of other sense experiences than taste. This can easily be demonstrated by holding the nose in such a manner as to eliminate smell when a substance is tasted. Without odor a meal would be insipid indeed. With smell eliminated it is almost impossible to distinguish a bit of onion from a bit of apple. [2]

Heat and cold, pressure, kinesthesis, and pain all help to complicate tastes. In fact, tastes are modified by the social atmosphere of a meal, the aesthetic effects, worry, and a number of other factors.

After all these extraneous influences are eliminated there remain four elementary tastes: bitter, sweet, saline, and sour.

The typical stimuli which will give rise to these primary tastes are: Sweet 

For sour: weak hydrochloric acid 

For saline: common salt 

For bitter: quinine 

For sweet: cane sugar

While the relationship between these four primary taste qualities has not been definitely determined, they may be tentatively related as shown in the taste tetrahedron in Fig. 113. Saline Sour Bitter

Taste results from the stimulation of specialized cells in the small nipple-shaped elevations (papillae) of the tongue and in certain parts of the mouth and throat (see Fig. 114). Some of these papillae respond only to sweet, some only to sour, some only to bitter; but many of them respond to all four tastes, some to two or three.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Different parts of the tongue are differentially sensitive. The upper front part of the tongue is not sensitive to any tastes. Salt is best sensed at the forward tip of the tongue; sensitivity to sweet is highest at the tip and is lower at the back; sensitivity to bitter is low at the tip and increases around the side edges, FIG. 114.-Transverse section through a small portion of the sensitive area of the tongue. Some phenomena of taste. It is particularly difficult to conduct exact experimentation in the field of taste. The receptor organs are in grooves and can be reached only by chemicals in solution. After one stimulus has been used it is difficult to

It is almost impossible to exclude such extraneous factors as smell and cutaneous impressions. In addition, most subjects rebel against acting as subjects in taste and smell experiments. In spite of these difficulties, the following taste phenomena have been observed. 

1. Certain tastes may fuse with each other and form taste

blends. As already noted, most taste blends contain smells, touch, and temperature stimuli as well as taste. When these other sense modalities are excluded, there are still blends which depend upon the combination of primary taste qualities. For example:

Potassium sulphate ... ..saline and sour . saline and bitter . saline and sweet sweet and bitter .sweet and sour bitter and sour Some component tastes in a blend can be readily distinguished, whereas others are difficult to analyze.
