Salt-sweet blends are difficult to analyze. The flat taste of unsalted oatmeal is not easily recognized by the untrained person as a lack of salt. Add salt and the effect seems to be an increase in sweetness. 

2. Some tastes tend to neutralize other tastes. Mix salt and sour tastes and the resultant fusion tends to mask the components so that each is less intense than it would be alone. In maple sugar season, after one has eaten too much maple sugar, he may overcome the effect by eating something sour; and thus be able to eat more of the sugar. 

3. Adaptation for tastes is rapid. After tasting a substance for some time, some of its flavor is lost. Such adaptation is greatest for sweet, next for bitter, and comparatively slight for salt and sour. It reaches its maximum effect after about two minutes, and is much more of a factor when the taste is strong. 

In addition, it has been found that a salty substance tastes more salty after one has become adapted to a sweet taste. 

KINESTHETIC SENSATIONS 

Kinesthetic sensations are those attending movements of any members of the body whether those movements are actively initiated by the individual or are passive responses to outside forces. The muscles, tendons, and joints are sensitive to pressure, pain, strain, fatigue. When these are added to information derived from the skin senses, which we shall examine shortly, the

PSYCHOLOGY 

individual is able to gain important information about the weight of objects, their resistance to manipulation, their hardness or softness, their relative positions, the position of members of the body, and the like. Furthermore, vision contributes to our knowledge of position and movement. 

It has been definitely established that there is no simple sense of weight, or sense of the amount of force exerted in the execution of a movement. A sensation of position or movement is a learned pattern. Some individuals become adept in learning delicate muscle cues. For example, in the ordinary parlor game of "mind reading," the individual whose mind is to be read grasps the wrist of the person who is to do the reading and then thinks of what the "reader" should do next (such as go forward, go backward, or stoop). Involuntary muscular movements give cues which a sensitive person can interpret and follow with success. 

CUTANEOUS SENSATIONS 

Most persons do not use their skin senses as extensively as they do their hearing and vision for the simple reason that they do not need to do so. In cases where persons have been deprived of vision or hearing, remarkable abilities in the use of touch have been developed. Blind persons can read Braille by the expert use of their finger tips. Deaf persons have been able to interpret speech by placing their finger tips upon a vibrating diaphragm. 

Since most of us do not need to develop our cutaneous senses to an extreme degree, we have an inadequate notion of the possibilities of cutaneous sensory development. [6] All psychologists are agreed that there is not a single sense of touch. There is less agreement upon how many separate cutaneous senses there are. Four have been distinguished: warmth, cold, pressure, and pain.

Punctate skin sensitivity. If a small area of the skin is explored, spot by spot, by different stimuli (such as a tiny bit of cotton, a sharpened horsehair, a heated piece of pointed brass, and a cooled pointed piece of brass), it will be found that the skin is not uniformly sensitive to these different stimuli. It will be sensitive to pressure at certain points, to pain at others, to warmth at others, and to cold at still other points. 

The frequency of these spots varies. For example, on the

volar or palmar surface of the forearm, there will be, per square centimeter, about 200 pain spots, 15 touch spots, 6 cold spots, and 0.4 warmth spots.

The discovery of these spots led to the theory that "touch" was composed of four separate senses, each with its own peculiar sense organ in the skin. This theory has been questioned on the following grounds: 

1. The spots are not fixed and stable. The location of the spots shifts on different trials. Furthermore, intensifying the stimulus will increase the number of spots found, and may even change the qualitative nature of the resulting sensation. 

2. Careful search has failed to reveal specific end organs at the spots. In other words, histological examination of the skin. has not disclosed one type of nervous end organ at the pain spots, another type at the touch spots, another at the warm spots, and another at the cold spots. 

In addition to these two negative arguments, there is some positive evidence that cold and warmth are based on the same receptor organs, and that pressure and pain are closely related. 

The two-point threshold. When two points in the same region on the skin are stimulated simultaneously, they will feel like a single point unless separated by a sufficient distance. The amount that they must be separated in order to be felt as two points is called the two-point threshold. This threshold varies strikingly for different parts of the body, as shown in Table VIII.

WARMTH AND COLD

The sensitivity of the skin to changes in temperature varies with different parts of the body; it also varies in the same area

with such factors as health, degree of activity of the individual, surroundings, the general tonus of the body, and adaptation. 

For any specific area of the body an indifference point may be found. For example, an average person, in a room with a temperature of about 70° F., will be indifferent to a temperature stimulus of 98.6° F. applied under his tongue, to a stimulus of about 95° F. applied to a normally clothed part of his body, to a stimulus of about 92° F. applied to his hands, or to a stimulus of about 79° F. applied to the lobes of his ears. The contrast between the indifference point of the hand and the ear lobe can easily be demonstrated by grasping the lobe with the fingers. 

The ear lobe will feel cool to the fingers and the fingers will feel warm to the ear lobe.

If the temperature of the air or other contacting surface is raised above the indifference point of the area it strikes, it will be felt as warm. This sensation of warmth will grow in intensity (for an ordinarily clothed area of the body, for example) up to about 115° F. As the stimulus is raised above 115° F., the sensation of warmth is lost and the experience becomes a complex mixture of pressure and pricking until about 125° F., above which only pain is felt. A similar change occurs as the temperature of the stimulus is decreased below the indifference point. 

A stimulus will feel increasingly cold until about 54° F., when it will become a complex of pressure and pain, the sensation of cold gradually disappearing. At about 35° F. and below the individual will feel only pain. [6] 

However, these ranges of sensitivity can readily be changed by adaptation. If the hand is placed in water whose temperature is 98° F., the water will feel definitely warm at first. Soon it will not feel warm but, if the hand is put into water of 92° F., which would ordinarily feel neither cold nor warm, it will feel cold.

Furthermore, the same temperature may feel warm to one hand and cold to the other. This may be effected as follows: 

Have three bowls of water whose temperatures are 65° F., 85° F., and 105° F. Hold one hand in the warm water (105° F.) and the other in the cool water (65° F.) for several minutes and then transfer them both to the medium water (85° F.). The water of medium temperature will feel cold to

PSYCHOLOGY 

the hand that has been in the hot water and warm to the hand that has been in the cool water. 

The cold points in the skin respond differently from the warm points. The cold flashes out quickly, clearly, and vigorously, whereas the warm comes in slowly and wells up in a leisurely fashion. The average reaction time for warm is about twice that for cold. [3]

Another interesting phenomenon is that of paradoxical cold. 

A pointed warm stimulus may sometimes arouse a sensation of cold when applied near a cold spot. Although not so easily obtained, it is possible to arouse a sensation of warmth by the application of a cold stimulus to a warm spot. This mistaking of heat for cold and cold for heat is more pronounced when the stimuli are intense, that is, near the pain point. In other words, as warmth and cold approach the pain region they become qualitatively alike and may be mistaken for each other. 

While no specific end organs have been found to correspond with warm and cold spots (although the Krause end-bulb has been suggested as the possible sense organ for these sensations), it has been found that these cold spots are always near tufts of blood vessels. One interesting theory to explain these facts is that cold sensations result from the sudden contraction of the blood vessels in the skin and that warmth sensations come with their relaxation. Extreme heat or cold will cause spastic contraction of these vessels and give the experience of pain. [6] 

This theory also accounts for various other facts: (a) The puncture of arteries is accompanied by cold and hot flashes which could correspond with vascular contraction and relaxation. (b) 

The reaction time for cold corresponds with the contraction time of smooth muscle, while the reaction time for warmth corre sponds with the relaxation time of smooth muscle. (c) The blood vessels are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and so may be affected by events ordinarily called emotional. For example, the cold chill that comes from certain screechy sounds may be explained on this basis. The chill during a fever does not depend upon the cooling of the skin but upon the autonomic contraction of the smooth muscles in the blood vessels. (d) 

Mechanical rubbing of the skin may cause a warm glow because of the relaxation produced.

It does not follow that all constriction of blood vessels is felt as cold, nor all relaxation as warmth. There are probably certain patterns of constriction and dilation that produce these sensations. Those which do not conform to these patterns do not give rise to conscious experiences of cold or warmth. 

PRESSURE AND PAIN 

The sense of pressure varies greatly at different parts of the body, depending partly upon the thickness of the skin and partly upon the amount of nerve supply. The amount of pressure necessary to produce a touch sensation varies from 2 grams per square mm. on the tip of the tongue to 250 grams per square mm. on the thick part of the sole. The sensation of pressure is produced only when the skin is forced inward, pulled outward, or deformed in some manner. When the pressure is too light to indent the skin, the sensation may be produced by the movement of a hair. [6]

There is some reason to believe (although there is still controversy on this point) that the sense organs for pressure are the free nerve endings in the skin and that these same organs mediate sensations of pain: The difference comes from a difference in intensity of stimulation. Strong pressure may cause pain while light pressure at the same spot may cause only a sensation of contact.

However, pain is not limited to excessive stimulation of the pressure end organs. Pain may be caused by excessive warmth or cold, destruction of tissue by chemical action, the action of foreign substances in the blood, electrical stimulation, and the spastic contraction of a muscle. In short, pain may be explained as resulting from continuous stimulation at relatively high intensities. A single application of an intense stimulus may not cause pain, whereas a number of successive applications of the same stimulus will. In other words, there is a summation effect in pain.

Most of the common words used to describe pain refer to patterns in which pain is combined with other factors: (a) Pain mixed with other qualities: cold-pain, warm-pain, smart, severe tension, cramp, pressure-pain. (b) Pain limited to certain areas:

PSYCHOLOGY 

crick, headache, stitch. (c) Those referring to temporal changes: throbbing pains and pulsating pains. 1 

VISCERAL SENSITIVITY 

Visceral sensitivity is vague and rather inaccurately localized as compared with cutaneous sensitivity. It is dependent upon elaborate patterns involving sensations of pressure, pain, warmth, and cold. The visceral sensitivity is so inadequate as compared with the sensitivity of external portions of the body that, for a time, it was thought that the viscera were completely insensitive to surgical manipulation. Later studies have shown that there is a slight amount of sensitivity to violent abdominal disturbance. 

It is probably not true that visceral organs may be cuf, burned, pressed, stretched, or torn without sensation. However, even though there is some evidence for visceral sensitivity, there is no evidence for a visceral sense. Most afferent impulses from the viscera are not accompanied by conscious states. 

An interesting phenomenon is that of referred pain. It is the localizing a pain at one place when the stimulus is actually located at another. It may depend upon irradiation in the nervous system, a strong stimulation spreading to remote parts, or it may depend upon a strong sensation overshadowing a smaller one and being felt at the site of the weaker pain. When a place of low sensitivity located near a place of greater sensitivity is stimulated painfully, the experience is felt at the place of greater sensitivity if the two places are supplied by the same spinal nerve.

SENSATIONS OF POSITION AND MOVEMENT 

A reference to the model of the inner ear as shown in Fig. 104 will serve as a reminder that only a part of the inner ear (the cochlea) is connected with hearing. The other parts, notably the semicircular canals and the vestibule, are concerned with sensations of position, of movement, and of balance. [7] 

The peculiar position of the semicircular canals has given rise to a theory that the movement of fluid in them, which must take place with changes in the position of the head, provides the essential stimulation for their functioning. From Fig. 118 it will be clear that they occupy the three planes of space, each at right angles to the others. They all open into an enlarged

5 WAL space, called the ampulla, containing a transverse membrane on which are sensitive hair cells. It is supposed that the nerve endings in these hair cells are stimulated by the changes in pressure of the fluid which fills the canals. This fluid (called endolymph) contains small hard particles (called otoliths) which impinge upon the hair cells with any movement of the fluid in which they float. When the head is moved, the fluid, because of its inertia, lags behind and thus presses against the sensitive 

FIG. 118.-Diagram to show the position. 

of the semicircular canals in the head. 

The external, or horizontal, canals (E) of the two sides are in the same plane. 

The canal A on one side is in a plane parallel to P on the other side. cells. If this theory is sound, only the starting and stopping of a movement of the head or a change in relative speed of movement would be effective. When the head moved at a constant rate there would be no inertia or lag of the fluid behind the walls of the canal. Some experiments seem to show that this is the case.

There are some other arguments which seem to contradict the theory. One is that the tubes are so tiny that adherence of the fluid to the walls would more than counterbalance any force exerted by inertia. Movement is not the only stimulus that can affect the canals. They can be effectively stimulated by irrigations of the external ear by hot or cold water, by an electric current, by certain drugs, by reflex excitation from the eyes or the stomach.

Stimulation of the semicircular canals affects movement or position in different ways.

PSYCHOLOGY 

1. Movement of the body causes compensatory movements of the head and body. This can be observed by the balancing movements made by birds when they are perched on a swaying wire. A test of this same type of compensatory movement can be observed in the laboratory. If a person sits in a barber's chair with his eyes closed, his head will tend to turn in the opposite direction from any turn given to the chair. If the chair is made to turn at a uniform rate, the subject will become adjusted to the movement and report that he is not rotating at all. Then, as the chair is stopped, he will report that he has been turned in the opposite direction. 

2. The canals assist in the maintenance of muscular tonus. 

Animals deprived of the canals will show a marked decrease in tonus. It is probably the shock imparted to the semicircular canals by a knockout blow to the jaw that causes the boxer to lose his tonus and fall to the floor.

It has been made clear, however, that the ability to maintain tonus, to be aware of movement and position, and to compensate for turnings by muscular readjustments is not wholly dependent upon the semicircular canals. When pigeons, for example, have had the canals removed by surgical operation they show marked disturbances. They will flop to the floor when they attempt to walk or to fly. If they attempt to peck at a grain of corn their head is likely to turn to one side and they will miss the grain. They lack tonus and appear to have lost all motor control. However, after a period of time they will recover and will gain remarkable control over their postures and movements. 

It is quite probable that the normal person uses his semicircular canals rather extensively but in co-operation with kinesthetic sensations, visual cues, and cutaneous sensations. Should he suddenly be deprived of the semicircular canals, he is greatly disturbed for a time but has the ability to substitute the other means of control for the cues he ordinarily would receive from the semicircular canals.

Chapter XV PERCEIVING 

P ERCEIVING may be defined as the process of becoming aware of external objects, qualities, or relations. It is a complex procedure involving several factors: (a) It presupposes general awareness., A person cannot perceive when he is in a coma. He perceives dimly when half asleep. He perceives most clearly when keenly alert. (b) It involves some sort of immediate interpretation of the objective world. When perceiving, a person makes such remarks as: "I see a dog." "I taste an orange," "The apple is red." Even when there is no clear interpretation, there is an attempt to arrive at some significance. It may not be clear whether a noise is thunder, the backfire of a car, or a gun; but the experience does not stop with a mere auditory sensation. (c) A perceptual interpretation seems trustworthy. In most cases a perception is uncritically accepted as the last word in evidence of reality. Even when we discover that we have been deceived by some queer arrangement of things or events, the perception does not seem less real. We are bewildered by the fact that we were deceived. We may think it odd that it seemed so real when it actually was unreal, but it did seem real nonetheless. (d) A perception provides the basis for action. When we perceive, we act accordingly.

ANALYSIS OF THE PERCEIVING PROCESS 

We have perceptual problems but they seem different and are handled differently from logical problems. A perceptual problem may lead to such a question as: "What do I hear?" "What do I see?" "What do I taste?" The answer is reached not by logic, but by listening, looking, or tasting again. 409

PSYCHOLOGY 

Untrustworthiness of perceptions. Not every perceptual experience is accompanied by any such clear-cut question. Instead, there is usually emphasis upon the answer, often with such a degree of confidence in the answer that the observer does not even realize there was a question. The answer comes so spontaneously, so quickly, and with such assurance that there is often a refusal to admit that there could have been any other interpretation. The observer says, "I saw the man on the stage pull a rabbit out of the hat . . . I saw him eat a whole paper of needles and then pull them out of his mouth again all strung on a thread.” 

He may admit bewilderment as to how the trick was done, but he does not question the fact that he saw it done. As a matter of fact, he did not see it done; he merely thought he did. magician fooled him. The

Our perceptions are continually fooling us; but the mistakes we make do no harm so long as we do not take them too seriously. 

Perceptions are hypotheses at best, usually mere guesses. There is this distinctive difference between logical hypotheses and perceptual hypotheses. Logical hypotheses lead to delay and further investigation before action is taken. Perceptual hypotheses lead to immediate action.

The selection of significant cues. It is an undisputed fact that many of the elements in our environment pass unnoticed, not merely because they are too weak to affect our sense organs, but because we tend to select only certain aspects of the total situation for our consideration and response. If our selection includes the proper combination of factors, we will make a satisfactory response. If we select the wrong ones, failure will follow.

An interesting parlor game is based upon this principle. Select some ordinarily trivial or incidental element and make it the dominant one in a problem situation and watch the guests fumble in their attempt to be more observing. For example, go through some complicated movements with the hands and ask the guests to imitate the pattern. If the significant factor is à clearing of the throat (or some similar other apparently irrelevant act), the guests will not be very likely to discern this coughing and will become increasingly zealous in their attempt to move their hands .n exactly the correct manner. 

Many situations in life are of a similar order. The success-

PERCEIVING 

411 ful man is the one who can discern the significant factor that others do not see. However, it is possible for one to take this lesson too seriously and to go through life looking for all sorts of irrelevant details. Such an individual becomes "scatterbrained."

Essential characteristics of perceptions. This sketchy description of a perceptual process needs to be rounded out by an examination of some of the essential characteristics of the act of perceiving. [1] 

Perceiving involves jumping at conclusions without weighing the logical justification for such conclusions. For example, suppose that a prankster tickled a man's neck with a feather. Without hesitation the man would brush at the bug he perceived crawling over his neck. He would not stop, propose to himself the various possible interpretations of his tactile sensations, consciously decide it might be a bug, and then tentatively brush at the spot in order to verify his hypothesis. To him it was a real bug. He responded with all the violence that would ordinarily go with complete knowledge that it was a bug. Only after he saw the grinning boy did he find it necessary to revise his interpretation of what he felt. Even so, after he knew it was a feather he still knew it felt as real as though it were a bug. 

In other words, in perceiving we act with complete conviction and with little regard for the completeness or accuracy of knowledge concerning the circumstances. Intuitions, hunches, and convictions are all part and parcel of the same process. Why do we jump at conclusions? Merely to shorten the process of living.

A great proportion of living is taking things for granted. If you hear a horn behind you, it will pay you to jump for the sidewalk; and then find out later whether it really was an approaching car or some friend playing a trick on you.

A perception may or may not conform with objective reality. Perceptions are working hypotheses with major emphasis on the working aspect and little on the justifying reasons for accepting them. They are premature conclusions and, consequently, need not conform with reality. Perceiving a thing is no reason for believing it.

Individuals differ in the way in which they perceive the same objective facts. The observer distorts what he takes in

PSYCHOLOGY 

through his sense organs in order to make these incoming impressions conform to what he has come to believe they should be. 

A rose looks red regardless of the way in which it is illuminated, and it takes a trained artist to observe that it changes color in different settings. A wheel looks round no matter from what angle it is seen. We make allowances for a great many distortions, and are aware of these distortions only when some unusual circumstance makes them apparent. We shall see this principle clearly demonstrated in some of the illusions which we shall shortly study.

When an individual develops a certain attitude, distortions may become even more marked. Lovers may be intrigued by the sounds of crickets, tree frogs, and owls, and by the moon shadows; the boy who has run away from home may perceive them only as fateful warnings of danger. Just how much any perception is determined by objective circumstances and how much by the attitude of the observer it is almost impossible to detect. 

Perceptions vary in reliability. Certainly no perceptions are infallible, and probably none are absolutely untrustworthy. 

Since this is so, it may be of some value to know some of the factors affecting the degree of dependability of perceptions. 

1. The various senses differ in their ability to give accurate information. In general, vision is the best source for information as to spatial relations. We can more easily see where an object is than hear where it is or smell where it is. Ventriloquism is an illustration of how easily we can be deceived as to the location of a sound source. We can sense wetness better by feeling than by seeing. We can hear rhythms and music better than we can see them. We can gauge the time taken in the execution of a movement more accurately than we can determine the energy consumed in making the movement. Sometimes we must make a perceptual response when deprived of the use of the sense best suited to give accurate information. In such cases, our degree of error is sure to be greater and due allowances must be made. 

2. The past experiences of an individual are highly important in present perceptual interpretations. If a child has had little experience he will make many errors in attempting to adjust to various situations. He will have all kinds of accidents because he has not learned to interpret spatial relationships: he will fall

PERCEIVING 

413 down stairs, he will bump his head, he will push his toys and dishes off the table, and attempt to reach for remote objects. 

Some of these accidents and errors may be due to motor awkwardness, to be sure, but many of them depend strikingly upon perceptual inexperience. 

The confusion that a child manifests when he first adjusts to using a mirror illustrates the forcefulness of past experiences in guiding perceptual interpretations. The child has learned to look at his mother directly and to hear her speak to him and has thus built up certain expectations and reactions to his mother's acts. Let the mother stand behind him so that he can see her by looking in the mirror and then let her speak to him. He will show the greatest confusion. He acts as though he might expect to creep into the mirror to her, turns his head when he hears her voice and then looks at her alternately by turning his head and by looking at the image in the mirror. Having learned one set of spatial reactions, he must now learn new ones to fit this strange new situation. The reactions of the child in such a situation are certainly different from the smooth reactions of the adult who uses a mirror to guide his movements while shaving or combing his hair. 

3. Momentary conditions affect perceptions. The setting in which an experience occurs, the events which led up to the experience, and the attitude of the individual, all affect his perceptions. There is, for example, the factor of contrast. A tall man looks shorter when in the company of a taller man. A color looks brighter by contrast with a dull color. A dollar seems bigger to a poor man than to a wealthy one. 

Then there is the phenomenon of irradiation. A man who has just heard of the death of his best friend is likely to see everything in drab tones. A man who has just received a promotion is likely to observe how brilliant everything seems. Everyone is familiar with the importance of what is called a "build-up.” 

A girl who has just heard tales of housebreakings will hear all sounds as burglars, especially if she is alone in her home. A yell is always more startling after one has been prepared for it by a good ghost story. 

4. The unreliability of perceptions is accentuated by the fact that we are usually in ignorance of the cues upon which our

PSYCHOLOGY 

1 perceptions are based. When we recognize that attitudes affect perceptual interpretations, it should make us skeptical when things appear the way we want them to be or the way we are afraid they might be. We glibly admit at one moment that our perceptions are distorted, if the situation is not of vital importance; and then at another time we try to convince ourselves that they are not affected by our desires. We admit in general that we see the world through colored glasses; but we refuse to try to discern the color at each particular moment and to make allowances for the distortion. 

5. Furthermore, there is a tendency for us to develop a perceptual intolerance. We know an event is so, we assert, because we saw it, we heard it, we tasted it, and the like. We are sure of our own perceptions and doubtful of the perceptions of others. We would come nearer the truth if we were to reverse the process and say: Our prejudice colors our perceptions; perhaps the other fellow is nearer right than we are. 

Perceptions are continually changing. The incessant changing of perceptual interpretations has long been known and universally recognized. These shifts have been given the popular name of attention. The reasons for changes in attention can be divided into two general groups: (2) factors inherent in the external stimulating circumstances, or objective factors; (2) those dependent upon the perceiving individual, or subjective factors. [5] 

1. Objective factors of attention. We are all familiar with the objective methods for gaining the attention of a person. 

We call his name, yell, wave something at him, nudge him, or punch him if he is unresponsive to milder stimulations. (a) Other things being equal, an intense stimulus will be more effective than a weak one. A loud sound, a bright color, a pungent odor, a sharp pain are more effective than weaker stimulations would be. A large display heading in the newspaper gains attention quicker than a heading in small type would do.

Anything that gives a situation intensity value gives it attention value. While it might be desirable to give each possible stimulus a quantitative attention value, this has not been done. We cannot say that a bright light is more effective than a certain loud sound, nor how much more effective the bright light is than a weaker

PERCEIVING 

415 one. One reason for this is that attention factors shift in themselves and never have any constant value. (b) A changing stimulus is more effective than a stationary of constant one. This factor has been utilized extensively in advertising. The ordinary man is constantly bombarded by signs which jump on and off, which portray all kinds of activities. The locomotive or the fire truck with a rotating headlight clears the road much better than one with a stationary light, even though they may be of equal luminous value. (c) Repetition makes a stimulus more striking. Even when the repetition becomes annoying, as often happens when a radio advertiser repeats the same phrase incessantly, the words arrest attention in spite of the antagonistic appeal. In fact, the irritation may help in gaining attention. (d) All these objective factors may be summed up by the term "novelty" or "change." It is probable that change is the most effective objective determinant of attention that we can discover. Even a striking stimulus will lose its value if repeated monotonously or if kept at the same intensity. A person will go to sleep to the regular ticking of a clock at his ear but may be wakened by the sudden stopping of the clock. 

2. The subjective factors of attention. The subjective factors that favor attention may be summed up in the word “interest." Other terms have been used to express the same condition. Set, attitude, or priming may be used to indicate a readi→ ness on the part of an individual to be responsive to a certain pattern of stimuli. These may all have value in designating a condition that is easily observable but they do not explain the process. The fact is, we cannot derive any formula to explain the fact that certain situations are favored, because each experience is a specific one and is effective because of a unique combination of factors which probably never will be duplicated exactly. 

Life is a changing process and each perceptual process is merely one step in living.

There is an objective constancy behind perceptual change. 

An interesting factor that stands out in all this welter of change is the ease with which an individual attributes constancy to objects and circumstances involved in his perceptual world. An object changes appearance with position and circumstances and yet it

PSYCHOLOGY 

continues to be the same object to us. The sensations which give us information about objects in our world change in value, but the objects from which these sensations originate are perceived as unchanged. We see a wheel from different angles, and it may change from a round object to an oval object; and yet it continues to be 'perceived as a round wheel. We see snow as white no matter how much illumination is reflected. Such constancy of objective perceptions must make allowance for all sorts of changing circumstances. Such qualifications are made without any conscious intent to do so. Indeed, the process is just the reverse. 

We are so sure of the constancy of the object perceived that, in many cases, we do not realize that the stimulus values are different.

Perception is, consequently, a reaction to cues which are accepted as significant and any irrelevant factor that would tend to distract us from the immediate interpretation of a situation is distorted or ignored. Perception is thus a laborsaving, timesaving, and efficient way to meet our environment. It comes to be utilized because it is an efficient working basis for behavior. To avoid egregious error, however, it must be tempered by a willingness to change when it becomes apparent that our interpretation has been incorrect.

Rules for making perceiving more adequate and reliable. 

On the basis of these general characteristics of perceptual processes, certain rules for adequate perceiving can be formulated. 

If they are carefully kept in mind, their value will be vindicated as we examine the way in which perceptions operate in the perception of form, space, time, and the like. 

1. Be alert to sense all the cues that are present. Alertness is relative. It varies all the way from the unresponsiveness of the man who goes through life almost asleep to the individual who misses nothing. 

2. Be willing to change when it is discovered that an interpretation is incorrect. The best guesser is the one who does not stick to a guess any longer than succeeding events warrant. 

3. Play with different interpretations. Even if one meaning seems to be correct, it is of practical benefit to play with the possibility of other interpretations. 

4. Avoid emotional prejudices. When a perceptual inter-

PERCEIVING 

417 pretation comes, it often does so with a queer feeling of satisfaction or relief. One says, "Aha, I have the answer." What a person may fail to realize is that the "Aha" experience of satisfaction may just as easily accompany a mistaken perception as a correct one. Once the satisfaction comes, it provides an obstacle against change. 

5. Avoid habitual interpretations. Habits are prejudicial to good perceptions. The essential element in a good perception is plasticity and when a person gets into the security of a habit he is thereby avoiding any further perceptual development. He learns only by getting a rude jolt, whereas the slightest cue should be enough.

THE PERCEPTION OF FORM 

When a number of elements are grouped and are perceived as a whole, the whole presents characteristics which cannot be explained by the parts into which the whole can be analyzed. 

Squareness or roundness is not an essential function of the elements which make these forms. The tune transposed into another key is made up of different notes, but it is still the same tune. 

The form of an object does not reside in the constituent elements but in their patterning and mutual relations. [21, pp. 623–650] 

Factors which affect form perception. In some instances the possible forms which a grouping of stimuli take is limited; in others, the possibilities are almost innumerable. In most situations a number of factors operate; hence, our outline of the influence of different features should not be construed to mean that each perception should be traceable to any one or even to a small combination.

Ambiguous figures. With the same objective setting, an observer may be impressed by some aspects more than by others. 

This dominance does not persist, for features which were unnoticed a moment ago may now be the salient features. As pointed out at the beginning of the chapter, shifting characterizes all perceptions; ambiguous figures merely illustrate this general principle.

There are wide individual differences in this shifting from one aspect to another. Some persons are very distractable and cannot prevent themselves from jumping from one thing to another. Others seem to be oblivious to most of the conditions around them and are lost in the contemplation of an event that happened an hour ago. For example, a student complained that it took him half a class period to get his attention fixed upon the subject at hand because he found he was absorbed in reviewing

in his mind what had taken place in the preceding hour. After the present class was half over he could get his attention shifted, only to find his mind reverting to this material in the following hour. In short, he was so slow in shifting his attention from subject to subject that he found himself always about half an hour behind time.

By way of contrast, the distractable person shifts his attention so quickly that he misses little, but is unable to utilize what

Figure and ground. We do not react in a uniform or a constant manner to specific stimuli. Instead, the nature of the setting in which they are found determines the mode of response to some extent. Normally, when an observer looks at Fig. 121, he 

FIG. 121.-Figure-ground reversal. 

(After E. Rubin.) sees only a plain black vase on a white background. After a period, longer or shorter, the perception of the figure may change and he sees no longer the vase but, instead, two white profiles facing each other across a black background. The experience is quite similar to that which comes from inspection of the ambiguous picture in Fig. 120. After considerable practice, the observer may see either the profiles or the vase alternately or he can maintain one to the exclusion of the other; but he cannot see both at the same time. One cannot see the same part of a situation as figure and ground simultaneously. [12] 

This simple figure illustrates a phenomenon that is continually operating in all perceptual fields. From the conglomeration of impressions, certain aspects stand out as figure and the remaining parts retire into the background. The distinguishing characteristics of a figure as contrasted with the background are as follows:

PSYCHOLOGY 

1. The figure has form, whereas the ground is relatively without form. This does not mean that the background has no form in and of itself but that at this particular moment it appears formless to the observer. 

2. The figure has definite limits, whereas the ground seems to extend continuously behind the figure and not to be interrupted by it. 

3. The figure has the characteristics of a thing, whereas the ground appears to be unformed material. 

4. The figure tends to stand apart from the ground. It more often appears to be in front of the ground but the direction of the differentiation is not the important factor. 

5. The figure is more impressive, better remembered, and more likely to suggest meaning. There is a tendency to see the same figure on a second observation of the same situation than to see a new figure.

To state these facts in a slightly different manner we can say: 

An object is that part of the environmental setting which has form, definite limits, individuality, contour, and impressiveness to such a degree that it can be identified as standing apart from the rest of the situation, and can be remembered and recognized on some future occasion. We see things or objects and not sensations, and these figures or things are real to us. We need get into no discussion as to the objective existence of these figures or things; as psychologists, we need not prove that they have eternal existence. For the individual they are vital experiences. 

These facts are most clearly observed in visual perceptions but the same factors hold in other fields. For example, the melody can be regarded as the figure in a musical composition and the accompanying sounds as the ground. In a musical composition the figure is likely to be higher in pitch, louder, have a different timbre, to be played by a different instrument, to move differently, to have a different rhythm, or to start and stop at different times than the ground. In some way the figure must be given individuality and meaning. In fact, one of the pleasures in listening to symphonic music arises from trying to recognize the figure (or theme) when it appears in different settings or grounds.

Time. Experiments in the field of vision demonstrate that it takes a certain amount of time for the figure to emerge from the background. If a subject is shown an irregular enclosed white patch, as in Fig. 122, for a period of time less than 10 msec., he will see little differentiation between the white and the black. 

With an exposure of 14 msec., he will see good contour; and after 

FIG. 122.-Figure to illustrate time factor involved in distinguishing figure from ground. See text. about several seconds he will see the white figure distinctly and may even imagine it to be a flying witch or other object. The amount of time required to get a good figure-ground distinction depends greatly upon the nature of the situation; but time is an important factor even though no definite rules have been discovered.

Contrast between the figure and ground is an important factor. In the field of vision the greater the brightness differences between the figure and ground the easier it will be for the subject to get the figure-ground experience. 

Clear-cut characteristics will make a figure stand out. In the visual field a figure is more likely to emerge from the background if it has sharply projecting points. In music a quickly struck note, a loud note, or an unusual rhythm will make the figure easily apparent. 

Size. It is easier to see a small concise part as the figure and a large broad expanse as ground. 

Perspective. If the situation can be viewed in three dimensions so that the object may be nearer to the observer or farther away than the ground, the figure stands out more easily Ithan if the whole situation is two dimensional.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Meaning. The ability to give the figure a name or relate it to some known group of objects makes it easier for it to separate itself from the ground. 

Masking of figures. From the preceding analysis it would seem that the whole process of distinguishing figure from ground can be viewed as a method for getting meaning from a situation. 

The observer tends to select objects from a background; and when one thing emerges, it is usually difficult to replace it except with some other object or figure.

It is also clear that there is much in our environment that we never perceive. There are combinations and patterns that we never discern because they are concealed or masked by others which claim our interest or attention first, and which then dominate the field. At the same time that we are interpreting our environment in terms of dominant figures, there are other parts which are thereby lost. Many sleight-of-hand tricks are based upon this principle. The performer masks the essential part of his trick by getting the observer to attend to another aspect of his act.

VISUAL PERCEPTION OF DISTANCE OR DEPTH 

The eyes have often been appropriately called our most important "distance receptors." Some have argued that we get our early conceptions of space from tactile and kinesthetic sensations and have contended that vision comes in merely to supplement these cues. Experimental evidence has not vindicated these arguments. Instead, it has been shown fairly conclusively that the eyes play the predominant role in space perception. [4]

427 It is clear that a child is not born with a knowledge of spatial relations, of distance, or of the solidity of objects. He learns these relations. The way in which this learning takes place and the contribution made by the different visual factors is an interesting study. The usual method for determining the significance of any one factor is to keep all other factors as nearly constant as possible and then to vary the one under consideration. This method has demonstrated the importance of a number of visual processes in space perception.

Any characteristic of an object or a situation which changes consistently with changes in distance can be used by an individual as an index of distance. Nevertheless, although different factors may be isolated experimentally, it is not likely that an individual, in judging distance, isolates these same factors. Instead, he utilizes a number of cues in combination at any moment, without any analysis on his part and usually without awareness of the factors he is using.

The factors contributing to the perception of distance, depth, or solidity may be divided, for purposes of discussion, into two kinds: (1) those which can be utilized with a single eyemonocular factors; (2) those which depend upon the mutual activity of both eyes-binocular factors.

Monocular factors in the perception of distance or depth. 

There are eight monocular factors that may be distinguished: (1) attached shadows; (2) cast shadow; (3) linear perspective; (4) detail perspective; (5) superposition; (6) movement parallax; (7) relative size of familiar objects; (8) the shape of familiar objects. [17] 

1. Attached shadows. A shadow above a high light indicates a dent; a high light above a shadow indicates a bulge. Experience probably teaches this because we are accustomed to viewing objects illuminated from above. If Fig. 131 is turned upside down, the effect of shadows will be clearly seen. 

2. Cast shadows. A cast shadow is one cast by an object on the ground or on a near-by object and thereby reveals spatial relationships between objects. The effect of cast shadows is clearly seen in Fig. 132. 

3. Linear perspective. With increased distance there is a diminution of angular size of objects; at the same time parallel

PSYCHOLOGY 

lines seem to run together as they recede from the observer. In 

Fig. 134 there is a conflict between these two factors, giving an illusory effect. The three blocks are actually the same size; but 

FIG. 134.-Relation of apparent size to perception of distance. The converging lines suggest distance. The block at the right would therefore appear smaller if it were the same size as the block at the left. The three blocks measure the same size, but the one. at the left is much smaller perceptually. perceptually the one at the right is much larger than the one at the left. 

4. Detail perspective. As objects recede from the observer they lose some of their clearness of detail owing to loss of visual acuity with distance, the haziness of the atmosphere, fog, or smoke. Consequently, haziness in detail suggests distance. The effect of this factor becomes evident when one attempts to drive a car in a fog. When an approaching car is first seen it is judged to be much farther away than it really is, and then suddenly it seems to jump from a distance right upon one. This accounts for many an accident in foggy weather. Distance also changes the colors of objects, so that a change in the hue of objects judged to be the same color gives a distance cue. [19] 

5. Superposition. If an object cuts off part of another object in the visual field, the observer judges the covering object to be nearer. In Fig. 133 there is little doubt that the right hand is in front of the left, or that both hands are on top of the unholstered object. 

6. Movement parallax. As we move forward, nearer objects increase in size more rapidly than more remote objects; hence, the relative change in the size of objects as we approach them gives the observer a clue as to their relative distance. A forward motion also changes the clearness of outline, detail, and

PERCEIVING 

429 coloring of objects in the field of vision and the observer through experience learns to judge those that change in these particulars with the greatest speed to be nearer than those that change more slowly.

PERCEPTION OF MOTION 

Anyone who has driven a car knows that individuals differ strikingly in their ability to judge motion. What appears to be reckless driving may be caused by sheer inability on the part of the driver to compare the speed of an oncoming car with that of the car in front of him. This practical need for skill in the perception of motion is enough to stimulate the psychologist to study this complex problem. Other practical interests are involved in sign displays and in the development of better motion pictures. [6]

Conditions under which motion may be perceived. 

Motion may be perceived under different circumstances. 

1. When a single object is observed to change its position

PSYCHOLOGY 

in relation to other objects it is seen to move. This gives the clearest perception of motion. If an object is seen at A and then gradually changes its relative position and finally stops at B, the observer not only gets the perception of change of position but is able to follow the course over which that change of position was attained. 

2. When an object is seen at one position and then at another position, after having been invisible in the interim, the observer gets practically the same perception of motion as though he had seen it change position. If the time interval between exposures was long, the perception of motion may be dependent upon logical inference, but when a single object is seen in rapid succession at two different but relatively close places, the observer has a perception of movement that is just as real to him as though he had followed it from one spot to another, although it has really been invisible to him between exposures. [14]

Apparent movement. Apparent movement, called the phi phenomenon, has been studied extensively by an analysis of the ways in which temporal and spatial factors may be manipulated to give illusory perceptions of motion. [10] Various types of apparent motion have been described, as follows: 

Alpha motion. Alpha motion is the type of apparent motion produced when there is an illusory change in size owing to a change in some part of the total pattern. This is illustrated by changing the direction of the wings on a figure known as the 

FIG. 144. The Müller-Lyer figure. The lines between the points where the feathered lines join are equal in length. 

Müller-Lyer figure. This figure is shown in Fig. 144. If in successive exposures of the figure the wings change in the sequence shown in Fig. 145, and the central horizontal line remains the same, it will seem as though the line between the two centers of rotation grows larger and smaller. It will seem longer when the wings extend outward and shorter when they are turned inward. 

Beta motion. When two successive figures are shown which actually differ in size or position, the observer will get

PERCEIVING 

437 the perception of actual growth or movement. This is called beta motion.

Gamma motion. Gamma motion is a type of apparent motion that results from sudden exposure or withdrawal or a change in the illumination of a single figure. When a simple form is exposed rapidly, there is an appearance of movement from the center outward; when the exposure ceases, there is apparent movement from without toward the center. When a dark figure is exposed on a white ground, the dark figure spreads out; or when one looks at a large uniform surface illuminated by 

FIG. 145.-Figure to illustrate alpha motion. Let this complex figure represent the Müller-Lyer figure with the oblique lines circling to occupy successively the following positions: AAAA, BBBB, CCCC, DDDD, CCCC,

D BBBB, AAAA, BBBB, CCCC, A A 

A A etc. The line between the rotation centers will appear to grow correspondingly longer and shorter. a momentary flash of light, the light appears to spread from the center to the periphery and then to shrink toward the center again. 

Delta motion. When two figures are shown successively in adjacent areas, one of which is more impressive than the other (that is, one is larger, more intense, or more complex), the more impressive member tends to move toward the less impressive; the two then unite and seem to return to the position of the more impressive one. For example, if one exposes two lights successively, the first being more intense than the second, there is an apparent movement from the second to the first and back again. 

Epsilon, or positive-negative, motion. When a white line on a black ground is succeeded by a black line on a white ground with a change in position, motion is seen from the first to the second. 

Factors affecting apparent motion. Apparent motion is 'influenced by a number of factors:

PSYCHOLOGY 

Time factors. The phi phenomenon is modified by the time between successive exposures, and the length of time that each stimulus is shown. For example, if two parallel lines, as shown in Fig. 146, are presented at the same time or at an interval 11 

FIG. 146.-Beta motion stimuli. 

of less than 30 msec., they will appear as two lines. If the interval between presentations of the two lines is somewhere around 60 msec., the first line will appear to move to the second. If the interval exceeds 200 msec., the two lines will be seen in succession with no apparent movement between them. 

The length of time that each of the component stimuli is shown is important. If they are exposed briefly, the observer may not clearly get the identity of either but seem to see only a movement. If they are exposed long enough, the observer may see first the one line, then it may disappear and he sees only the second.

Furthermore, the optimum time interval between exposures is affected by the distance between the two stimuli and by their intensity.

The distance between the two stimuli. If intensity is kept constant, the greater the distance between the two stimuli (that is, the larger the visual angle subtended by the two stimuli) the longer must be the time interval between exposures in order to get good apparent movement. 

The absolute intensity of the stimuli. Other factors being equal, the greater the intensity of the stimuli the longer must be the time interval between exposures in order to get the best apparent movement.

The relative intensities of the stimuli. If, for example, the second stimulus exposed is more intense than the first, the apparent motion begins between the stimuli, goes toward the stimulus first exposed (the weak one), and then returns to the posi-

PERCEIVING 

439 tion occupied by the second, or stronger, stimulus. This is the delta movement.

The character of the stimulus. The simple lines that have been used in experimental studies are not conducive to the most effective demonstrations of apparent movement. The more nearly the object seen in movement has correspondence to our everyday perceptions of moving objects the greater will be the ease of seeing movement even if the other factors of time, space, and intensity are not at their optimum values.

For example, when one holds a pointed object between his fingers and strikes some other object with the end, it is customary for the object to penetrate the object that is struck. Consequently, if one holds a cigarette in his fingers and stabs it at his ear, the cigarette may be slipped behind the fingers but the observer will get the impression that the cigarette has penetrated the ear. 

Another illustration is the "Yogi" toy shown in Fig. 147.

This is a circular toy with a sword or ax pivoted from the center much as the hand of a watch is pivoted. At the position which B ၁၉ AO

It seems to the observer that the sword has gone directly, in a clockwise direction, from II to IV and thus has cut off the head

of the girl. He is mystified to see the head unharmed. In reality the sword has traveled the long way round, in a counterclockwise direction, from II to IV. He sees the sword only at the beginning and at the end of its movement, but he has the definite impression that he has seen it move from one spot to the other. [16] 

The experience, attitude, temporary set, or expectation of the observer. Whereas movement may be seen when the observer takes a naïve attitude toward the situation, a searching or analytic attitude may eliminate or impair the apparent movement. On the other hand, whereas a movement that is not natural may not be seen by an instructed subject, he may see the movement easily when told what to expect.

Retinal factors. A change in the visual fixation point may change the character of the apparent movement. The waterfall illusion is an illustration of the influence of this factor. Let an individual first fixate his vision on any portion of a waterfall and then shift his gaze to some portion of the surrounding scenery. The scenery will appear to move in the opposite (upward) direction. 

FIG. 148.-Spiral illusion. Re produce this figure on a circular card, spin it slowly on a pin through the center, for about ten seconds, then quickly stop it, and continue to look at it after it is stopped. It will seem to expand or contract, depending on the direction of rotation.

New York: D. Van Nostrand Co.) 

The afterimage of movement may best be produced as follows: Let an observer fixate the center of a disk containing a spiral as shown in Fig. 148, while it is rotated at the rate of one or two revolutions per second for about twenty seconds. Let him then turn his gaze to a blank object the same distance from

PERCEIVING 

441 him as the disk. He will see a spiral moving in the direction opposite to that of the motion when the disk was fixated. 

From all these facts it seems clear that the perception of motion depends upon temporal and spatial factors, as suggested at the beginning of this section. If two objects appear simultaneously, no motion is perceived. The two objects merely stand side by side. If too long an interval is allowed to elapse between exposures, and the stimuli are separated far enough in space or are different enough in some other characteristics, the observer sees first an object here and then an object there. If he sees an object and then, after a suitable time interval, sees the same object or one not too much changed, at a different spot, he gains the experience of motion whether he sees the actual motion or not. 

The truth of the matter is that, in ordinary life, we actually see very little motion and most of our experiences of motion in external objects are based on the principle of perception set forth at the beginning of this chapter; namely, that perception is a guess or immediate inference.

PERCEPTION OF TIME 

Time is ordinarily perceived with great inaccuracy. Experimental evidence seems to favor the opinion that learning modifies skill in judging time intervals and that accuracy of judgment is affected by apparently irrelevant factors. [2, 9] Perception of time dependent upon succession of events. 

Time can be conceived only by reference to a certain succession of events. Physical time implies a succession of irreversible changes in the physical universe, such as the movement of the earth in relation to the sun. Physiological time might be conceived to imply a succession of changes in the physiological universe, and psychological time might imply a succession of psychic processes. There is evidence that the perception of time is influenced by all three types of succession. 

1. The estimation of time is probably affected by physiological activity. If physiological activity is retarded, physical time will appear to move more rapidly by contrast. This may be a factor in the familiar fact that time flows more quickly in old age than in youth. This effect can be understood if physical time is represented by one train moving at constant speed and

PSYCHOLOGY 

physiological time by another train moving on a parallel track. 

In youth they might be running neck and neck; as the person becomes older, the physiological train will slow down and the other increase its relative speed.

Experiments dealing with the effect of drugs on time estimation substantiate this point of view. Drugs which accelerate the metabolic rate-that is, cause the individual to live faster-cause an individual to underestimate a definite time interval; drugs which slow down the metabolic rate lead to overestimation of a definite time interval. 

2. Estimation of time depends upon some frame of reference. 

Suppose that a subject is given the task of estimating the interval between two sound stimuli. If the first sound is prolonged, the interval between it and the second sound is judged to be longer than if the first sound is short. That is, the observer tends to judge the total interval including the sounds as well as the silent interval between them. 

3. The happenings during an interval of time affect the judgment of time. Filled time seems shorter than empty time. 

An interval of time filled with rhythmic music seems shorter than time filled with a monotonous tone. If an individual is made totally unconscious for a period of time by means of an anesthetic, the interval between going to sleep and waking will appear shorter than an interval of wakefulness because of the complete emptiness of the period during which the anesthetic operates. 

The perception of rhythm. Rhythm is a regular recurrence of groups, of patterns, or of successive impressions. It can take the form of a pattern of movement, as in dance steps; of a pattern of sounds, as in music; of a visual pattern, as in a decorative border; or of a pattern of words, as in poetry. 

Some rhythms may be inherent in objective events. This occurs in music, where the sequences of tones may be stressed by time relationships, by relative stresses, or by regular changes in pitch. Rhythm may occur in such movements as marching, swinging on a bar, waving a part of the body, or the like. It occurs naturally in poetry where the stress on different syllables gives the words a pronounced regularity. From a study of such natural rhythms it appears that they are perceived because they correspond to some real or fancied movement. If a person is

PERCEIVING 

443 observed closely when he is attempting to interpret some complicated rhythm he can be seen to move different parts of his body. 

Those rhythms which he can follow with his hand, arm, foot, or head are most easily recognized.

When a series of impressions have absolute uniformity, the recipient does not usually perceive them as a succession of unitary events occurring in sequence. He tends to group them, to stress certain ones, and to introduce rhythm into the series. In other words, he gives a subjective rhythm to physical events which are spaced identically in time and stressed equally in force. This tendency makes it easier to perceive a long string of events, it makes it easier to recall them, and it makes them more interesting so that attention can be maintained for longer intervals. In other words, rhythm is a way of introducing meaning into successions of events. When there is a natural rhythm inherent in the events themselves, this process is easy. When such a natural rhythm is absent, the observer creates one in order to assist him in perceiving these events.

The tau effect. The tau effect is the name given to an illusion in which judgment of spatial intervals is influenced by the temporal intervals involved. For example, if three stimuli are presented in succession at equal spatial but unequal temporal intervals, and if the time between the first and second stimuli is shorter than that between the second and third stimuli, then the first and second stimuli appear to be closer in space than the second and third stimuli. The tau effect can be observed in vision and in touch. It persists even when the observer attempts to allow for it.

In vision the tau effect can be brought out by the following procedure: Three discrete points of light are successively presented. The distance between the points of light are equal but the time interval between the first and second points of light is greater (or less) than the time interval between the second and third. The perceived space between the first and second will be greater (or less) than the perceived space between the second and third points of light.

This tau effect is a neat illustration, which may be used as a parlor trick or game, of the relationship of time and space.

PSYCHOLOGY ILLUSIONS 

An illusion is a misinterpretation of the sensory impressions upon which a perception is based. We have already examined a number of situations in which the observer is likely to have difficulty in interpreting his sense impressions correctly, some in which a number of different interpretations are possible and some in which his perceptions did not agree with the external stimulating conditions. These illusory factors were most striking in the perception of movement, or the phi phenomenon. 

It happens in some situations that the observer recognizes such errors while they are being made. He sees the discrepancy and attempts to effect some sort of compromise. His reaction to such situations is characterized by bewilderment or amusement, and is usually accompanied by a recognition of his error. He usually experiments in some manner, repeats his experiences if possible, or tries in some way to determine the true state of affairs. 

His attitude is the same as that of a person witnessing a sleightof-hand performance. He perceives events which are incongruous with other known events or which violate his reason. He attempts to understand but, when he cannot, is willing to admit that there is something wrong even if he does not know what causes the incongruity. We shall review some typical illusions and examine some of the theories advanced to explain them. [15] 

Geometrical illusions. Geometrical illusions result from misinterpretations of total geometrical figures owing to errors in determining the length, area, direction, or curvature in patterns of lines. They make an interesting study because they are common to practically all individuals and so must depend upon some common characteristics in human beings. They are, however, so diverse that it would be a mistake to attempt to explain them all by means of one general or common principle. Since there is disagreement about the factors accounting for them, the beginning student can do little more than become acquainted with the different kinds. 

1. Vertical distances are perceived as greater than physically equal horizontal distances. A pole or a tree is generally judged to be longer when it is standing than when it lies on the ground.

PERCEIVING

2. Small angles are relatively overestimated, and large angles are relatively underestimated. This distortion of angles shows

This illusion is shown in various forms.
