Explanations of illusions. Psychologists have been concerned with discovering one general principle to explain all geometrical illusions. It should be apparent that such an undertaking is destined to fail because each illusion probably depends upon a different combination of factors. Nevertheless, the student should know what theories have been advanced to explain them. 

The eye movement theory. This theory assumes that the impression of length is obtained by moving the eye along a line from one end to another. If vertical movements are more strenuous than horizontal, a given vertical distance calls for more effort than the same horizontal distance and therefore seems longer. 

The strongest argument against this theory is that numerous experiments, in which the eye movements have been photographed, show no such movements of the eyes during examination

PERCEIVING 

449 of the figures as this theory would require. If eye movements play any role, it certainly is a minor one. 

The perspective theory. It is a fact that a line drawing readily suggests to the observer objects in three dimensions and, while studying the perception of depth, it is shown that the perception of depth in line drawings is subject to error. However, many other geometrical illusions cannot be explained by this factor.

The empathy theory. Empathy means the imaginary projection of oneself into some objective situation. Applying this theory to such an illusion as the vertical-horizontal illusion, it is contended that a vertical line by resisting gravity suggests effort and thus appears longer to the observer. This theory is purely speculative and is not backed by any experimental evidence. 

The good-figure theory. Those who would explain illusions by the good-figure theory define a good figure as one which expresses some characteristic fully, or is complete in its meaning. 

When one observes a figure having some characteristic, his tendency is to see this characteristic as fully as the conditions will allow. A near-circle is seen as a true circle or as a better circle than it is; if compactness is suggested by the figure, it will appear to be more compact than it is. This is merely a description of what seems to happen in some illusions and is not an adequate explanation of illusions in general. 

The wrong-response theory. This theory is not so satisfying to some individuals as some of the others but it seems to get at the root of the matter better. If a person sees a figure incorrectly, he has no notion of his error unless that is forced upon him by some other aspect of the situation. He measures a line and finds it is not curved as it seems. He finds the center of a circle and completes the part omitted or distorted and thus proves that he saw it incorrectly. He measures two lines which appear unequal and finds that they are equal. Thus, he finds by experiment, by the test of other senses, or by evidence of some sort that he was wrong. An illusion is not an illusion until it conflicts with other perceptual data. 

The explanation of any illusion must be an account of why the observer's first reaction and subsequent data do not correspond. The actual facts will probably be different in every case.

PSYCHOLOGY 

To attempt to explain them all on one basis is equivalent to explaining every trick of a clever sleight-of-hand performer by the same device. Illusions are tricks our senses and past experience play upon us and these tricks are probably extremely numerous.

The impossibility of deriving some simple principle to explain all illusions will become still more apparent by an examination of some illusions involving factors other than geometrical distortions.

The size-weight illusion. The size of an object has a definite influence upon judgment of its weight. If two objects are the same in weight, while one is larger than the other, the larger weight will be judged lighter. A pound of lead will feel much heavier than a pound of feathers. Load two pillboxes, one much larger than the other, with paraffin and shot so that they both weigh the same. Your friends will invariably judge the smaller one to be the heavier. 

This illusion is usually explained on the basis of set or expectation. Since the two boxes are of the same material, one unwittingly judges them to be of the same specific gravity. 

Having picked up the smaller one, the observer expects the larger one to be heavier. When he finds that it is not so heavy as he expected it to be, it actually seems lighter. In short, it is judged lighter than the other box because it is lighter than he expected it to be.

Cyclorama illusion. An interesting and useful illusion of spatial relations can be produced by placing in the foreground a number of solid objects and have them melt into a painted background, so that the observer seems to be in the midst of a great open area. Objects of natural history are often mounted in glass cases in such a way that they occupy the foreground with an almost imperceptible transition to painted scenery in the background. This illusion probably depends upon the fact that the perception of depth is definitely created by the disparate images and binocular parallax of the near objects and the use of other monocular cues for the painted wall effects. 

The confused finger-movement illusion. This illusion illustrates the fact that visual and kinesthetic cues may combine in a perceptual situation and, when the visual cues are reversed,

PERCEIVING 

451 confusion results. With the hands held in the position indicated in Fig. 155, have someone instruct the subject to move a specific finger by pointing to it. He is likely to move the corresponding finger of the other hand.

When the subject closes his eyes and is instructed to move a certain finger he can do it without error. In other words, when he looks he uses visual cues and moves the finger that would 

FIG. 155.-Illustration showing the position of the fingers ready for a demonstration of the confused fingermovement illusion. ordinarily be pointing in the direction of the finger designated but which is now reversed. 

With practice the illusion disappears, not so much from a conscious differentiation between right and left hands as from gradual and almost unconscious fusion of visual cues with the correct kinesthetic and tactual cues. 

HALLUCINATIONS 

A hallucination is a perception that occurs when there is no objective stimulus to give rise to the perception, or a perception that is so gross a misinterpretation of the objective stimulating factors as to have little or no apparent relation to them. In an extreme and pathological form a person may hear voices talking to him when there is no objective source of such voices; he may see visions when there is no objective visual stimulation; he may feel objects touching his body when there is nothing in contact with the area indicated by his perceptions; or he may feel himself 1

PSYCHOLOGY 

being transported through space when absolutely motionless. 

However, the term "hallucination" should not be limited to pathological conditions. Since misinterpretation is a relative term, there is no possibility of making sharp distinctions between illusions, hallucinations, and pathological hallucinations. 

Factors which contribute to hallucinatory experiences. 

While it is true that everybody is sure to misinterpret his sensory experiences to some degree, it is also significant that each individual attempts to correct any perceptual errors that arise so that his final interpretation of objective conditions be as nearly accurate as possible. This being true, an examination of some of the factors contributing to hallucinatory experiences may indicate what precautions an ordinary person should take in order to avoid being deceived too completely by his perceptual mistakes. [13] 

Predominance of subjective components characterize hallucinations. In any perception there are individual factors. In a hallucination these subjective components are given undue weight. For example, the lone person in a large house at night, after having been told of recent burglaries in the neighborhood, is more likely to interpret a sound as the entrance of a burglar than if the fear of burglars were not so pronounced. 

Resistance to contradictory evidence contributes to gross distortion of perceptual interpretations. Persons who have pathological hallucinations demonstrate clearly the presence of this factor. For example, if a person is tempted to do some immoral act, he may be frightened by the very thought of such an act. 

Instead of recognizing the temptation as a part of his own thinking, he may interpret it as the suggestion of some outsider. If he can interpret it as a voice coming to him he thus escapes selfcondemnation. Any evidence against the reality of the voice is rejected because such evidence would make it clear that his temptation was part of his own personal thinking. He rejects evidence against the error of his perception because such an error is more comfortable than the truth would be. 

A hallucination is likely to be acted upon as though it were real in spite of evidence of its falsity. Action is the final test of how seriously a person takes his perceptions. In a simple illusion the person is not likely to act on the basis of a perception that he

PERCEIVING 

453 knows is wrong. He takes objective checks as the final test and acts accordingly. When a person rejects factual evidence and acts on his own errors, he certainly is evidencing an unwholesome interest in maintaining such errors. For example, when a woman leaves her real husband to live with an imaginary husband and considers this fictitious man the only real husband, she is manifesting an extremely morbid hallucinatory trend. When a young man sees only the beauty in his chosen girl he is doing a similar thing, although there is a vast degree of difference in the amount of distortion involved. 

It should be apparent, from the numerous kinds of perceptual errors that are possible, that the normal man should never be sure of what he sees, hears, tastes, smells, or touches. He is continually checking his perceptions by additional evidence from the various senses, by experiment, and by the ways in which others around him behave. At the same time he must act as though his perceptions were accurate. The normal procedure is to make the best interpretation that one can, but at the same time accept corrections without hesitation. It is when one does not accept corrections that he develops pathological hallucinations. 

If I hear a voice calling my name and, upon investigation, find no source for the sound, I should admit that I was mistaken. If I insist that it was a departed loved one speaking to me I am giving an unwarranted interpretation to an error. 

Sometimes it may be difficult to determine whether a perception has or has not a relevant sensory basis. An interesting illustration came to light in one case when a man heard radio broadcasts without being near a receiving set. It appeared that these broadcasts could not be wholly subjective, for they corresponded in content and time with broadcasts actually being given. 

Investigation showed that the fillings in his teeth combined with carborundum deposits on his teeth to form a crystal receiving set. 

He was not hearing hallucinations; he was hearing actual broadcasts.

Factors which cause hallucinations. Genuine hallucinations require a set of conditions which permit drastic distortion of sensory experiences. They cannot all be explained upon the same basis, any more than any perception can be attributed to the operation of any one factor. Causal factors may be divided. 1

PSYCHOLOGY 

into two main groups: (1) those producing a malfunctioning of the sensory processes and (2) those depending upon an attitude or set in the individual which makes it advantageous to him to distort his sensory experiences. 

1. Physiological factors favoring hallucinatory experi ences. Any condition that impairs the efficiency of the sensory mechanism may contribute to perceptual distortion. Some of these conditions are: fatigue, fever, deliria, diseases of the sense organs, and poisoning by such drugs as alcohol, cocaine, morphine, mescal, or hashish.

Such hallucinations frequently take a form corresponding to the nature of the physiological disturbance. For example, alcohol may disturb the ears and thus make it easier for an individual to experience auditory hallucinations; cocaine may cause a disturbance of the touch sense organs and be interpreted as the activity of tiny animals crawling over the skin; mescal may stimulate acute visual imagery. Unless the disturbance is extreme, however, the individual who has a hallucination based on a purely physiological background is likely to have some notion that his perception is not real. The man with delirium tremens sees snakes, but at the same time he has a suspicion that they are not real snakes. When subjective factors dominate, the individual is more likely to believe that his perceptions are real. 

2. Attitudes which favor hallucinations. When an individual has a need for a certain interpretation he is likely to distort his perceptions in a direction that makes it more adequate to meet the need. Three subjective factors which favor such distortion may be outlined as follows: (a) The habit of daydreaming. Individuals vary in the ease with which they can let their imaginations play. When such imaginings are so clear that the observer claims they equal actual sensory impressions in vividness and liveliness, they have been called eidetic images. Such images occur most frequently in uncritical children, almost never in adults who have an objective, critical, and unemotional outlook on life. Although no such relationship has been demonstrated, it would be logical to suppose that a person who finds it easy to develop eidetic images would also find it easy to have hallucinations. (b) Emotional tensions. In inflammation of the ear

PERCEIVING 

455 caused by fatigue, disease, or drug there may be buzzing sounds that will be heard as simple sounds by an emotionally stable individual. Suppose, on the other hand, that certain emotional tensions are added to the physiological disturbance. A person who is afraid that he may be caught in a lie he has just told may hear the buzzings as voices calling him a liar. A person who is having difficulty in making an important decision may hear the buzzing as an answer to his problem. The mother who is worrying about her son on the battlefield may hear the buzzing as his voice. (c) Persistent temptations. All individuals have impulses to commit acts or at least to think thoughts which they would rather avoid. When such impulses become too unpleasant, it may be easy to explain them on the basis of impressions from the outside world. Such projections free the subject from guilt. 

If someone puts the ideas into his head, he is not to blame, so he feels. When he is tempted to steal he can deny any impulse by stating that some voice from outside told him to steal. Having resisted such a suggestion, he may feel genuinely virtuous. Thus, the hallucination has value for him and he wants to believe it.

Chapter XVI PROBLEM SOLVING 

A

PERSON may be said to be confronting a problem when he is in a situation containing some elements, factors, or conditions that are known and others that are unknown; and when he is somehow stimulated to achieve a result that depends upon his discovery of how to utilize some of the unknown elements, factors, or conditions. A problem involves uncertainty and the solution of a problem entails clearing up the uncertainty, the finding of a path or course of action that has not been clear and open.. Problem solving is a type of adjustive behavior. 

KINDS OF PROBLEMS. 

Variations in clearness. Problems vary greatly in the clearness with which they may be formulated. The most clearly formulated problems can usually be answered by a simple yes or no. For example: Shall I take the road to the right at this fork?

Shall I buy this article? In some problems a simple discrimination is all that is required. For example: Which of two colors is more pleasing? As the factors involved in a problem increase in number, the part played by each element becomes more obscure and, for this reason, the formulation of the problem itself becomes difficult. In the most intricate problems, the individual confronting the situation usually does not know much more than that he is uncomfortable and must do something; but what to do he cannot discern. [57] 

Variations in openness or accessibility of relevant factors. In some problems, success is largely dependent upon ability to select from a great many elements those which are most relevant in the present situation. Some brain-teasers and puzzle problems give false cues as to the importance of various factors, and thus tempt the one who is trying to solve them to make 458

PROBLEM SOLVING 

459 continued false responses. On the other hand, a person may become so intent in searching for some hidden or intricate solution that he fails to discern a correct procedure that is clearly apparent. 

An interesting parlor game illustrates this principle. Various objects, such as a penny, a hairpin, a cigarette, a match, a piece. of string, are placed around a room in plain sight, so that nothing need be moved to see them.. Each member of the group is given a list of the "hidden" objects and is required to designate where they are. Searchers will mill around, hunting for these objects, and frequently will look straight at them without discerning them. 

When an object is noticed, the finder is usually surprised that he had such difficulty in seeing it. 

Variations in the number of processes necessary for solution. Some problems involve only one step. Once the point of the problem is discerned, that one step may be taken and complete solution effected. After such a solution, repetition leads to no improvement, except possibly a slight decrease in the time required to repeat the correct act. A simple puzzle illustrates this principle: This puzzle consists of a trough in which are two BB shot. The problem is to get one in a socket at one end of the curved runway and the other shot in the socket at the other. If the whole puzzle is tipped toward one end the shot will drop into one socket. When the puzzle is tipped in the opposite direction far enough to permit the second shot to drop into its socket, the first shot will come out into the runway. The correct solution is to spin the puzzle so that centrifugal force will throw each shot in a separate direction, and each will fall in its appropriate socket. 

Once the trick is learned, it takes but one flip to solve it, whereas the novice will toy with the apparatus indefinitely trying to roll one shot into its socket without dislodging the other. 

On the other hand, a problem may involve so many movements or factors that even after all the essential steps are known their operation takes considerable time, skill, and patience. An example of such a problem is the disk transfer puzzle. [48, p. 472] In this problem, ten disks would require 1,023 moves; twenty, over a million; and thirty, over a billion. Certainly, the learner cannot go about solving such a complicated problem in the same manner that he would set out to solve a puzzle which depended upon one trick act.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Variations in urgency. Problems differ in the degree of intensity of the demand for solution. To extricate oneself from a wrecked vehicle would be a problem; but the need for a solution would become much more urgent were the wreckage to catch fire. 

An emergency should not be regarded merely as a single new element added to a systematic problem that would customarily be solved by fixed methods; the emergency transforms the routine problem into a totally new situation requiring different treatment. 

New techniques in industry, new procedures in surgery, and the like, have often arisen when it has been discerned that the present situation could not be met adequately by a speeding up of old methods. Emergencies have contributed extensively to human progress and invention. 

Variations in ability of challenged individual. Problems vary in relation to the training and ability of the individual who confronts the problem situation. No problem exists except in relation to an individual to whom it is a challenge. If the situation is so far removed from the experience of the individual that he has no comprehension of its significance, it certainly is not a problem so far as he is concerned. The two-year-old boy cannot be made to search for a solution to the problem of unemployment or surplus production, but he can be very much alive to the need for recovering the ball that has rolled under a hot radiator beyond his reach.

Variations in methods for solving problems. There is no one solution for any problem. Instead, most problems have more than one solution, and these can be reached by different routes. One solution may be better than another, or one method may be more expeditious than another; two facts which suggest that we probably do not have the ultimate answer to any problem. 

Problem solving is thus an intriguing game. Even if we have a solution, there may be a better one if we hunt long enough, and with sufficient experience and intelligence; and even if we have found what appears to be the best answer, there may yet be a better way of reaching that goal.

Having arrived at a solution for a problem, the problem solver is losing much of the benefit of his endeavors if he becomes self-satisfied. The greatest value of success is not success itself, but the guidance it may provide for the finding of a better

PROBLEM SOLVING 

461 solution or the reaching of a goal by different routes. We shall find that success may be a matter of chance or may be the result of careful analysis and clear thinking. If an individual complacently congratulates himself for a chance success he is less likely to advance from random methods to more rational procedures than he is if his interest is centered in problem solving as a game. Success should be only a temporary stopping place; it should be a period of respite during which to get one's wind, a time during which one may pause long enough to analyze his · methods critically.

TOOLS FOR SOLVING PROBLEMS 

A good mechanic may need few tools, but the expert knows how to use the finest of tools. Since problem solving is the most important task that confronts a human being, it is important for him to utilize the best tools that are available and to select the correct ones to fit each need.

Random activity. Could an individual be placed in a totally new situation, one in which he had no conceivable cue as to what kind of behavior to favor, he probably would respond in a random fashion. Purely random activity would imply that there was as great a probability of any one act being made as any other act; a person would show no preference for any of the innumerable possible responses he might make. Since we all have been modified by past experience, we never act in a purely random fashion. 

If we see a puzzle we are more likely to manipulate it with our hands than to use our feet, to begin to scream, eat, go to sleep, or sing a song. In other words, there are all degrees of specificity of behavior from sheer chance or random behavior to completely directed and specific acts. The newer a problem, that is, the less apparent relationship there is to past experience, the greater will be the random nature of any attempts to solve the problem. 

Random activity may be in the motor realm and easily observable to an outsider, as is the case when an animal is confined in a cage and tries to escape; or it may be in the thinking of an individual who is confronted with a reasoning problem that is strange to him. [49]

Random activity is a substitute, and a good one, for giving up. Suppose that one never tried a problem until he knew what

PSYCHOLOGY 

to do; he never would accomplish much. Instead, he begins flourdering around, trying any hunch he may have. Eventually, if he varies his activity enough he may happen upon some act which gets him nearer his goal. He takes advantage of this lead and makes his floundering a little more specific until he falls upon another happy move.

When, in psychology, we speak of random behavior, we do not imply that there is no direction. Instead, we mean that the individual is in a dilemma from which he would be unable to extricate himself should he wait until he knows exactly what to do, and that he resorts to undirected activity with the hope that he may happen to do the correct thing. He watches closely, if he is intelligent enough to do so, the relation of his various acts to success and failure and, in the long run, tends to avoid those acts which he learns lead only to failure and to repeat those acts which seem to be related to success. [35] Such behavior has been variously named "trial and error," "trial and success," and "fumble and success." It is a valuable tool and the good problem solver usually has learned when and to what extent to "take a chance." It is valuable in the solution of puzzles or games engaged in for pure fun. [12] It becomes rather dangerous and costly in solving problems which involve human life or human welfare. It may be a sensible thing to make a random trial in the attempt to solve a puzzle, but an unintelligent act to stake one's fortune on the turning up of a card in a poker game.

Past experiences. Utilizing past experiences in problem solving is more than repeating an act in a habitual manner. As a matter of fact, habitual behavior is inimical to problem solving. 

If all a person does in a new situation is to act in the same manner that he did in similar situations in the past, he thereby ignores the new elements in the present situation and, consequently, fails. 

Instead, a problem demands that the benefits of more than one past experience shall be somehow combined and used in the present situation. We shall see how sagacity in recombining past experiences is a most important element in solving problems. 

Orientation. In problem solving, orientation is used to mean the act of determining or correcting one's relation to the goal or objective of the problem situation. Various terms have

PROBLEM SOLVING 

463 been used by different psychologists to express the same factor: set, schema, direction, pointing. They all imply more or less the same set of processes. To keep oriented one must have a clear conception (as clear as possible) of the goal to be reached, one must be alert to the effects of various acts in relation to that goal (do they bring one nearer or take: one farther away?), and one must be alert to cues in order to keep one's bearing. [65, p. 137] 

Incentives. Before am animal will run through a maze he must be hungry or uncomfortable enough to be stimulated to do something. The best setup for giving an individual an incentive to solve a problem is to make the separation from the goal: the direct cause of the discomfort and to make the attainment of that goal a direct relief from the discomfort. This will not only stimulate the individual to do something, but will give his activity some point or direction. Where the goal is not clearly seen in relation to the challenged person's activity the result will be activity, but activity of a more or less random nature. 

In Chapter V we learned how certain physiological processes incited the individual to activity. In Chapter VI we found that the experiences of an individual modify the strength of certain drives. Furthermore, in Chapter VII we learned that emotional tensions, which result from certain maladjustments, are essential to problem solving. The individual has to do more than perceive a goal in order to make active attempts to get it. He has to want that goal to such an extent that he will continue his efforts to attain it in spite of temporary defeats, the need for delaying final gratification of his desires, the temporary failures which meet his efforts, and the necessity for giving up of other desires which are more immediate. 

In human individuals who have had much experience in solving problems of various sorts, the mere presence of a problem is challenge enough to enlist their finest efforts. The so-called pure scientist is probably a person of this sort. He is not so much concerned with the immediate application of what he discovers as he is in the fun of solving the problems that confront him. He will forget his meals, his sleep, or his appointments with friends in the search for some elusive answer to an abstract problem. The outsider cannot understand this zeal because he

PSYCHOLOGY 

has not learned that a problem itself can be the greatest challenge to prolonged effort. 

Language. As we proceed with our study of problem solving we shall make some comparisons of the problem-solving ability and methods of animals as compared with human beings. These studies will make apparent the tremendous advantage that language gives to the problem solver and to the thinker. Of all the tools that man uses in his thinking processes, language stands out in a unique way. At this point we shall merely point out some of these advantages so that the tremendous significance of language will be more apparent as we proceed with our survey of problem-solving methods. 

By means of language (a) we are able to name objects so that they can be more readily identified on future occasions; (b) we can compare objects and experiences more easily with each other; (c) we can state relationships between objects and experiences; (d) we can classify information for future reference; (e) we can formulate abstractions and deal with abstract concepts in a manner that would be impossible without language; (f) we can state general principles or laws; (g) we can carry out logical deductions which enable us to make correct statements about situations we have never experienced on the basis of what we have learned in the past.

THE SOLUTION OF SIMPLE PROBLEMS 

A puzzle is a complex combination of objects or circumstances that is mystifying or perplexing. In a sense every problem is a puzzle, but the term "puzzle" is more appropriately used when the challenging situation presents a novel arrangement of familiar elements. Once a puzzle is solved it usually looks absurdly simple.

Puzzles involving a hidden element. A common illustration of a puzzle of this sort is the picture in which there is a hidden figure. Until the figure is discerned it may be hard to locate; once it is discerned it is almost impossible not to perceive it. In many situations the significant element is embedded in apparently irrelevant factors and is consequently overlooked. 

This fact was clearly seen in our study of perceiving. In order to discern which elements in a situation are significant and which

PROBLEM SOLVING 

465 are not, the individual must be able to shift his attention quickly over all possible factors, not slighting any and not becoming fixed on any one. Alert attention, keen discrimination, and minute comparisons are essential.

For example, one experimenter created a situation in which a monkey was fed whenever the experimenter picked up the food with his left hand, but was never fed when it was picked up with the right hand. The monkey had to learn to discriminate between the two hand signals, to learn that the raising of the left hand was a cue or signal that food was to be given, and to learn that the raising of the right hand was a cue or signal that no food would be received. [58] This same experimenter tried a more complicated arrangement of the same process with a kitten. The kitten was accustomed to climb up the wire netting of his cage whenever it expected to receive food. Whenever the experimenter said aloud, "I must feed those cats," the kitten was always fed; whenever the experimenter said, "I will not feed them," the kitten was never fed. It took the kitten 380 trials to learn to distinguish between the two verbal signals and to climb up the netting only when it heard the words, "I must feed those cats." [58] The student will recognize that this process of comparison and the acceptance of one factor as a cue for food involves the same sort of learning that was involved in the conditioned reaction discussed in Chapter IX. 

In such an experiment the learner is helped because of the fact that the experimenter is consistent. He always arranges matters so that food will come with one signal and will never come with another. The difficulty is accentuated when the signal is one that is strange to the animal. Should the experimenter always give three signals-raise his right hand, stamp his left foot, and open his mouth-when the animal is fed, and should he never feed the animals unless all three signals were present, such a complication would tremendously increase the difficulty of the problem.

Whether the deception in a puzzle is purposely introduced by an experimenter or whether it merely happens to be present does not change the significance of the problem to the one required to solve it. In fact, most problems are deceptive and are difficult for this very reason. They give the investigator a false clue, a

PSYCHOLOGY 

suggestion which he must be able to override netone success can be achieved. If one knows he is being tricked, he can give his attention to trivial incidents and details; but in natural problems one never knows whether the solution is to be found in a trivial incident or in some factor which appears to be important. 

Puzzle-box experiments. In order to analyze the procedures involved in problem solving, investigators have placed dogs, cats, chicks, monkeys, and children in cages of various sorts from which escape could be gained only by performing some specific act or series of acts prescribed by the experimenter. Some boxes require the pulling of various strings or loops, or the utilization of certain objects within the cage. In some situations the essenFIG. 156.-Double-platform puzzłe box used with white rats. The rat enters in front of the door d.

This door opens only after platforms a and b are successively pressed down. tial act is simple, in others it is made complex. An illustration of a difficult puzzle box is given in Fig. 156.

A fact of first importance that appears in these experiments is that individuals differ in the way they act under such circumstances. Not only do animals of different species behave differently, but animals within the same species vary in their reactions. 

Some quietly lie down and must be taught the need for getting out of the pen to get the reward (for example, something to eat) by being taken out and fed and then returned. Some are violent in their attempts to get out, while others are relatively docile. 

Some work intermittently and others continuously. To attempt to generalize and say that all animals do certain acts in response to a problem is obviously an error. They do what their individuality, past experience, and present stimulations and irritations make them do.

PROBLEM SOLVING 

467 When the experimenter succeeds in setting a problem that is quite new to the animal, or very difficult for him, the animal is likely to resort to trial-and-error, or fumble-and-success, behavior. That is, when the animal does not know what to do, his behavior is helter-skelter, performed in a hasty, disorderly, and confused manner.

More critical observations have shown that, after his first success, the behavior of the animal in the puzzle box is not purely random. Instead, the animal tends to give more of his time, and to devote more of his attention, to the parts of the box where he succeeded in previous trials; and to abandon, or give less attention to, those aspects of the problem which were apparently unrelated to his successful performances. In other words, there is a gradual change from aimless and random activity to restricted acts. After an animal has released himself from a puzzle box by turning a certain button, he is likely to spend much more of his time in the vicinity of that button than in some remote portion of the cage, even though he has not learned just how to turn the button to release himself. [35]

Sometimes the animal wil persist in an act that is useless; but this is probably because it has not been made clear to him that it is useless. For example, suppose that an animal is pulling at the wrong bar with his right paw, when his left paw accidentally pushes the correct bar, and the door opens. Is it strange that, on succeeding trials, he continues to pull at the wrong bar with his right paw? Such persistence should not be called random behavior. Instead, he is adhering to a false cue or hypothesis. 

The problem solver, be he animal or man, often deceives himself by accomplishing his end in some unnoticed manner while devoting his attention to some irrelevant feature. Furthermore, if some new element is added after he has solved a problem in one way, this success tends to interfere with an adequate regard for the new feature. Because new parts of a situation are similar to a familiar one, an individual tends to ignore the new features and to act as though the new situation were identical to the known situation in all particulars.

This tendency was clearly demonstrated in an experiment with door-button manipulation by a chimpanzee. The chimpanzee saw a banana placed in a box through a doorway. She set about

PSYCHOLOGY 

trying to open the door by pulling, pushing, and shaking it, but with no specific attention directed toward the button which held the door shut. Eventually, after much banging and shaking, the button was pushed into the vertical position so that the door could be pulled open. From then, in succeeding trials, she devoted her time to the button or to the door near the button, and after three trials was able to open the door by a prompt turning of the button. Then another button, just like the first one, was added at a higher position, as shown in Fig. 157. The chimpanzee 

FIG. 157.-Diagram of a door button puzzle box. The box was first presented to the chimpanzee with only the lower button. 

After this problem was mastered the upper button was added. The animal did not immediately note this addition. Instead, her failure to open the door by turning the lower button led to increased excitement and to a reversion to random activity. neglected this new button and continued to devote all her energies to the first button which, she had learned, held the secret to opening the door. When this did not succeed she became more energetic in her attack on this first button, turning it back and forth and pulling at the door. Only after a considerable amount of time did she discover the second button. [65, p. 755] 

We might state the situation something like this: The chimpanzee learned that a certain button had to be turned before the door could be opened. She did not learn that doors in general may be opened by turning buttons in general. When button B was added, it was not immediately grasped as a specific instance of a general principle. Nevertheless, learning the second button was easier than learning the first one, and there was some carryover from the first problem to the second. There was also some interference because of a tendency to adhere to the type of behavior that had already proved of value.

Detour problems. Many problems cannot be solved directly. Instead, they require either deliberation or some roundabout activity. The more intelligent solver is able to turn his back upon the goal when he discerns that a direct approach is Bars Objective

Important factors in problem solving are the recognition of an error when one has been made, and the substitution of some other line of action to replace the erroneous one.

One experimenter tested the ability of chickens to solve a problem which demanded a detour. Hens were separated from a visible supply of food by a fence through which they could project their heads without being able to reach the food, as shown

Solution came when a hen, in her excitement, extended the length of her runs and, by accident, ran far enough from the food to come to the gate. We shall encounter the same principle when we study the thinking processes in human beings. The intelligent thinker is the one who can discard a hypothesis, a theory, or a method of attack when he has evidence that he is in the wrong and can consider some factor that may appear to be taking him away from the problem itself. The unintelligent thinker is dominated by habit and tradition. The intelligent thinker is willing to do unusual things, to try anything once; but he is also willing to discard a procedure once he finds that it is erroneous.

Box-stacking problems. The setting for the box-stacking problem is to suspend some coveted object, a bit of food for an animal or a toy for a child, beyond the reach of the subject and, at the same time, place a box in the vicinity which, if properly used, will enable the subject to reach the food with its help. In one experiment a hungry chimpanzee was placed in a cage, from the ceiling of which was suspended a banana, with a box thrown casually on the floor of the cage some distance from the point where the fruit hung suspended. The chimpanzee spent many hours in his unsuccessful attempts to get the fruit, jumping up toward it, climbing the walls, and the like. After the animal had shown that he was incompetent to cope with the situation, the experimenter dragged the box across the floor of the cage to a point beneath the banana, climbed upon the box, reached the banana, and then got down and threw the box to one side of the cage. The animal profited from this example, pulled the box over under the banana, climbed upon it and reached the banana. 

The same experiment, when tried on a stupid ape, was not successful. He climbed upon the box, raised it over him, but never learned to use the box as an instrument for obtaining the banana. [34] 

Another experimenter tried a similar test using both a child (age 15 months) and an ape (age 12½ months) as subjects. A cooky was suspended from the ceiling and a chair was used as the tool upon which the subjects could climb to get the cooky. The preliminary instruction consisted of placing the chair beneath the cooky and permitting the subjects to climb upon the chair and get it. After these preliminaries they were given trials of five minutes each, during which they could manipulate the chair as they saw fit. The ape secured the cooky in the first trial, the child in his fourth trial. The ape failed only once in twenty attempts, the child four times. Furthermore, the ape seemed to grasp the significance of the problem more clearly than the child, keeping his eye on the cooky while manipulating the chair, whereas the child would push the chair around without much regard for the location of the cooky and seldom looking at it (see Fig. 164). [32] 

Once a subject, animal or human, has learned how to utilize one box or chair as a means for reaching a dangling object,

Delayed reactions. It is a wise man who knows when to act and when to wait. In some situations it is profitable to act even though the outcome of activity may not be clear. When an animal is placed in a puzzle box, it pays him to get up and move around and try to get out even though he has not the remotest idea of how his release may be effected. When a man is attempt-

PSYCHOLOGY 

ing to solve a typical mechanical puzzle, he will accomplish more by manipulating the puzzle in a haphazard manner than he will by attempting to solve it by purely analytical methods. On the other hand, mistakes may be costly, and, in such cases, it pays to delay when uncertainty exists.

Delay should not merely be idle waiting; it should be occupied with a comparison of one suggestion with another so that, when a final act is made, it may be more suitable than would have LC 

FIG. 165.-Diagram of apparatus for testing delayed reactions. The subject is placed in the release box (R). One of the three lights (L) is flashed on a sufficient time for the subject to see it and is then turned off. After an interval of time the subject is released. 

If he goes to the light which flashed he finds the door (D) open and gains food or some reward. If he goes to one of the other lights, he finds the door (D) closed and he gets no reward. (From W. S. Hunter, Behavior Monogr., 1913, 2, 23.) been the case had not deliberation preceded it. It is, consequently, an important consideration how long an individual can retain the benefits of a cue or a hypothetical solution without acting upon it.

This can be tested with animals by a simple type of experiment. [25] An animal is taught that he can get food only when he goes to one of three boxes. This correct box may be distinguished by a light, a geometrical figure, a color, or some similar means. After the animal has learned that the lighted box always contains food, he is placed where he can see all three

PROBLEM SOLVING 

477 of the boxes but cannot reach any of them. Such an apparatus is shown in Fig. 165. One box is lighted, and then the light extinguished. After prescribed intervals of time, the animal is released and permitted to choose any one of the three boxes, which now are all dark. If he chooses the right one consistently, it would appear that he profited from seeing the box lighted even though he was prevented from going to it at once. 

The length of the period of delay with animals varies from a few seconds up to about 20 when there are three alternatives from which to choose, but increases to 30 seconds when the number of alternatives is reduced to two. The interval of delay is also lengthened as one advances in the animal scale, that is, there is an increase with the intelligence level. With three alternatives rats were able to delay 10 seconds, a raccoon could delay 25 seconds, a 22-year-old child 50 seconds, and a 6-year-old girl twenty-five minutes. [67]

In another experiment, all the doors were exactly alike except for position. An animal has no means of identifying relative position by language. He cannot say to himself, “that was the middle door" or "the door to the left," or "the door to the right." 

He merely is given the cue that a certain door leads to food and then the means of distinguishing that door from the others is removed. How does he then make the distinction and go to the right door when he is released? In these early experiments the animals were observed to maintain a posture which oriented them in relation to the correct door. Sometimes they pointed their heads toward the door and kept them there.. Whatever part of their body was used, the essential element was to maintain a constant postural relationship to the correct door. [25] 

On the other hand, such bodily orientations are not an absolute prerequisite for correct delayed responses. Where the cue is more complex it may offer other means of identification and the animal does not need to maintain a posture in order to make the proper selection after a delay. [14] In another experiment a cat was restrained in a cage while the experimenter walked across the room with a plate of food and out one of two doors. After thirty seconds the cat was released and made a correct choice of doors in 68 per cent of the trials. The cat did not maintain a rigid posture pointing toward the correct door during this interval.

PSYCHOLOGY 

[7] In still another experiment the reward was placed under one of three cups in the presence of a child and the child could make a correct selection after a considerable interval with no maintenance of posture during the interval. [27] 

An actual movement in the direction of the correct response enables the animal to delay his final reaction even longer than is possible if he maintains a postural' orientation or pointing. It would seem that an incipient movement functions as a means of partial identification and helps the animal to make the correct choice when he is free to make a complete response. [22] 

The efficiency of a delayed response depends upon a clear identification of the choice to be made. After it is clear what should be done at some later time, the interval may be filled with rest or other activity. If the only identifying factor is an object in a certain location, the only successful way of delaying, and then making a correct response, is to maintain a bodily orientation with respect to the correct object. If the correct object can be identified by some other characteristic than its position, the animal need not maintain a bodily posture during the waiting interval. Fairly complicated problems can be solved by monkeys if the setting is so arranged that the animal can utilize some cue to identify the correct response. [60] In human beings the use of language makes possible more accurate identification and a much more prolonged delay than is possible in an animal, which cannot use language.

These experiments with delayed reactions in human beings and animals show fairly decisively that, if an individual is to withhold his response to a certain problem, he must have some sort of device which will guide him at the time he does respond. 

Becoming aware of some identifying cue is a form of preliminary set or incipient response which is not consummated because of some restraining influence. With the animal, it is a cage that restrains him; in human thinking, caution is probably the restraining force-a fear of error from precipitate or hasty reactions. 

At any rate, the preliminary response creates a "set," or readiness, to consummate a specific reaction when the time is ripe to do so. 

In some of the lower forms of animal life, and if the situation offers no cue except a spatial one, the animal may be forced to use a posture, or pointing attitude, to keep himself oriented to the

PROBLEM SOLVING 

479 problem. When other cues are present the animal can forgo the postural set and utilize some other cue for identifying the correct response. The ideal cue to use is a verbal one and this is the type used by human beings in most situations calling for delayed reactions.

Multiple choice. Choosing between possible alternatives certainly is a prominent feature of problem solving. While this is so, a choice may be a quite different act depending upon other circumstances than the act of choosing itself. Choices may be classified in different ways: 

1. Choices may be random or rational. If the alternatives are so nearly alike to the observer that he has no grounds for making a selection, his choice must be as purely random as the tossing of a coin or the throwing of dice. At the other extreme are selections based on complete knowledge of the factors involved so that the person making the choice is practically certain of the outcome of his choice. Most of the choices made in problem situations involve some degree of uncertainty. 

2. Choices may be final or tentative. The chooser may in some instances reserve the right to retrace his steps and make another selection after he has examined some of the results of his choice. In other instances, an act may be irrevocable. 

3. Choices may be real or imaginary. In some cases the thinker may imagine what the outcome would be were he to choose the different alternatives, in others no such imaginary speculations are possible. Imaginary choices are prominent in certain kinds of reasoning, where the thinker withholds a final act while speculating as to the possible results of various selections he might make. 

4. Choices may involve two or more alternatives. In some instances there are only two possible alternatives from which to choose, in others there may be a great number. One of the obstacles in the way of clear thinking is the tendency to devote exclusive attention to the most obvious alternatives and thus fail to discern others. The individual in the problem situation becomes so engrossed in trying to decide whether to make selection A or B (both of which could be wrong choices) that he fails to note the possibility of the correct alternative C, D, or X. 

If problem solving is to be efficient, an individual must dis-

PSYCHOLOGY 

cover rational bases for choice, with the consequent diminution and elimination of chance selections. Were this not so, it would be just as sensible for a person to carry with him a coin, a die, or numbered chips to use whenever alternatives presented themselves. If there were only two, the flip of a coin could be used to determine the selection. If there were six possibilities, one could throw the die. If there were more, he could shake up the chips, using one for each possibility. Students have been observed answering true-false examinations by flipping a coin, but it is hardly conceivable that one could make a successful journey through life using no other methods than these chance throws. 

A problem that has been uppermost in the minds of experimenters in multiple-choice problems, using animals and human beings as subjects, has been to discover how progress is made from purely random selection to selection by rational cues. In such experiments, the subject is presented with a number of choices (from two to eleven have been used) offering no clue as to which one is correct. The subject must make some choice by chance. If it is the wrong one, he is not rewarded and may be punished. He may then make other selections and is informed that he has made the correct choice by the absence of punishment or by receiving a reward.

The problem to be solved is arranged arbitrarily by the experimenter and the subject of the experiment is given the task of discovering the solution. For example, the correct selection may always be the object at the left of all the others, the object at the right of all the others, the second object from the left, the second from the right and the second from the left alternately. [68] One type of apparatus for testing multiple choice behavior consists of a room into which the subject is admitted by a one way door and from which he can depart only by selecting one of four exactly similar doors, equidistant from his point of entry (see Fig. 166). These doors may be opened outwardly by a push upon them except when they are fastened by a catch that is not visible to the subject entering the compartment. The problem confronting the subject is to select the door that has been left unfastened. This he can ascertain only by actually pushing against the doors. He must search for the only unlocked door

PROBLEM SOLVING 

481 until he finds it. If the first one he tries is locked, he may go to another. Various problems can be set by means of such a device. 

A typical one required that the subject learn that he could not gain exit by means of the door which had been unlocked on the preceding trial. The experimenter had a schedule, determined by chance, by means of which he determined which door to keep unlocked for each trial. [16] 2 Ent. 3 4

FIG. 166.-Diagram of a mul tiple-choice apparatus. The subject, animal or human, is equidistant from each of the four exit doors after he has entered the apparatus and reached the point O. The experimenter determines in advance which exit is correct at any one trial, and it is the task of the subject to determine what is the basis for the selection of the correct exit.

The poorest type of reaction to such a choice problem is where the subject seems to profit little from his failure. For example, he may try a door, leave it, and then return and try it again without having tried any other door. Or, he may try repeatedly two or three of the doors without trying all of them. 

In other words, the subject does not seem to grasp the principle that, if an act fails, it may pay to try a different one instead of repeating the identical act which brought failure. A little higher, or more intelligent, type of response is where the animal returns to a door he had previously tried before having explored all the doors. For example, he might try the sequence, 4, 1, 4, 3, 4, 1, 4, 2. A still better type of response is to adopt a pattern of trying all the doors from left to right, or from right to left, regardless of the results of preceding trials. Still better is the method of trying each door only once but in irregular order. 

The best type of reaction for this particular problem is where the subject learns to avoid the door that had been left open on the preceding trial and to try each of the three other doors only

once and in irregular order. This highest type of selection was possible: only for human beings above eight years of age. Animals never advanced above the more random types of choice. [16] These results may be interpreted as indicating that the animal cannot learn a temporal sequence; whereas in problems involving spatial factors the animals are able to learn the solution and make the correct choices. 

The method of gradual correction. An uncritical observer is much inclined to credit an animal with "human" cleverness or with "reasoning power" when the animal demonstrates his ability to do such acts as to open a gate, to ring a doorbell, or to pull the cover off a table in order to get food that was on the table beyond his reach. The earliest workers in animal psychology argued against such an explanation and attempted to demonstrate that the ingenuity of animals in solving puzzles could be explained on a simpler basis than by attributing human intelligence to them. [45]

One of these investigators reported an experiment in teaching a dog a practical problem in mechanics. The ordinary dog usually has learned to pick up a stick in his mouth by grasping it near the middle. The stick is thus balanced and is easily carried without undue strain or dragging on the ground. In this experiment, the stick had a heavy ball on one end. To carry such a stick by grasping it midway between the two ends would result in an unbalanced and awkward act. When this stick was thrown, the dog, who had learned to carry sticks in the ordinary way, ran to retrieve it and, of course, took the middle of the stick in his mouth as he had been accustomed to do.. Again and again, the stick was thrown to be retrieved, and gradually the dog learned to seize the stick nearer and nearer to the heavy end until, after an hour or two of practice, he had learned to carry it in a well-balanced manner. [45] 

The early writers called such learning "trial-and-error" learning, contending that the dog learned to carry the stick correctly by making errors which were finally eliminated by chance. Probably a better name for the process would have been learning by gradual correction. This is actually what these experimenters had in mind, because, when they went on to explain what they meant by trial-and-error learning, they described it as a method

PROBLEM SOLVING 

483 whereby the performance became more and more perfect owing to the gradual discovery of the best way of doing the act. The dog, for example, gradually found the most comfortable way of carrying the stick and then adopted that method. 

This method of solving a problem is illustrated also by the parlor games commonly known as "hot and cold" and "tom-tom." 

In either game the subject is sent from the room and the other members of the party decide upon some act to be performed by him. Suppose he is to get on his knees before a certain girl. 

When he comes in he is told that he is getting hotter or colder (or the tom-tom is beaten more or less violently) according as he is approaching the required objective. As he walks toward the girl he gets his cue and continues; as he moves away he is told he is getting colder (or the tom-tom is beaten less loudly). He thus learns that he must stay at a certain spot but also knows that he must do something else. He may try various acts until finally, by permitting himself to vary his activity and at the same time correlate it with the signals, he does the right act. 

Solving a problem by the method of gradual correction depends upon three factors: 

1. Variability of performance. Learning by gradual correction certainly depends upon the fact that the learner does not perform in exactly the same manner each time. If performances were identical, there would be no basis for judging the relative value of one act as compared with another. For example, if the dog always grasped the stick at exactly the same place and in exactly the same manner each time he performed he would never learn to improve his technique. At the end of a thousand trials he would still be grasping the stick in the exact center. The fact that changes in performance occur is often due to extraneous influences. The dog may have had the carrying of ordinary sticks pretty well mastered and might have kept on in his accustomed manner were it not for the fact that a new type of stick was presented to him. The new element in any situation makes the old performance faulty. It is the changes in the challenging situations themselves that provide the need for solving problems. 

Variability of performance is absolutely essential because life itself is continually changing, because the old behavior does not fit.

PSYCHOLOGY 

2. Comparison of performances. Problem solution de pends upon some discernment of the relative merits of different acts. In many situations a person does not know what to do and his activities are purely random so far as progress toward any goal is concerned. If each of these random acts appeared to be as significant as any other act, the problem might be solved by accident, but each succeeding solution would also be accidental. 

When a series of variable acts is followed by a successful solution of the problem, the subject tends to make comparisons of his various acts and to interpret some acts as more related to the correct solution than were others. For example, if a cat in a pen effects his release when he has been clawing at a particular part of his cage, he will tend to stress pawing in the same general region rather than in some remote region. He has discerned some differential in value between different parts of the cage. 

After he has learned to favor á certain corner, he can then begin to compare the various acts which he does in that corner, and thus select one act in preference to those which are apparently unrelated to success. For example, if an animal raises his paw against a lever and gains food, whereas he gains nothing when he lowers his paw against the same lever, raising the paw against the lever will have preferential value. It should not be assumed that an animal makes a deliberate comparison and choice in his solution of such problems. Even many adult human beings do not weigh two alternate acts and choose after deliberate comparison. If gold is found more often in California than in the Ozarks, men will devote more energy to searching in California than in Arkansas although none of them can give any reason why there should be more gold in one place than in the other. In short, as a result of the fact that, while varying his performances, an individual observes that some acts are more often followed by nearness to an objective than are others, he comes to favor those performances which make his actions quicker, easier, more comfortable, or more successful; and he comes to avoid those which make his performance more unsatisfactory. 

3. The formulation of some principle or rule as a guide for future action. A rule based upon this method is faulty unless it is pursued further and is modified in such a manner that some

PROBLEM SOLVING 

485 This reason for the effectiveness of the behavior is discerned. is done by isolating all the component acts in a situation, holding all constant, or making them ineffective, while varying one and observing its relation to success or failure. This is the analytical procedure of the scientist, but it is seldom carried out by the majority of individuals, rarely by children, and probably never by animals. The ordinary individual accepts his majority experiences as rules for further guidance and ignores the exceptions. 

The scientist knows that the exception to the general expectation probably signifies some new or unusual factor and tracing its effect makes possible the formulation of rules that are more accurate than the "rule of thumb" which results from repetition of experiences with no attempt at critical analysis or interpretation. 

In other words, the method of gradual correction through repeated trials is merely the exploratory stage of problem solving. 

It is used primarily when situations are so strange that analytical procedures are impossible.

PROBLEM SOLVING BY HUMAN ADULTS 

The experiments on problem solving in animals have demonstrated clearly that there is no one way for solving problems in general. The challenged individual must let himself be guided by the problem in hand and adapt his reactions to the situation. This same principle holds with human problem solving. There are some general principles which will help in understanding some of the procedures that may be used, but we cannot expect to find any rigid form of thinking which holds for all situations. Thinking involves variability from fixed habits. The person who acts according to fixed patterns is not thinking. A number of experiments have been performed to illustrate this fact. 

Principles of puzzle solving by human adults. One experimenter used a large number of puzzles in an attempt to discover the procedures that human adults used in solving them. 

He kept time records and took elaborate notes on the comments of those individuals who were subjects in the experiments. [54] 

Some of the conditions affecting solutions are as follows:

Solution depends clearly upon variations in method. Such variations may be made unconsciously but those adopted consciously are most effective. The ease with which a subject is able

PSYCHOLOGY 

to vary his method depends strikingly upon his attitudes and upon. his ability to avoid explicit assumptions. 

1. Certain attitudes may interfere with problem solving. 

The two attitudes which are most detrimental to puzzle solving are sensitivity to the approval or disapproval of observers, and self-attentiveness. In the case of the attitude of sensitivity to, observation, the solver is more interested in watching the observer than in the puzzle. In the self-attentive attitude, the subject is more interested in himself than in the puzzle. The subject. with such an attitude becomes self-conscious, thinks he is on trial, and has his attention centered upon his own ineptness and ignorance. When success comes to such an individual, he is so elated that he fails to profit from it; when he does not succeed, he is so chagrined that he fails to study the significance of such a failure. 

It has been clearly demonstrated by experiment that problem solving depends upon the substitution of an objective attitude for the self-attentive attitude. Consciousness of the problem must be placed before self-consciousness. In 2. Assumptions may inhibit variation in method. many instances the first glance at a puzzle may result in some assumption which may be clearly formulated or may be a mere 8388802 FIG. 167.-A six-piece cross puzzle. A, the component pieces; B, the cross after the pieces are correctly assembled. vague attitude. No matter how it originates, such an assumption often tends to be maintained in spite of evidence that it is erroneous. The individual may begin to work on the wrong part of the puzzle, may turn it in the wrong direction; but the interesting part of the whole performance is the persistence with which the error is maintained.

PROBLEM SOLVING 

487 Solution is often the result of accident rather than of analysis. In puzzle solution, success is more often the result of random activity than of straightaway thinking and the consequent formulation of a thoroughgoing plan of action. Regardless of whether success comes as the result of anticipatory analysis, of pure accident, or of a combination of both,. subjects are able to benefit from such success. They often, for example, notice the final position of the parts of the puzzle just before the solution is

Solution is often aided by conscious analysis of the problem resulting from repeated successes or failures. By analytical procedures, (a) it is possible for subjects to develop hypotheses bearing on the problem; (b) to render these hypotheses more explicit with succeeding attempts and, at the same time, keep them flexible; (c) to keep up an active search for new points of view and to escape the tendency to be governed by fixed assumptions;

PSYCHOLOGY 

(d) to adopt some form of registration, such as naming or numbering, to avoid mere repetition; and (e) to evaluate different possibilities and to test the selected ones with a critical comparison of the results.

Effects of success and failure upon solution of puzzles. 

Near-success interferes with the ready acceptance of evidence of failure in a new situation. This is illustrated in experiments with reaching for objects with sticks. If the object is just beyond the reach of the animal when he is using the shorter of two sticks, the fact that he has almost solved the problem will tempt him to persist in his present activities rather than stimulate him to discard it for the other, longer, stick or to utilize the short stick to get the longer stick. A complete failure leads to a quicker change to other methods than does a near-success. Puzzles invariably incorporate this principle. They can almost be solved by some wrong method and this approximation to success tempts the solver to continue the wrong method. Since he is almost there, a little persistence should get him to the goal, he feels. 

Many experiments indicate that sheer persistence is not a valuable adjunct in problem solving. The person who cannot admit defeat is a poor problem solver because such an admission is the first step toward changing methods or looking for some novel approach. However, the admission of defeat must be a challenging element and, instead of leading to the abandonment of the problem, must incite to further effort. The clever thinker admits that he has been wrong in the past, but refuses to stay wrong. 

Insight. Other experiments show that a subject, whether an animal or a human being, acts differently when he has become aware of the nature of the trick involved in a puzzle. His activity becomes quicker and smoother. Besides, when confronted with a similar situation, he may hesitate before making any overt response, and then attack the problem in the correct manner. The onlooker, whether he is a psychologist or a layman, is certain that the subject knows what he is about. This knowing the solution has been called insight. It is indicated in the solution of mechanical puzzles in human beings (a) by a sudden drop in the learning curve, (b) by regularity of performance, and (c) by the report of the subjects that they knew how to work the puzzle. [54]

PROBLEM SOLVING 

489 The term "insight" has been used at times as the sudden apprehension of meaning without reference to previous experience, but this exclusion of previous experience as a step toward insight is gratuitous. [34]

The pendulum problem. The subject is given: two burette clamps, one table clamp, four pieces of chalk, two pieces of wire, eight pieces of lead tubing, and four poles. He is asked to construct with these materials two pendulums which can be swung so as to make chalk marks at specified points on the laboratory floor. The correct solution (as shown in the illustration in Fig. 

169) is as follows: The two pieces of wire are attached to the opposite ends of the poles. To the free end of each wire a piece of chalk is fastened by means of a burette clamp. The other two poles are clamped together with the table clamp so as to make a pole of the right length to stand on the floor and hold the single pole against the ceiling in the form of a T. The position of the pole on the ceiling and the length of each pendulum are then adjusted so that one piece of chalk touches each of the marks on the floor.

This problem was used in an experiment to determine the significance of preliminary instructions in problem solving. In order to accomplish this purpose the instructions that might be given were outlined and different groups were given different combinations of these directions. The directions were as follows: (a) A demonstration showing how to make a plumb line out of a cord, a clamp, and a pencil. (b) A demonstration showing how to make a long rod out of two short rods and a clamp. (c) A demonstration showing how to hold a bar against the vertical edge of a doorway by wedging against the bar's mid-point another bar which reached to the opposite vertical side of the door. (d) 

A direct hint for solving the problem as follows: "I should like to have you appreciate how simple this problem would be if we could just hang the pendulums from a nail in the ceiling. Of course, that is not a possible solution, but I just want you to appreciate how simple the problem would be if that were possible." 

This experiment showed clearly that preliminary instructions certainly help in problem solving. The amazing part was that only one person in sixty-two who were not given all the instructions outlined above could solve the problem. PSYCHOLOGY 

The subject was required to tie together the free ends of the two cords as they hung from the ceiling. Several solutions to this problem are possible: (1) One cord may be lengthened. (2) One cord may be tied to the chair and pulled over toward the other cord so that the subject can reach it when holding the second cord. (3) One cord may be pulled with a pole while the other cord is held. (4) The pliers or clamp may be tied to one cord and the cord swung as a pendulum, enabling the subject to hold the other cord and catch the pendulum as it swings toward him.

The experimenter decided in his own mind that only the fourth solution would be "correct." If the subject solved it by any of the first three methods, he was told to look for another solution.

In this experiment the subject was given ten minutes in which to solve the problem in the approved fashion by making one cord into a pendulum. If he failed, he was given the following hint: The experimenter brushed against one cord, thereby imparting to it a swinging motion. If the subject did not take this hint within a reasonable time, another hint was given: The experimenter gave the subject the pair of pliers and told him that with the aid of that tool alone the problem could be solved. 

The hints were effective in aiding the subjects to solve the problem. In many instances, the subject was not conscious that a hint was given, even denying afterward that he had received any hint, although he had obviously profited from it. When the solution did come to the subject, it was the same sort of quick transformation that takes place when the hidden figure in a puzzle picture becomes apparent. [8] 

Unwarranted assumptions interfere with problem solving. Whenever a new problem is presented, there is a tendency to get clues as to possible procedures from past experiences. This, of course, is absolutely essential and, in many instances, of value. 

In other situations the new problem has a similarity to previous problems; which fact merely detracts the attention of the solver from the essential element in the new problem. The similarity to some past problem leads the solver to make unnecessary and unwarranted assumptions, which keep him from getting the proper solution. [3]

The limitations placed upon our thinking by such unwarranted assumptions are the most potent source of failure in problem solving. Having tried a few of the procedures which suggest themselves to us, we assume that we have tried all the possibilities. Instead, failure should stimulate us to look beyond our limitations. [19]

MAZE LEARNING 

A maze is a device consisting of a system of pathways, with turns, branches, and blind alleys, through which the subject must Start

Platform 

Food box

FIG. 175.-Diagram of plan of ele vated maze for use with animals.

The parallel lines represent elevated runways along which the animal must travel from the starting box to the food box. The whole maze can be turned so that the animal cannot use objects in the room to guide his movements. (Adapted from Honzik, C. H., "The Sensory
