Monogr., 1936, 13, No. 64.) find his way from the starting point to the goal. In most mazes there is but one correct pathway, although some offer alternate routes. The kinds of paths vary with different mazes. In the enclosed-alley maze the pathways are between walls so that the subject cannot see any of the maze except the small portion in which he happens to be. In the elevated or open animal maze the passages are strips supported from beneath at such a height that the animal will not jump down and far enough apart to prevent jumping from one passage to another. In the elevated maze vision is unobstructed.

Any maze resolves itself into a series of choice points. The subject starts from the entrance and comes to branching pathways

PROBLEM SOLVING 

497 between which he must choose. If he makes the wrong choice he finds himself in a blind alley and must retrace his steps to the point where he made the wrong choice.

Different methods are used to indicate when a maze is learned and to measure progress in learning. The most widely accepted criterion for successful mastery of a maze is the standard of three successive perfect runs. Sometimes the standard is nine perfect runs in a sequence of ten runs; or the experimenter may set his own arbitrary standard. Measures of progress may be the total number of errors committed (that is, the number of entrances into blind alleys) before reaching the criterion of mastery, the total time consumed in attaining mastery, the total time or errors in a specified number of trials, or the errors per trial. The two latter methods enable the experimenter to construct a learning curve.

Sensory cues used by animals in maze running. Much experimentation has been done in the attempt to determine which sensory cues an animal uses in learning a maze. One method has been to make the different senses inoperative in turn to discover the effect of such deprivation on learning the maze. By such methods it has been found that blind animals, anosmic animals (that is, those deprived of the sense of smell), deafened animals, animals with their vibrissae removed, animals whose feet were anesthetized [63], and animals whose kinesthetic sensitivity was eliminated [37], could learn a maze about as readily as a normal animal. [31] In other words, each sense has been excluded without producing a marked disturbance of the ability to learn the maze. The conclusion that follows from this work is that maze learning is not dependent upon any one set of sensory cues, although the animal must have some sensory cues in order to learn the maze. [64] The animal uses what sensory apparatus he has. 1 This conclusion was checked by a different type of experiment, in which it was found that if a rat has learned a maze by the aid of visual cues and is then transferred to another maze of the same pattern, but one in which visual cues cannot function, the animal has to learn the maze all over again. Blind rats are at a disadvantage in mazes which depend primarily on vision but are not handicapped by blindness when placed in the enclosed type

PSYCHOLOGY 

of maze where they can use other sensory cues than vision. These experiments confirm the previous conclusion; namely, that no one sense furnishes any indispensable cues. The animal uses the cues which he is most accustomed to use and if these are not permitted to function he does the best he can by utilizing cues from another sensory field. [65, p. 129]

Importance of goal in maze learning. There are a number of experiments which indicate that the paramount problem for the animal is to get from the starting point to the goal. The experimenter may see the animal learning the maze but from the point of view of the animal he is learning to reach the goal as expeditiously as possible. He is hungry and wants the food Food

[23] 

The conclusion from these experiments seems to be that animals learn maze problems not by mastering certain fixed motor acts or certain sequences of acts, but by spatial and directional cues. Such cues are in the nature of guides toward some goal. 

When the cues are clearly apparent, learning is easy for the animal; when they are absent, the animal cannot learn; and when they are confused, the animal has difficulty. Spatial and directional factors make maze learning possible for animals. If solution depends upon temporal sequences or upon verbal cues, the animal finds himself unable to solve the problem. 

Explanations of animal maze learning. Various theories have been advanced to explain animal maze learning. One writer suggests that the animal puts together in one act what has been learned at different times. [41] Another writer argues that the animal forms hypotheses in his early trials and then discards or corrects these hypotheses on the basis of further trials. [35] 

Another believes that the choices in a maze are reactions to cues which are essentially symbolic substitutes for the postural pointing reactions which animals show in delayed reaction (see page 

477) experiments. [25] These are all probably partial truths; they are correct as far as they go but they do not explain adequately the whole procedure of mastering the maze. 

There are probably three processes in learning a maze: (1) getting acquainted with the maze in a general way, including

PROBLEM SOLVING 

501 the recognition that the problem required is to proceed from the starting box to the goal; (2) learning a path within the multiplicity of paths offered which will enable the animal to reach the goal; and (3) developing some skill in following this pathway efficiently, with the elimination of errors that might have been present in the earlier runs. [65, p. 137]

These steps correspond roughly with what is observed in any form of problem solving. There is (a) a general orientation to the problem in hand; (b) the working out of some sort of S

FIG. 179.-A typical stylus maze. (From J. C. Warden, J. exper. Psychol., 1924, 7, 101.) crude solution; and (c) the improvement of this solution by the elimination of irrelevant factors on the basis of repeated trials. 

A comparison of human maze learning with animal maze learning. Human beings have been given the problem of solving mazes which are quite similar to animal mazes. Some human mazes are merely enlargements of the enclosed-alley type. 

Other human mazes, such as the one illustrated in Fig. 179, have depressions which are covered and which must be traversed by a stylus held in the hand of the subject. The finger maze illustrated in Fig. 180 has elevated ridges along the top of which the subject moves his finger. In some human mazes the major portion of the maze is hidden from view, in some the subject

Some valuable principles have been secured by comparing human and animal maze learning. Human beings profit more quickly from errors, they adopt superior modes of attack, they orient themselves to new problems more quickly and accurately, and they are able to maintain interest on the essential problem more persistently. 

Maze learning is easier for those individuals who profit most quickly from their errors. An experiment was conducted by making an enlargement of a maze that had been used for animals. Blindfolded adults and children were taught to run this maze and their performance compared with that of rats. It took all three groups (the blindfolded adults, children, and rats) practically the same number of trials to learn the maze, but adult human beings excelled in speed and made many fewer errors. In the first trial the rats averaged seven entrances to each blind alley, the children averaged four, and the blindfolded human adults averaged only one. There is a striking difference in the quickness with which the different groups profited from their mistakes. 

This is apparently an important factor in problem solving. The most intelligent individual quickly profits from false moves and erroneous cues. The child, the animal, or the dull adult has to repeat an error more frequently before he discovers its significance and is able to eliminate it. [20]

PROBLEM SOLVING 

503 S

Year XII FIG. 181.-Pencil mazes. The subject is permitted to see the whole maze as he threads his way from S with a pencil. 

Success is definitely related to the mode of attack upon the problem. Human individuals show marked differences in their approach to maze problems. [46] Furthermore, the same individual will show a greater tendency to change his method during an attempt than will an animal. This variability of performance is an asset; it enables the individual to compare methods and to select those most suitable for the problem at hand. [29] 

When naïve human subjects were permitted to choose their own methods for running a maze their methods fell roughly into three main groups: (1) the word reaction method, in which the subject named his turns left-right; (2) the visual imagery method, in which the subject attempted to visualize the maze pattern; and (3) the motor method, where the subject permitted himself to be guided by motor cues. [62] 

While the majority of subjects used more than one method in the course of their trials, most of them favored one method or the other. [30] The greater number (42 per cent) favored the word reaction method, the fewest (28 per cent) the motor method, while the visual imagery method stood between the two (30 per cent). [62] The most efficient method was the word reaction method. It required less than one-quarter as many trials as did the motor reaction method, and about one-half as many trials as the imagery method. Human subjects vary their pro-

PSYCHOLOGY 

cedure during the course of their work, and the more alert ones tend to select the more efficient methods. 

Quick and accurate orientation to a problem helps in its solution. When human subjects were given the task of going blindfolded through a large outdoor maze, they quickly oriented themselves, usually during the first trial. They learned the relation of the entrance to the exit, the general course of the true path, and became familiar with certain of the paths so as to get specific cues. [2] 

There seems little doubt that an important element in solving any kind of problem is the ability to discern clearly just what the problem is. If an individual waits for someone to explain exactly what should be done, it is apparent that someone else has previously solved the problem. The sagacious individual does not wait to be told what a problem is; he discerns it himself from the nature of the situation; and while his less astute comrade is. still groping, he is on his way toward solving it. 

Attention to the central problem should overshadow interest in irrelevant details, distractions, and failure. This ability to maintain the central problem in spite of changes in certain aspects of the problem was demonstrated in an experiment in which human subjects were made to solve various forms of mazes. 

After the blindfolded subjects had learned their way through the large maze, they were given the following problems while still blindfolded: (a) they were required to trace their way with a stylus through a small maze of the same pattern; (b) the maze was rotated through 90° and 180°; (c) they were required to retrace their pathway from the exit to the entrance; (d) they were required to trace it with their left hands after they had done it with their right hands. [38] The subjects adjusted themselves to all these changes with surprising rapidity, showing that they had the ability to maintain the central problem and to utilize that knowledge to solve what might otherwise have been a relatively new problem. [46]

It is an essential element in problem solving to get the proper balance between this ability to avoid irrelevant distractions or to follow circumscribed channels and, at the same time, to grasp any tiny cue that relates to the problem at hand. Poor thinkers may make an error in either direction: (a) they may

PROBLEM SOLVING 

505 be so eager to let no clue slip that they become lost in a confusion of details or (b) they may be so anxious to retain the central problem that they fail to see the means of solution even though these should be clearly apparent.

Procedures involved in finding the principle of a maze. 

The derivation of rules, principles, or laws from a series of concrete experiences (the process of induction) is an important element in human thinking and reasoning. Human maze learning has been used to study the procedures by means of which such generalizations are effected.

The importance of language cues to assist an individual is demonstrated clearly in the solving of a temporal maze, where spatial factors are entirely eliminated. In the temporal maze the alleys are changed with succeeding runs so that the animal may be required to make a right turn at a certain point on one run and then to make a left turn at the same point on a later run. 

Where the animal has to depend upon the sequence of his movements instead of spatial orientation, he has trouble. [33] 

The temporal maze is built upon the principle of a double square (see Fig. 182) with gates that can easily be changed from trial to trial in such a manner that the animal cannot tell how they are arranged until he has completed a run through an alley involving two turns. For example, in the first trial he may be required to go to the left to get food but on the next trial the gate at the end of the alley to the left is closed and he finds he should have gone to the right. He must learn the sequence and orientation in spatial terms does no good. All the choices are made at the same point, whereas in the ordinary maze the choices are made at different places. The rat has great difficulty in learning such a simple sequence as right, left, right, left (RLRL), and finds it almost impossible to learn the sequence RRLL. [28] [28] In contrast with this difficulty in the lower animals, children and human adults find such a maze relatively easy. They soon catch on to the nature of the problem, even though they have been given no verbal instructions, and formulate their solution in words: right, left, right, left; or twice to the right and twice to the left; or three times to the right and twice to the left. With verbal interpretations the cues become very simple. [15]

INDUCTIVE REASONING 

We now have the task of considering in more detail those forms of problem solving where the great proportion of work is internal and the results of which manifest themselves in a final act that is precise and correct. 

The use of language in problem solving. We have already seen how the use of words can be of assistance in problem solving. In working on a temporal maze, the solver can formulate the succession of turns as right, right, left, left, right, right, left, left, etc. In multiple-choice problems, he can formulate the problem in words such as: "Always take the smaller door." "Never select the door which led to food on the previous trial." 

In solving more intricate problems, work is facilitated if accurate meanings and definitions can be formulated to guide the thinker. 

Abstractions. An abstract quality is some attribute which is found to be common to a series of experiences. For example,

PROBLEM SOLVING 

509 by observing iron, copper, and silver it may be observed that they all have the common quality of hardness. Hardness may then be considered without reference to any of the other characteristics of the three separate substances in which it was observed; it can be thought of as a separate entity although it has never been observed in isolation. A clear-cut abstraction helps to guide us in our behavior. For example, we treat hard objects differently from the manner in which we treat soft objects. 

Formulation of definitions. Clear thinking depends upon definitions which are so clear that they prevent misunderstanding between persons who use them, so precise that they enable users to be consistent, so fixed that they prevent changes in their meaning during the process of thinking.

The ability to define varies with intellectual maturation. [57] The very young child defines with increasing skill, passing through the following stages: (1) by pointing to an object; (2) by repeating the name of an object (“A chair is a chair"); (3) by giving the use of the object (“A chair is to sit on"); (4) by describing the object in some detail as to its form, size, color, or appearance; and finally (5) by telling to what class the object belongs or its relation to other classes of objects. 

Formulating a mature definition consists of showing the relation of a less inclusive group of objects (called the species) to a more inclusive group of objects (called the genus). In the simplest type of definition the mere relation of genus and species may be accepted as satisfactory. For example, it may be stated that man is an animal. This definition leaves something to be desired for it does not differentiate between man and the other species of animals. A good definition requires not merely the statement of a more inclusive group into which the word to be defined may be placed, but it requires as well some distinguishing characteristics (differentia) between the object to be defined and other members of the genus into which it is placed by definition. 

Thus, a man is an animal, but in addition, a man is an animal belonging to the class of primates, and distinguished in behavior by language, civilization, and the elaborate use of tools. 

In order to be considered a first-class definition, the following requirements should be fulfilled: (1) the definition should be more than a mere synonym of the word defined. (2) The defi-

PSYCHOLOGY 

nition should not be in terms less familiar than the term defined. (3) The differentia should clearly distinguish the term defined from all other species of the same genus. (4) The definition should be in positive terms, that is, it should indicate what the word is, not merely what it is not. 

Inductive and deductive reasoning. Induction, or generalizing, is the process of reasoning from particular to general. 

It is the development of a hypothesis, theory, principle, or law after discerning certain uniformities or common factors in successive situations. Inductive reasoning is often contrasted with deductive reasoning, which is reasoning from general premises or propositions to more concrete and specific applications of the general rule.

The distinction between induction and deduction lies largely in the nature of the problems to be solved. In an inductive problem the given factors are specimens, and from these individual specimens of objects, acts, or situations the thinker endeavors to formulate a definition, some working principle, or some rule to guide him in dealing with those specimens. For example, a child may have learned that whenever he has put his hand on a hot stove he has been burned. From these experiences he derives the general rule that a hot stove will burn one's hand. Such a rule is of service to him; for he refrains from touching hot stoves, and does not burn his hand.

Deductive reasoning, on the other hand, attempts to discover the implications of certain given propositions. For example: 

If Bill is at the right of Paul, and if Paul is at the right of Sam, what can be said as to the relative positions of Bill and Sam? 

In actual thinking processes, induction and deduction are utilized in conjunction, the one tending to reinforce and support the other.

The development of class concepts. The general plan of experiments directed toward an understanding of the development of class concepts is to present the subject with a number of specific examples of a class, giving him the name of the concept at the same time; after which he is asked either to define the concept or to recognize whether other succeeding illustrations should or should not be included in that same class. 

For example, suppose a dar is a circle with two dots, the

511 one dot being inside the circle and the other dot outside the circle. The experimenter shows (Fig. 185) various illustrations of the class dar and after the subject has examined them he is asked to tell what a dax is. If he cannot define the concept correctly he is shown further illustrations of dar interspersed with others which are not dax. 

All of the figures above are DAX

With a number of concepts studied in this manner, it has been found: (a) Individuals may learn concepts with sufficient accuracy to identify them and to distinguish them from objects which should not be included in the class and still not be able to define the concept with accuracy. (b) The process of concept formation involves grouping of objects. Sometimes the basis for such grouping is vague even though it may correspond closely with the definitions arbitrarily given by the examiner but not revealed to the subject. (c) The clearing up of a vague concept involves a tentative definition and the corroboration, rejection, or correction of that tentative definition with succeeding experiences. [13, 55]

PSYCHOLOGY 

Concept formation involves not only the statement of essential qualities but the exclusion of irrelevant qualities. This is brought out in a test of concept formation conducted about as 

The subject has spread before him 22 blocks. Each block has a name but the names are turned down so that the subject cannot see them. (a) There are six flat blocks with relatively large top surfaces of varied shapes and colors, and these are named bik. (b) There are six flat blocks with relative small top surfaces of varied shapes and colors, and these are named cev. (c) There are five tall blocks with relatively large top surfaces of varied shapes and colors, and these are named lag. (d) There are five tall blocks with relatively small top surfaces of varied shapes and colors, and these are named mur. 

The subject is told that there are four different kinds of blocks, each with a distinctive name, and he is to sort them out into four different groups according to these four kinds. His task is to discover that the bases of distinction are height and top-surface area and that shape and color are irrelevant. 

In an experiment where the class concept was a grouping of lines buried in other lines so as to give the subject the impression that he was looking at a Chinese character, it was found that the subjects experienced great difficulty in discerning the common element involved. They would experience a vague feeling of familiarity, discern some family resemblance, but could not identify the specific lines upon which this resemblance was based. [24] 

When confronted with a novel object, two general methods are used in classifying that object. One method is to assimilate it to some class of objects with which one is already familiar. 

The second is to analyze the new object into parts and then to fit the parts into separate categories. The first is the method of everyday experience; it is quicker and not so accurate in its results. The latter analytical method is more dependable and is the method which scientific thinkers attempt to use. [5] 

Classification, then, depends primarily upon a clear delineation of the essential qualities which distinguish a class of objects, with an exclusion of those qualities which are irrelevant. In addition, classification should adhere to the following rules:

PROBLEM SOLVING 

513 (a) Some controlling principle should be followed in a system of classification. For example, it is faulty to classify books into quartos, octavos, duodecimos, and paper covered. (b) The species into which the genus is divided must not overlap but must be mutually exclusive. For example, men cannot be divided into good and bad because goodness and badness are not mutually exclusive and men overlap in the possession of these traits. (c) The constituent species in a classification must, taken together, exhaust the genus; no part of the genus must be omitted in the classification. If all the members of the genus cannot be named specifically, there can be created a miscellaneous group. [4] It should be apparent from the study of concept formation and the rules for correct classification that the primary need is to strive continually for greater precision in meaning. It is failure in this respect that leads to much fuzzy thinking. 

The process of formulating a principle. Usually, in the first contact with a problem whose solution is sought, the puzzled individual does not even know in what area the solution lies. 

It takes more than one contact to formulate any generalization whatsoever. Succeeding experiences are different but are not totally new; they combine some new elements with elements which have been present in preceding experiences. As life rolls on, the animal or human being uses the familiar aspects of his environment as cues to guide him. For example, after an animal has learned to escape from a puzzle box by turning a certain button, he will restrict his activities to the location of the button in succeeding attempts and not scratch at all parts of the box indiscriminately. He has isolated a certain part of the box for his activities. Furthermore, after he has learned to escape from one box by turning a button, he will tend to isolate a button for his attention when placed in a new puzzle box, provided there is a button for him to manipulate. If the solution of this new puzzle involves the manipulation of the button, his past experience may help him even though he may have to do something different with the button in this new box. If, on the other hand, the new box must be solved by raising a latch in a different part of the box, his past experience will prove a handicap. He will take the button as a cue, but it will be a false one. In some cases generalization may help in solving problems; in others it may

PSYCHOLOGY 

interfere. The puzzled individual may profit from generalizing from past experiences, but he cannot take his generalizations too rigidly or he may be acting upon some irrelevant or misleading factor. If it is a puzzle, he manipulates it in his search for a clue; if it is a definition, he searches for identical elements in a series of experiences; if it is a rule, he searches for essential sequences.

One experimenter studied the method of deriving a general principle by means of a game played with matches. Seven matches are presented and the rules of the game are stated about as follows: Each player is to take, alternately, either one or two matches and to manipulate his plays so that he will always take the last match. Sometimes a subject can learn to win at this game without being able to formulate any law or principle which enables him to win. If he watches his plays he may be able to formulate the rule, which is: To win always draw enough matches to leave your opponent a number that is a multiple of three. 

If your opponent is left with three matches, he may draw one and leave two, in which case you may take them and win; or he may draw two and leave one, in which case you take the one and win. When only seven matches are used, a learner may formulate the partial rule that it is always desirable to leave your opponent with the last three matches, but when given a larger number to begin with-say ten or thirteen-he may find that he cannot manipulate matters so as to accomplish this end unless the formulated rule is applied early in the series of plays. In order to help him learn the rule, the game may be varied by using ten, eleven, thirteen, or any number of matches which is not a multiple of three. [48] 

Such a generalization may be reached in various ways: (a) One may be told the rule as the reader has here been told. 

All he needs to do is to verify it. (b) It may come as a sort of guess, which is found to hold upon experimentation. (c) It may come partially and be corrected with succeeding trials. (d) It may come as the result of analysis and comparison of one trial with another, the learner varying his procedure and studying the effects of such variation. Individuals vary greatly in their insight into the significance of the generalization or the ability to state it

PROBLEM SOLVING. 

515 clearly. Some learners become proficient in learning to play the game but are unable to state the rule. 

Imperfect generalizations. The greatest enemy to a wholesome use of the inductive method is the temptation to make hasty generalizations. A hasty generalization is the fallacy of assuming that a result has wider or more dependable application than is justified from the information or experiences at hand. 

Hasty generalizations take various forms: 

False analogy. A belief should not be accepted upon the basis of some superficial resemblance between the situation in question and some known principle. Many superstitions are based on false analogies. For example, when the moon is waxing the crops should grow likewise. We judge a man to be tenacious because he has a broad jaw like a bulldog. One striking illustration will convince the ordinary man of a proposition in spite of a great amount of definite evidence that the proposition is false. 

When this method is applied to our judgment of individuals, it has been called the "halo" effect. When we like a man because he has favored us, this fact is likely to color our estimate of his intelligence, his honesty, or even his sanity. 

When you wish to convince a person, use illustrations and analogies; when you wish to ascertain the truth, avoid them. 

Giving weight to accidental concomitance. Because the stop light always turns red when your car is approaching it is no evidence that the approach of your car causes the light to change, as some disgruntled souls have been heard to complain. 

Nevertheless, there are devices to cause the light to change to green when a car approaches an intersection. How can one tell whether his approach is really a factor in the change of the light or an accidental circumstance? If he observed the light over a long period of time and noticed that it never changed unless a car approached and that it always did change whenever a car approached, he might assume that there was some connection. 

Because the street lights come on in a city exactly ten minutes after sunset is no reason to assume that the movement of the sun turns on the lights.

Extending the reach of generalizations. Suppose that one, by prolonged observation, came to the conclusion that a go light

PSYCHOLOGY 

came on upon the approach of a car. 

He could make the generalization that that particular light responded to the approach of a car, but he would not be warranted in assuming that all go lights were operated by oncoming cars. It is told that when the king of Siam heard a Dutch traveler tell how the water in Holland became so hard that people could walk across it, he exclaimed: "Now I know you are lying." A law may be general in one set of circumstances and still not hold in others. Can you imagine the comment of a man a hundred years ago were he told that a man would be able to sit in his study and talk in a whisper and yet be heard by millions of people at distances ranging up to thousands of miles?

The tendency to generalize instances because of their number alone. The acceptance of testimonials is evidence of this fallacy. It is all too common to find the tendency to generalize on insufficient evidence, even from a single instance. In escaping from this tendency it is easy to fall into the related error of thinking that the accumulation of illustrations provides sound evidence for the truth of a proposition. A million persons might testify that after anointing with bear grease the knife by means of which they cut themselves, the wound healed. Would this prove, or be the slightest evidence, that the anointing of the knife was directly related with the healing of the wound? Even though the million testimonials included those of intelligent and famous men, the generalization would still be invalid. 

Reasons for imperfect generalizations. A great many factors enter into the tendency to maintain false generalizations. 

To mention a few of them briefly: (a) We dislike to remain in suspense. Once having found some satisfactory way of meeting one situation, we tend to utilize it quickly rather than remain in suspense while hunting something better. (b) Once we have accepted a position, personal pride makes us tend to retain it even though we may have severe doubts as to the wisdom of so doing. (c) A firmly established emotional prejudice will tend to crush any factors which might make this prejudice doubtful. (d) Hero worship of others who maintain a position may make us slow to accept evidence which runs counter to their views. (e) Mental laziness or inertia. [4]

PROBLEM SOLVING 

517 

DEDUCTIVE REASONING 

Deductive reasoning should normally take the form of a syllogism; although this form is often hidden in language in such a way as to disguise it.

Form of the syllogism. The syllogism consists of three propositions, two of which are premises and one of which is the conclusion. Each of these three propositions contains two terms connected by a copula-is or are. In the whole syllogism there can be only three terms. The conclusion must contain one term from each of the premises and must omit the term common to each of the premises. This term which is present in each of the premises and is absent from the conclusion is called the middle term. This middle term is the link between the two premises and must be used in strictly the same sense in both premises, otherwise the conclusion will not be valid. 

An illustration of a syllogism is the following: 

All books are made of paper. (first premise) 

The Bible is a book. (second premise)

The Bible is made of paper. (conclusion) 

While the logic in this syllogism is valid, the conclusion is not true necessarily because one of the premises is not true; not all books are made of paper. The logical soundness of a syllogism may be correct, but, if the premises are not true, the conclusion may not be true. Each premise should be considered as an if proposition. If all books are made of paper; and if the Bible is a book; then, but only under the conditions stated in the premises, the Bible is made of paper. When this qualifying if is kept in mind, the thinker will be reminded that his conclusion is also a qualified statement. A conclusion can be considered true only when the premises are true and the reasoning valid. 

Significance of relationships. The deductions made in syllogistic reasoning depend upon relationships. When we know the relationship of term A to a middle term and, at the same time, the relationship of term B to the same middle term, what do these facts tell us (if anything) about the relationship between terms A and B? The best way to think clearly is to reduce the propositions in any syllogism to some diagram which clearly indicates the relationships involved.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Linear relationships.

Some syllogisms can be reduced to simple linear relationships. [6] 

For example: 

If Bob is heavier than Fred; and if Dick is lighter than Fred; then is Dick heavier or lighter than Bob? 

Weight can be represented in linear terms. If we conceive the lightest to be on top and the heaviest to be on the bottom, we have the following arrangement: 

Dick-lighter than Fred 

Fred-middle term 

Bob-heavier than Fred

The conclusion (Dick is lighter than Bob) is clearly seen from inspection of the arrangement of the three. Any propositions that can be reduced to a straight-line relationship could be handled in a similar manner. East-west, right-left, inner-outer, and earlier-later can all be represented in this manner and propositions based on such relationships clearly tested. 

Suppose we have the two propositions: 

If Bob is heavier than Fred; and if Dick is heavier than Fred; then is Dick heavier or lighter than Bob? 

An attempt to reduce these propositions to a diagram will show that nothing can be deduced because both terms (Dick and Bob) vary in the same direction from the middle term (Fred), and nothing is said to indicate which varies more. 

Relations of inclusion and exclusion. Relations of inclu sion and exclusion are best symbolized by circles to represent the terms of the propositions. If we let X equal one term and Y equal another, it is possible to have them related in the different ways represented in Fig. 186.

By reference to the diagrams in Fig. 186, any proposition depending upon the relation of inclusion and exclusion may be reduced to graphic form. Such a representation of the syllogism usually reveals immediately which conclusions are valid and which are invalid.

4. When the premises are both particular-negative propositions, no conclusion can be drawn about the relation of X and Z. 

For example:

This syllogism may be represented equally well by the same three diagrams shown in Fig. 190. Nevertheless, 70 per cent of those tested gave the conclusion: Some X's are not Z's. 

A great deal that passes for reasoning is not reasoning at all, but merely a foreknowledge that a conclusion is wrong or right.

523 

For example: 

If: Some men are liars; and 

Some women are liars: then 

How many men are women? 

Everybody would quickly answer: No men are women.

However, this is not the result of his reasoning. The premises are both particular-affirmative propositions, which, when reduced to abstract terms, were answered in a way equivalent to saying that "some men are women" by 90 per cent of the individuals tested. As shown in Fig. 190, it is no more logical to say that "no men are women" than to say that "some men are women.' 

It seems apparent from these experiments that accurate syllogistic reasoning demands some method for escaping from atmosphere effects and extraneous influences. 99 1. Where the material is couched in ambiguous language, it must be reduced to terms which can be rigidly defined and these definitions must be maintained throughout the logical processes. 

2. The propositions should be clearly stated and should be reduced to syllogistic form. If the premises are not true, no conclusions deduced from them can be valid. 

3. The syllogism should never contain more than three terms. 

4. The relations involved should be clearly recognized. This is best accomplished by means of symbolic diagrams.

Chapter XVII  

P TO this point our study has been analytical. We have isolated successively different aspects of the psychological individual and studied each feature to the exclusion of others. 

Now we plan to study the individual as a whole. 

COMPLEXITY OF THE PSYCHOLOGICAL INDIVIDUAL 

We are immediately struck with the difficulties involved in undertaking the study of the entire individual. No two persons are exactly alike and the same person changes from day to day. 

Shall we study the areas in which some similarity exists between individuals and ignore the points of difference? Shall we hunt for the more stable factors and ignore the changing ones? Or shall we go to the opposite extreme and take cognizance only of each individual as an entity and stress his unique and changing characteristics? We might venture the statement that the pure scientist would prefer to hunt for common elements and the pure artist would prefer to stress individual differences or unique characteristics. On the other hand, no one is either a pure scientist or a pure artist; each student will have his own preferences. 

These personality preferences in those who have studied human nature have kept the study of psychology from becoming stereotyped.

This diversity of interest with its consequent multiplicity of approaches does no damage so long as the student realizes that he is driven by his own interests rather than by objective facts. Everyone likes to consider himself a "student of human nature." Let anyone study who cares to do so; but let each 530

beware of the temptation to believe he has the last word. Each one is almost sure to emphasize one particular aspect, to favor some particular method, and to give too much weight to congenial conclusions.

METHODS FOR STUDYING INDIVIDUALITY 

This diversity of interests in people is well illustrated when one begins to outline the different ways in which people may be studied. One author lists fifty definitions for personality, and has listed fifty-two methods for studying personality. [1] 

Another author, in a fairly comprehensive outline for personality study, lists for investigation 11 main items or areas of study, 79 subitems under these 11 main ones, 304 subsubitems, and 486 subsubsubitems: 880 in all. No one man would be competent to secure all the information contained in this outline for any one individual. [14]

The complexity of our study will be apparent by a reading of the following list of methods, all of which have been seriously utilized to study individuality: [1] 

1. Influence upon the individual of the cultural setting in which he lives. For example, two young men may join the 

Communist party. Superficially, it is the same act by both; but the unique significance of each man's act may only appear when it is learned that one man is the son of a wealthy banker, while the other is the son of a disgruntled laborer. 

2. Language analysis. Individual analysis may be sought by a study of the language preferences of the person, or by the size of his vocabulary. General analyses may be made by a study of the words in a language which are used to describe personal traits, 'by a study of proverbs, by an analysis of the figures of speech, or the like. It has been assumed that if the language of a people contains a word descriptive of individuality there must be some trait to correspond to that word. One study of the English language found 17,953 terms descriptive of personality or behavior. 

3. Hereditary background. 

4. Family situations in which individual was raised. These include the study of the interaction with the personalities of parents, siblings, and other persons in the home. 

5. Biochemical factors. These include psychogalvanic re-

PSYCHOLOGY 

flexes, circulatory peculiarities, blood composition, brain waves, and endocrine make-up. 

6. Constitutional factors. Such characteristics as weight, skin texture, coloring, bodily proportions, and the like play a part in individual development. 

7. Socioeconomic status. 

8. Play history. 

9. Work habits. These include jobs held, length of tenure, and circumstances surrounding changes. 

10. School history. 

11. Response to other people. Very important are the reactions of a person to others when he has been irritated, thwarted, punished, rewarded, cheated, or loved by them. 

12. Response to difficulties. Comparisons of responses to social, economic, physical, moral, or romantic problems are often illuminating. 

13. Diaries. Whether or not a person enjoys keeping a diary may be significant, as would be an analysis of the contents of a diary.. 

14. Analysis of correspondence. 

15. Analysis of written or oral themes. 

16. Analysis of expressive behavior of the individual. Individual study may be approached by an analysis of facial expression, mannerisms, dress, drawings, speech, writing, emotional behavior, postures, and the like. 

17. Rating scales. Hosts of rating scales have been devised. 

These include ratings of character, conduct, good citizenship, executive ability, teaching ability, leadership, and a host of other so-called personality traits. 

18. Psychograph methods. Various traits may be isolated, and the person scored by some means on each of these traits. The psychograph is a graphic representation of these scores. 

19. Tests. In recent years much effort has been devoted to the development of a great variety of personality tests. 

20. Questionnaires. 

21. Behavior scales. 

22. Attitude scales. 

23. Statistical analysis. The most recent of these is the method of factor analysis.

24. Taking time samples of an individual's life. 

25. Behavior in a miniature representation of a real life situation. 

26. Trap situations. On the theory that an individual will reveal his true characteristics better when in a challenging situation than when he is in complete control of himself, many experiments have been conducted where the unexpected happens or the subject finds himself confronted by an apparent danger. This method has been used, for example, in studying such characteristics as honesty and loyalty. 

27. Psychoanalysis. 

28. Dream interpretation. This would include interpretation of both night and day dreams. 

29. Analyzing the significance of slips of speech, forgetting, losing objects, and the like. 

30. Free association. 

31. Study of involuntary movements. 

32. Hypnosis. 

33. Interviews. 

34. Biographies. 

35. Complete case studies.

Having read this array of methods, the student should be thoroughly bewildered at the complexity of the problem of individual analysis. This is as it should be. Any satisfyingly simple procedure is sure to tempt one to accept it, and this outline has been given to make clear the absurdity of any claim for the adequacy of a simple system.

The student should also be on his guard against the opposite error; namely, that of saying that he has an intuitive understanding of "human nature" which he does not wish to mar by any analysis of the components of individuality. A good artist is never injured by a study of techniques, whereas a potentially good one may remain a dauber if he refrains from detailed study. 

Psychology is the scientific study of the individual; the artistic study of the individual may involve the application of all that psychology has to teach. There is a place for the abstract scientist; there is a place for the artist; but there is little place for the individual who tries to take a short cut and to make personality analyses with no basis for his work. [16]

PSYCHOLOGY HISTORICAL SURVEY OF THE SEARCH FOR COMMON FACTORS 

The study of individuality has a long and interesting history. 

A review of its course will reveal an incessant search for common factors. There is an admission by all that the differences between persons are extremely striking; but it does not satisfy the inquiring mind to stop with the assertion that no two persons are alike. 

People are different, but there must be common factors. One group of students will seem to work out certain common elements and classify people on those bases; the next group will show that the classification is untenable and propose a new classification. 

Historically, we have a sequence of fads in personality analysis and the present era is no exception. [1] 

The doctrine of humors. The oldest classification of personalities of which we have any record comes from the Greeks. 

It ascribed the peculiarities of temperament to the "humors," or fluids, in the body. Persons were classified according to the predominance of these fluids. A person with a large supply of blood was sanguine; one with a large supply of black bile was melancholic; one with a large supply of yellow bile was choleric; while one with a large amount of phlegm was phlegmatic. We still use the descriptive names to designate certain temperaments; but the relation of these to the original "humors" is thoroughly discredited. According to present-day usage, a sanguine person is one who is confident, lighthearted, vivacious, and enthusiastic. 

A melancholy person is one who is habitually low-spirited, downcast, and dejected. A choleric person is irascible, fiery, hightempered, and easily provoked to anger. A phlegmatic person is cool, calm, composed, and emotionally indifferent. 

The theory of body types. Men have long thought that general body build was related in some way to mental characteristics. The fat man was supposed to be happy, successful, and aggressive. The lean man was unhappy, dissatisfied, and dangerous.

Rather recently, attempts have been made to construct a rather comprehensive classification on the basis of body build. 

People are divided into four groups: [16] 

1. The asthenic (or tall, slender, and weak person) is temperamentally shut-in, idealistic, romantic, silent, unhappy; a retir-

ing person who tends to retreat into his own emotions instead of meeting life in an objective or heroic manner. 

2. The pyknic (or short, heavy, small-boned, and corpulent individual) is likely to be genial, easy to meet, happy, goodnatured, objective, and realistic. 

3. The athletic (or tall, muscular individual) is active, fond of physical activity, but less happy about his adjustments than the pyknic individual. 

4. The dysplastic (or physically deformed person) tends to be odd, peculiar in disposition, with a freakish temperament which often is appropriate to his deformity. 

While it may be possible arbitrarily to classify people into these four types, extensive studies of the relationship between these physical characteristics and the personality ascribed to them have shown that such a classification is purely conjectural. Where differences in personality are found connected with physical types, these may be explained on the basis of differences in experiences which go naturally with physical build. For example, boys who have solid and substantial physiques (whether pyknic or athletic) tend to develop personalities that are aggressive and realistic, partly because such a physique disposes them to act in an aggressive manner. 

Personality classifications based on endocrine factors.

The most clear-cut classification of this sort is into sexes: male and female. We are all familiar with the so-called secondary sex characteristics, such as the pitch of the voice, the distribution of hair, the bony structure, and the like. That these characteristics are directly related to the sex glands has been demonstrated by extirpation and transplantation experiments in animals. 

However, some of the traits that we recognize as being different in men and women are not clearly and arbitrarily dependent upon the endocrine glands. Many recognized sexual traits depend upon differences in social treatment. With no social influence it would be hard to imagine that most boys would prefer to play baseball and marbles instead of choosing to knit and to play with dolls. 

Endocrine factors and physical make-up probably do have some influence upon personality characteristics; but a classification

PSYCHOLOGY 

based solely upon such factors is certainly hopelessly incomplete.

[1] Phrenology. Although the attempt to localize functions at various areas of the brain was begun by scientists, the idea of such localization struck a popular note which led to an exploitation of the belief in phrenology. In spite of its manifest absurdity, this belief still creeps up in modern life. According to this system, the mental life of the individual may be subdivided into specific traits which actually have no existence: inhabitativeness, alimentiveness, ideality, sublimity, form, weight, color, time, tune, and the like. To these they add others which are loosely descriptive of human beings but hard to define: destructiveness, acquisitiveness, amativeness, mirthfulness, and the like. 

The phrenologists have listed forty-two of these "faculties" and have plotted them on the cortex of the brain. They are supposed to have the seat of their functioning at these areas. Furthermore, it is assumed that as these traits develop they cause increases in brain mass at these points which in turn push out the skull located above such areas. Character can thus be read by studying the bumps on an individual's skull. These views have been totally discredited. 

Stigmata of degeneracy. This theory maintained that the presence of certain bodily peculiarities, which were called stigmata of degeneracy, indicates a tendency toward traits of instability and degeneracy. Some of the stigmata that have been named are: woolly hair; peculiarities in the shape of the skull; scanty eyebrows; absence of body framework of the nose; extremely large or thick ears; wrinkled, pale, or sallow skin; deeply cleft lips; peculiarities in the formation of the teeth. This theory has been thoroughly discredited. 

Physiognomy. Physiognomic systems attempt to interpret human characteristics from the form of the face and other outward appearances of the individual. Some of these systems have been based upon hypotheses of reputable scientists. Physiognomy has been shown to be erroneous but has, nevertheless, been exploited by uncritical individuals and widely publicized. One physiognomist, for example, divided the human personality into three types: the mental, the motor, and the vital. The mental type was supposedly indicated by an elongated or triangular face with

the base across the top of the head, and the apex pointed downward at the chin. The motor type could be recognized from a square head and face. The vital type had a round, flabby countenance.

Numerous studies have shown that there is no relationship between such physical characteristics and temperament. In spite of this negative evidence, the belief in such relationships is persistent. It has been found, for example, that the unlettered individual incorrectly and with no sound reason believes that certain physical traits are connected with distinctive personality traits: 

Thick bushy eyebrows, to these persons, suggest sternness. A receding chin suggests vacillation and lack of initiative. Small eyes suggest greed. Small bones they believe to mean high ideals and delicate feelings. Fine hair indicates fine temperament. 

Coarse hair suggests toughness, meanness, and low ideals. Small ears suggest thrift. Big ears suggest eloquence and excellence of speech. A thin sharp nose suggests shrewdness in business. 

Thick lips suggest passion, strong feelings, and impulsiveness. A high forehead suggests great intellect. A receding forehead suggests low intelligence and criminal tendencies. A square jaw, to these people, suggests stubbornness. [16]

Regardless of where these superstitions originated, and in spite of their unsoundness, some people believe that they can judge by such characteristics. The important consideration is not to guard against judging others by these methods but to counteract the tendency of others to judge us according to some such physical trait. The logical procedure is to get rid of characteristics which produce unfavorable impressions or, if they cannot be eliminated, to counterbalance such impressions by exaggerating our manifestation of counterbalancing physical traits.

Contemporary attempts to classify personalities. Modern investigators have endeavored to avoid the mistakes which this historical sketch of personality study has revealed. Of those methods listed on pages 531 to 533, they have found the following to be the most valuable: clinical studies, rating scales, questionnaires and inventories, tests, experiments, and statistical analyses. These are not mutually exclusive and some of them depend upon or presuppose the others. We shall deal with these in

PSYCHOLOGY 

greater detail presently, although we shall not take them up in regular order. [24]

THE GROWTH OF  

Whereas the individual is complex and defies classification into any limited set of categories, he still has a coherence and a unity which mark him off from every other individual. Even identical twins are separate, unique personalities in spite of the fact that one may be mistaken, at times, for the other. 

Individual unity is, nevertheless, not a static entity. Some persons are more unified than others. Some easily fall apart physically, emotionally, and intellectually. Some resist the most violent disrupting influences. 

Furthermore, there are changes in the degree of unity as life proceeds. The thread of unity runing through a single life is a somewhat elusive thing. A person is born, goes through his life, and dies; we consider that he is the same person all the way along and, in a sense, he is. On the other hand, the infant John 

Jones is not the same John Jones whom we see in grade school, in high school, as a mature businessman, or as an irascible man of eighty-five who cannot remember at ten o'clock what he had for breakfast.

People differ in their reactions to this phenomenon of changing personality. Complacent, self-satisfied persons tend to dislike the notion of change. They would like to remain as they are because they believe they have "arrived." Ambitious persons, who are still dissatisfied with themselves, like to believe that there are better things ahead for them; so they stress the changing factors in life. In other words, whether one wants change depends upon where he thinks he is in relation to the top or the bottom. 

If one is at the bottom of the social ladder, any change is more likely to be up than down; if one is at the top, any change is more likely to be down than up. The psychologist should not permit such personal considerations to enter into his study of individuality.

How can continuity of individuality be reconciled with the fact that a person is continually changing? The answer probably lies in the fact that the degree of change at any one time is small in relation to the whole individual. When changes become

too great there is disruption or death. The slow, continuous nature of development is clearly manifest when one attempts to divide a life into periods. It is almost impossible to indicate exactly where infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into maturity, and maturity into senility. 

Interaction between environmental and hereditary factors. Each individual is a product of hereditary processes and of the experiences through which he passes after conception. A man's structure is certainly the result of hereditary factors. 

Hereditary accounts for such facts as that he is a human being and not a goat, that he has two feet and not six, that he can live in air rather than in water, and that his larynx, tongue, lips, and lungs are adapted to speaking. Certain activities also are determined by such inherited structures. A man walks as he does because of his structure, he breathes air instead of water not from choice but from necessity. He talks partly because he has the organic structures which he has. However, what he says does not depend upon heredity. Perhaps a safe generalization would be that there is more dependence upon heredity in those characteristics which are relatively closely tied to the structure of the individual, and more dependence upon experience in those traits which are not closely linked with structure. 

The way in which heredity and environment are related to each other has often erroneously been regarded as a summation effect. A certain percentage is presumed to come from heredity and another percentage from environment; the sum of the two must be 100 per cent. The two are not added in any such fashion. 

The relationship is better expressed by multiplication than by addition. The individual is the product of heredity times environment. With such an equation, if either factor is reduced to zero the product is zero. With no environment, heredity cannot produce an individual. Without heredity, environment is just as powerless.

The relative weight that should be given to each factor is certainly not a constant. It probably varies with individuals, and in the same individual it varies in different situations. This being the case, it is futile to attempt to assign relative weights to each, and statements which presume to do so are probably in error.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Relative value of maturation and learning. Those who stress hereditary factors encounter a striking difficulty when they study the development of the human infant. The equipment of the human infant is certainly meager and he is exceedingly incompetent. If most of his ability comes through inheritance, where is it during infancy? The concept of maturation was conceived to escape this difficulty. According to this theory, there is a ripening of innate behavioral tendencies in the absence of any training and experience. The infant is incompetent, but ripening makes up for his deficiencies without the benefit of teaching or experience.

As we have shown in a previous chapter (page 46), there is little reason to reject the concept of maturation or ripening as a factor in physiological development. One cannot learn to use an arm until the arm has reached a stage of development that will permit its use. An individual cannot become a parent before adolescence. No amount of training can teach a person to perform an act unless the structural mechanism for its performance is present.

On the other hand, there is no justification for reasoning from analogy and contending that elusive personality traits await personality maturation. There is reason for thinking that such characteristics as deceitfulness, neatness, humility, aggressiveness, or fidelity are dependent more upon learning than upon the ripening of some innate mechanism.

This does not carry with it the implication that innate structure, or structure acquired by maturation or even by accident, is not effective in the direction of intricate traits. One might easily expect that a weak, sickly child is more likely to be dependent, shy, and fond of the mother who nursed him incessantly than is the robust child who has had less need for his mother's care. 

Learning should be viewed in its broadest sense when we are considering the part it plays in individual development. It may be unintentional learning; it may be that the child was "taught" one thing but learned something entirely different; it may be that some violent shock was more effective than long periods of training; a vague attitude may be the result of learning as much as is the ability to hit a target with an arrow.

The role of conflict in the growth of individuality. In our study of emotional adjustments we found that when a person was confronted with some emergency situation, he mobilized his energies and reacted in a more violent way or in some new manner. We discussed the adequacy of such different responses. 

There is another aspect to emotional situations; namely, the permanent or semilasting effect they have upon the one who experiences them. The traits which we class as personality traits are more likely to be based upon emotional experiences than upon routine events. To state the issue in another way: Personality traits contain a large proportion of emotional habits. 

One can imagine situations which, when repeated with a child, could develop various so-called traits, to wit: 

Suggestibility might be taught to a child if he found solutions for his difficulties by taking the suggestions of others; a nonsuggestible child might be developed by seeing to it that he gained nothing but more trouble by taking suggestions. 

See to it that a child is happier when he daydreams than when engaged in objective and active pursuits, and it should be possible to develop in him the tendency to daydream. 

See that a child repeatedly gains his ends by stealing and that he is caught and suffers infrequently; and he may thereby learn to be a sneak thief.

Qualities of the mature individual. If we accept the developmental conception of individuality, we should interpret the changes which we see in the growing person as pointing toward 

FIG. 191.-A cycloid curve. The imag inary representation of an undisturbed life cycle. a condition of ripeness or maturity. Ripeness, however, is never static; rather, it carries with it the implication of retrogression, deterioration, and decay. The curve of an individual life has never been precisely determined, but we can imagine it to be in the form of a cycloid. A cycloid is represented in Fig. 191. 

Such an imaginary representation of a life cycle is, doubtless, an oversimplification.

Maturation is not definitely related to chronological age.

PSYCHOLOGY 

Some individuals reach the highest level of development earlier in life than others; some continue to grow longer than others; some are cut off, so that the curve may make an abrupt drop from any conceivable point.

Furthermore, growth and maturity are the product of a number of different factors. An individual may be relatively mature in some respects and infantile in others. Such infantilism may never be overcome, or it may be followed by a period of rapid development.

All these qualifications indicate clearly that the idea of individual maturity is a vague and unmeasurable concept. In spite of this, clinical studies have shown that the following aspects of individual maturation are of some significance. 

The mature individual should be well rounded. By this is meant that he should have a normal amount of development in all aspects of his individuality. Such an individual is equipped to compete on an even basis with other individuals. A case can be made, nevertheless, for the lopsided individual-the freak or the genius who has some quality lacking, or some trait present in a grossly exaggerated form. An extreme oddity may give him a decided advantage in a competitive society. For example, the late boy giant of Alton, Illinois, who was over eight feet tall, had a decided advantage in playing forward on a basketball team. He merely stood under the basket, received the ball from his teammates, and dropped it into the basket. 

The mature individual should have achieved a fair amount of objectivity. He should be well adjusted to his environment. 

Such maturity shows itself in the preference for dealing with the actual world rather than for solitary daydreaming, in the variety of interests shown in objective life, in the ability to become absorbed in work, in play, in civic activities, and in the ability to meet a challenging situation by cool analysis. 

Such an objective adjustment can be accompanied by a desire to change situations and does not involve docile acceptance of unfavorable aspects of living. There should be an active planning for the betterment of conditions instead of the more infantile reaction of whining, complaining, or solitary retreat.

The mature individual should have insight. Insight is essentially knowledge of oneself; it is freedom from self-decep-

tion. It is not unusual to see a child boasting loudly about his prowess while, at the same time, he is failing completely. He lacks the self-criticism which a mature individual should possess. Insight is more likely to be accompanied by a modest appraisal of oneself than by exaggerated statements of ability. 

Insight is manifest also in the willingness of an individual to take the responsibility for his own acts when these are not so excellent. One lacking insight takes the credit for his successes and blames others for his failures. Maturity brings a reversal of this process. 

A genuine sense of humor about oneself is a good index of insight. The young child usually lacks such humor. He laughs readily at the misfortunes of others, but seldom sees a joke on himself as really funny. He takes himself so seriously that his failures cannot amuse him. It is seldom that a man admits that he has no sense of humor; and probably all men have some. It is the direction that his humor takes which indicates his degree of maturation. The mature man genuinely enjoys a good joke on himself more than he does a joke on others. 

The mature person is socially adjusted. Probably no other quality measures the maturity of an individual more than the degree to which he has developed a consistently mature type of social philosophy. Perhaps the significance of this characteristic can be made clear by drawing some contrasts between the individual who is still infantile in his social adjustments and one who is relatively mature: 

1. The social infant needs others; the socially matured person helps those who need him. 

2. The social infant tries to impress others with his virtues; the socially matured person appreciates the good points in others. 

3. The social infant is fortunate if he is able to get along with one person-his mother; the socially matured person understands individual differences and gets along well with persons of widely different types. 

4. The social infant wants to be understood; the socially matured person wants to understand others. 

5. The social infant wants others to contribute to his hap-

PSYCHOLOGY 

piness; the socially matured person gains his greatest happiness by contributing to the happiness of others. 

6. The social infant wants others to like him; the socially matured person is so busy liking others that he has no time to consider whether they like him or not. 7. The social infant takes; the socially adolescent person gives and takes; the socially matured person gives. 

UNIFYING FACTORS IN THE INDIVIDUAL 

Even while subjecting the human individual to the process of psychological dissection, it is apparent all along that there are numerous integrating or unifying factors. It may be of value to summarize these factors briefly. 

Each cell in an individual contains the same essential pattern of chromosomes. In the early stages of growth, each division of a cell leaves the daughter cells with the same pattern as the parent cells because reproduction is by division. Even when cells become highly specialized this pattern remains the same. 

However, in the adult individual, identical chromosome pattern is not so essential as might be imagined for continued unity. For example, the individuality of a person is not much affected by having a part grafted to him from another person or even from an animal.

Specialization of parts of the individual does not destroy unity. In the analysis of early development, it was found that the individual was, at first, a mass of cells which acted as a whole, and that development proceeded by the process of individuation. 

One part of the body learned to do some specialized act; there was the emergence of a specific and local activity out of general mass activity. Instead of being a breakdown of the original unity of the individual, as it might seem to be at first glance, individuation is essentially the beginning of a unity of a higher order. 

It enables the growing organism to deal with a local situation effectively while still free to attend to other matters. Individuation proceeds, however, only so far as the welfare of the individual is served. Instead of differentiation of function leading to civil strife and disunity, it makes for increasing efficiency. 

Unity is accentuated by teamwork. Orderly performance requires that each contributor (or actor) not only becomes

individually efficient, but that he knows when to join with other contributors, when to sit back and wait, and just what degree of assistance or restraint to exercise. In other words, unity of function requires accurate timing. This is illustrated well in skilled motor acts, but it also appears in every function where specialized individual contributions are made. Parts of the body have to learn cues as to when they should come in; and the study of conditioned reflexes showed us how such learning takes place. 

There must be profiting by mistakes, which involves memory; there must be proper co-ordination, which comes with practice; and there must be a unifying objective at any one moment, which requires consistent motivation. 

Unity requires the avoidance of dangerous excesses. 

In times of stress, we found that various parts of the body changed their function to maintain what has been called homeostasis. If there was an approach to the danger line away from balance in such essential conditions as water content, salt content, temperature, and the like, there was a mobilization of energy to bring the organism back to safety. It would do no good for a hand to continue practicing some motor trick when the total individual was threatened by death from loss of blood. The hand would be forced to stop its specialized performance so that all available energy might be utilized to meet the emergency. 

The nervous system is a unifying instrument. By means of the nervous system, every part of the body has a line, or lines, of communication with every other part. All these connections, moreover, are effected through central connections of a complex order. The brain is the essential switching center and co-ordinator of activity in such a complex organism as an individual. 

Simple reflex patterns can operate without the co-operation of the brain, but the solution of a difficult intellectual problem requires more than local reflexes. It requires a mechanism to mobilize all the energies of the individual, all his past experience, all aspects of the present, and the possibility of making tentative responses to test the validity of possible solutions. 

Different parts of the body are more important than others; but the brain outranks them all. One can live when large parts of the brain are not functioning (as in sleeping sickness), but not

PSYCHOLOGY 

effectively. The arm might go on a strike (because of a motor paralysis) and efficiency might be somewhat reduced; but the individual could get along much better than if the brain went on strike.

Unity is helped by shifts of interest. When an individual is bombarded at one time with a number of problems demanding solution, an attempt to deal with them all simultaneously could end only in disruption. The ordinary procedure is to give complete attention to one at a time. This leads to the phenomenon commonly known as a shift of attention. When this process does not function adequately, various forms of individual disruption may occur. Extreme efforts to deal with all issues at once leads to "jitteriness." If too much attention is given to one problem and the others are completely ignored, so that they do not get their attention in turn, there may be dissociation owing to a memory blocking. The individual forgets instead of delaying action. In an extreme form of this type of behavior there may appear a complete dissociation of the personality. The individual forgets who he is. He starts life afresh because he does not remember who he was or what problems he had. Shifts of attention, with successive attention to different problems, is an important aspect of psychological unity. 

Every person evolves individual codes for living. 

Although these may be difficult for a person to formulate, each individual is continually building up a body of principles or points of reference for the regulation of his own behavior. Various names have been suggested for such life codes: philosophy of life, world outlook, ideology, creed, belief, point of view, way of thinking, or confession of faith.

Probably in most instances an individual is unable to formulate in words what his own set of rules for living are. He may state one rule and live another. He may have evolved his own, or he may have accepted them from others. 

Normally, every experience modifies them continually in some manner, although a person may believe that he is living consistently by the same rules through a period of years. They may contain many inconsistencies, or may be fairly well integrated. It might be safe to say that, in most instances, the guid-

ing rules are not those verbally enunciated by an individual, but a set of attitudes or emotional habits which come to the foreground especially in times of crisis. 

THE MEASUREMENT OF TRAITS 

A trait may be defined as a distinctive mode of behavior. It is purely a descriptive term, an index of an outsider's interpretation of the behavior of another. We observe the indications of a trait in another person; we infer the presence of a trait if those indicators are consistent with our definition of the trait in question. The measuring of a trait is the process of determining the degree to which a person fits such an arbitrary definition. 

Suppose a boy has been guilty of an act which he has been told was bad and that he is reasonably certain that his father does not know he did it. Suppose, further, that this father approaches the boy with anger written all over him, and screams at him, "Did you do that?" The boy knows if he says "yes," he will be whipped. If he says "no," he has reasonable assurance that he will not. Consequently, if he says "no," he is making an intelligent response. Does this make him a liar? He certainly should not be classified along with the pathological liar who tells lies in all sorts of circumstances, who prefers a lie to the truth, and who can always be counted upon to tell a lie if it is at all possible to do so.

Suppose we wish to measure to what degree a certain person tends to tell falsehoods. Whether he told the truth or told a lie would depend upon: (a) The amount of pressure put upon him to tell a lie. (b) The number of equally promising methods of adjustment apparent to him. The observer might see other ways of adjusting, but the important consideration is whether the subject sees them. (c) The strength of the habit of telling lies without waiting to look for other reactions or considering them if they were present; that is, the degree to which he has specialized in lying. (d) The attitude of the subject toward the particular lie in question. [12] 

In no psychological experiment designed to measure traits have all the variables been controlled or measured. Hence, the student should be warned that the status of trait measurement

PSYCHOLOGY 

is unsatisfactory. We shall, nevertheless, review some of the methods that have been used.¹

Ratings of others. In a rating scale the individual under consideration is assigned a score, rank, mark, or position on the trait under consideration.

Requirements for a valid rating scale. In order for a rating scale to be valid certain basic requirements should be met. 

The neglect of these has made many ratings of little or no value. 

1. The rater should have a clear conception of the trait he is judging. If the trait cannot be clearly defined, it is futile. to attempt to rate any person on it. 

It has been found that definitions in terms of what a man does, or the effect that the man has on the persons or things with which he comes in contact, are much more valuable than descriptions in terms of so-called traits or personality characteristics. 

2. The rater should know the person he is rating. The rater should have observed the one he is rating over a long enough
