3. Allowance should be made for the halo effect. The halo effect is the tendency (to which any rater is subject) to be influenced, in rating one trait, by an estimate of some other trait or by a general estimate of the person. A teacher, for example, would be inclined to rate a boy high in studiousness if he is attentive to her or if she liked him. 

4. The ratings of several judges should always be considered. If there is little or no consistency among them, the ratings are worthless. 

5. The selection of judges from different areas of contact with the subject is important. It might be possible, for example, for all the teachers in a school to rate low in desirable traits a boy who had the reputation of being bad; on the contrary, other persons who knew him under different circumstances might give him an entirely different rating. Prejudiced ratings can be cumulative. 

6. Attempts should be made to determine the competence of each rater. It has been found there are wide individual differences in ability to judge the significance of behavior in others. Some persons are so low in this ability that their ratings are worse than useless. There is no easy way to judge a person's rating ability. One method has been to compare the ratings of each rater with the composite score of the other raters. The one who disagreed most with this composite score was judged the poorest rater. This may not always hold. A trained psychologist might disagree with a host of gossipmongers in a community as to the rating of a boy in that community in some trait, and yet the psychologist might be the only one who was even close to a correct judgment. 

Self-rating methods. Self-rating is the attempt made by an individual to evaluate himself in some characteristic. There are obvious limitations in this method. [24] 

Errors in direct self-ratings. The most apparent error arises from the fact that it is easy for a person to lie in the estimate he renders, provided he knows the significance of the trait he is rating. On the other hand, even if a person attempts to be honest in rating himself, it has been found that he tends to make consistent errors which tend to make self-ratings unreliable.

PSYCHOLOGY 

A person tends to overestimate himself on desirable traits and to minimize the undesirable ones. However, this tendency is not always in conformity with the social standards of his community. If a person believes a trait to be desirable, and the community believes it to be undesirable, the person will rate himself high on the traits he prefers rather than on those the community prefers. In other words, he manifests his overestimation of himself even in his judgment of the significance of traits. About all that can be told from direct self-ratings, then, is how conceited a person is by comparing his estimate of himself with the estimate of his peers.

Indirect self-rating methods. Various means have been devised for disguising the significance of a person's rating of himself. 

1. Comparison with an imaginary person. In one test for children, the subject is required to make a direct comparison between himself and some imaginary character with certain characteristics.

For example, the child is told that "Peter is a big, strong boy who can beat any of the other boys in a fight." The child is then asked to indicate on a graphic rating scale the degree to which he thinks he is just like Peter. After this comparison has been made, he is asked to indicate on another graphic scale the degree to which he wishes to be just like Peter. Other hypothetical characters are given (each with a different name and with girls' names when the subject is a girl) and the same procedure repeated for each. Some of the characters are: 

George likes to read. He has read all the books he can get about cowboys. 

Ed is the best ball player in school.

Sam gets good marks on all his schoolwork. 

Allan has make-believe friends and a make-believe world which is much nicer than the real world. He sits and dreams of all sorts of make-believe adventures with these make-believe friends.

Joe is a leader. All the fellows do what he tells them to do.

The psychological questionnaire. A questionnaire consists of a group of questions submitted to a number of individuals with the request that they give an answer to each item. There are certain characteristics which distinguish a questionnaire from a test. In a test the issue is whether the person can answer the question; in a questionnaire the issue is whether he will answer the questions truthfully. In a test a person's score is determined by his ability and the test is made difficult in order to offer a challenge to ability. A questionnaire is made as easy and as simple as possible, and the person given as much time as he desires to answer it. Tests are designed to find out what a person can do, while questionnaires are designed to find out what a person has done, will do, or how he thinks, feels, or believes. While the questionnaire method may be used to discover facts, the psychological questionnaire is designed primarily to learn about reactions of the individual who answers it, such as beliefs, preferences, likes and dislikes, wishes, judgments, and choices. 

Two main kinds of questionnaires have been used in attempts to study individuality: the adjustment inventory and the expression of wishes. [21] 

1. Adjustment inventories. It happens to be a delicate

matter to inquire directly into the adjustment problems of an individual. Since a questionnaire may be answered truthfully or untruthfully, with or without bias, and may include any degree' of distortion; its use to study psychological adjustments is particularly difficult. In order to surmount these difficulties it is customary to have a relatively large number of questions in the questionnaire (or inventory, as it is euphemistically called), ranging from highly significant ones to jokers which have no significance. It is assumed that the one who answers will not be able to distinguish all the significant items and thus will probably reveal his maladjustments by the number of such items he answers in a manner characteristic of the maladjusted person. 

This method has been grossly overworked. It was developed in order to meet an emergency, in 1917. A widely publicized form was later developed because a psychologist was assigned the task of examining a large incoming college class in order to select those who might be in need of psychiatric assistance. Those who developed the method have pointed out its crude nature, but others have tried to use it as though it were a psychological micrometer. 

With ordinary common sense a person can answer such a questionnaire in a manner that would indicate that he needed help or in a manner that would make him well balanced. What it reveals, then, is whether the one who takes it wants sympathy and attention or wants to be let alone. If he is a neurotic of the complaining variety he will give a large number of "neurotic" answers. 

Other workers have evolved much more elaborate lists, But have not improved much on the original ones, for the simple reason that the basic flaws are intrinsic in the method and cannot be removed by increased complexity of formation. Inventories have been designed to measure the following: various kinds of psychotic tendencies, such as tendencies toward hysteria, neurasthenia, psychasthenia, paranoia, schizophrenia and the like; introversion and extroversion; family relationships, such as relationships with parents, siblings, and wife or husband; love affairs; vocational adjustments; general emotional stability; school and social adjustments; ascendance-submission; negativism and suggestability. 

2. Expression of wishes. The expression of a wish is not frowned upon violently even when the wish is nonconven-

PSYCHOLOGY 

tional. Consequently, the expression of wishes has been used to secure an index of personal adjustment. For example, children have been asked to state three wishes, the examiner then attempting to interpret the significance of the replies.

Objective tests of personality. A test has a definite advantage over a rating scale or a questionnaire. Instead of basing judgment on crude opinion or on an answer that may be biased or may be a downright lie, in a test the individual's score is determined by what he does in the test situation. 

Many ingenious tests have been devised to measure personal traits. As an illustration of a typical test approach to this field of study we shall describe some tests devised to measure honesty and trustworthiness. [10, 11, 12] 

The duplicating test technique. Two tests of equal difficulty are made. One test is given under conditions in which cheating is impossible; while in the other test ample opportunity for cheating is given. If there is a difference in favor of the one taken where cheating is possible (a larger difference than might be expected by chance), the presumption is that cheating took place.

The self-scoring technique. A test is given and the student then permitted to score his own paper. Various devices have been used to detect any changes made while the student scores his own paper.

One is to secure a paraffin impression of all markings made on the original performance. Another more laborious method is to collect the papers and make a duplicate copy of the answers, then to return the papers and permit each student to score his own paper. 

Another type of self-scoring can be used with tests of motor skill or strength. Students are put in competition with each other in such performances as strength of grip, lung capacity, chinning, and broad jump. Motivation is secured by offering prizes of various sorts. Each contestant is given three trials, which are scored and records kept by the examiner. Then each child is permitted to make five additional trials in which he scores himself. Since practice effects are small, a marked increase in

PSYCHOLOGY 

grade when the child scores himself is presumptive evidence that he cheated when permitted to keep his own record. 

The improbable achievement technique. Subjects are given tasks impossible of accomplishment to determine whether they will cheat in order to achieve success. (10 1 2 Circles 12345678910T Trial 1 H 2 3 4 5 SCORE

Total 

3 6 1 FIG. 192.-Circles test for honesty. The subject is required to keep his eyes closed while putting digits in order in circles as indicated. 

He makes five trials and records his own scores. It is impossible to accomplish this task without the help of vision. A high score is presumptive evidence of cheating.

For example, the subjects may be required to perform a motor task which can be done successfully only with the aid of vision, with the requirement that they keep their eyes closed. 

A successful performance indicates peeping. The circles test, shown in Fig. 192, requires that the subject with closed eyes make marks in irregularly placed circles of decreasing size, a

task which no subject has ever been able to accomplish with eyes closed. Another is to trace a pencil maze with eyes closed without touching the sides.

Still more ingenious is the weight test. Seven boxes, each one varying from the other by one tenth of a gram, are marked correctly on the bottom with numbers one to seven. The subject is asked to arrange the boxes according to weight. He is then to turn the boxes over and mark the numbers on a score sheet, being told at the same time that the correct order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Then he is told to turn the numbers down and arrange them again. Success in succeeding trials is an indication of peeping.

Overstatement techniques. A typical example of this technique is found in the "Books Read Test." The test consists of a number of book titles, some of which are fictitious. The subject is asked to check those he has read. The subject may check titles of books which do not exist. 

Another is to give the subject a list of questions with the requirement that he check all questions to which he knows the answer. Such questions as the following are given: Who discovered America? Who saved the life of Captain John Smith?

Where are the pyramids? After fifty such questions have been examined (or have been asked orally) the subject is given a chance to give the actual answers. His overstatement is found by comparing those he actually knows with those he claimed to know.

Cheating in games. Various games are played with opportunities for cheating.

Stealing tests. Various opportunities are given for stealing coins or other objects under circumstances where the subject is made to feel that he will be able to steal without detection. 

The Character Education Inquiry used thirty-two tests similar to those just described to make an extremely comprehensive study of cheating, lying, and stealing. The interesting part of their work is the revelation that there is so little relation between the results of the different tests that it makes any such trait as honesty a dubious entity. Instead, each test indicates what the subject will do in that particular situation and gives little basis for predicting what he will do in another specific situa-

PSYCHOLOGY 

tion, supposed to measure another aspect of honesty. A single test of deceit has little value as an index of deceit in general. The child does not respond to honesty in the abstract, but to such concrete things as the teacher, paper, pencil, school marks, coins, the urge to succeed, imminence of detection, ease of cheating, and the like.

The implication from these studies is that most of the traits about which we talk so glibly are merely abstractions based on outside observation. What we do depends upon the needs of the moment and is not determined by any abstract traits in us. 

THE MEASUREMENT OF ADJUSTMENT 

The futility of attempts to measure abstract traits in individuals has pointed toward the need for emphasis on adjustment processes. Instead of attempting to find whether a person is honest or dishonest, aggressive or retiring, conceited or modest, more interest is being devoted to the significance of what a person does when he is confronted with some difficult problem. [22] 

Any individual's life can be looked upon as a succession of problems which must be solved in one way or another. There is little uniformity in the pattern of these problems. They come in no regular sequence; they manifest little equality or uniform intensity; the periods between them may be long or short; and the degree of success in one may have no relation to the relative success in another. Furthermore, each problem carries with it the seeds for new problems whether one makes a satisfactory adjustment or not. As long as a person lives he must adjust, adjust again, then readjust, ad infinitum. Death is the only final adjustment. It is nonsense for a living person to speak of being adjusted.

Dual effect of adjusting. Now, there are two ways of looking at an adjustment process. The first is to judge the whole sequence of actions in terms of how well the individual solved his problem. Did the person win or lose? How efficient were his methods? Could he have done better? How does his solution compare with the solution of others? What is the effect of his solution on other problems? Such are the questions that the observer is likely to ask when objective accomplishment is made the issue. Even most psychological studies of human adjustment

tend to stress the adjustment process in terms of its merits in meeting the actual problem presented.

The second method of viewing adjustment processes is that of attempting to discover the effect of the whole situation on the individuality of the one who makes the adjustment. Every problem a person solves, or fails to solve, leaves him a different individual from what he was before. The curious and fascinating part of this residual effect is that it is not dependent upon the degree of success as judged by objective standards. The important consideration for the psychologist should be: What did this experience do to the person involved? 

Furthermore, the only way in which we can determine the effect that previous adjustments have had upon the individual is by what he does and says now. This is not easy. A response at the moment is partly determined by the needs of the moment, by the tendencies in an individual based on habitual adjustments in the past, by the need for concealing some motives, by the necessity of making a good impression upon observers, by other problems which exist simultaneously with the one that appears momentarily dominant, and other factors that might be listed. 

Consequently, it is not possible to observe a person make a single adjustment reaction and, on the basis of that one situation, arrive at any pronouncement as to the kind of person he is. 

Circumstances under which dominant trends are revealed. Certain situations tend to bring out habitual trends in an individual more readily than do other situations. [9] 

Emergencies. It has been found that the way a person behaves when everything is moving smoothly is not so likely to be indicative of his customary trends as is his behavior when he is confronted with some emergency. This is one of the reasons why clinical methods have been so valuable in the study of individuality. The clinician is called upon to examine a person after he has been more or less shattered by unusual circumstances and he thus has the opportunity to study how the patient behaved when he was hard pressed.

The frequency with which a trend is used. Other things being equal, if a person is given frequent opportunities to make a number of responses and tends to choose a single one repeatedly,

PSYCHOLOGY 

it may be inferred that the preference thus demonstrated indicates a personality trend.

Trend manifested when individual is free from social restraint. A third method is to compare the behavior of an individual when he believes he is being observed with his behavior when he is reasonably sure he is not being watched. 

In short, a person's habitual trends are manifested by the way in which he behaves in an emergency, the preference he shows for one type of response when he has the freedom of choice, and the way in which he behaves when free from any of the inhibitions arising from being observed by others. 

Unwholesome effect of excessive use of a single trend. 

Because these tendencies are so easily and clearly observed when the person gets into some adjustment difficulty, they have been called defense mechanisms. This is merely another way of saying that anyone uses his favorite means of adjustment when pressed the hardest. The use of this term is likely to obscure the real significance of the tendency thus manifested. It gives the impression that such behavior is abnormal and that it should be avoided. 

This is not so. Some habitual methods of solving problems are desirable and some are undesirable in and of themselves. Some good ones can be overworked and some poor ones should be used on occasion.

The ideal person, from the adjustment standpoint, is the one who has a vast number of ways of reacting to life's problems and has the facility for choosing the one best suited to each problem as it arises. The most undesirable person is the one who has but one device, which he tends to use on every occasion whether it is suitable or not. Most of us fall somewhere between those two extremes.

According to this analysis, the poorly adjusted person is the one who has specialized in a few types of adjustment behavior to the exclusion of others and, further, that the types of behavior he has chosen are those which have a bad residual effect upon his general personal structure. The best type of person is no specialist in the use of any one adjustment pattern. He adjusts his behavior to the needs of the present situation. In other words, he is more likely to be guided by objective circumstances than by his individual habits. This conception of traits is a dynamic one

and is in marked contrast to that conception which looks for some fixed abstract quality in the individual. 

CLASSIFICATION OF ADJUSTMENT TENDENCIES 

Many abnormal individuals are characterized by the fact that they have a relatively small group of characteristics developed to an unusual degree. Such exaggerations really provide an excellent opportunity to study these characteristics. [19] 

Nevertheless, in giving a classification of behavior tendencies, or adjustment mechanisms, there is no implication that each kind stands for a type of person. Any one person may use a combination of a great number. Some do not fit together so well as others and are not so likely to come in combination; others fall together very easily. The grouping, then, is in terms of habit patterns and not in terms of personality types. 

Responses which are primarily objective. From the point of view of making the best adjustment to any situation, it is better to be objective about the problem than to let personal bias influence one. The best synonym for objectivity in this sense is rationality. The rational approach to a problem involves interest in the problem itself, the study of all factors that can be observed, the making of tentative reactions while observing their effect upon some hypothesis that has been formulated, the realization that the situation is unique, and the recognition that a successful response at one moment may not be the successful one at the next moment.

Such complete objectivity and rationality of behavior is the exception and represents an ideal. Some individuals come nearer to it than do others. There are persons who are more objective than subjective in their attack upon life, but who, at the same time, are not so ideally rational in the way they go about meeting the objective situation. These less perfect objectivists may be grouped as follows: 

Objective perseveration. Perseveration is the tendency to continue a type of response once it has been used. It is a relatively nonintelligent type of behavior. Of course, one may persist in a type of response without regard for the objective world at all. 

Objective perseveration implies that the subject made his first response in relation to the objective situation and then continues

PSYCHOLOGY 

to use it rather than to attempt some new reaction when he discovers that his is inadequate. As an illustration, a woman asked for help in breaking her child of the habit of sucking his thumb. 

She asserted that she had tied his hands up in tin cuffs for six years and that it did no good. When it was suggested that she discard this practice, she seemed surprised. Here was a woman who admitted that she had done the same thing 2,190 times, who recognized that it was futile, and who yet insisted that she must continue to do it. 

Overactivity. Sometimes it is advisable to try a little harder before giving up an attempted solution. If a door sticks, it may open if it is pushed a little more vigorously. There are times when this simple procedure is inadequate. It might be better to observe some peculiarity in the sticking, whether at the top, at the bottom, or at the lock. Even on a football field, there are times when some indirect attack is better than an attempted drive through center. 

Distinctively habitual responses. Some defense reactions are effective because they influence others to respond favorably. 

Tears are a good example. A child soon learns that he can produce results with his mother in a great diversity of situations if he makes the proper use of tears. Some of the habitual reactions, which a person tends to use primarily because he has acquired the habit of so doing, are: 

Playing upon the sympathy of others. Here the attention is not directed toward the actual problem at hand but at the reactions of those whose help is sought. It is a form of parasitism. The individual expects someone else to solve his problems and his main concern is to manipulate them effectively. 

There are hundreds of ways of eliciting the sympathy and help of others. These vary in subtlety, in the extent to which society tolerates them, in the ease with which they may be applied, as well as in the effect their continued use has upon an individual. 

1. Getting ill. Children learn this easily because they are treated with more consideration when ill than when well. Many adults continue to exploit others by this means. 

2. Display of affection. The little boy who has been naughty softens his punishment by a vigorous demonstration of affection for his mother. The man who has been out half the

night playing poker softens the jolt by bringing home a gift to his outraged wife. 

3. Working on the other person's self-esteem. This is found effective and is utilized by great numbers of persons. It takes a multitude of forms: (a) A direct "build-up" is effective more often than one might suppose. (b) Indirect compliments are usually effective; that is, tell A how fine a person B is on the theory that A will tell B what you said and thus make B take a favorable attitude toward you. (c) Let the other fellow think he is the boss while you are getting your own way by some indirect process. (d) Let the other fellow win the argument while you get your way. (e) Being an attentive listener does wonders. (f) Showing interest in the hobbies or fads of the other person makes him proud of his choice of occupations. 

Children learn all these tricks. The amazing part is the way their effectiveness persists through the older years. 

4. Making some problem into a moral issue in order to enlist the help of others. It is much easier to get people on your side if you are espousing a cause than if you want direct personal help. Most "moral issues" are disguised personal aims.

Distracting devices. Many a problem is solved if one can get the attention of others centered on some irrelevant factor in the environment so that the real issue is hidden. One can easily get in the habit of stirring up the mud instead of trying to see a problem clearly. Rationalization, that is, pretending to argue the question out by excessive talking, is a good illustration. This habit can be initiated easily by a parent who has the theory that he should "reason" things out with his child. Such a process often is not reasoning in any real sense but a contest to determine who can talk the longest. Much of our so-called reasoning in adult life is merely a continuation of these talking contests. 

Blaming others. The habit of blaming others for our misfortunes and failures may begin as a form of distraction. 

There is no better way to distract the teacher's attention from the essential problem than for all the students to engage in the mutual game of blaming the other person. By the time the guilt of all concerned has been evaluated, it is spread out so thinly that no one gets much punishment. 

Conventionality. A person may easily learn that the ob-

PSYCHOLOGY 

servance of conventions can be a means of gaining ends that are otherwise elusive. Here is an illustration where the method did not work: A little girl brought in two apples which her mother had told her to share with her brother. One apple was large and one small. She wanted the large apple but had been taught to be unselfish. How could she get it? She put the two on a plate and holding them both out asked her brother to take an apple. 

He (being unconventional) took the big one. Whereupon the girl complained that he was selfish for taking the big apple. He asked her which one she would have taken had he presented them both to her. "The smaller one," was her moralistic answer. "Well," her brother replied, "you have it, so why do you crab at me?"

Revolutionary behavior. Children learn that they often gain their ends by making a scene-starting a revolution. Older persons carry out the same type of behavior. A revolutionist has nothing to lose and he may gain something. Hence, when you don't like what is going on, start something and try to grab off what you want in the turmoil.

Exploitation. Because of the spoiling by doting parents or, conversely, because a child has been neglected, the habit of exploiting others by fair means or foul, with little regard for their feelings, may be learned. Persons thus develop the attitude that the world owes them a living and set out to collect, feeling injured if anyone stands in their way or if they are called to task for their lack of conformity to law and order. 

Compromise adjustments. Compromise adjustments are the rule rather than the exception. Few individuals actually reach the goal they set for themselves, and most of us must be satisfied with some sort of compromise. These compromises take a multitude of forms.

The sweet-lemon outlook. This is a form of consolation in which the loser tells himself that he gained more in other ways than if he had received the prize. 

Sour grapes. After losing, one tries to convince himself that the prize was not worth having anyway.

Hero worship. When a person knows he cannot achieve some objective, he worships someone who does, thus getting some

vicarious satisfaction through the activity of one who is more successful than himself.

Sublimation. When a person is thwarted, another goal may be substituted in place of the lost one. Thus, a woman whose desire to become a mother has been unfulfilled, may mother other children as a substitute form of satisfaction. 

Daydreaming. Building air castles is a common way of adjusting to failure.

Compensation. Compensation is the process of covering up, or making up for, deficiency in some particular by excellence in another. For example, the girl with the unattractive features may compensate by developing exceptional excellence in social graces. The boy with the weak physique may compensate by superiority in his studies.

Withdrawal reactions. Withdrawal may, at times, be a sensible reaction. When it becomes habitual it may make failure certain. It takes various forms. 

Forgetting. After an individual discovers that genuine forgetting has the added effect of enabling him to avoid unpleasant obligations or to forget unpleasant events, he may cultivate convenient forgetting to such an extent that it becomes habitual. He may begin the habit of forgetting as a side issue in trivial situations but, once started, the habit may grow until large sections of his life may be lost. 

Sleeping. Sleeping is the natural way in which an individual recovers from fatigue. At the same time, it may come as a welcome relief when a person has been hard pressed by difficult situations. In one sense, this is not an unwholesome type of withdrawal. It gives a person a temporary relief, and when he wakes he will probably be in better condition to face his difficulties than he was when tired. There have been a few cases where individuals learned to sleep as a chronic means of escape but, on the whole, sleeping over a problem is a useful procedure. 

Procrastination. Delay, when used wisely, is a valuable device; when used habitually, with little regard for the nature of the difficulty to be met, it may be a mere way of avoiding an urgent responsibility. 

Drug addiction. The use of drugs as an escape from unpleasant or difficult situations is, on the whole, a dangerous

PSYCHOLOGY 

and unwholesome procedure. In their place, drugs have value in helping an individual avoid pain. The use of anesthetics in surgical operations, the professional use of sedatives to bring relief from physical distress, and the administration of specific drugs to treat certain ailments are instances of wise application. 

The degeneration of what may be a beneficial treatment under professional guidance into habitual drug addiction constitutes one of the most unintelligent forms of evasion. 

Worry. When a person is in the presence of a real danger, it pays him to be emotionally aroused and to use the energies thus set loose to attempt to reach some solution to his problem. Worry, on the other hand, is a form of ingrown emotion which turns the emotional energy away from the active pursuit of some solution to the nursing of one's own feelings and to self-pity. By becoming engrossed in worry the victim of this habit evades any active attempt at adjustment and settles down to chronic evasion. 

Living in the past. The lasting value of any experience is the help it provides in meeting some new situation. We learn from both the successes and the mistakes we have made. Evaders escape a present problem situation by dwelling upon the failures of the past, becoming emotionally depressed, and arguing that there is no use in trying again; or they may evade a present challenge by continual prating about the victory they once achieved. 

Reminiscence is a form of consolation to be expected in an old person who has lived his life; it tends to reconcile him to the fact that there is little ahead for him. In a younger person who should be actively engaged in the challenging issues of the present, such premature old age is certainly an unwholesome escape device. 

Extreme introversion If an individual pauses long enough in the process of living to take a good look at himself, to make a personal inventory so that he can be more sure of his personal assets and liabilities, he can doubtless profit thereby. The chronic introvert, on the other hand, might be compared with the businessman who has turned miser. He becomes so engrossed in the contemplation of himself that he ignores the environment in which he lives as well as the ways in which he might utilize his personal qualities. The ironical part of such a procedure is that the very

qualities that the introvert guards so jealously slip out of his grasp through decay, and atrophy from disuse. 

Self-destruction. Most of the adjustments we have outlined to this point may have their bad features eliminated and the good elements cultivated as experience points out these qualities to the individual who uses them. Even though some may be inherently less wholesome than others, all can be changed and used more intelligently as life proceeds. The tragic part of selfdestruction is that it is final. Once having exercised this method of retreat from the problems of life, there is no turning back. 

Intelligent adjustment. Intelligent adjustment involves the use of that form of reaction which is most appropriate at the moment, the checking of the results of each trial adjustment, and the modification of the next reaction accordingly. Please note carefully: The essence of intelligent adjustment is variability of response-the selection of one of many possible reactions; it is not the blind repetition of one type of reaction merely because it was successful at one time. The specialization in one type of adjustment reaction is inefficient, nonintelligent, and may easily lead to a pathological condition. The mother who complains that her son is unpredictable, that he is continually getting into one unexpected situation after another, is really describing the adjustment behavior of an intelligent and forward-looking child. 

Pity the child whose mother can always depend upon him. He will become the cog in some machine that is controlled by his more intelligent comrades.

A trait is, then, essentially the habit of responding in a distinctive (or habitual) manner to a great number and variety of situations requiring adjustment. If a person has a definite personality trait, it means that his friends can count on a certain type of behavior which characterizes that trait. 

Various social organizations laud certain traits and stress the importance of their development. In an army situation, blind obedience is held up as a virtue. In a fraternal group, loyalty is desirable. In a group of salesmen, aggressiveness is praised. 

The good referee is characterized by quickness of decision. The development of such a trait is more a convenience for the particular society than for the individual. Of course, if the person is to live in that group he needs to have the trait that the group

PSYCHOLOGY 

demands. When he joins himself to any group he tacitly or openly agrees to cultivate the traits which that group commends. 

Should he change his mind he should get out. For example, when a boy comes to college he tacitly agrees to attempt to develop the trait of studiousness. Having entered, he may assert his independence and revolt against concentrating on study, attempting to turn the college into a social club. 

This brings us to a common performance by an individual who finds that he has become too specialized. Instead of reverting to the intelligent objective type of behavior, he picks some other type of defense behavior and begins to specialize in it. 

The boy who feels too dependent tries to become independent. 

Such independence tends to show itself in silly negativism or nonconformity in nonessentials. The overdisciplined two-year-old child often shows stubbornness. He shows he is a real man by refusing to eat his food, by refusing to lace his shoes, by refusing to fold his napkin. All you need do to get him to do a thing is to tell him to do the opposite of the act desired. The extreme of this sort of thing is found in a symptom in some pathological cases known as approximate answers. The patient knows the right answer but shows his independence by refusing to give it. 

Ask him how much twenty-five minus four is, and he will reply successively with the answers: twenty, twenty-two, nineteen, eighteen, twenty-three, seventeen, twenty-four, and the like.

The best adjusted man is the one who lets "traits" control settled issues, but who is versatile in his adjustment behavior in any problem situation. He uses intelligence to guide his behavior instead of relegating his decisions to habits.

A change in the sensitivity of a sense organ by means of which the sense organ accommodates to changes in the stimuli affecting it. A picture in which certain parts are open to two interpretations. In one type of ambiguous figure the same part may be interpreted either as the essential figure or as part of the background. In another type the same element may be interpreted as nearer the observer or farther away than the adjacent elements. analogies test. A type of mental test designed to measure the familiarity of the subject with certain relations, such as causeeffect, part-whole, genus-species, etc. Example: As fire is to heat, so ice is to analytic method. That method of investigation which proceeds by breaking down compounds, or intricate situations, into more elementary units. apparent movement (or motion). The perception of movement experienced when stationary stimuli are exposed in brief succession. Five types have been differentiated: alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and epsilon. appetite. An inborn or habitual desire or propensity for some personal gratification. aptitude test. A test designed to measure the fitness of a subject

for undertaking a specific kind of activity, for example, music, mechanics, language study, etc. aqueous humor. The transparent, watery fluid which fills the space in the front part of the eye between the cornea and the lens. association. The establishment of functional relations between psychological activities following individual experience. For example, if A and B are associated, the appearance of either one at a later time will tend to be accompanied by the other. association, controlled. A response or a series of associative responses conforming to some previously announced restriction. 

Example: words are presented to a subject, who is required to give the opposite of each. association fiber. Nerve fibers which connect different nerve centers. association, free. An associative response, or a series of such responses, which is unrestricted. association tests. Tests designed to measure some aspect of response sequences. Example: a subject may be presented with a standard list of words to each of which we must give an associative response. association time. The interval elapsing between the giving of a stimulus and the associative response made by the subject. asthenia. A lack of general strength. Weakness. ataxiameter. An apparatus that measures the swaying movements of a subject who is trying to stand motionless. attention. A set, attitude, priming, posture, or adjustment which makes it easier for one to respond to a certain stimulus. attitude. A muscular posture, mental set, or mood which influences in a general way a person's behavior in a variety of situations. audiometer. An instrument for measuring the acuity of hearing. automatograph. An instrument used to make a graphic record of unrestricted movements of a part of the body. autonomic nervous system. The division of the nervous system which activates the smooth muscles of the body and certain glands. It functions predominantly in emotional behavior. autoscope. A general term for any one of a number of devices by means of which imperceptible, involuntary muscular movements are intensified and thus become significant. Illustrations are the planchette, the divining rod, the ouija board, and tables for table tipping.

The two groups are then treated in ways differing in some measurable fashion and are subsequently compared. Resultant differences are presumably the result of the specifically different treatment. convergence, visual. The fiber of a neuron which conducts the nerve impulse toward the cell body. Contrasted with the axon, the fiber of a neuron which carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body.

The turning of the two eyes outward so that both eyes may remain fixated on the same object as it moves farther away from an individual, or the movement that occurs when the eyes change from fixation on a near object to fixation on a distant object. dominant character. Mendel's law. A principle of hereditary transmission, discovered by Gregor Mendel, which states: When parents that are opposite in a particular genetic character are crossed, the progeny of the first generation will all be like one of the parents with respect to the character in question. When the hybrid offspring of this first generation are, in turn, crossed with each other at random, they will produce a mixed progeny, 25 per cent of which will be like one grandparent, 25 per cent like the other grandparent, and 50 per cent like the hybrid parents. mental age. Any small nipplelike projection.

591 paradoxical cold. A sensation of cold in response to a typically warm stimulus. paradoxical warmth. A sensation of warmth in response to a typically cold stimulus. parallax. The apparent shift in relative position of two unequally distant objects with a change in position of the observer. parasympathetic nervous system. The sacral and cranial segments of the autonomic nervous system conceived as functioning in opposition to the sympathetic system. parathyroid glands. Four small glands located on the surface of the thyroid glands, which secrete a hormone that regulates blood calcium. partial tone. One of the simple harmonic components of a compound tone. The first partial is the fundamental tone; the second partial is the first overtone; the third partial is the second overtone; and so on. patella. The kneecap. pendular motion. The motion made by a body so suspended from a fixed point that it can swing freely to and fro under the combined action of gravity and momentum. perceiving. The process of becoming aware of external objects, qualities, and relations. performance test. A type of mental test in which the factor of language is eliminated or greatly diminished. perilymph. The fluid that fills the bony cavities of the inner ear. phase. In simple circular motion (or simple harmonic motion), the point to which the rotation has advanced from its starting position. phi phenomenon. A term sometimes used to designate apparent motion. photopic vision. Color vision, that is, vision occurring when the illumination is sufficiently bright to permit color discrimination. phylogeny. The origin and development of various animal species. 

Contrasted with ontogeny, the origin and development of the individual. physiological limit. The limit of excellence of performance in a given motor act, which is determined by such factors as speed limitations, strength limitations, and the like. pitch. That characteristic of a tone which makes it possible to differentiate it from others in terms of high and low, or acute and grave. It depends primarily (but not entirely) upon the frequency of the sound wave.

PSYCHOLOGY 

pituitary gland. A ductless gland situated at the base of the brain. that secretes several hormones, some of which affect growth, sexual development, sexual activity, the production of fat, and the general tension of the body. planchette. See autoscope. plantar reflex. A reflex movement consisting of the flexion of the toes in response to the stroking of the sole of the foot. plateau. A temporary halt in the progress of learning, which manifests itself as a flat portion of a learning curve and indicates a period of inability to increase speed or to decrease the number of errors. plethysmograph. An instrument used to record changes in the size of a part of the body resulting from changes in blood supply. pneumograph. An instrument used to record the rate and extent of breathing movements. polygraph. An instrument that makes a simultaneous graphic record of several physiological processes, such as heartbeat, breathing, and muscular contractions. premise. A proposition from which a conclusion is to be drawn. prenatal. Before birth. prestige suggestion. A suggestion that depends for its effectiveness upon the personal influence or reputation of the one who gives it. problem solving. A type of adjustive behavior in which an individual is stimulated by some uncertainty in the situation to discover how to use some of the unknown elements, factors, or conditions in order to achieve some definite end. protoplasm. The essential living substance of the cell. psychogalvanic reflex. The change in resistance of the skin to the passage of electric current (presumably caused by physiological activity under control of the autonomic nervous system) which follows sensory stimulation or accompanies thinking processes. psychology. The study of how people act and why they act as they do. 

Purkinje phenomenon. A name used to designate the various changes in color values resulting from decreases in general illumination. As the spectrum is darkened, the long-wave end darkens more rapidly than the short-wave end. radiant energy. Electromagnetic waves traveling through free space at a velocity of about 186,000 miles per second, those

GLOSSARY 

593 wave lengths ranging from about 400 to 760 millimicrons being known as light. rating scale. A method of securing and recording judgments by indicating where each judgment should fall on a prearranged set of values. rationalization. The process of justifying an act or opinion by excuses displayed in the guise of reasons. reaction time. The interval of time between a stimulus and the beginning of a response to that stimulus. reasoning. A way of solving problems involving a departure from routine reactions and frequently making use of words or other symbolic devices. recalling. The process of making use at a given time of what was memorized in the past. receptor. A general name for sense organ. recessive character. A biological term used in contrast to the term "dominant character." Each biological factor is presumed to have two aspects, one dominant and one recessive; the dominant always suppressing or preventing the appearance of the corresponding recessive character, when two factors are associated. reflex. recognizing. The process of identifying an object or of locating it in the setting in which it occurred in some previous experience. 

A simple form of response which involves a sense receptor, a central nervous connection, and a motor organ (or gland). refractory phase, refractory period. A brief period of time, following the excitation of a nerve, during which it is inexcitable. reminiscence. The tendency of an experience to become more firmly fixed, or more easily recalled, with the passage of time. reproductive interference. The interference with what has just been learned, by intense activity following the learning. resonance. The vibratory response of a body to a harmonic motion imposed upon it. retained members, method of. A memorizing method in which the score is the proportion of material previously memorized that can now be reproduced. retaining. The process of keeping intact what has been learned as evidenced by subsequent recall. retina. The innermost of the three coats of the eyeball, which contains the essential receptors for light; namely, the rods and cones. retinal rivalry. An experience that results when radically different

PSYCHOLOGY 

colors or figures are presented simultaneously to congruent areas of the two eyes, consisting of a fairly rapid alternation between the two stimuli-the individual sees first one and then the other instead of a fusion of the two. rod, retinal. A rodlike structure found in the retina of the eye and functioning as a receiving apparatus for light. round window. See window, round. s factor (specific factor). A specific factor that is supposed to be distinct from a general intelligence factor, to play a part in the performance of individual intelligence tests, and to account for individual differences between those who have equal general ability. saccadic movement. The sudden movement of the eyes from one fixation point to another. sacral segment. That portion of the nervous system which is situated near the lower part of the human body and the tail end of animals. saturation. The degree to which any color possessing a given hue differs from a gray of the same brightness. sclerotic coat. The outermost of the three coats of the eyeball. scotopic vision. Vision that occurs in faint illumination. semicircular canals. Three canals in the inner ear lying at right angles to one another and serving as sense organs to detect changes in general position or balance of the body. sensation. An experience resulting from the stimulation of a sense organ. set. A posture, attitude, interest, or other condition of the individual which facilitates a certain type of activity. sibling. One of two or more children of the same parents, regardless of sex. size-weight illusion. An illusion based on the common tendency to judge objects of greater size as lighter in weight than smaller objects of the same actual weight. smooth muscles. Muscle fibers which are smooth in appearance (i.e., not striated), are innervated by the autonomic nervous system, and operate the internal viscera. Their period of contraction and relaxation is much slower than that of striped muscles. somesthesis. A general term used to designate all sensations from the skin and underlying tissues, as well as sensations from the internal organs of the body.

GLOSSARY 

595 sound. The mechanical disturbance that is produced when harmonic motion affects some material substance capable of being moved by its pulsations or pistonlike movements. spinal animal. An animal in which the entire head part of the nervous system has been severed from functional influence upon the spinal cord. sphygmograph. An instrument for recording pulse movements. stapes (stirrup). The third of the little bones (ossicles) in the middle ear; it is articulated with the incus (anvil) and fits into the oval window of the inner ear. stereoscope. An optical instrument, consisting of a prism placed before each eye in such a manner that, while each eye is seeing a different picture, the two pictures are superimposed and combine with each other. When the two pictures are of the same objects and have been taken by two cameras separated by a distance equal to the distance between the two eyes, the observer has a perception of depth when he views them through the stereoscope. stroboscope. An instrument for producing a static effect from a rapid series of periodic visual stimuli. subliminal. Below the threshold. suggestibility. The characteristic of an individual that shows itself in his tendency to be responsive or obedient to other persons. syllogism. A pattern for a formal argument, consisting of (1) a major premise, (2) a minor premise, and (3) a conclusion. For example: (1) All men have heads, (2) Joe is a man, (3) therefore, Joe has a head. symbol. An object, letter, character, sign, movement, or emblem used as a representative substitute for something other than itself. sympathetic nervous system. The central portion of the autonomic nervous system, concerned primarily with emergency functions of the organism. synapse. The region of functional contact between two or more neurons; usually the region where the branchings of the dendrites of some neurons are intermeshed with the axon branchings of other cells. tambour. A device for making a graphic record of changes in air volume. It consists essentially of a small vessel, one side of which is covered with an elastic membrane to which a writing

PSYCHOLOGY 

lever is attached. It is connected with a tube through which changing impulses are communicated as changes in air volume. taste tetrahedron. A figure designed to show the mutual relations of the four principal tastes. tau effect. An illusion in which judgment of spatial intervals is influenced by the temporal intervals involved. technique. The specific way or means of securing data or of working on an experimental problem. threshold, difference. See difference threshold. threshold, stimulus. That magnitude of a stimulus at which a transition occurs from no sensation to sensation. thyroid gland. A ductless gland, located in the region of the neck, which secretes a hormone that regulates the basal metabolic rate of the body. . tone. An auditory sensation aroused by a periodic sound wave. trial-and-error method. The name applied to a method of learning characterized by a series of rather blind and random attempts to solve a problem. twilight vision. See scotopic vision. twins. Offspring produced at one birth. Fraternal twins are those which develop from separate fertilized ova and have no more similarity in heredity than any other pair of siblings. Identical twins develop from a single fertilized ovum and thus have identical heredity. tympanic membrane. The eardrum membrane. unconditioned stimulus. The original, or adequate, stimulus which naturally initiates a certain response. valence. The effective combining power of a chemical element. 

The term has been used by analogy by psychologists to designate the interacting attracting and repelling values of various objects or activities. vascular system. The system of blood vessels in the body. vertical axis. The axis of reference of the human body passing from head to feet. viscera. The large internal organs of the body. visual axis. A straight line passing through the external point of visual fixation and the nodal point of the eye to the fovea. window, oval. An oval opening into the inner ear into which fits the stirrup, the innermost of the three bones (ossicles) of the middle ear.

GLOSSARY 

597 window, round. A round opening between the middle and inner ear, just below the oval window, and closed by a flexible membrane. yellow spot. A pigmented spot about 2 mm. in diameter in the central area of the human retina, in the center of which is the fovea, the point of clearest vision.
